name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear, GOP again in a tizzy over fair board after KY Farm Bureau submits names for seat
description: Republicans in Frankfort and Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear are once again butting heads over the Kentucky State Fair Board.  The Senate Republican caucus highlighted comments in a Monday press release made by Kentucky Farm Bureau President Eddie Melton during a recent agriculture committee meeting regarding KFB’s representation on the state fair board. Rep. R[...]
text:
Kentucky State Fair (Kentucky Lantern photo by Sarah Ladd)Republicans in Frankfort and Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear are once again butting heads over the Kentucky State Fair Board. 
The Senate Republican caucus highlighted comments in a Monday press release made by Kentucky Farm Bureau President Eddie Melton during a recent agriculture committee meeting regarding KFB’s representation on the state fair board. Rep. Ryan Bivens, R-Hodgenville, asked Melton if he had submitted names to the governor to select a KFB nominee for the fair board. 
Melton said he had given six names, including Marshall Coyle, who had been serving as the KFB representative on the fair board. 
“I received an email back that said that the governor rejected those six names and asked me for six more names that would work in an honest and transparent manner,” Melton told lawmakers. “At that time, I chose to not resubmit six more names because I felt like that I sent six names in that were more than qualified to be able to serve in an honest and transparent manner.” 
The fair board’s governance was entangled in turmoil this summer after the Kentucky Supreme Court overturned a state law that aimed to shift control of the board from the governor to the agriculture commissioner. Within days of the ruling, Beshear appointed new members of the board, which then moved to fire former CEO and President David Beck. At the time, Beshear said Beck “was not willing to work with me, and made that pretty clear” and had “led a charge to prevent any form of accountability from a governor.” 
In response to Melton during the legislative meeting, Bivens criticized Beshear. 
“He’s got a job to do. Whether you like doing it or not, you have a job, and there was a list of six names, and he has not done his job,” Bivens said, adding “it is a shame that an agricultural group like Farm Bureau is not being represented right now on that board, and they have committed so much to that fairgrounds.” 
After the Senate Republicans’ press release, Beshear’s office sent a Monday letter to the co-chairs of the committee to “correct the record about statements” regarding an open seat on the fair board, according to a letter reviewed by the Kentucky Lantern. Signed by Executive Director of Boards and Commissions Matt Osborne, the letter said before the law was overturned by the Supreme Court, “the State Fair Board operated with an unconstitutional governing structure” for nearly four years while the law was challenged in courts. 
Osborne wrote Beshear rejected KFB’s list in early August and requested a new list of names, which is allowed under state law. 
“Unfortunately, we still have not received the requested list from Farm Bureau. At last week’s Committee meeting, Farm Bureau admitted to not sending the requested list,” Osborne wrote. “The Governor will make a timely appointment to the Kentucky State Fair Board to represent the Kentucky Farm Bureau when he receives the requested list and considers them.”
Melton did not say during the meeting who else was on the initial nomination list he submitted to the governor. A KFB spokesperson declined to publicly share the names, but said the individuals have “valuable experience and a strong commitment to Kentucky agriculture.” 
“Kentucky Farm Bureau remains committed to working toward a resolution that ensures Kentucky farm families continue to have a meaningful voice on the State Fair Board,” the spokesperson said. “We recognize the importance of this appointment and remain hopeful that a path forward can be found.” 
It’s not the first time in recent weeks the governor has been criticized for rejecting nominations. Beshear also drew ire from Republican Auditor Allison Ball for rejecting a list of nominations she gave for a spot on the Executive Branch Ethics Commission last month. Her initial list had three names Beshear had complicated histories with. 
Ball submitted a second list, but a spokesperson for her said the office has not yet received a response from Beshear. The names on Ball’s new list are former Deputy Chief Justice of the Kentucky Supreme Court William T. Scott, Dinsmore & Shohl partner Sarah Billiter Cameron, Partner at Dinsmore & Shohl LLP, and Larry Brown, an attorney and former Republican state representative who defeated former Democratic House Speaker Greg Stumbo in 2016.

title: Messy-ssippi: This state has a history of elections that don’t end on Election Day
description: Ronnie Musgrove's Mississippi gubernatorial victory in 1999 was not finalized until January 2000. Musgrove signs first law of his administration, a plan for the state to set aside more money to encourage young people to move into areas with teaching shortages, as Lt. Gov. Amy Tuck, left, Jackson State University student Candace Carter and state lawmakers wat[...]
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Local election officials in Mississippi have spent more than a week counting votes in a hard-fought U.S. Senate race between Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom.
More than 957,000 ballots had been counted by Wednesday, eight days after people voted. Colom opened up a narrow lead on election night, Nov. 3. The vote count remained close, but his lead grew as officials examined provisional ballots.
A victory by Colom would be historic in a state that did everything it could, for generations, to block Black people from voting. He would become the first Black senator in Mississippi since Reconstruction – and the first elected here by popular vote, because senators during Reconstruction were chosen by state lawmakers. 
This isn’t the first election that has extended into overtime. The state has a history of messy contests that took a while to resolve.
Party like it’s 1999
The 1999 governor’s race dragged on until January 2000. Republican Gov. Kirk Fordice couldn’t seek a third term, and the top candidates were Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Parker and Democratic Lt. Gov. Ronnie Musgrove.
Musgrove was known for his get-up-early-and-stay-late work ethic, and he campaigned the same way. Parker? Not so much. He was at a golf course during the crucial final days before the election.
Two other candidates were on the ballot. The Reform Party’s Jerry Ladner and independent Helen Perkins ran low-budget campaigns but collected enough votes to create chaos.
Back then, winning a statewide race was a multi-step process. In addition to receiving a majority of the popular vote, a candidate had to prevail in a majority of the 122 state House districts – essentially the equivalent of the Electoral College.
Musgrove received 49.6% of the popular vote to Parker’s 48.5%. Ladner got just over 1% and Perkins got just under that amount.
Weirdly, Parker and Musgrove split the House districts right down the middle, winning 61 each. 
Former U.S. Rep. Mike Parker, the 1999 Republican nominee for Mississippi governor, is photographed with his wife Rosemary Parker on Tuesday, Jan. 4, 2000, in Jackson on the day he finally officially lost the Mississippi gubernatorial election.
Those requirements threw the race to the House of Representatives, where members had no obligation to vote as their districts did. The two months between Election Day 1999 and the opening day of the 2000 legislative session saw some of the most intense politicking of the season as Parker and Musgrove courted House members.
Democrats controlled the House by a wide margin. But, the party label was more a decorative item than a declaration of ideals for many lawmakers, so the Democrat was not a shoo-in for governor.
Musgrove ended up prevailing in an 86-36 vote that was split largely along party lines. Notably, a Republican lawmaker from DeSoto County, Valeria Robertson, cast her vote for Parker, even though Musgrove carried her House district.
Mississippi eliminated the complicated process of electing statewide officials in 2020, switching to a runoff if no candidate receives a majority. The 2023 election cycle was the first time that system was in place, though no runoffs were needed.
Gunn vs. Barbour, 2003
Republican Philip Gunn became one of the most powerful figures in state government during three terms as the speaker of the Mississippi House. But he had a rocky time even winning his first House race.
Gunn, of Clinton, challenged Republican Rep. Jep Barbour of Yazoo City in the 2003 Republican primary, the same year that Jep’s uncle, Republican Haley Barbour, unseated Musgrove in the governor’s race.
Jep Barbour was initially declared the winner of the House primary, but Gunn challenged the results and a judge ordered a new round of voting in two precincts. Gunn won the primary and the general election, starting the first of his five terms in the House. He chose not to seek reelection in 2023, and he is now among the Republicans in the 2027 governor’s race.
Tea party vs. the establishment, 2014
State Sen. Chris McDaniel of Jones County came close to unseating longtime U.S. Sen. Thad Cochran in a three-person Republican primary in 2014. It was a race that dragged on well past when the votes were counted because McDaniel refused to concede, even going to court.
Cochran surprised even some of his ardent supporters by announcing in late 2013 that he would seek reelection rather than retire. After a career of easy victories, he conducted what can generously be called a lackadaisical campaign in which he often appeared unfocused.
McDaniel started strong, but his momentum sputtered after some of his supporters were caught breaking into the nursing home room of Cochran’s wife, who had dementia, and taking photos of her. The images briefly appeared in a blog post implying that Cochran was stepping out with another woman while his wife was incapacitated. Cochran’s camp said he had not engaged in any improper relationship.
McDaniel aligned himself with tea party folks who wanted to upend the Republican establishment. Cochran served six years in the U.S. House before winning the Senate seat in 1978, and he epitomized the establishment, bringing billions of dollars to Mississippi as chairman of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee.
McDaniel led the first round of Republican primary voting with 49.5% of the vote to Cochran’s 49%. A candidate who spent little, Thomas Carey, received the remaining sliver of votes. 
In the weeks between the primary and the runoff, Cochran actively sought support from Black voters. McDaniel protested that people who usually support Democrats should not vote in the Republican runoff. But Mississippi voters don’t register by party. The only people prohibited from voting in a Republican runoff are those who voted in the Democratic primary that cycle.
Cochran won the Republican nomination, but McDaniel asked the state Republican Party to overturn Cochran’s victory on a claim that Democrats had improperly crossed over to vote in the runoff. The party did not act on his appeal, so McDaniel challenged his loss in court. A judge dismissed that case, saying McDaniel waited too long to file it.
Cochran defeated Democratic former U.S. Rep. Travis Childers in the 2014 general election. After serving less than half of the six-year term, Cochran retired in early 2018 and Republican Gov. Phil Bryant chose Hyde-Smith, the state agriculture commissioner, to go to the Senate. 
Drawing straws but coming up short
About 9,000 people voted in a 2015 race for a Mississippi House seat, and it ended in a tie between 20-year Democratic incumbent Bo Eaton of Taylorsville and Republican challenger Mark Tullos, an attorney from Raleigh. The tiebreaker? A drawing of straws.
Republican Delbert Hosemann, who was secretary of state, held a ceremony in a state office. Each candidate reached into a bag and chose a silver-plated business card case engraved with the word “Mississippi” – one containing a green plastic straw, the other containing a red one.
Eaton, a farmer, won by drawing the green straw, and he declared: “There’s always happiness in a good crop year.”
But it was a temporary victory. 
Tullos filed an appeal, which was considered by a committee in the Republican-majority House. That committee tossed out five affidavit ballots that were in dispute. With that decision, Tullos was sworn into the House, where he still serves in the Republican supermajority.

Mississippi Today Editor-in-Chief Emily Wagster Pettus has covered state politics since 1994. She worked for The Clarion-Ledger and The Associated Press before joining Mississippi Today.

title: Michigan lawmaker seeks to make ‘rolling coal’ a crime
description: A Michigan lawmaker has introduced legislation that would make it a crime for drivers to intentionally direct vehicle exhaust at other people, a practice commonly known as “rolling coal.” House Bills 6459 and 6460, introduced Tuesday by state Rep. Brenda Carter (D-Pontiac), would make it illegal to intentionally aim vehicle exhaust at individuals and establi[...]
text:
A pickup truck lats down thick exhaust as it passes a rally outside Howell City Hall held in response to recent white supremacist demonstrations on Nov. 23, 2024. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)A Michigan lawmaker has introduced legislation that would make it a crime for drivers to intentionally direct vehicle exhaust at other people, a practice commonly known as “rolling coal.”
House Bills 6459 and 6460, introduced Tuesday by state Rep. Brenda Carter (D-Pontiac), would make it illegal to intentionally aim vehicle exhaust at individuals and establish sentencing guidelines for the offense.
Rolling coal involves modifying a diesel-powered vehicle to emit thick, dark exhaust smoke. The modifications, often achieved by tampering with a vehicle’s emissions-control equipment, allow a driver to direct the resulting smoke at pedestrians, cyclists or occupants of other vehicles. It has also occurred at political protests, including last year in Howell.
Michigan already has a law making it a felony to operate or possess a motor vehicle equipped with a device to produce excessive smoke or gas. This new legislation would address the intentional targeting of individuals with that exhaust, rather than the equipment used to produce the excess emissions.
HB 6459 would add a new section to the Michigan Penal Code, making a first offense a misdemeanor with a maximum 93 day jail sentence and/or  a $500 fine. A second offense would also be a misdemeanor, but with a maximum one year in jail and/or a $1,500 fine. A third offense, however, would be a felony punishable by up to two years in prison and/or a fine of up to $2,500. HB 6460 would add the proposed offense to the state’s criminal sentencing guidelines. 
While the bills are tie-barred, meaning one could not take effect without the other, they were both immediately sent to the House Committee of Government Operations, usually a repository for legislation with little to no hope of getting a committee hearing, much less making it to the House floor for a vote.

The Delaware Department of Labor’s Office of Wage & Hour announced Holiday Helper: Hiring Teen Workers 101 in a release posted Nov. 10. The 20-minute, on-demand webinar became available Nov. 1 and requires registration and the link for the on-demand options will be emailed to you.  Photo courtesy of the State of Delaware, image created on 11/11 using ai
 
Free online session covers work permits, scheduling, pay, and safety for young workers, parents and employers
WILMINGTON, Del. — Delaware’s youngest holiday workers and the businesses hiring them have a new resource to help prepare for the first shift: a free online workshop explaining work permits, scheduling restrictions and workplace protections.
The Delaware Department of Labor’s Office of Wage & Hour announced Holiday Helper: Hiring Teen Workers 101 in a release posted Nov. 10. The 20-minute, on-demand webinar became available Nov. 1 and requires registration and the link for the on-demand options will be emailed to you.
Designed for ages 14 to 17, it also serves parents, educators and employers. The video expands access to material used in the department’s in-person HireME! Teen Job Readiness Workshop.
“Every young person deserves the opportunity to enter the workforce feeling informed, confident, and prepared,” Labor Secretary LaKresha Moultrie said in the release.
A teen presenter guides viewers through workplace scenarios involving six young workers. Topics include permits, hours, breaks, hazardous tasks, pay protections, and fraudulent job advertisements.
Start with the work permit
For jobs covered by Delaware’s child labor law, employers must keep a validated work permit on file for each employee under 18. A new permit is required when a minor changes employers.
The teen and employer complete their portions of the form before an authorized issuing officer approves it. For 14- and 15-year-olds, a parent or guardian must also sign.
Issuing officers are available through schools and the Department of Labor. The state’s form also provides instructions for submitting paperwork by email. Employers should accept only permits signed and dated by an issuing officer.
Check both state and federal scheduling rules
Employers must account for both Delaware and federal requirements. When both apply, the more protective rule controls.
That distinction matters for 14- and 15-year-olds. Delaware’s permit form lists a four-hour limit on school days, but federal law generally limits covered nonagricultural employment to three hours on a school day, including Friday.
Federal rules also generally limit those workers to 18 hours in any week when school is in session, even for only part of the week. The limits are eight hours on a nonschool day and 40 hours in a week when school is not in session.
For ordinary holiday-season scheduling, 14- and 15-year-olds may work only outside school hours, between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Delaware also limits them to six workdays a week. The later summer cutoff of 9 p.m. ends on Labor Day.
Under Delaware law, 16- and 17-year-olds cannot spend more than 12 hours a day in school and work combined. They must have at least eight consecutive hours free from school and work in each 24-hour period.
Minors cannot work more than five consecutive hours without a nonworking break of at least 30 minutes.
Match the duties to the worker’s age
Scheduling is only part of the responsibility. Delaware law generally bars workers under 16 from operating meat slicers, deep-fat fryers and certain other powered equipment. Hazardous-occupation restrictions also apply to older teens.
A work permit does not authorize an employer to assign duties prohibited for that worker’s age. Employers with questions about a particular job or piece of equipment should check with the Department of Labor before assigning the task.
To Go Box

What: Holiday Helper: Hiring Teen Workers 101.
Format: Free, 20-minute, on-demand online workshop.
Who: Teens ages 14 to 17, parents, employers, educators and community organizations.
Register: Holiday Helper workshop registration.
Work permits: Download Delaware’s work permit form.
Permit submissions: workpermits@delaware.gov.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Voters adopted transgender sports restrictions in blue states. Officials are pushing back.
description: Activists who want to keep transgender athletes out of girls’ sports think they now have a playbook that works in Democratic states: Put the issue on the ballot. Even amid an overwhelming blue wave on Nov. 3, voters in four states chose to restrict transgender rights in youth athletics. Two of those states — Washington […]
text:
A canvasser with the Protect Girls Sports campaign looks on as a voter signs a petition to restrict transgender students’ access to sports and school facilities at the Green Ladle culinary school in Lewiston on Nov. 4, 2025. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star) 
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters

Activists who want to keep transgender athletes out of girls’ sports think they now have a playbook that works in Democratic states: Put the issue on the ballot.
Even amid an overwhelming blue wave on Nov. 3, voters in four states chose to restrict transgender rights in youth athletics. Two of those states — Washington and Colorado — have been havens of inclusive transgender policy. But their voters easily approved ballot measures limiting transgender sports participation while also handing Democrats supermajorities in their state legislatures.
Those and other results highlight an increasingly hostile political landscape for transgender rights in schools and elsewhere. Yet LGBTQ advocates and their allies in elected office are not backing down.
Parents of trans and cisgender athletes, along with the Washington state teachers union, sued Monday to block Initiative 638, which requires healthcare providers to verify girls are girls before they can play sports. And the Seattle school board voted unanimously to pursue its own legal action over fears that complying with the initiative would mean violating other state laws.
In Colorado, Democratic Governor-elect Phil Weiser is already talking about making “adjustments” to ballot measures that say students must play on teams that match their biological sex and that bar gender-affirming surgeries for minors.
School sports have become a fierce battleground over the rights of transgender children, even though most states count fewer than a dozen such athletes at any given time. Conservatives found that restricting sports participation did much better in focus groups and in polls than banning transgender adults from using bathrooms that matched their gender identity. They built a broader cultural agenda that includes parental rights and curriculum restrictions around the issue.
Starting with Idaho in 2020, 29 states adopted laws or policies restricting transgender athletes — most often transgender girls — from joining teams that match their gender identity. President Donald Trump made the issue a centerpiece of his approach to Title IX, and this June, the U.S. Supreme Court found these bans to be constitutional.
But the court did not rule that states must exclude transgender athletes from girls’ and women’s sports teams. That kicked the issue back to the states.
Both supporters and opponents of restricting transgender sports participation expect to see ballot measures in more states.
Groups renew multi-pronged effort to alter Maine’s inclusive trans athlete laws

“Voters generally don’t like discrimination, but conservative groups have been very successful about framing the sports issue as not about discrimination but about fairness and about biology,” said Joanna Wuest, a political scientist at Stony Brook University who has written extensively about LGBTQ rights.
Anti-transgender ballot initiatives could mark turning point
Supporters of sports restrictions describe them as common sense steps that recognize innate biological differences between the sexes and protect athletic opportunities for girls and women.
Jennifer Sey, a backer of the Colorado ballot measure and an activist who achieved prominence by opposing COVID-era school closures, said Democratic leaders need to pay attention to what she called a “watershed moment.”
“The midterm results proved — despite deep-pocketed interest groups efforts to label the initiatives as ‘right wing’ and ‘bigoted’ — that protecting girls’ sports was never about right versus left; it’s about right versus wrong,” Sey said in an emailed statement. “Now party leaders must take heed: Your own base has spoken decisively.”
This year, Arizona voters expanded an existing ban about school sports to include recreational sports like Little League, even as Democrats flipped control of the state legislature and the state superintendent’s office. In Nebraska, voters enshrined an existing ban into their state constitution by a far wider margin than the one by which they reelected their Republican U.S. senator.
But Aidan Key, co-founder of the Washington state advocacy group Gender Diversity, who helped develop the state’s transgender sports policies, believes those policies have been working.
Since 2007, Washington state has allowed K-12 students to participate in sports that match their gender identity without having to undergo medical treatment. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association estimates that roughly 10 transgender athletes participate each year out of roughly 250,000 student athletes.
Dozens of athletes have participated over the years without drawing much notice at all while getting the benefits of physical activity and team comradery, said Key, who also heads TransFamilies, one of the organizations suing over Initiative 638. Even those transgender athletes who have excelled locally post stats well within the normal range for high school girls nationally.
“I want the will of the people to be an informed will,” he said. “I want them to know the bragging rights we should have as a state for how well this policy has worked. If a legal challenge can help us continue the conversation, then that seems worthwhile.”
Seattle school board member Joe Mizrahi opposed Initiative 638 as a father of three daughters who play sports. But he said at Monday’s meeting that his vote to sue was about legal concerns.
The school district, he said, doesn’t know how to comply with the new law while also abiding by state laws protecting student privacy, barring discrimination, and guaranteeing equal access to educational opportunities.
“Those laws didn’t come out of nowhere,” Mizrahi said. “They came from the democratic process, from representatives, from votes, and from our constitutional principles. So those protections also reflect the will of the people.”
The issue has particular prominence in Washington. In 2024 and 2025, a transgender track athlete won back to back state titles in the 400 meter event. The Trump administration opened an investigation into state policies last year. This fall, another Washington transgender runner made national news when teammates protested her inclusion.
And a high school female wrestler who said a transgender opponent sexually assaulted her during a match is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to find that inclusive sports policies violate the civil rights of female athletes.
Brian Heywood, a hedge fund founder who put his personal wealth behind Washington Initiative 638, said female athletes there felt pressured by “bureaucratic bullies” to accept what they viewed as unfair competition and intrusions into private spaces. “Someone had to punch back,” he said.
In an interview, Heywood consistently referred to transgender girls as boys, but said the initiative is “not a MAGA thing,” not part of a national movement, and not a step toward broader discrimination.
But Sey argued in her Substack that people who agree with her on sports “know that a person is male” and can’t change sex, which means public policy shouldn’t accommodate gender identity.
The 2026 midterms did deliver wins for out transgender lawmakers in Alabama and Georgia. And voters in Vermont overwhelmingly approved a state constitutional amendment that bars discrimination on the basis of gender identity.
At the same time, some red-state Democrats ran ads promising to keep biological males — a term many transgender people find derogatory — off girls’ and women’s sports teams.
Wuest said the rhetoric used to support sport restrictions often depicts transgender women and girls as threatening or predatory. That “puts a target on trans kids’ and trans teachers’ backs,” she said, and also gets used to justify restricting bathroom access, another Trump administration priority.
At the same time, she said, “I don’t think most Democrats want to go out of their way to talk about trans issues right now.”



Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news site covering educational change in public schools.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: After North Idaho’s Latah County found 2,300 of unreported ballots, recount shows no races changed
description: In Latah County in North Idaho, a full recount — prompted by the discovery of thousands of unreported ballots — showed that the outcomes of all races and ballot issues in the county remained unchanged, state election officials said. The recount came after the Latah County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, discovered that […]
text:
Staff with the Idaho Office of Secretary of State oversaw a full recount of all ballots cast in the Nov. 3 general election in Latah County on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Office of Secretary of State)In Latah County in North Idaho, a full recount — prompted by the discovery of thousands of unreported ballots — showed that the outcomes of all races and ballot issues in the county remained unchanged, state election officials said.
The recount came after the Latah County Clerk’s Office, which runs the election locally, discovered that 2,343 ballots were not added into the state’s system to report unofficial election results on Election Day. 
The ballots — from a portion of early voting  — had already been counted by tabulation machines, but the results weren’t uploaded to the state’s reporting system, state officials said. Those ballots represented 12.9% of all 18,104 ballots cast in Latah County, according to state election officials.
The Latah County Clerk’s Office conducted the recount Tuesday, which was overseen by the Idaho Office of Secretary of State, the state election agency. The secretary of state’s office announced the recount was completed early Wednesday morning.
“We take our responsibility to accurately report election results seriously, and this error should not have happened,” Latah County Clerk Julie Fry, an elected Republican, said in a written statement. “I’m grateful to our election staff and the Secretary of State’s Office for their work to verify the results and ensure every ballot is properly accounted for.”
The new results for Latah County are available online. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The closest issue there, according to state election officials, was the Moscow School District Plant Facilities Reserve Fund Levy, which narrowly passed with 60.34% of the vote. It needed 60% support to pass.
A race for county commissioner in Latah got even closer. Republican Dan Schoenberg had won with 129 more votes than Democrat Laura Heinse, who had submitted a complaint to Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane on Monday over the unreported ballots. 
“Elections have built-in safeguards to ensure votes are accurately counted and reported,”McGrane said in a statement. “When this discrepancy was discovered, our team jumped into action and headed immediately to Latah County. For the recount, we went back to the source, which is the paper ballots. That’s how we verify the results and give voters confidence that their voices are accurately reflected.”
The results from last week’s election remain unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which is scheduled to meet Nov. 24.
The Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which certifies the state’s election results, is set to meet at 1 p.m. Friday to select counties and precincts that will undergo audits of election results, including hand counts and reviews of reported results.
In eastern Idaho’s Bannock County, Idaho election officials reported on Tuesday that 333 ballots went uncounted but would not change the outcomes of races there.

description: Kentuckian and conservative political commentator Scott Jennings is asking a federal court to dismiss a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against him from progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.  Attorneys for Jennings filed the motion Tuesday arguing Piker’s initial complaint fails to state a claim.  “Specifically, he fails to plausibly plead either that Mr[...]
text:
GOP pundit Scott Jennings spoke live on CNN from the Fancy Farm political picnic on Aug. 5, 2023. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Austin Anthony)Kentuckian and conservative political commentator Scott Jennings is asking a federal court to dismiss a $72.5 million defamation lawsuit against him from progressive Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. 
Attorneys for Jennings filed the motion Tuesday arguing Piker’s initial complaint fails to state a claim. 
“Specifically, he fails to plausibly plead either that Mr. Jennings acted with actual malice, or that the alleged defamatory statements are actionable,” the motion says. 
Last month, Piker’s attorneys filed a complaint in federal court in Washington, D.C. and alleged Jennings “falsely told a nationwide podcast audience that Hasan Piker was ‘out there calling for Black voters to be lynched.’” The claims stem from an edited video Jennings shared on his show and on social media in August.
“Mr. Jennings’ filing today puts great trust in the US Constitution, the truth, and the right of Americans to speak… even if Mr Piker doesn’t like what they have to say,” said Benjamin G. Chew, one of Jennings’ attorneys. 
Jennings’ motion says the footage in the video he shared came from an X account belonging to Senate Republicans, @NRSC. It also says Jennings “did not create, edit, or manipulate and had no reason to doubt based on the source of the video and the totality of what is known about Mr. Piker’s general worldview—was defamatory, as was Mr. Jennings’s accompanying commentary.”
A Snopes review  from August of the video the Senate Republicans shared found that Piker was sarcastically mimicking others’ opinions and the clips were from hours-long streams and heavily edited without full context. 
Jennings, who now frequently appears on CNN to discuss Republican politics, is a former staffer of Kentucky U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell and a founding partner of RunSwitch PR, one of Kentucky’s largest public relations firms.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Death row pastor calls on Byron Donalds to halt executions for six months after he takes office
description: No state has executed more death row inmates over the past two years than Florida, but with a change of administrations taking place in January, anti-death penalty advocates are calling on Gov.-elect Byron Donalds to pause on any further executions. The Rev. Jeff Hood is spiritual adviser to two men scheduled to be executed within […]
text:
Screenshot of Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood holding the remains of a recent Florida death row inmate executed by the state.No state has executed more death row inmates over the past two years than Florida, but with a change of administrations taking place in January, anti-death penalty advocates are calling on Gov.-elect Byron Donalds to pause on any further executions.
The Rev. Jeff Hood is spiritual adviser to two men scheduled to be executed within the next month. He is urging Donalds to commit to a six-month moratorium, between Jan. 5, when he takes office, and July 5.
“We’re asking for this to be a moment in which the state takes the opportunity to investigate what 40 executions in multiple years has cost,” Hood said Wednesday in a remote press conference. “We are asking the governor to lead the way in taking the opportunity to see what pieces are not in place to support those who are being pushed and forced to carry these executions out. We should be knowledgeable about how much these executions are costing.”
Hood said he would like the governor-elect during that pause to create an independent commission to determine whether the existing process, which has conducted more executions than any other part of the country, is reliable, fair, and gives courts and defense attorneys adequate time to prepare.
Florida had never executed more than eight inmates in a single year until last year, when Gov. Ron DeSantis signed death warrants for 19 people, nearly four times as many as any other state. The state has executed 19 people again this year, and the governor has signed death warrants for three more executions before the end of the year.
Donalds told the Miami Herald and Tampa Bay Times earlier this year that he supports the death penalty.
“This is not California,” he told the paper. “Chaos will not run our streets, and criminals will not run our communities. In Florida, we don’t play that game. Harm a Floridian, and you will face the consequences.”
Noting the reference to California, Hood said Wednesday that the Golden State has not carried out an execution in 20 years. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced last week that he was commuting the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in California.
In addition to the call by Rev. Hood, a group of Florida death row exonerees and criminal justice advocates are scheduled to gather at the Capitol Thursday to call upon Donalds to pause executions. Thirty death row inmates since 1976 in Florida have been released due to a lack of evidence, more than in any other state in the country.
Hood is also spiritual adviser to death row inmates in Texas. In the past week, he has sent a letter calling upon Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa to stop all executions there. Hinojosa told CNN last month that she while she personally opposes the death penalty, she would take each situation on a “case-by-case basis.”
Hood says his ask for Donalds doesn’t go as far because “we are trying to meet him where he is.”
Next
Three executions scheduled in Florida in the coming weeks:

Thomas M. Overton on Nov. 19 for the 1991 murders of a Florida Keys couple. At the time, the female victim was eight months pregnant. The unborn child did not survive the attack. The case went unresolved for years until Overton, 70, was charged with the rape and murder of the woman and the murder of the man. Overton was convicted in 1999 and sentenced to death on both murder counts, although the jury’s recommendations for death were not unanimous.
Ricardo Gonzalez, 56, on Dec. 1 in the 1994 first-degree murder of  a North Miami police officer in 1992.
Willie Seth Crain Jr., 80, on Dec. 10 in the 1999 first-degree murder and kidnapping of a seven-year-old girl in 1998 in Tampa. Her body was never found.

In August, Hood called on DeSantis to personally view the execution of death row inmate William Silvia. The governor has not attended an execution since he’s been in office. Hood says that if Donalds doesn’t suspend the death penalty, he should sign a proclamation shortly after he is sworn into office declaring that he will be present at every execution for which he signs a warrant.
“That will make it a lot more believable that he believes in execution,” he said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Congress has to act first before nuclear campuses take shape, US Energy secretary says
description: The Trump cabinet’s top energy official acknowledged Tuesday that Congress will have to approve the creation of a second U.S. nuclear waste disposal site before the administration’s nuclear energy visions can become reality.
text:
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright greets attendees Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, at the Dufresne Community Center in Luling. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)LULING — The Trump cabinet’s top energy official acknowledged Tuesday that Congress will have to approve the creation of a second U.S. nuclear waste disposal site before the administration’s nuclear energy visions can become reality.
Chris Wright, secretary of the U.S. Department of Energy, said he believes lawmakers back the agency’s proposed nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses. The sites would encompass all aspects of nuclear energy production — from uranium enrichment to permanent storage of the end waste product.
“I think we have bipartisan support on the effort that we’re doing, so we don’t expect trouble getting that done,” Wright said during a visit to Louisiana to announce a federal loan for energy exploration off the state’s coast.    
Earlier this year, the Energy Department asked states to submit proposals to host nuclear lifecycle innovation campuses and received applications from 26 states. Idaho, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and West Virginia were chosen as finalists.
West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey has since backed out of the competition, under pressure from residents who oppose storing nuclear waste inside old coal mines. 
For any campus to move forward, Congress has to approve a permanent storage location for the waste material left over from spent uranium rods. Nuclear facilities currently store the used material on site, first in steel-lined, covered concrete pools and then years later in steel and concrete dry casks after they have cooled.  
The only existing approved permanent storage site is Yucca Mountain in Nevada, which was first proposed nearly 40 years ago and has yet to accept any waste. There’s been no federal funding provided to complete the project since 2011, and the site’s neighbors have opposed advancing with permanent waste disposal plans.    
“We do need to have a statutory change to make it so it’s not exclusively tied to Yucca Mountain,” Wright said. “… To actually move forward, we need an act from Congress.” 
No one in Congress has stepped up to carry the needed legislation since the Energy Department first asked for nuclear campus applications in January. Republicans will lose their majority in both chambers on Jan. 3.
Louisiana’s pitch to the Trump administration calls for using underground salt domes off its coast as permanent nuclear waste storage sites, which the legislature would also have to approve. State officials also envision Louisiana becoming a hub for uranium fuel rod recycling, noting that only 5% of the fuel they contain is used in reactors. They have pointed to technology in France that can extract 80% of the unused uranium.
Gov. Jeff Landry has also championed bringing nuclear energy manufacturing to Louisiana in anticipation of growing demand for small modular nuclear reactors. Their proponents say they are ideal for localized placement to meet the high electricity needs from industrial facilities such as data centers. 
The industrial construction company Turner Industries announced in April it would add a combined 1,000 jobs at its New Iberia and Port Allen facilities to create components and piping for the next generation of nuclear reactors.
The Department of Energy could pick more than one state for a nuclear lifecycle innovation campus, though only one site in each state will be chosen. Wright confirmed Tuesday the choices are still expected to be made public later this year or early 2027.
St. Charles Parish and West Feliciana Parish, both home to nuclear power plants, have expressed interest in being selected for a nuclear campus, as have East Feliciana Parish and the authority that oversees Port Fourchon, the closest point of access for proposed salt dome storage.  
The Trump administration has not pledged any financial support or preferential permitting treatment for the states picked, while promoting the concept as an avenue toward building the U.S. nuclear industry. 
China is projected to overtake the United States in nuclear power production within the next 10 years, according to the Institute for Energy Research. Only one nuclear energy project, the Vogtle 3 and 4 reactors in Georgia, has come online in the U.S. in the past 10 years. China, meanwhile, has tripled its nuclear generating capacity over the same period.

Sophia Paffenroth, women’s health reporter for Mississippi Today, has been selected for the Association of Health Care Journalists’ International Health Study Fellowship. 
Through this international fellowship, Paffenroth will compare and contrast reproductive health policies and practices in Mississippi with those in the United Kingdom to better understand how access and affordability shape infant mortality rates in both places. 
Sophia Paffenroth Credit: Courtesy of Sophia Paffenroth
Paffenroth will build on her existing reporting. In August 2025, State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney declared Mississippi’s infant mortality rate a public health emergency at 9.7 deaths for every 1,000 live births, higher than the national average. Research has shown that Black babies in Mississippi are more than twice as likely to die in infancy than white babies. More than a year later, experts say the state should do more to improve outcomes for its children, including focusing on equity. 
“I’m so excited by the opportunity to provide Mississippi with a meaningful international comparison of maternity care as stakeholders in the state navigate a maternal-infant health crisis,” Paffenroth said. 
Through her reporting in the United Kingdom, Paffenroth said she hopes to learn more about the country’s “rich history of community midwifery care” and how it has boosted outcomes for pregnant people and newborns from households across all income levels while also lowering costs.
“We are thrilled to see Sophia take her reporting on this important issue to the next level,” said Laura Santhanam, health editor at Mississippi Today. “The insights and data she returns with will help our audiences make more well-informed decisions on matters of life and death.”
Launched in 2018, this fellowship is sponsored by the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit research foundation. The program has sent health journalists from across the United States abroad to ask questions – and seek answers to – some of this nation’s most demanding health challenges. 
In this latest cohort with three other U.S. journalists, Paffenroth will travel to New York to gain insights into reading international health statistics, navigating a new country as a journalist and understanding systems of care and patient concerns. Then, Paffenroth will travel to the United Kingdom to conduct her reporting.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska approves 50-year land lease for large natural gas-powered data center in the Arctic
description: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources on Tuesday approved a 50-year land lease for a proposed large-scale computing data center on the North Slope near the Dalton Highway, the trans-Alaska oil pipeline and the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline. In its final approval, the department said the lease is in the best interests of the […]
text:
The Trans-Alaska Pipeline is seen in the northern Brooks Range on June 20, 2007. Alaska. Rocks in the background produce oil on the North Slope, and running along the pipeline is the Dalton Highway. (Photo provided by the U.S. Geological Survey)The Alaska Department of Natural Resources on Tuesday approved a 50-year land lease for a proposed large-scale computing data center on the North Slope near the Dalton Highway, the trans-Alaska oil pipeline and the proposed trans-Alaska natural gas pipeline.
In its final approval, the department said the lease is in the best interests of the state of Alaska, and additional permits will be needed before construction takes place.
The proposed “STAK Energy Campus,” estimated to cost $500 million, would include a multi-gigawatt natural gas power plant fired with gas produced locally on the North Slope. 
Writing in response to public comments about the plan, the DNR wrote, “this proposed development presents circumstances that are, in important respects, without direct precedent in the State’s historical management of its lands and resources.”
To date, Alaska has no large-scale commercial computing data centers.     
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

The data center complex, which is expected to cover about 715 acres, would be air-cooled and would not be tied into the electrical grid that covers Alaska’s Railbelt, though operators could sell power to customers in and around Prudhoe Bay.
“Construction is expected to require a peak workforce of up to 1,500 workers, while ongoing operations are anticipated to employ between 50 and 150 permanent personnel on rotating shifts,” DNR wrote.
The state intends to charge the owners of the data center a fee based on the amount of electricity produced and used by the data center, as well as rent on the land, with the amount to be determined after market appraisal.
Construction on the privately financed project is expected to take six years, according to information shared with DNR officials, but additional permits — including a federal wetlands permit and a state air quality permit for the power plant — are needed first.
Earlier this year, DNR extended a public comment period on the proposed land lease and received more than 1,200 public responses, most in opposition to the proposal.
Many commenters raised environmental concerns, which DNR addressed in a 30-page response filed alongside Tuesday’s approval.
Unlike data centers in the Lower 48, which use liquid cooling, the proposed STAK data center would be air cooled, raised above a gravel pad in order to allow Arctic air to circulate above and below an array of modular computer buildings.
“STAK’s Cumulative Impact Analysis (CIA) estimates that this approach will reduce direct operational water consumption by 90 percent or more compared to evaporative cooling at lower-latitude data centers,” DNR wrote.
Some objectors raised concerns about STAK’s ability to finance and actually build the data center complex, but DNR officials said that doesn’t fall within their purview. 
“The Division is not … obligated to conduct a general corporate or financial investigation beyond what bears on the decision of whether the proposed disposal is in the best interest of the state,” it wrote.
As for the long lease term, DNR wrote, “STAK requested a 50-year lease term, and the Division’s determination that a term of that length serves the State’s best interests reflects the capital intensity of the proposed development: a project requiring approximately $500 million in initial capital expenditures, a multi-year construction buildout, and an operational life extending well beyond that buildout entails a lease term long enough to allow STAK to recover its investment and operate the facility over its designed useful life.”
Some commenters raised noise concerns.
“The facility will be visible from the Dalton Highway at roughly one mile and will operate a 1-3 gigawatt generation system, producing continuous turbine, cooling, and equipment noise that could carry across several miles of flat Arctic terrain,” DNR wrote, but said that any noise must be considered against the fact that the data center would be placed within the busy industrial corridor connecting the oil fields around Prudhoe Bay to the rest of the state.
The data center will be 60 miles from the nearest inhabited town, and its buildings and a supporting gas pipeline will be designed to avoid impacts on nearby caribou.
“Project-specific baseline environmental studies – including site-specific air quality monitoring,
wetland delineations, and water quality assessments – will be required by other agencies as part of subsequent permitting processes that follow this lease decision,” DNR wrote.
Some commenters expressed concerns about the potential greenhouse gas emissions caused by the natural gas power plant, but the DNR division in charge of ruling on the lease said that analysis is not part of its job.
“The Division is not the agency responsible for establishing or enforcing greenhouse gas emission standards, conducting statewide climate monitoring, or making technical determinations regarding the causes, extent, or future trajectory of climate change,” it wrote.
Tuesday’s decision is subject to a 20-day reconsideration period and could be challenged in court. If no challenge is filed, the project may advance to the next phase of permitting.

Fiscal 2028 request includes $500,000 more for education assistance and $6.8 million for a new readiness center
DOVER, Del. — As Delaware honors veterans on Nov. 11, the Delaware National Guard is seeking more state money to help its members pay for college and develop a new readiness center in Cheswold.
The Guard’s fiscal 2028 budget request includes a $7.26 million operating budget and $9.8 million in capital funding. Its priorities include an additional $500,000 for education assistance and $6.8 million for design, site preparation and construction of the Cheswold facility.
The Guard presented its requests at a Nov. 4 public hearing before the Office of Management and Budget. The proposals require further review by the governor and approval by the General Assembly.
Tuition help leads operating requests
The Guard says the additional education money would “mitigate the continual budget shortfall and offset rising costs.”
The request puts a benefit used by service members at the center of the Guard’s budget priorities, alongside facilities and staffing needs.
The state tuition program is available to eligible Army and Air National Guard members in good standing who attend accredited public or private institutions in Delaware. Participants must meet program rules, including a six-year service requirement. Graduate-level reimbursement depends on funding remaining after undergraduate benefits are paid, according to the Guard’s education services office.
The operating request also includes $113,200 for a new state public affairs position. The presentation says the change would have no net effect on the number of full-time equivalent positions.
The Guard seeks another $46,588 to add two Army-side student slots to its co-op program. Approval of its full $64,676 discretionary increase would secure two existing Air Guard co-op slots previously supported with other funds.
The presentation lists an authorized force of 1,693 Army Guard soldiers and 1,128 Air Guard personnel. Those figures represent authorized positions rather than the number of members currently serving.
What a possible cut would mean
The Guard also submitted a contingency plan showing how it would absorb a 1% reduction. The proposed reductions total $64,700 against a fiscal 2027 general fund appropriation of approximately $6.47 million.
The reductions are planning proposals, not approved cuts.
They include $38,500 in contractual services and $14,000 in supplies and materials. The Guard says reduced maintenance funding would cause backlogs, facility deterioration, readiness risks and safety concerns.
Other proposed reductions include $3,200 in travel, $4,000 from the State Partnership Program and $5,000 from the unit fund supporting morale, welfare and recreation.
The Guard warns that reducing the unit fund would affect service members and their families, with consequences for morale, retention and readiness.
Cheswold leads facility requests
The largest capital item is the $6.8 million request for the Cheswold readiness center. The Guard also seeks $475,000 to replace trailers at the Bethany Beach Training Site.
Another $2.3 million would support minor capital improvements, including an HVAC replacement at the Duncan readiness center, demolition of Wing E at the Wilmington readiness center, roof replacements at the Scannell and Georgetown readiness centers, and interior and exterior work at the 1401 readiness center.
The presentation identifies approximately $5 million in federal funding associated with minor capital improvements this year. It separately requests $200,000 for maintenance and restoration.
The facilities support the Guard’s dual responsibilities: responding to emergencies and other needs in Delaware while maintaining trained, equipped forces for federal missions.
What happens next
Gov. Matt Meyer is expected to release his recommended budget in January. Legislative review follows in the spring, with final budget bills considered before the new fiscal year begins July 1, 2027.
For service members, the outcome will help determine the resources available for education benefits and the facilities where they train. For taxpayers, the process offers an opportunity to examine the state’s share of maintaining a force that serves both Delaware and the nation.
To Go

Read the request: Find the Delaware National Guard presentation on the Office of Management and Budget’s fiscal 2028 public hearing documents page.
Learn about tuition assistance: Visit the Delaware National Guard’s education services page.
Tuition questions: Call the State Tuition Program office at 302-326-7012 or email ng.de.dearng.mbx.state-tuition-program@army.mil.
Follow budget hearings: Check the Delaware Public Meeting Calendar for meeting notices and participation instructions.

title: New Mexico Gov.-elect Haaland names transition and inaugural teams, including former US Sen. Udall
description: New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland this week announced a slate of well-known New Mexico Democrats charged with leading her transition and inauguration ahead of her taking office in January.
text:
Former U.S. Sen. Tom Udall (D-N.M.) will serve as honorary chair of New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland’s transition team, according to an announcement from Haaland’s campaign Nov. 10, 2026. (Screenshot of Udall’s announcement endorsing Haaland)New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland this week announced a slate of well-known New Mexico Democrats charged with leading her transition and inauguration ahead of her taking office in January.
Former U.S. Sen. Tom Udall (D-N.M.) will be the honorary chair of Haaland’s transition team, Haaland’s team announced Tuesday. He represented New Mexico in the U.S. Senate between 2009 and 2021, following terms in the U.S. House and as the state’s attorney general. Udall most recently served as U.S. ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during former Democratic President Joe Biden’s single term in office ending in 2025. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The Haaland Administration will be laser-focused on delivering for working families by bringing down costs and putting money back in people’s pockets,” Udall said in a statement, adding that the team is committed to Haaland’s “vision to create opportunities for New Mexicans and protect our state for future generations.”
In addition to Udall, Haaland named 16 “honorary co-chairs” of her transition team, including all five members of New Mexico’s current congressional delegation; leaders of the state House and Senate; and governors of four New Mexico pueblos that endorsed her during the primary or general election campaigns. 
Those pueblos include Jemez Pueblo Gov. John Galvan, Picuris Pueblo Gov. John Galvan, Zuni Pueblo Gov. Arden Kucate and Santo Domingo Pueblo Gov. Raymond Aguilar Jr. Navajo Nation President-elect Crystalyne Curley is also on the list of co-chairs. 
Incoming state Senate Majority Leader Sen. Linda Trujillo (D-Albuquerque) said in a post on social media Wednesday morning that she has watched two gubernatorial transitions “from the sidelines” as a longtime lawmaker and former cabinet secretary. 
“Those experiences gave me a deep appreciation for the thoughtful planning, collaboration, and hard work that go into preparing a new administration to serve,” she said. “I’m grateful for the trust and excited to help lay the groundwork for New Mexico’s next chapter.”
Haaland’s team also named former Albuquerque Mayor Martin Chavez, who recently spearheaded the planning stages of a large New Mexico State Fairgrounds redevelopment project on behalf of outgoing Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham, as chair of her inauguration efforts. Alongside him is Clara Apodaca, who served as New Mexico’s first lady when her husband, the late Jerry Apodaca, served as governor between 1975 and 1979. 
Serving as inauguration director is Britton Hansen, Haaland’s campaign’s former state and events director. The deputy director is Leah Johnson, who served as the campaign’s finance director, according to the announcement from Haaland’s campaign.  
Last week, Haaland named state Department of Workforce Solutions Secretary Sarita Nair as her chief of staff. Nair’s responsibilities also include guiding the transition to Haaland’s administration, as well as coordinating her staffing, cabinet appointments and policy priorities.

name: Mississippi Today
title: 6,000 acre Hinds County solar farm can proceed, appeals court rules
description: Hinds County residents not in favor of the building of a solar farm in their area packed the meeting of the Hinds County Board of Supervisors, Monday, June 17, 2024 in Jackson. Supervisors voted 3 - 2 in favor of the solor farm.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A large solar power project that would take up close to 6,000 acres near Bolton can move forward, the Mississippi Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday, over two years after Hinds County officials initially greenlit the facility.
“Soul City Solar,” an idea brought to the area by Virginia-based company Apex Clean Energy, drew pushback in 2024 from nearby residents who were worried about what a massive solar facility would do to the area’s natural ecosystem. The company agreed to lease land for the project from Gaddis Farms.
Despite the loud protests, the Hinds County Board of Supervisors approved the application with a 3-2 vote in June, 2024.
One of the opposing residents, Allison Lauderdale, appealed the decision to the Hinds County Circuit Court, arguing that the Board of Supervisors didn’t offer a written finding with its decision and that it should have required further environmental assessment. Lauderdale raised nearly $4,000 through a GoFundMe campaign to back her legal effort.
But the local court ruled against her, finding that the board did what was required of it. The Court of Appeals, after taking the case last year, affirmed the lower court’s decision on Tuesday.
Protesters against the building of a solar farm in their area gathered outside the Chancery Court building, Monday, June 17, 2024. The Hinds County Board of Supervisors voted 3 – 2 in favor of the solar farm. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
In its opinion, the court pointed to measures Soul City agreed to after hearing the community’s objections. Those included offering to repair nearby roads, using trees as a visual screen around the facility and putting up “fencing” and “corridors” to allow wildlife to move through the project area.
“Soul City voluntarily accepted conditions that concerned the community. The fact that these conditions were taken on voluntarily, rather than imposed by the Board, does not negate the fact that they exist,” Appeals Court Judge Amy Lassitter St. Pé wrote in the decision.
Advertising the project in 2024, Apex Clean Energy said the new facility would produce 396 megawatts of electricity, or enough to power 95,000 homes. That production would make it the largest solar producing facility in the state, officials at the time told Mississippi Today.

Officials in Hinds County began processing long-awaited affidavit ballots on Wednesday in the historic Mississippi U.S. Senate race between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom.

Election workers in Hinds County, a traditional Democratic stronghold and one of Mississippi’s largest counties, counted 67 outstanding mail-in ballots and were on track to process 817 accepted affidavits. Once the officials tabulate those affidavits, it could decide the outcome of the race.

name: Washington State Standard
title: O’Donnell declares victory in tight WA Supreme Court race
description: After a week of ballot tallying, Washington’s closest race for state Supreme Court has a winner. King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell claimed victory Wednesday morning over appeals court Judge Ian Birk. He leads by 39,000 votes, or 1.4%, with fewer than 100,000 ballots left to count statewide. “I am thrilled to be elected […]
text:
King County Superior Court Judge Sean O'Donnell at a candidate forum in September. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)After a week of ballot tallying, Washington’s closest race for state Supreme Court has a winner.
King County Superior Court Judge Sean O’Donnell claimed victory Wednesday morning over appeals court Judge Ian Birk. He leads by 39,000 votes, or 1.4%, with fewer than 100,000 ballots left to count statewide.
“I am thrilled to be elected to the Washington State Supreme Court,” O’Donnell said in a statement. “In electing me the voters of Washington demonstrated that they want judges who are experienced and impartial. They also demonstrated that they will not be fooled. I hope we will reflect on how and why so much outside money flooded into this race and work to ensure judicial races remain non-partisan.  
O’Donnell was referring to a decision from the state’s Public Disclosure Commission days before the election to not enforce limits on how much money political committees could accept.
After the move, Service Employees International Union 775 contributed $250,000 to the progressive-backed Beware the Attack on Our Courts political action committee. The money went toward boosting Birk and undermining O’Donnell, as part of a flurry of last-minute spending. 
The five Supreme Court races on this year’s ballot presented a proxy battle between Republicans and Democrats without any other statewide elected officials on the ballot. Five candidates, including Birk and two appointees of Gov. Bob Ferguson, had support from Democratic groups, while their five opponents, including O’Donnell, were supported by the state GOP. 
Birk’s campaign claimed O’Donnell was a closet Republican running on a “partisan agenda.” It was a rare example of typically sleepy races turning overtly partisan. 
Dozens of judges came to O’Donnell’s defense, calling out Birk for what they called “false partisan attacks.”
O’Donnell stressed that he had support from both sides of the political spectrum. 
Ian Birk, 2026 candidate for Washington state Supreme Court. (Photo by Jerry Cornfield/Washington State Standard)
The four other Democrat-allied candidates sailed to victory by double-digit margins. Ferguson’s appointees, Justices Colleen Melody and Theo Angelis, will retain their positions on the court. Chief Justice Debra Stephens won another term easily, and King County Superior Court Judge Jaime Hawk, who was previously an attorney for the American Civil Liberties Union, will join the high court. 
The races were all expensive, especially for Supreme Court campaigns, but none more than the battle between O’Donnell and Birk. O’Donnell raised $614,000, while Birk brought in $643,000. No other judicial candidates raised within $100,000 of those totals.
More than $1.3 million in additional outside spending flooded the O’Donnell-Birk race. 
All of the races drew more attention than usual in part because of the recent heavy turnover on the court and the looming legal challenge to the state’s new income tax on high earners, passed by voters. The measure is headed for a test at the high court.
Birk didn’t respond to requests for comment.
O’Donnell, in his statement, issued a “heartfelt thank you to the more than 1.4 million Washington voters who made their voices heard by entrusting me with the incredible responsibility of safeguarding our democracy in this perilous time, and ensuring justice is accessible to all.”
“I wish Judge Birk all the best,” he continued. “Now more than ever, our judges must uphold the rule of law and apply it equally to everyone, no matter how powerful they are. I have dedicated my life to public service and will work every day to ensure Washingtonians have faith in the impartiality, fairness, and thoughtfulness of our highest court.”
O’Donnell, elected to a six-year term, will replace Justice Charles Johnson, who wasn’t eligible for reelection; the state constitution requires justices to retire at age 75. Johnson has served on the court since 1991.
O’Donnell has served as a King County Superior Court judge since 2013, and has previously been a pro tem, or substitute, justice on the Supreme Court. He is also a past president of the Superior Court Judges’ Association. Before joining the bench, O’Donnell was a senior deputy prosecutor, and was part of the team that investigated and prosecuted Gary Ridgway, the Green River Killer.
During the campaign, he often discussed the importance of the Supreme Court setting rules for the use of generative artificial intelligence for judges and lawyers.

text:
The Oklahoma state Capitol dome is pictured on Dec. 13, 2023. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Newly elected Oklahoma state lawmakers will be sworn into office next week.
Senators will be sworn into office at 2 p.m. Monday while House members will take the oath of office at 10 a.m. Tuesday.
The recent elections didn’t change the balance of power in the Senate.
Six of the eight Senate Democrats were reelected unopposed.
The Senate will have 40 Republicans and eight Democrats with the lieutenant governor casting a vote if there is a tie. T.W. Shannon, a Republican and former House Speaker, was elected lieutenant governor, replacing Matt Pinnell, a Republican who could not run again due to term limits.
Some more vocal members of the conservative Freedom Caucus lost their bids for reelection, including Sen. Dusty Deevers, R-Elgin. Deevers didn’t make it out of the primary in Senate District 32. Republican Curtis W. Erwin was elected to the post.
Democrats picked up six seats in the House by defeating five Republican incumbents and taking an open seat previously held by the GOP.
The election results bring the balance of power to 75 Republicans and 26 Democrats in the 101-member body. 
Statewide officials will take their oaths of office in January.

title: GOP incumbent Britt maintains 228-vote lead in closely watched NC Senate race
description: Republican state Sen. Danny Britt maintained a narrow lead over Democratic challenger Catina Hamm in North Carolina’s 24th Senate District. The candidates were separated by just 228 votes Wednesday after officials counted provisional and cured ballots as the race moves toward its official canvass Friday.  Britt received 28,047 votes, or 50.2%, compared with [...]
text:
Republican Sen. Danny Britt (left) and Democrat Catina Hamm (right). (Photos: NCGA and Hamm campaign) Republican state Sen. Danny Britt maintained a narrow lead over Democratic challenger Catina Hamm in North Carolina’s 24th Senate District.
The candidates were separated by just 228 votes Wednesday after officials counted provisional and cured ballots as the race moves toward its official canvass Friday. 
Britt received 28,047 votes, or 50.2%, compared with 27,819 votes or 49.8% for Hamm, according to unofficial results from the North Carolina State Board of Elections. 
The margin leaves the contest in recount territory. Under North Carolina law, Hamm can request a recount if Britt’s lead remains less than 1% after the county canvasses Friday. 
The district includes Robeson, Hoke and Scotland counties. Britt has represented it since 2017.
The race could determine which party controls the state Senate when lawmakers convene in January. 
Republicans entered Election Day with a 30-20 majority in the chamber. Democrats picked up four seats in the Nov. 3 election, leaving them with 24 seats and Republicans with 26 if Britt holds his lead. 
If Britt wins, Republicans would retain a narrow majority and control of Senate leadership, committee assignments and the chamber’s legislative agenda.  But the party would still lose its veto-proof supermajority, meaning it would need Democratic support to override vetoes by Democratic Gov. Josh Stein. 
If Hamm were to win, the Senate would be evenly divided, with 25 Republicans and 25 Democrats. Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt, a Democrat, would be the tie-breaking vote.
Democrats have already taken control of the state House of Representatives for the first time since 2010. 
The deadline to file a recount request is noon on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: ICE agent in fatal Biddeford shooting had expedited training, held anti-immigrant views, NYT reports
description: The immigration agent who allegedly shot and killed a Biddeford man was fast-tracked through training and had expressed anti-immigrant views, according to new reporting from The New York Times. Media reports identified David Brouillette as the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July. [...]
text:
The site where Johan Sebastián, 25, was fatally shot by ICE agents is outlined in flowers on Wednesday, July 15, 2026,  in Biddeford, Maine. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)The immigration agent who allegedly shot and killed a Biddeford man was fast-tracked through training and had expressed anti-immigrant views, according to new reporting from The New York Times.
Media reports identified David Brouillette as the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who fatally shot 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in July. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security has not officially released the agent’s name. Guerrero, who was from Colombia, was not the intended target of the ICE operation and had a pending asylum case and a valid work permit, according to his family and lawyer. 
The Times obtained a series of emails that Brouillette, a former U.S. Army sergeant, sent in 2021 criticizing his sister’s relationship with a Colombian man, with whom she had two children.
“He can takes his non citizen ass back to his country and enjoy his third world luxuries,” Brouillette wrote in an email riddled with typos. He continued that the man’s “bloodline knows nothing about what it takes to earn and then CHERISH the freedom America offers.”
The reporting also revealed new details about Brouillette’s ICE training, citing anonymous sources who were briefed on his work history with the agency.
Brouillette applied at ICE in the fall of 2025 and was cleared to start on Dec. 1 after being fast-tracked through preliminary vetting, according to the sources. That was amid a hiring surge after President Donald Trump’s administration called for doubling the number of deportation officers. 
Brouillette skipped ICE’s full training course in Georgia, in line with ICE’s practice of recruits with some law enforcement experience completing a shorter online training program, and his background check was done by an outside contractor. However, officials still hadn’t checked his background for red flags that could result in his termination at the time of the Biddeford shooting, an anonymous source with knowledge of his hiring told the Times. 
Brouillette declined to speak with the Times. He has not responded to Maine Morning Star’s repeated attempts to contact him through phone or email. When Maine Morning Star asked ICE in July about Brouillette’s alleged involvement, an unnamed spokesperson said, “The ICE officer in question has nearly a decade of federal law enforcement experience with required training,” but declined to share a name.  
The 911 calls made after ICE fatally shot Biddeford man

The new revelations about Brouillette’s background come after earlier reporting revealed complaints of domestic abuse. 
Court documents show that one of Brouillette’s ex-wives filed several requests for protection from harassment and protection from abuse orders against him, for herself and on behalf of their minor child. Most of those were denied, though a judge required him to temporarily relinquish his firearms. Brouillette also filed several requests for protection against an ex-wife, including on behalf of their children.
Benjamin Gideon, attorney for Guerrero’s wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, and estate, called Brouillette “the poster child for what happens when our government chooses to recruit agents to carry out a campaign of hate against immigrants, hires those agents without adequate screening and places them on the street without basic training.”
“Johan Sebastián’s death was not an inevitable accident,” Gideon said in a statement Wednesday. “It was a natural and predictable choices of the policies of our government and its political leadership.”
The federal government has yet to tell Guerrero’s family anything about a federal investigation, according to Gideon. U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine said the latest reporting makes the need for a full, independent investigation even more urgent.
“Who authorized his deployment? What would a thorough review have revealed?” Pingree questioned in a statement. “An agency whistleblower has already warned the DHS Inspector General of an ‘unprecedented lowering of standards.’ How many other agents are carrying guns in our communities without completed vetting?”
The state has its own investigation underway. Another lawyer for Guerrero’s family, Sean Murphy, told the Times that investigators said Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey, who terms out at the end of the year, plans to announce any decisions in the case before he leaves office.
Maine Morning Star’s requests for records of communications between federal agencies and the state attorney general’s office and the coroner’s report have been denied as they remain confidential while the investigation is ongoing.
