title: Nevada braces for more SNAP cuts proposed by Trump administration
description: The Trump administration moved on Tuesday to cut millions of Americans from the nation’s largest food assistance program even after voters signaled grocery costs were a major concern during the midterm elections. The Department of Agriculture (USDA) published a proposed rule that would end provisions that automatically make households eligible for the Supple[...]
text:
Since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect, Nevada has seen a 23% reduction in SNAP participants, or more than 100,000 Nevadans. (Photo: New Jersey Monitor)The Trump administration moved on Tuesday to cut millions of Americans from the nation’s largest food assistance program even after voters signaled grocery costs were a major concern during the midterm elections.
The Department of Agriculture (USDA) published a proposed rule that would end provisions that automatically make households eligible for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) if they also meet requirements for the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).
According to an analysis posted by the USDA, the proposed changes would cut SNAP benefits by more than $45 billion over five years and remove about 17% of SNAP beneficiaries from the program — or 6.3 million people — beginning in 2029, the first year the rule takes full effect. 
Under the rule, about 1.8 million children would no longer be automatically eligible for free school meals, and 5,500 households would lose access to TANF, the agency estimated.
In addition, the agency estimates that about 42,000 children nationally could potentially lose Summer EBT beginning in 2029.
It’s unclear how many Nevadans would be affected by the rule, if implemented. 
“The Division of Social Services was recently made aware of this matter and will need additional time to thoroughly review the information, evaluate any potential impacts, and gather the necessary details,” said a spokesperson for the Nevada Department of Human Services Division of Social Services. 
The proposed rule would end a policy known as “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which allows states to expand SNAP access to households that receive aid from TANF but have assets above the normal SNAP threshold. 
“Broad-based categorical eligibility has bloated the welfare rolls for decades,” a USDA spokesperson said in a statement. “It has allowed States to take short cuts, error rates to balloon, and those with income and assets far above federal limits access to a benefit meant for the neediest among us. Correcting this loophole is long overdue.”
Advocates argue the rule allows states to streamline SNAP applications for households already deemed eligible for other assistance programs, reducing administrative costs and improving efficiency.
USDA estimates the rule would increase state administrative costs by nearly $930 million.
“Eliminating [broad-based categorical eligibility] does nothing to reduce hunger, and it doesn’t improve program integrity,” said Crystal FitzSimons, president of the Food Research & Action Center in a statement.
Thousands of Nevadans have already been removed from SNAP since the passage of the Republicans One Big Beautiful Bill Act last summer, which enacted stricter work requirements. 
Since the law took effect in July 2025, Nevada has seen a 23% reduction in SNAP participants, or more than 100,000 Nevadans. 
States have also faced rising administrative costs under the bill. In Nevada, administrative costs associated with implementing the new federal requirements are estimated at $19 million for the 2025–26 biennium and approximately $50 million for each future biennium, according to the Nevada Division of Social Services. 
“It is unconscionable that the Trump administration would attempt to issue this proposed rule again now given the harm that the budget reconciliation law, H.R. 1, has already unleashed,” said FitzSimons. 
The Trump administration proposed a similar rule in 2019, during the president’s first term, but never finalized the regulation. The Biden administration withdrew the proposal in 2021.
Food banks in the state raised concerns about the proposed rule, noting that for every meal food banks distribute, SNAP provides nine.
“Food banks will do everything we can, and we already are, but the charitable food system was built to supplement SNAP, not replace it,”  said KC Kappen, a spokesperson for Three Square. “When thousands of people lose benefits at once, it creates immediate pressure on food banks and nonprofit partners. Every family that loses SNAP becomes another family in line at a pantry that’s already stretched.”
It’s unclear whether the proposed rule will ultimately be finalized following changes in leadership after the midterms. Democrats, who took control of both houses of Congress last week, have vowed to roll back SNAP cuts.
But “broad-based categorical eligibility” has long been a target of Republicans. The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 policy blueprint, which the Trump administration has closely followed, targets the policy.
Retail groups in Nevada also called out the proposed rule change. Bryan Wachter, the president of the Retail Association of Nevada, urged federal lawmakers to assess the potential impacts on Nevada’s retail sector, noting that every dollar in SNAP benefits directly benefits the local economy. 
“This proposed rule will have the exact opposite effect that the administration seeks to accomplish. This rule will create more government as families and businesses try to navigate an already complex system. The negative effects go far beyond those who will be removed from the program, and we urge the next Congress to examine this issue closely,” said Wachter.

name: California
title: Bad news for California school repairs: nearly half of bond measures on track to fail
description: Voters rejected billions of dollars in bonds that schools use to pay for repairs and modernization to aging campus facilities.
text:
In summary
Voters rejected billions of dollars in bonds that schools use to pay for repairs and modernization to aging campus facilities.


Last week’s election was full of surprises, especially for California school districts seeking to fix leaking roofs and broken air conditioners.
Although election officials are still counting votes in many parts of the state, the preliminary results show that nearly half the school bonds on California ballots are failing. 
“It’s a shocking outcome,” said Sara Hinkley, director of policy and research at UC Berkeley’s Center for Cities and Schools. “This leaves some school districts with very few options. I’m sure they’re sweating.”
Eighty-six school districts put bonds seeking to do school repairs and modernization on last week’s ballot, totalling $12.4 billion, a relatively low amount of money compared to other big election years. Two years ago, school bonds totaled almost four times that and most of them passed. 
As of late Tuesday, 50 bonds had either passed or were leading, with the rest failing. Bonds need 55% to pass. 
Painful cuts
School district officials blamed the shaky economy.
“Everyone wants what is best for the kids, but when gas, groceries and utilities are cutting into people’s budget, they have to find places to save,” said Mays Kakish, superintendent of Beaumont Unified School District near Banning in the Inland Empire. “In the short term, this loss of funding will be painful.” 
Beaumont, one of the few districts in California where enrollment is increasing, desperately needs the $86 million the bond would have brought in. Last year, its schools had 138 roof leaks, district spokesman Thomas Guzowski said. In addition, the district needs to replace 81 portable classrooms.
A 2024 state bond — Proposition 2 — that provided $10 billion for school construction, is an alternative source of money for some school districts. But districts need to provide matching funds to get Prop. 2 money, and if the bond fails Beaumont will not qualify, Guzowski said.
Regardless, most of the Prop. 2 money set aside for school repairs is already spoken for. There’s still money available for new construction projects and emergencies, but there’s a long waiting list for the remaining money to fix leaky roofs or make other maintenance repairs.
Rich get richer
John Affeldt, managing attorney at the public interest law firm Public Advocates, said he wasn’t surprised at the outcome of the school bond elections. Many bonds in wealthier areas like the Bay Area and Orange County tend to be for more money and usually pass, enabling those districts to get Prop. 2 money using matching funds. Bonds in lower-income areas, meanwhile, tend to be for less money and fail.
“Those who have more, get more,” Affeldt said. “It’s an unfair system, and part of a long pattern of the state’s failed system of financing facilities.”
Affeldt’s firm sued the state over the alleged inequities in Prop. 2 and is awaiting a judge’s decision on whether to grant the state’s request to throw out the case. Earlier this year, a judge denied the plaintiffs’ request for an injunction but said they had a “reasonable chance of succeeding” on at least part of the case.
Windfall in San Diego
San Diego Unified is on the other end of the school bond fortunes. Voters said “yes” to its $3.4 billion bond, the largest in California, ushering in a windfall for swimming pools, new performing arts venues, staff housing, new air conditioners, security systems and other upgrades. Homeowners will pay an average of $294 a year. 
“It was a great night. I’m still on a high,” said school board vice president Sabrina Bazzo. “This means that all students in our district — not just those in wealthy neighborhoods — will get access to high-quality facilities.”
Basso attributed the bond’s success to plenty of community support. Labor unions threw their weight behind the measure, in part because the district agreed to hire local union workers for much of the work, Bazzo said. Even the local taxpayers association supported the bond, largely because it wasn’t a new tax; it replaced a previous bond from 2022.
Repair and replace
Visalia Unified near Fresno doesn’t look to be so lucky. Its bid for a $158 million bond is trailing and expected to lose. 
“The economy is challenging right now for a lot of folks,” said Superintendent Kirk Shrum. “I’m disappointed, thinking about what we could have done — upgraded bathrooms, new furniture — and now we have to wait.”
More than 70% of the district’s buildings are 50 years old or older, and are in dire need of repairs, Shrum said. A few years ago, the district assessed the condition of its buildings and the total for repairs came to $600 million. That seemed too high for a bond, so the district went with $158 million, the amount needed for only the most urgent projects.
Without the bond money, the district will shift funds around to pay for repairs when needed, but “we’ll never be able to get ahead of it,” Shrum said.
“You get stuck in a cycle of replace and repair when things break,” Shrum said. “But you can patch a roof only so many times.”

name: California
title: With California’s insurance crisis at an impasse, it might be time for a different approach
description: California Insurance Commissioner-elect Jane Kim's plan to set up a fire insurance system warrants an independent and authoritative examination.
text:
Nobody really likes writing those premium checks to insurance companies that always seem to be increasing — until they need their insurance to cover losses from auto crashes, fires or other calamities.
The conflict between those two priorities has been particularly acute in California in recent years as a series of horrendous wildfires swept through the state, taking lives, destroying billions of dollars in property and disrupting lives — even of those who escape direct losses.
Californians spend more than $100 billion a year on what the industry calls “property and casualty” policies, according to the state Department of Insurance.
Bills for fire and homeowners coverage topped $19 billion in 2025, but thanks largely to the destructive fires that hit Los Angeles and its suburbs 22 months ago, insurers incurred more than $31 billion in losses on those policies — more than four times the losses in 2024.
As payouts mounted over several years of wildfires, insurers began either pulling out of the California market or imposing tighter restrictions and higher premiums, forcing millions of property owners to scramble for coverage mortgage lenders require.
The state’s last ditch “FAIR plan” was deluged with applications for coverage that was both costly and minimal, putting its finances in jeopardy.
It was — and is — a genuine crisis, needing a solution that provides consumers with adequate coverage at affordable prices and makes insurance profitable enough to keep insurers in the market.
After the Legislature failed to come up with a solution, Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara weighed in three years ago with a plan he said could advance both priorities, allowing insurers to base rates on estimates of future losses, rather than past experience, while requiring them to meet coverage quotas.
Lara has taken heat from consumer groups, such as Consumer Watchdog, accusing him of caving in to insurers.
Oddly, however, the industry and consumer groups forged a strange bedfellows alliance this year to oppose a scheme Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed, limiting the liability of electric utilities such as Pacific Gas & Electric when their transmission lines fail and spark fires.
Without such limits, utilities argued, their financial stability would be undermined, making it difficult for them to borrow money and attract investors. The plan would, in effect, shift more of fire losses to insurers or property owners.
However, adding utilities’ liability to an already dicey insurance coverage crisis was too much to swallow, and as the legislative session ended that plan remained on the table.
Lara could not run for another term, and the election of his successor this month adds still another factor to a situation already fraught with political complexity.
Two Democrats, former San Francisco Supervisor Jane Kim and state Sen. Ben Allen, finished in the top two in the June primary, putting both on the Nov. 3 ballot. Their duel took on an ideological aura. On the left, Kim proposed that the state set up its own fire insurance system, while Allen, a moderate, said Kim’s proposal would cost too much and the state should build on Lara’s plan.
Kim won decisively, one of many political races that progressives claimed this year. Her victory sets the stage for another legislative struggle.
Kim’s notion of having the state directly provide at least some coverage is not particularly novel. The state already has an insurance program for workers’ compensation, and it offers earthquake insurance. 
Nor is it fatally unworkable, as Allen and the industry contended. Having base coverage provided by the state through taxes or mandatory fees tied to property value — and backed by reinsurance — could, if designed adroitly, protect insurers, utilities and consumers from the economic jolts of catastrophic wildfires.
At the very least, it warrants an independent and authoritative examination.

name: California
title: Election integrity is becoming a partisan prize. California voters did not take the bait
description: California voters saw Proposition 39 for what it was: not an attempt to solve any problem, but a ploy to use "election integrity" for partisan gain.
text:
The sheer magnitude of the Republican Party’s election defeat suspends, but does not extinguish, a dangerous and growing assault on U.S. elections. 
If Democrats had won only the four seats they needed to gain control of the Senate in the 2026 midterms, President Donald Trump would again have had the sort of incentive he had after losing Georgia in his 2020 election defeat — incentive to pressure state election officials to “find” non-existent votes, threaten poll workers with criminal charges, allege interference with voting machines, claim victory despite obvious defeat and attempt to thwart certification of the results.
If Senate control in the 2026 midterms turned only on Mississippi, for example, where a Democrat currently leads by a hair or two, Trump might have lost Congress in the end yet still advanced a far more nefarious campaign — to sow doubt and thereby undermine public confidence in fundamental institutions of American democracy.
To proclaim that U.S. elections are “rigged.” To have millions of Americans believe it. To have millions more question whether any given election will be free and fair.
The threat to American elections has little to do with the actual freeness or fairness of voting, or the accuracy of reported results.
The threat is to public confidence in that freeness and fairness. If election outcomes perfectly reflect the will of the voting majority, but the voters don’t believe that they do, democracy cannot survive.
Or if a segment of voters believe the results are accurate but reject them anyway and falsely claim “fraud” — again, democracy cannot survive. Victory and power become things snatched by aggressors, liars and crooks, not by candidates with winning campaigns and majority support. 
Voter confidence in the instruments and processes of democracy is precious and fragile. Once lost, it is not easily recovered.
Close elections test that confidence, strain it and tempt cheaters.
But this election was not close. It was a broad and historic repudiation of the president in the form of a “bluenami” that rolled over Texas, the Carolinas, Kansas, Iowa and other GOP strongholds, bumped Republicans from statehouses and delivered control of both the House and Senate to Democrats by — and again, this is key — large margins. Democrats won not just four but at least seven, and possibly eight or nine, Senate seats. 
That’s a scale too big to look “rigged.” 
By Monday, Trump was up to his old tricks and suggested on Truth Social that it was, but the post seemed mostly for form. No one seemed to be taking the bait.
The Democratic (and democratic) wave also helped derail the administration’s odious and easily disproven allegations of widespread non-citizen voting and its attempt to compel California to sequester 20,000 supposedly suspect ballots, plus its threats to criminally charge county elections officials. It is one thing for courts to reject such gambits, as they did — first and forcefully in the district court, then twice in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and finally in the U.S. Supreme Court. It is another thing altogether for the federal prosecutor, Bill Essayli — who was disqualified from representing the Trump administration in court but purports to do so anyway — to ultimately acknowledge futility and to drop the suit.
Also, in California, voters soundly rejected Proposition 39, which would have required them to present government-issued identification the next time they go to the polls, and forever after. 
It was never an unreasonable-sounding idea on its face. Only citizens may lawfully vote, so how can a poll worker know if a person, absent identification, is entitled to cast a ballot? Most other states require ID. If the goal is not just free and fair elections, but broad voter confidence in that freeness and fairness, what would be so bad about requiring ID?
But a majority of California voters saw the measure for what it was: not an attempt to solve any problem that actually exists, but a ploy to use the banner of “election integrity” for partisan gain. 
Many states have a long, sordid history of efforts to disenfranchise whole swaths of American society by making it harder, more expensive or more risky to register and to vote. If you must pay a fee to replace a lost California drivers license ($37) or to get a U.S. passport ($165), and if you need to present one of those documents when voting, what practical difference is there between that and an unconstitutional poll tax? (The “free” ID that Prop. 39 would have required would have cost the state millions).
Or if armed federal agents routinely arrest or threaten to arrest naturalized citizens because their language or their accent or their skin supposedly make them suspect, how is that different from threatening Black voters in the South with arrest in the days before the Voting Rights Act of 1965?
Now that the Voting Rights Act has been all but extinguished by the U.S. Supreme Court, California and some other forward-looking states have expanded and protected voting rights by permitting everyone to choose to vote by mail, and by rejecting onerous ID requirements in favor of proven safeguards and audits.
That’s important. The right to vote, like confidence in elections, is fundamental and precious. Indeed, when voting is disparaged, discouraged or disputed, elections are by definition neither free nor fair and we can have no confidence in them.
And there’s the rub. Political parties and their adherents have made not just electoral victory but also election integrity a prize to be grabbed from the hands of one another. One side argues that elections are unfair if the franchise is restricted, and the other side argues that elections are fraudulent if the franchise expands. At this moment in history it is Democrats who are protecting voting rights, but a quick look at the Alaska Senate ballot and the multiple Dan Sullivans fiasco demonstrates that they are hardly on the side of the angels. 
No party, candidate or leader is standing up purely in defense of democracy and confidence in democratic institutions.
And yet, in a delicious irony, one American did step forward to rescue democracy, in spite of himself, by encouraging a large voter turnout and an unmistakable electoral verdict.
It was Trump. So many voters of various political stripes found him to be such a clear and present danger to American liberty, American leadership, American justice, the American economy, America’s capital city, America’s allies, American decorum and yes, American elections, that millions of Americans set aside their differences in order to go to the polls and say “no.” 
Trump gifted us with the unassailable margin of his own defeat. That margin buys us a temporary period of shared belief in election integrity.
States can use those 18 months or so to hammer out mutual political and racial gerrymandering agreements, accords on election security, compromises where possible — an array of projects to firm up not just actual election integrity, but restored and enduring confidence that our elections are indeed free and fair.
It’s that, or the further and perhaps permanent degradation of democracy.

name: California
title: This law was supposed to force more Californians into mental health treatment. What happened?
description: A new law was supposed to keep severely mentally ill Californians from falling through the cracks. So far, it’s resulted in few people getting long-term care.
text:
Californians braced for major upheaval three years ago when Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law meant to bring people with severe mental illnesses and addictions off the street and into involuntary treatment. 
Families who championed the measure hoped it would be the answer to their prayers – a tool that finally would compel their loved ones to receive treatment through conservatorship. 
Disability rights advocates who opposed the law warned it would traumatize large numbers of people by forcibly medicating them and removing their rights to make decisions about their own care.
County behavioral health officials worried the legislation would unleash a torrent of new referrals on programs that didn’t have the resources to keep up. 
And leaders of already overcrowded hospital emergency rooms and psychiatric facilities braced themselves for a large influx of new patients.
So far, little of that seems to have happened.
In fact, data obtained by CalMatters shows that, in most of the state’s largest counties, the number of conservatorships has barely budged. 
“It was not at all as big an impact as we thought it could be,” said Toni Navarro, director of behavioral health for Santa Barbara County, where the number of conservatorships has dropped 1% since the legislation took effect there in July 2025. 
Senate Bill 43, signed into law in 2023, broadened a nearly 60-year-old framework known as the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act for determining when someone is so “gravely disabled” that they can no longer care for themselves.  
The new law allows more people to qualify for involuntary treatment. “Gravely disabled” used to mean someone could not provide for their basic needs of food, clothing or shelter due to severe mental illness or chronic alcoholism. Now, it also includes people who cannot provide for their safety or medical care, as well as people who are incapacitated due to severe substance use disorder.
The state allowed counties to wait until January of this year to start using the new parameters, and many did. Some experts say in those counties, the real effect of the law won’t be apparent until more time has passed. 
Annis Pereyra, whose son was shot and killed by Walnut Creek police in February, said she believes the new law could have saved his life — if the county had used it to compel him to take an antipsychotic medication that had worked for him in the past.
“His needs were ignored at every turn that happened. Every single turn,” she said. “He wasn’t put on the only medication that saved him from the horrors of his illness.”
A picture of Annis Pereyra’s son, Joaquin Anthony “Tony” Pereyra, in the garden of her home in Walnut Creek on Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters
To assess how the law is working, CalMatters requested data from the state’s 25 most populous counties comparing the number of people under a one-year mental health conservatorship right before the legislation went into effect with the number under a conservatorship now. The majority of counties that provided data reported that their numbers did not increase significantly. 
There could be a number of reasons the numbers haven’t shown a dramatic increase. Some counties reported improving their voluntary mental health services around the same time that the new conservatorship law went into effect. As a result, more people chose care and fewer people were forced into conservatorships – something that’s widely considered a positive outcome. 
Another reason could lie in the way the law was written, county behavioral health directors say. It tried to push addiction treatment into the existing mental health conservatorship framework, which isn’t necessarily a good fit. 
But even though the new law doesn’t appear to have gotten many more people off the street and into conservatorships, health officials say it’s still accomplished good things, such as facilitating better addiction treatment for people on conservatorships and other involuntary psychiatric holds who have both a mental illness and an addiction. 
“It has given us quite a lot of positive things that I think that no one is looking at,” said Veronica Kelley, director of the Orange County Health Care Agency. “But I think the end that everyone’s interested in: Did we get everyone now into (a Lanterman-Petris-Short) conservatorship? No, that hasn’t happened.”


How we obtained data for this story
CalMatters requested conservatorship data from the state’s 25 most populous counties for this story. We asked each county for the number of conservatorships on the day before SB 43 went into effect in their county (start dates range from Jan. 1, 2024 to Jan. 1, 2026) and the current number of conservatorships. 
Nineteen counties provided that point-in-time data. For most, the data on “current” conservatorships is from September 2026. Two counties instead provided data from June and one from October.


Her agency has seen a 2% increase in conservatorship cases since January, when the law went into effect in Orange County. 
Disability rights advocates, who strongly opposed the law, caution that it’s too soon to measure its impact, which they still expect to be significant. Once more facilities are built, said Samuel Jain, a senior policy attorney at Disability Rights California, he and others anticipate seeing a lot more people forced into involuntary treatment, 
Former Sen. Susan Talamantes Eggman, a Democrat from Stockton and the author of the legislation, didn’t respond to multiple calls requesting an interview.
Sen. Roger Niello, a Republican from Roseville and one of the legislation’s 23 co-authors, worries society’s reluctance to overrule someone’s civil rights and compel treatment is jeopardizing the law’s effectiveness – but he said the jury’s still out because the law is so new.  
The other thing standing in the way is money, Niello said. 
“First we need funding,” he said. “If we’re not going to have funding, if we’re not going to increase the capacity for treatment, then I’m not sure there’s any (amount) of time that would show success.”
Some family members of people with serious mental illnesses say the law is just the latest in a series of failed promises made by the Newsom administration. A CalMatters investigation of CARE Court, Newsom’s signature effort to use the courts to get people into mental health treatment, found that program has helped fewer people than anticipated and left many families disappointed. A recent bond the governor backed has doled out billions for mental health treatment beds and treatment slots, but CalMatters found all the projects slated to open last year were delayed or canceled.   
“It’s scary, the gaps are scary,” said Teresa Pasquini, a long-time mental health advocate whose own son lives with mental illness.
When it comes to the new conservatorship law, the biggest failure Pasquini knows of is the case of her friend Annis Pereyra’s son. 
Begging for conservatorship
By the time Walnut Creek law enforcement officers shot and killed Joaquin Anthony “Tony” Pereyra while he was in the middle of a mental health crisis last February, his mother, Annis, had been begging Contra Costa County to force him to take medication for months. 
Even before the new law took effect in the county, Annis had asked local leaders whether they could use it to compel her son to receive treatment. 
Growing up, Tony had been a cheerful, brilliant child. In fifth grade, he started having irrational thoughts. In junior high, he began hearing voices. During his sophomore year, he experienced his first psychotic break and dropped out of high school. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia soon after. 
In those early years, the county frequently placed Tony under temporary conservatorships and sent him to locked facilities, his mother said. After trying several other medications without lasting success, he finally landed on clozapine in his early 30s. It transformed him, his mother said. She described 15 good years, during which he was able to hold down a job, live independently and help her with myriad projects around the family home. 
Annis Pereyra in the outdoor patio of her home in Walnut Creek on Oct. 28, 2026. Pereyra’s son, Joaquin Anthony Pereyra, was killed by law enforcement during a mental health crisis. Photo by Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters
Then, in the summer of 2024, Annis had a medical emergency. His mother’s frailty terrified Tony. Now in his 40s, he took himself off clozapine. The voices, long quieted, grew louder. 
On March 24, 2025, a distressed Tony appeared at his parents’ home and violently attacked them.
The couple told police they didn’t want to press charges. They just wanted someone to help their son. Tony was placed in locked facilities for several months under a temporary conservatorship, but was released to his apartment without going back on clozapine, his mother said.
The county’s attempt to reach Tony through CARE Court also failed, Annis said. So she turned her focus to the new conservatorship law. Her son was dangerous to himself and others, he wasn’t able to care for himself and he wasn’t able to recognize that he needed medication, his mother said. Surely, she thought, that would make him a candidate for a longer-term conservatorship.
Diane Burgis, the chair of the Contra Costa County board of supervisors, didn’t weigh in on Tony’s case, but said county leaders were aware of the high expectations families had as the new law rolled out and are “so committed to this work.” 
“It wasn’t as far-reaching as expected, we kind of saw that coming,” she said. “As someone that has personally experienced the frustrations of trying to help someone that you love get the care you need, the system still has so much that it needs to do to be better.”
What the numbers show
The new law affects a range of involuntary treatment options, from a 72-hour hold (also known as a 5150 hold) to a one-year conservatorship. After a 72-hour hold, if someone is still unable to care for themselves, they can progress through the system and eventually be placed under a conservatorship. Then, a judge orders a conservator to take over their treatment, and they often are placed in a locked psychiatric facility.
Of the 19 counties that provided point-in-time data, 12 reported increases of less than 5% or decreases in their one-year conservatorship case load after SB 43 went into effect. On average, counties saw an increase of less than 6%. The overall number of cases in the counties CalMatters analyzed increased by 4%. 
Only three counties said they had used the new law to conserve anyone solely because of a substance use disorder, amounting to a total of six people. Most counties CalMatters received data from aren’t tracking whether people are conserved under the law’s other expanded criteria.
Some counties saw larger increases in involuntary 72-hour psychiatric holds. In San Mateo County, for example, the number of people on those short-term holds increased by more than a quarter in the six months after the new conservatorship law went into effect, compared to the six months before. Los Angeles County wrote more than 500 72-hour holds for severe substance use disorder – as newly allowed by the recent legislation – between January and June 2026. 
But those short-term holds don’t always lead to the type of lasting treatment patients need. Instead, people placed on 5150 holds often cycle repeatedly between the hospital and the street.
Licensed clinician Ernesto Alvarado negotiates with a man reluctant to be placed on a mental health hold in Penn Valley on March 15, 2022. Alvarado is part of Nevada County’s Mobile Crisis Team. Photo by Max Whittaker for CalMatters
Even in counties that are seeing more conservatorship cases, it’s difficult to draw a direct connection between the increased case load and the new law. In San Luis Obispo County, which began using the new law as soon as it could (in January 2024), the number of people on one-year conservatorships has increased by more than a quarter – but none of those cases were for substance use alone, and the county isn’t tracking cases under the law’s other expanded parameters. The same is true in Tulare and Placer counties, which each saw conservatorship cases increase by nearly 17%.
San Francisco, however, does attribute its 7% increase in conservatorship cases at least in part to the new law. It strengthened the city’s ability to help those who are most at risk of fatal overdoses and who are repeatedly harming themselves, the San Francisco Human Services Agency said in a statement.  
When it began using the new law at the start of this year, Sonoma County braced for an expected 20 or 30 more cases per year – an influx that would have taxed the mid-sized county’s already scarce resources, said Jasdeep Singh, the county’s chief deputy public administrator-guardian-conservator. 
Instead, cases are down slightly. 
When the county recently tried to get someone into a conservatorship using the new law, by arguing that the person’s personal safety was at risk, the court rejected the petition, said Singh. It was frustrating for staff who thought the person needed more time in treatment. 
“Just going off of that, what feels like a recent experience, it wasn’t helpful,” he said. 
Could it have saved him?
Contra Costa County, where Tony Pereyra lived, has seen one-year conservatorships increase by 13% since the new conservatorship law went into effect, more than many other counties. In actual numbers, it’s gone from 98 cases to 111.
Contra Costa’s behavioral health department declined to make anyone available for an interview.

Annis Pereyra wears a pin dedicated to her son, Joaquin Anthony Pereyra, during a vigil honoring the memory of him and others impacted by mental illness, outside of the Contra Costa County Administration Building in Martinez on Oct. 6, 2026. Photo by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters

Early on the morning of Feb. 26, less than two months after the new law rolled out in Contra Costa County, Walnut Creek police responded to a report of a man in dark clothing shining a flashlight into people’s cars and homes. They found Tony Pereyra around the corner from his parents’ house. Body-worn camera footage released by the department shows officers issuing multiple commands for Tony to show his hands and drop to the ground . “I ain’t messing with you, man,” one officer shouted. After shooting Tony, the officers discovered he had been holding a pellet gun. He died at the scene.
After her son’s death, Annis Pereyra went to the apartment where he lived. Garbage was piled up to the railings on his back patio. Tony had ripped up the flooring, dismantled the plumbing, pulled out the light switches, and used the racks from the refrigerator to block off the kitchen cabinets. 
She believes he was trying to make the voices stop. How, she wonders, did the county not consider him sick enough to use the new law to force him to restart clozapine?
A square peg in a round hole
Why isn’t the new law getting more people into conservatorships? 
It turns out addiction, one of the main expanded criteria of the legislation, doesn’t fit as neatly into the conservatorship system as lawmakers hoped it would, said Kelley of Orange County. The first step toward involuntary care is a 72-hour psychiatric hold. If someone is held because of drug use, they typically regain the ability to care for themselves once the drugs wear off within that 72 hours. Then, they no longer qualify for a conservatorship.
In addition, many counties have little appetite for using lengthy involuntary holds to treat substance use. Research suggests that forcing people into addiction treatment doesn’t work, and can instead reduce people’s drug tolerance and make them more likely to overdose once they go back to using, said Michelle Cabrera, executive director of the County Behavioral Health Directors Association, citing research out of Massachusetts. 
“We can’t ignore that there isn’t a tremendous amount of evidence to support this treatment model,” she said. 
A man lights a pipe in front of a city worker during an encampment sweep in the Tenderloin in San Francisco on Aug. 8, 2024. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters
But the law has done some good work, say the people involved in its implementation. Including substance use on the list of criteria for a mental health conservatorship has forced counties’ mental health and addiction treatment departments – which are often separate – to collaborate more. That’s been helpful, Kelley said, as about 60% of the patients with a serious mental illness that her Orange County department sees also have a substance use disorder. The mental health facilities that serve people in conservatorships are now better equipped to also treat their addictions, she said. 
“We’ve been trying to merge those systems, because it’s the same brain, for decades,” Kelley said.
A vigil for Tony
Just before 9 a.m. on a Tuesday in early October, a group of 40 people formed a circle near the steps leading up to the Contra Costa County Board of Supervisors chambers in downtown Martinez. The group dedicated its vigil for the National Mental Health Day of Prayer to the memory of Tony Pereyra. 
“I’m tired of getting the phone calls that police have shot and killed another person with mental illness,” Gigi Crowder, chief executive of the local NAMI affiliate, told the group. Crowder is among those who believe the new conservatorship law could have been invoked to save Tony’s life. 
“This was a totally avoidable death,” she said.



First: Marissa Castill lifts her hands in prayer during a vigil organized by the National Alliance on Mental Illness honoring the memory of Joaquin Anthony Pereyra and others impacted by mental illness. Last: A sign shows faces of community members impacted by mental illness during the vigil outside the Contra Costa County Administration Building in Martinez on Oct. 6, 2026. Photos by Sarahbeth Maney for CalMatters
Burgis, the board chair, emerged from the chambers and stood quietly off to one side. She is intimately familiar with the heartache of having loved ones with mental illness.
“Sometimes, sitting up at the dais, people can get the impression that we don’t care,” she told CalMatters later. “I just wanted to be with those folks because I understand that experience. I share their frustrations. I understand there is a lot more work that needs to be done.”
Someone led the group in a hymn, and then many of the participants filed inside to attend the board of supervisors’ meeting. During public comment, Annis Pereyra approached the microphone. She wore a button with Tony’s picture pinned to her lapel and clutched a double-spaced printout of her message to the board. She described to them the bullet tearing through her son’s chest and the cold asphalt where he died.“Treatment before tragedy works,” she said.
Her two minutes were up before she could read the final line she had written on the paper: “Implement SB 43 to the fullest extent possible to save others.”

name: California
title: New governor begins the ‘Becerra era’ by making nice with Capitol Democrats
description: Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has evaded giving specifics about what policies his administration will prioritize. But some lawmakers are hoping for a more collaborative relationship
text:
In summary
Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has evaded giving specifics about what policies his administration will prioritize. But some lawmakers are hoping for a more collaborative relationship


Welcome to the “Becerra era,” where the incoming governor doesn’t share specific policy ideas, but really wants you to know that he’ll play nicely with Democratic leaders in the Legislature. 
“We’ve tried to make it very clear, through the fact that we are standing here just a couple of days after the election, to say, ‘We’re going to work together. This will be a partnership,’” Democratic Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra proclaimed to a crowd of reporters in the Capitol rotunda last week. 
“Get used to this,” he added, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with Senate President Pro Tem Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas.
Together, Becerra, Limón and Rivas — known collectively as the Big Three — will hold the ultimate decisionmaking power over California’s policy priorities. So far, all three have refrained from committing to any concrete legislative proposals on the major issues that lawmakers will confront when they return in January. 
California policymakers must navigate new federal restrictions, including cuts to Medi-Cal, the state program that provides healthcare to disabled and low-income Californians, that could cause more than 1 million to lose coverage starting Jan. 1. Lawmakers also need to resolve a debate over who pays for the damage from wildfires caused by utility equipment after a last-minute deal failed this year. Then there’s the mandates voters gave Democrats this election cycle to rein in artificial intelligence, root out corruption, lower everyday costs and increase available housing.
Becerra’s pledge to partner closely with the California Legislature from the get-go marks a pivot from Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature approach: jamming big policy proposals down the Legislature’s throat as legislative deadlines approach, using the time crunch to generate urgency while leaving as little room as possible for opposition to surface. 
The tactic backfired earlier this year when Newsom tried to push through major changes to the way utilities and insurance companies bear the cost of damages when utility equipment sparks wildfires. But for years prior, his last-minute maneuvers resulted in legislation to speed up infrastructure construction by limiting legal challenges and to carve out exemptions to environmental review for urban apartments and other projects.
Rivas acknowledged legislators have been irritated by Newsom’s last-minute jams for years, despite the speaker’s repeated efforts to communicate that early engagement is key to winning lawmakers’ support. 
“It’s pretty clear, based on the engagement we’ve had thus far, that it’s going to be a different type of relationship than what this Legislature has experienced over the past eight years,” Rivas said. 
“I fully expect and trust the governor-elect when he says that he’s going to do his best to work with the Legislature and do his best to not drop stuff on us unexpectedly.”
Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas during the swearing-in ceremony for Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón in the Senate chambers at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Jan. 5, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters/Pool
Becerra’s experience as an assemblymember and member of Congress enables him to be an “empathetic partner” to Limón and Rivas, said Richard Stapler, a Democratic political strategist and former senior aide to Sen. John Laird of Santa Cruz. Having served as the leader of the congressional Hispanic caucus, Stapler added, Becerra can appreciate the difficulties of managing a diverse caucus where members have conflicting priorities and policy ideas.
“The success of his governorship will largely ride on his ability to have a sound, thoughtful working relationship with the Legislature,” Stapler said.
Former Assembly Speaker Anthony Rendon said some tension between the two branches of government should be expected, no matter how harmonious they appear. He said when lawmakers chafed at what they called overreach from Newsom or his predecessor, Gov. Jerry Brown, it was often because they had given up their own power to push back, such as when lawmakers left Sacramento in the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.  
“It’s easier for one person to act than an entire body,” he said.
Since advancing from the primary as the sole Democratic candidate for governor, Becerra has met individually with several legislators, as well as the Senate and Assembly Democratic caucuses. 
Last month he joined Assembly appropriations committee chair Buffy Wicks, Democrat of Oakland, on a tour of a new transit-oriented affordable housing complex made possible through a 2025 housing law. 
Wicks, who has made housing policy one of her signature issues, said she told Becerra she plans to reintroduce a bill that died this year that will seek to increase the construction of condominiums — an important entry option for new home buyers — by updating state construction defect liability laws that have made developers reluctant to build new condos altogether.
“Because he’s been a legislator, he understands the pace and cadence of a legislative body, and you know, he also understands how we get very attached to our ideas — we get married to our bills, as they say,” Wicks told CalMatters. “Having more collaboration at the front end I think is going to be important and certainly welcome from the Legislature.”
When Sirat Attapit first started as director of legislative affairs in then-Attorney General Becerra’s office in 2017, her new boss instructed her to try to meet with all 120 California legislators and develop a rapport.
“Coming in as a former legislator … he really wanted to build a relationship with them,” Attapit told CalMatters earlier this year. 
She described Becerra as finely attuned to the smallest details of policy proposals. He would direct staff to mark bills as having a “fiscal impact” on the state even if it would only cost a few thousand dollars, or part of a full-time employee’s time, per year.
Becerra previously said he hopes to reduce the number of bills legislators introduce so the state has a clearer and more cohesive legislative agenda. Lawmakers showed slight restraint in 2026, introducing just under 1,850 bills as compared to the more than 2,100 they introduced in 2024 and 2025.
“That requires me to come to them early,” he told KCRA last month, “to talk to them, so they don’t feel like they have to plow forward and then find out at the end that I didn’t like what they were doing.”
Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra addresses the media during a news conference at the state Capitol on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters
Becerra has repeatedly played it safe, avoiding specifics on his agenda and instead opting for broad promises to prioritize issues like “affordability” and “fighting for working families” by making sure that “everyone pays their fair share.”
When asked if he would commit to reversing Newsom’s rollback of healthcare benefits for undocumented immigrants, which he seemed to endorse in an interview with KQED, Becerra bristled and lectured reporters for “playing politics” by asking him to make commitments before he knows all the details, such as the latest budget projections.
“Guys, don’t play this game about asking me to commit, because I didn’t get elected doing that,” Becerra said. “A lot of other folks make these wild promises, and they’re not the governor-elect.”
Pressed for details on how Becerra would differ from Newsom, Rivas said he didn’t know if their policies would diverge. Like Becerra himself, the speaker pointed mostly to the governor-elect’s experiences as a former lawmaker and a son of immigrants. 
One area where the three Democratic leaders have signalled early agreement is the Fair Share tax proposal, an idea pushed by liberal lawmakers to tax large corporations whose workers make so little that they qualify for public benefits like Medi-Cal. 
Facing federal cuts and budget deficits, Newsom began cutting Medi-Cal in recent years with lawmakers’ approval. Some in the Legislature pushed instead for the tax to backfill revenues. But Newsom is generally unwilling to raise taxes, and the Legislature compromised by instead directing the state to study how to implement such a tax. A report by the Department of Finance is due in March. 
Sen. Lola Smallwood-Cuevas, a Los Angeles Democrat who chairs the Senate labor committee, said she discussed the Fair Share plan with then-candidate Becerra early in the year. When she ran into him at an event for Black leaders last month, she said he told her he was all in on the idea.
“He stopped me and he said, ‘I really want to work on Fair Share. I want to get that done. I believe that that is important to how we move forward coming out of Trump’s attack on our healthcare system,’” she said.
“That was very encouraging, that he remembered the conversation, he remembered me raising that point, and that he sought me out,” she said.
Sen. Lola Smallwood-Cuevas chats with a lawmaker during a floor session at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Aug. 29, 2024. Photo by Florence Middleton, CalMatters. Photo by Florence Middleton, CalMatters
Rivas said he, Limón and Becerra have a “natural alignment and a willingness to do something” on the issue. But all three are waiting to see what the finance department recommends before proposing anything concrete. 
Legislative leaders were more restrained on another idea that Becerra proposed during the campaign, this one to require utilities to give low-income households two hours of free electricity during low-usage daytime hours. 
Limón said she believes such programs work “in the short term” to give families facing high power bills some relief and that her caucus “has always welcomed every idea.” 
Rivas said he still needed to consult Assembly Democrats on the details. 
“Could there be alignment?” he said. “Possibly.”

title: Utah is seeking diabetes patients’ testimony to include in insulin price lawsuit
description: Two years after Utah sued insulin manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers arguing they artificially inflated the price of the medication, the state is aiming to include personal testimony from diabetes patients in Utah in its legal strategy. “The Utah Attorney General’s Office and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection (Division) have filed a lawsuit a[...]
text:
According to the Department of Commerce, 200,000 people, roughly 8% of Utah’s population, are diabetes patients. (Javier Zayas Photography/Getty Images)Two years after Utah sued insulin manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers arguing they artificially inflated the price of the medication, the state is aiming to include personal testimony from diabetes patients in Utah in its legal strategy.
“The Utah Attorney General’s Office and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection (Division) have filed a lawsuit against these companies to fight for the rights of Utahns,” the Utah Department of Commerce wrote on its website. “To better represent consumers in this suit, the Division is inviting past and present Utah patients to share their experience buying and using diabetes medication in any period during the last ten years.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the Department of Commerce, 200,000 people, roughly 8% of Utah’s population, are diabetes patients. An additional 700,000 people have been diagnosed with pre-diabetes in the state. 
“It is estimated that diabetes patients statewide have collectively spent $1.7 billion dollars after their diagnosis,” the department wrote. “One out of every four dollars spent in healthcare is spent on diabetes.”
The case, filed in November 2023, has moved slowly in federal court with the pharmaceutical companies — including Eli Lilly and Company, and Novo Nordisk — denying the claims introduced by former Utah Attorney General Sean Reyes. 



Let us know what you think...


 


According to Utah’s complaint, the dramatic price hike of insulin coincided with the “rise to power” of pharmacy benefits managers, third-party administrators of drug benefits, in 2003. Since then, in some cases the list price of certain insulins has increased by more than 1000%, the lawsuit says. 
The state’s complaint says that manufacturers “allegedly raised wholesale insulin prices to provide higher rebates” to pharmacy benefits managers and that the administrators “allegedly prioritized high-rebate, high-cost drugs over more affordable options on health plan formularies,” the department said in a news release. 
“Insulin user experiences are critical evidence in Utah’s fight to stop these predatory pricing practices, recover damages, and protect Utah families going forward,” the department said in the release asking for insulin users’ input on its website. 
Submissions will be treated as formal consumer complaints, and while the department committed to make an effort to keep the information confidential, they said the testimonies may be subject to legal discovery and government records requests.
