title: Are Washington’s rules for bail unfair? WA Supreme Court hears arguments
description: Washington’s state Supreme Court is considering major rule changes that could lead to lower, and less, bail set for criminal defendants.  Public defenders support the changes. Public prosecutors don’t. The two sides made their cases to the court’s justices Tuesday.  Defense attorneys argue the current bail system disproportionately keeps people of color jail[...]
text:
King County Superior Court Judge David Keenan speaks in support of bail reform before the Washington state Supreme Court on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026, in Olympia. (Photo by Jake Goldstein-Street/Washington State Standard)Washington’s state Supreme Court is considering major rule changes that could lead to lower, and less, bail set for criminal defendants. 
Public defenders support the changes. Public prosecutors don’t. The two sides made their cases to the court’s justices Tuesday. 
Defense attorneys argue the current bail system disproportionately keeps people of color jailed and doesn’t help keep the community safe, as proponents maintain. 
Prosecutors, judges and bail bonds agents are opposed, saying the proposals limit judicial discretion and could lead dangerous people to commit further crimes when they could be confined.
Months ahead of the hearing, the proposed changes generated hundreds of comments to the high court from interested parties.
“All across the state, indigent people are being kept in jail for low-level offenses typically associated with poverty,” King County’s Department of Public Defense wrote.
“My father used to say, never underestimate the stupidity of large groups of people,” Pierce County criminal defense attorney Bryan Hershman wrote in opposition to the rule changes. “I assure you, no single person on this committee could have suggested something so silly as what is suggested in these changes.”
The justices pressed both sides with numerous questions over a nearly three-hour-long hearing at the Temple of Justice in Olympia. They wanted data to back up the myriad claims from both sides. They asked for more clarity regarding geographic disparities in bail approaches and a sense of why change is needed when the presumption in current court rules already favors release.
The U.S. and Washington constitutions prohibit excessive bail.
Many arrestees must post bail to be released from jail pending a trial on the charges they face. Bail is usually set immediately after arrest or arraignment. Judges typically impose higher bail, sometimes into the millions, for severe crimes such as murder, but people accused of misdemeanors may also have to pay to get out of jail. Time spent in jail before trial is usually credited as time served for a longer sentence, if found guilty.
Many people arrested by police are released from jail without having to post bail under the condition that they will appear at future court hearings. However, a defendant with a history of missing court appearances could face more expensive bail. 
Under current rules in Washington courts, the standard for a judge to set bail is a “likely failure to appear” for future court hearings. Judges also look at prior convictions and the risk to public safety when making bail decisions, among other factors.
The proposed rule change would raise that standard to a “high likelihood of willful flight from prosecution.” Illinois has moved to the latter standard.
The public defense proposal would also define willful flight as “intentional conduct with a purpose to thwart the judicial process to avoid prosecution.” 
Backers of the rule change contend that people usually miss court appearances for reasons other than trying to flee proceedings, such as transportation problems or conflicts with personal responsibilities like caregiving.
The plan would also cap bail at $200 for misdemeanor offenses, save for domestic violence and driving under the influence, unless the suspect is found to be likely to flee prosecution under the new standard. Vermont has imposed a similar $200 limit. 
Public defenders also want the accused to be able to post 10% of their bail amount with the court to secure release, with the promise they’ll get the money back so long as they don’t miss hearings. In essence, a $200 bail would require $20 for release. While allowed currently, public defenders rarely request the concession. The proposed rule change would set it as the starting point. 
The rules would also guarantee defendants a chance to appear for a hearing on their case while out of custody at least once before a judge can set bail based on the risk of flight. Judges could still impose bail for other reasons.
Courts usually order defendants to post either the full bail amount or a surety bond, which generally means paying 10% to a bail bond company to post the bond on their behalf. That 10% isn’t returned at the end of the case.
There is no timeline for a decision from the justices.
The arguments
The proposal’s proponents say the state’s current system is keeping people behind bars despite a presumption of release.
“For people with money, bail is a condition of relief,” said Katie Hurley, of the King County Department of Public Defense. “For people without money, it becomes an order of pre-trial detention. When bail becomes detention, we must ask ourselves what justifies taking away a person’s freedom.”
Some advocates, including multiple justices, suggest people plead guilty to charges they didn’t commit because they want to get out of jail but can’t afford to post bail. 
Rachel Sottile, president and CEO of the Washington-based Center for Children and Youth Justice said the harm that comes from pre-trial detention “may be the determining factor in a young person’s ability to achieve long-term stability and positive outcomes.”
Jailing people is also expensive. In King County, it reportedly costs more than $11,000 per month to detain someone before trial. Supporters of the rule changes say there are cheaper ways to get people to show up to court hearings, such as through text message reminders. 
Defendants can often appear virtually or waive their right to appear, but locales with fewer resources don’t provide remote access. In rural areas, hearings can mean a lot of travel, which leads to more people failing to appear. 
Prosecutors fear people released before trial will commit crimes that could be avoided if they were locked up. Justice Theo Angelis noted judges have an incentive to keep people confined so they don’t “commit a terrible crime that could effectively force you off the bench.”
“There’s no free lunch,” said Jefferson County Prosecutor James Kennedy. “You commit a crime, there’s going to be repercussions for it. You’re going to be inconvenienced for it.”
Some judges also said the “willful flight” standard could be impossible to apply in practice without a sense of what constitutes a “high likelihood.”
Some opponents also said the rule changes should be enacted through legislation, not by the court, as in other states, noting that more money would be needed for pre-trial services, such as electronic home monitoring.
“The dollars are not growing in availability, but in fact the fight is getting harder and harder,” said Snohomish County Prosecutor Jason Cummings, on behalf of the Washington Association of Prosecuting Attorneys.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Homeless encampments and the unsatisfactory feeling of unsolvable problems
description: Our nation’s homeless problem is very visible to anyone who lives in a large metropolitan area, including the Twin Cities.  We see unhoused people wandering the streets, on public transportation and at intersections soliciting money.  Not all unhoused people face the same challenges. Some experience temporary homelessness — moving to shelter or temporary hou[...]
text:
A tent with "Twin Citys" spray-painted onto it sits in an encampment along Franklin Avenue near Cedar Avenue Tuesday, Sept. 7, 2021. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer) Our nation’s homeless problem is very visible to anyone who lives in a large metropolitan area, including the Twin Cities. 
We see unhoused people wandering the streets, on public transportation and at intersections soliciting money. 
Not all unhoused people face the same challenges. Some experience temporary homelessness — moving to shelter or temporary housing, often on their way to permanent housing. Others may spend years chronically unhoused, often in and out of shelters or temporary housing before returning to the streets. 
Over the past several years the problem of chronic homelessness has manifested in a different way: encampments. 
The emergence of fentanyl on the streets — and in some encampments — has elevated community safety concerns of encampments, often pitting advocates for those living in the encampments against advocates for those who live in the surrounding community. 
From one perspective the encampments are people who — failed by our social service systems — have created communities to support and protect one another. 
From another perspective, encampments are trespassers who pose a threat to the safety and wellbeing of their residents and those living in the surrounding community, often communities that also struggle with poverty and inadequate housing. 
It is the sort of contentious, complex public policy issue that frustrates both the public and policymakers. 
We like to think that all problems are solvable, but that confidence can vanish when confronted by the limitations of politics and policymaking.  
Despite our wishes and best intentions, politics and public policy are imperfect tools for solving many problems. In policy school you learn that most policies are second-best solutions. There are always trade-offs — necessary political compromises, administrative barriers or budgetary constraints that work against getting to the best solution. 
The limitations of policymaking are particularly visible with the most complex problems, like what to do about homeless encampments. 
It is not just a housing issue. It touches on multiple policy domains, including poverty, mental health, substance use disorder, disabilities, veterans’ services, law enforcement, courts and health care, and crosses multiple jurisdictions and service providers. 
Many of the people living in encampments face multiple health conditions, often including mental illness and/or substance use disorder, conditions that can make rehousing challenging. In addition, encampments create tension with others who live in the community. On top of that, encampments can vary widely in size, needs of the people, and degree of tension with the community. 
When faced with complex problems we tend to default to simple solutions. Everyone thinks there is some panacea, something no one else has thought of or had the courage to try.  
For homeless encampments, the simple solution fallacy can be illustrated by two ideas from opposite ends of the political spectrum. 
Some on the right advocate a law-and-order approach, arresting everyone living in the encampment and plowing it down, while some on the left advocate that encampments be designated as safe spaces for people to use alcohol and other substances. 
Neither solution addresses the challenge of improving the services that have failed many of the encampment residents, and both avoid the difficult question of how to balance the rights of different groups. One solution criminalizes people for being unhoused, while the other ignores the rights of those who live in the surrounding community, as well as the public health risks of encampments.  
Each serves their ideology while avoiding the practical challenges of policymaking.  
Another approach frequently offered for complicated problems focuses on the root cause of the problem. 
On the surface this seems like a smart approach; solving a problem at the root can prevent the problem from recurring. 
Social psychologist Steven Pinker, in his book “Enlightenment Now,” calls this phenomenon “root-causism.” It seems attractive, but oversimplifies the problem and the solution. The reality is that the root causes of any social problem are usually just bigger, more deeply ingrained social problems. 
For example, I’d argue the root causes of homeless encampments are poverty, extreme income inequality, a fractured health care system and racism. We should solve these problems, but that’s a challenging and lengthy undertaking.  
In the meantime, though, we still need to do something about homelessness encampments. 
Although we’ve long been led to believe that treating symptoms is insufficient, Pinker advocates just that. 
Do what’s doable. 
And that’s pretty much what we have been doing with homeless encampments. 
Minnesota has a robust and effective strategy to re-house people experiencing homelessness. Thousands of people are rehoused every year. Outreach workers connect with unhoused people on the streets or in encampments to help them access housing. 
The challenge for encampments is that many of the residents face health, mental illness and/or substance use disorders, factors that make rehousing them more complicated. 
Many would benefit from supportive housing, a model that combines housing with services and ongoing care. 
But substance use disorder remains the biggest challenge to stable housing, and to any solution for encampments. We have struggled to establish viable models for housing people who are using substances. 
The best path to making a dent in the encampment problem is to improve the social services needed by chronically homeless people, including those living in encampments. 
Perhaps most critically, we need better community care for people experiencing mental illness, including more supportive housing. We need more robust addiction treatment programs. And we need to reduce the frequency of unhoused people cycling through the criminal justice system.
But those improvements take time and money. It won’t happen overnight.
In the meantime, we address encampments as we have been, continuing housing outreach, ensuring basic sanitary conditions and safety for people experiencing homelessness, and ensuring the availability of clean needles and overdose medication for those who continue to use substances. 
But that’s not all. When encampments become dangerous for their residents or for the local community, we should remove them, offering shelter to all who are willing to take it. 
And continued success also depends on political leaders who dig in and do their part to support these efforts rather than engaging in endless arguments.  
It may be frustrating that we can’t do more, that a better solution seems so elusive. 
But this is not giving up.  
It is doing what works and striving to do it better.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Dozens of immigrant children in KC face fast-tracked deportation after losing protections
description: They’re the immigrant children long considered to be the most vulnerable. Many traveled to the U.S. alone, unaccompanied by a parent or guardian. Some were trafficked for labor or sex. A state judge has ruled that each of them has experienced serious abuse, neglect or abandonment and is in need of the state’s care. For […]
text:
Artwork from children receiving counseling services while their immigration cases are pending (photo submitted). They’re the immigrant children long considered to be the most vulnerable.
Many traveled to the U.S. alone, unaccompanied by a parent or guardian. Some were trafficked for labor or sex. A state judge has ruled that each of them has experienced serious abuse, neglect or abandonment and is in need of the state’s care.
For decades, the U.S. treated these foreign-born youth from a child protection perspective. Policy, law and federal funding acknowledged their unique needs.
A special immigration status was available for them, which opened up the pathway to a green card. And while their cases moved through the country’s clogged-up immigration system, policy gave them protections from being deported.
But many of those protections have disappeared under President Donald Trump’s administration, affecting up to 150,000 children nationwide.
And now, at least two dozen such children in the Kansas City area are in active removal proceedings and could soon be ordered deported. And the organizations supporting the children have lost the federal funding that helped provide counseling and legal representation.
Hearings before immigration judges have been abruptly pulled from 2027 dockets. Some have been rescheduled for mid-November, leaving attorneys scrambling to jam six months or more of legal work into a matter of weeks.
“It’s nonsensical and it’s cruel because these children had already been told by the government that they wouldn’t be pursued for deportation,” said Aly Englander, senior staff attorney at the Asylum Clinic Kansas City.
Englander manages 113 immigration cases, about 80% of which are for children, including those whose deportations are being expedited.
The Trump administration maintains that it is focused on countering what it characterizes as Biden-era fraud within programs for unaccompanied children, and decreasing backlogs in immigration proceedings.
In a statement to The Beacon, federal officials with the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) said they’re just doing their job.
“Prior leadership may have allowed certain cases to languish indefinitely in violation of the law, and EOIR is working hard to correct those violations,” the statement read. “However, there is nothing novel about EOIR trying to ensure that cases are resolved as expeditiously as possible.”
 October change-ups

The Kansas City-area children most at risk of being ordered deported have either been granted or have a case pending to receive special immigrant juvenile status, a humanitarian designation for abused or neglected children that can lead to a permanent legal status, Englander said.
Previously, children with this legal classification were granted deferred action, an aspect of immigration law that allows for a suspension of deportation proceedings while cases progress. Since 2022, the children were also allowed to legally work, which provided them a government-issued identification as they waited for a green card to become available.
The Trump administration canceled those protections for new grantees and renewals of the special status, effective May 10, 2026.
In October, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. issued statements saying changes had been necessary to counter Biden-era fraud within the unaccompanied children programs.
Also in October, the government began offering $3,000 to unaccompanied children who are willing to self-deport, an increase of the $2,500 the administration set in 2025.
Around that same time, some of the children’s cases handled by the Asylum Clinic and assigned to the Kansas City immigration court were abruptly shifted to the docket of a Chicago immigration judge, worrying the children’s lawyers.
In addition, some of the families housing the youth, considered sponsors, have been put under heightened scrutiny by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
”They’ve started sending ICE to the houses of sponsors,” Englander said. “A lot of our clients have experienced ICE just going up to their house.”
The escalating tensions have left the local immigration attorneys, caseworkers and therapists scrambling.
”We took about 24 hours to freak out, and then we have not stopped since,” said Meaghan Fanning, youth program manager at Jewish Vocational Service, or JVS, which is coordinating with the Asylum Clinic to provide case management and therapy for some of the children.
“They’re kids,” Fanning said. “Either their life is unsafe, the people in their lives are unsafe, or they don’t have anybody else in their life at this point.”
The attorneys were told to appear with the youth in court in Kansas City on Oct. 29, despite the fact that such hearings were typically conducted virtually.
At the hearing, Judge Shawn Abraham appeared by teleconference and said he couldn’t access the Kansas City case files, pushing the cases back several weeks. Abraham agreed that at future hearings, the children could appear by video.
Court challenges to many of the administration’s new policies have also been filed.
 Who are Kansas City’s kids at risk of deportation? 

The Beacon is not identifying the Kansas City youth by name or complete biography, but attorneys and therapists outlined some of their circumstances.
One teenage girl lives in a Kansas City homeless shelter. She escaped what her attorney described as “intense labor trafficking.”
The girl doesn’t have steady access to food, an outcome of the Trump administration eliminating SNAP benefits for many immigrant classifications. Advocates deliver gift cards to her every two weeks, so she can purchase meals at Walmart.
One boy was homeless in Honduras from the ages of 6 to 10. He walked and hitched rides to the U.S. with a group of friends who were also homeless. The trip took several months until they approached Homeland Security agents at the southern border.
The boy was detained for a year in a U.S. government shelter for youth.
He’s 11 now, living with a relative and thriving at a local middle school.
Others among the children came to the U.S. as siblings. Older siblings often care for younger brothers and sisters as they walk across borders.
Some of the children have worked long hours in construction, roofing, drywalling and restaurants, with an adult confiscating their wages. A few have been unpaid nannies. Lawyers say at least five have been sexually exploited.
Many of the Kansas City children are Honduran or Guatemalan, but they also come from Vietnam, Mexico and several countries in Africa. The youngest is 6, and the oldest is 18.
Several are disabled, physically or intellectually. Some do not have a parent or other close relative in the U.S. and are in foster care.
For most, formal schooling was severely interrupted because of the abuse they fled or the exploitation they endured after entering the U.S.
 A departure from the status quo

The situation these children and their lawyers are navigating marks a major shift in how the government handles such cases, according to Mary Giovagnoli, a Kansas City native who is the former ombudsperson for unaccompanied children at the Department of Health and Human Services.
Giovagnoli, whom Trump removed from his administration last year, said she worries that the government is disregarding some of the children’s rights.
“They’re pushing these kids out the door so fast, there needs to be some attention paid to ensuring that their return to their home countries is safe,” Giovagnoli said.
That is not happening, she said, which comes up against provisions of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008.
The act expanded protections for trafficking victims, including setting standards to ensure they would not be persecuted or experience trafficking again if returned to their native countries.
In September 2025, Giovagnoli testified before a Senate subcommittee in oral and written comments. Her testimony outlined changes under the Trump administration that have shifted the care of vulnerable children from child welfare strategies to immigration enforcement.
In particular, she testified that decades-old positive approaches to funding work to protect children from trafficking were “all but abandoned in the provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.”
The Asylum Clinic is part of a network of agencies nationwide that received federal grants to represent abused and neglected children during their immigration cases. Those grants have been canceled by the Trump administration.
Similarly, some federal allowances for medical treatment for the children, therapy for trauma and help with food and housing have also been rescinded.
“The Trump administration’s policies pose the greatest risk to unaccompanied children in the U.S. today, as it systematically eliminates the protections and resources put in place by Congress to keep unaccompanied children safe,” reads a portion of Giovagnoli’s submitted testimony.
She accuses the Trump administration of “using children as pawns in its mass deportation agenda,” echoing a common charge by legal associations, nonprofits and some members of Congress. 
“We really need this next Congress to put a stop to this egregious treatment of unaccompanied children,” Giovagnoli said. “It should be, as with so many immigration issues, something that’s nonpartisan that everybody can agree on.”
The administration, in reply to such criticism, has released statements, often arguing that changes are necessary to correct fraud.
A statement released Oct. 1 said the government found fraudulent documentation, manipulated photographs, misrepresented or unverifiable addresses, problems with fingerprints and ages submitted and a failure to disclose household members of homes where the unaccompanied children were living.
“The Biden Administration failed in its most basic responsibility: protecting vulnerable children in federal care,” said Kennedy in a news release. “It weakened safeguards and prioritized speed over scrutiny, leaving children exposed to fraud, exploitation, and abuse.”
 Looking toward an uncertain future

Many of the children around Kansas City understand what is happening in their legal cases, or at least that their future is less certain, advocates told The Beacon.
“They can’t actually dream ahead because they either have lost their status or could lose their status at any time,” Fanning said.
Fanning said some of the students she worked with had a hard time starting school this fall.
Young people had absorbed the daily drum of news, she said, seeing video of ICE agents arresting people, sometimes in violent confrontations. Some of the children isolated themselves during the summer months, hesitant to be too far from home.
The administration’s actions upended how JVS therapists help the children process trauma.
“We work with kids on the stuff that they don’t want to say out loud,” Fanning said.
Talk therapy guides the youth in telling the story of their lives. They learn to speak about the abuse, the neglect, everything that they have faced until they arrive at surviving all of it, versus suffering.
Then they can set goals: graduating high school, obtaining a green card, planning for college.
The process also prepares the children for immigration hearings, where they’ll need to share details to an immigration judge and be ready to answer the questions of government attorneys.
“But how do you heal from your past when you cannot see a future?” Fanning said. “Now, it’s so unstable for them.”
Many of the youth lean into faith, often saying that God brought them this far in their lives and he will see them through, even if they don’t like the eventual legal outcome.
One child recently said this to Fanning: “‘I went through way too much to get here to just give up now.’”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Lame, suffocated and dead: The drug supersizing America’s cattle
description: This article was originally published by Investigate Midwest.  In 2018, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reviewed a first-of-its-kind cattle drug. Elanco Animal Health was seeking approval for Experior, a drug that contains an active ingredient from a controversial class of growth-promoting pharmaceuticals. These drugs can make farm animals gain more we[...]
text:
Cattle feedlot with a capacity of 68,000 animals in the Oklahoma Panhandle. A feedlot is where cattle spend the final months of their lives eating grain-heavy diets. Experior is mixed into the cattle feed. (Photo by Zach Lucero/Investigate Midwest)This article was originally published by Investigate Midwest. 
In 2018, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration reviewed a first-of-its-kind cattle drug.
Elanco Animal Health was seeking approval for Experior, a drug that contains an active ingredient from a controversial class of growth-promoting pharmaceuticals. These drugs can make farm animals gain more weight from the same amount of feed. Some are banned or restricted in more than 160 countries, largely over human safety concerns.
But the Indiana-based pharmaceutical company did not seek Experior’s approval as a growth-promoting drug. Instead, it submitted Experior as a novel solution to an environmental problem. Most cattle raised for beef in the U.S. spend their final months in feedlots, where manure and urine release harmful gases, including ammonia. Elanco claimed that Experior was able to reduce some of those emissions.
Some scientists within the FDA, however, had concerns. Investigate Midwest spoke to three former regulatory specialists at the agency’s Center for Veterinary Medicine on the condition of anonymity. Two of them described concerns common to other approved drugs in the same class; the third scientist had more serious concerns about the studies Elanco conducted and submitted with its application.
Across six studies, cattle that received the highest doses of Experior developed lameness more often than cattle in the control groups. In two studies, scientists diagnosed bloat — a dangerous condition that can cause cattle to suffocate and die — in cattle that received Experior; the control groups had no cases of bloat. In most cases, scientists diagnosed bloat after they found the cattle dead.
Despite these findings, the FDA approved Experior because Elanco showed that the drug could moderately reduce ammonia emissions from cattle.
There are no federal or state limits on ammonia emissions from cattle in feedlots. Yet, sales of Experior are booming: the drug generated more than $200 million in sales in 2025 alone, making it one of the leading drivers of growth for Elanco that year.
More than half of U.S. cattle in feedlots now receive Experior, and feedlot veterinarians are reporting the same issues seen in the studies — bloat-related deaths, lameness and other complications — in connection with Experior use. Data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture also shows a rise in health problems associated with heavier cattle. And a lawsuit by the Animal Legal Defense Fund questioned the safety of consuming beef from cattle raised with Experior.
The FDA approval of Experior raises questions about the influence pharmaceutical companies and the livestock industry can wield over the agency. The industry’s reach extends to taxpayer-funded public universities, where animal scientists often promote industry products, conduct industry-funded research and help shape policies that advance corporate interests. Investigate Midwest found that academics with close ties to Elanco helped drive Experior’s commercial success.
“The company used the FDA’s naivety,” said one of the former FDA scientists who spoke with Investigate Midwest. “Some people saw where this was going, but not everybody. So now we ended up with a drug that was not tested for growth being sold or being advertised as a drug for growth.”
In response to Investigate Midwest’s request for comment, an FDA spokesperson emphasized the agency’s role in ensuring the safety and effectiveness of new animal drugs. Elanco also defended Experior’s safety record.
“Experior’s safety profile is documented and demonstrated through nearly two decades of required scientific studies,” wrote Season Solario, a communications representative for Elanco, in an email. “Elanco remains fully confident in the safety and efficacy of Experior.”
Novel drug, shaky science
Experior brought the FDA into unfamiliar territory. The agency had never been asked to judge a feed additive, meant to be mixed into cattle feed, for its ability to reduce harmful gases released into the atmosphere.
The FDA’s public summary of its review of Experior explains how regulators concluded that Experior is safe and able to reduce ammonia emissions. Companies typically draft these summaries, and the agency revises and adopts them.
Elanco tested various gases, including carbon dioxide and methane, the greenhouse gases that put animal agriculture under scrutiny in the 2010s for its contribution to global warming. Ultimately, the company was able to show that Experior could reduce ammonia, which is not a greenhouse gas, by 14% to 18% per pound of animal weight. The drug did not have a significant impact on any of the other gases tested.
But Elanco never tested Experior in the places where it would ultimately be used: sprawling, open-air feedlots, which sometimes house more than 100,000 animals. The studies took place in small closed pens and environmentally-controlled chambers, some with just 12 animals. The FDA acknowledges that the environmental benefits of using Experior in real-world feedlots are unknown.
When assessing animal safety, reviewers found that two groups of Experior-fed cattle had a “numerically higher incidence of lameness” than the control groups across six studies.
But the FDA attributed the cases to the muddy conditions inside the pens and the animals’ diet, which they said contributed to foot rot. Because lameness improved in most cases after the animals received “medicated foot baths,” the FDA concluded that the issues were not related to Experior.
“This is scientifically not valid,” said one of the former FDA scientists. “It doesn’t mean that it didn’t happen or that it’s not due to the drug.”
The FDA also saw no reason for concern about the higher rates of bloat. Bloat is a life-threatening digestive emergency that happens when gas rapidly builds up in the rumen — the cow’s stomach — and the animal is unable to burp it out. This buildup puts pressure on the lungs, which can cause the animal to die quickly from suffocation.
In two studies, researchers diagnosed bloat only in Experior-fed cattle, most of them found dead. Despite recording zero cases of bloat in the control groups, the FDA did not conduct a statistical analysis to determine whether the difference was significant.
“The total number of cases observed across both groups was too low to support meaningful statistical comparison,” wrote an FDA spokesperson in an email.
Pushing cattle to their limits
As more feedlots across the country add Experior to cattle rations, feedlots are reporting some of the same problems documented in the studies.
Veterinarians or other feedlot workers sometimes notify a drug manufacturer when they suspect a drug caused a health problem or death. Federal law requires the manufacturer to report these cases to the FDA. As of July 2026, the FDA has received 75 adverse event reports involving lubabegron, the active ingredient in Experior.
Death linked to lubabegron appeared in 59 of the reports. One report from October 2024 documents 229 unexpected deaths in a single feedlot. Another one, from November 2024, lists the death of five Angus cattle weighing a staggering 1,800 pounds each, about 400 pounds above the average slaughter weight that year.
Many of the reports involving deaths also mention bloat and respiratory disorders, although the reports do not establish whether those conditions caused the deaths. More than a dozen reports show lameness and other mobility problems, including cases in which cattle were unable to stand.
“The FDA is aware of the adverse event reports associated with lubabegron and is evaluating them in accordance with the FDA’s post-market review processes,” wrote an FDA spokesperson in an email.
On its website, the FDA cautions that adverse event reports do not prove a drug caused the problem. The event could be related to other factors.
With cattle in feedlots receiving a range of pharmaceuticals, like hormones and antibiotics, an illness or death could be linked to more than one treatment. Experior is just one of several tools the industry uses to make cattle — and profits – bigger.
The average weight of heifer and steer carcasses has soared in recent years. Many carcasses often exceed 1,000 pounds.
Following a sharp increase in 2024, weights continued to rise through 2025 and into 2026. This trend raises questions about how far cattle can grow before reaching their physiological limits. While their bodies grow to unprecedented sizes, their hearts and lungs do not.
In 1975, the average cattle carcass weight — the combined average for steers and heifers after slaughter — was 615 pounds. By 2024, it had risen to 890 pounds, an increase of about 45%, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data.
One of the largest feedlots in the country is located in Nebraska near the Colorado and Kansas border. (Photo by Zach Lucero/Investigate Midwest)
It was also in 2024 that Experior achieved “blockbuster status,” meaning that it made at least $100 million in sales that year.
Beyond Experior, cheap corn has made it more economical for feedlots to extend feeding periods and bring cattle to heavier weights. At the same time, the expanding use of “beef-on-dairy” crossbreeding, which pairs dairy cows with beef bulls, is producing calves that tend to be larger than traditional beef calves.
Investigate Midwest obtained USDA data from federally inspected slaughterhouses for 2017 through 2025. The data shows that the number of cattle arriving at slaughterhouses dead or unable to stand increased among heifers and steers in 2024 and 2025.
The data does not establish a link between the increase in these conditions and cattle weight. But scientific research has found that heavier cattle are more likely to have mobility problems and are more vulnerable to heat stress. Heat stress is a particular concern during transportation to slaughterhouses and can, in some cases, result in death.
In 2024, the year when carcass weights surged, the number of cattle that arrived at meatpacking plants dead or unable to stand increased by approximately 20% compared to the previous year.
The trend continued in 2025. That year, compared with 2017, 44% more cattle arrived unable to stand and 36% more arrived dead — even though about 1.5 million fewer heifers and steers were slaughtered that year.
Is Experior safe for humans?
The Experior label instructs users to wear protective clothing, gloves and eye protection and to wash thoroughly with soap after handling the drug. “Individuals with cardiovascular disease should exercise special caution to avoid exposure. Not for human use. Keep out of reach of children,” the label reads.
In 2020, the Animal Legal Defense Fund and other groups filed a lawsuit against the FDA, arguing that the agency had insufficient information to determine the drug is safe for animals and consumers.
Dr. John Tegzes, a veterinarian and toxicologist with more than 25 years of experience who currently serves as dean of Western University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, filed a 44-page declaration in the lawsuit sharply criticizing the research behind the drug.
“There is currently no way to know whether consumers who eat beef with lubabegron residues will be affected,” Tegzes wrote, citing flaws in the research that Elanco relied on to determine human safety, including outdated studies and small sample sizes.
Tegzes warned that Experior’s effects on the heart and airways could pose a risk to people who consume beef containing residues of the drug, particularly those vulnerable to heart failure or respiratory problems.
He also objected to the software Elanco used in two studies, saying it allowed researchers to edit data without creating a log that FDA reviewers could see. Tegzes did not accuse Elanco of tampering with the data, but said that “the software did not assure the integrity of the study results.”
Perhaps most significantly, Tegzes challenged the FDA’s explanation of how Experior works. Elanco and the FDA say the drug makes cattle more efficient at using nitrogen, leaving less to be excreted and converted into ammonia. Tegzes said the data do not conclusively support that theory, proposing a troubling possibility: That cattle, despite their size, may be experiencing malnutrition or starvation, which could explain the lower ammonia emissions.
“[Cows] were starving, but still gaining weight,” says Cristina Kladis, the Animal Legal Defense Fund lawyer who led the case. “The FDA never could figure out how the drug works in cows’ bodies. They still don’t know. No one knows.”
The FDA submitted its own expert testimonies to refute Tegzes’ conclusions. One FDA scientist explained that federal law does not require understanding a drug’s exact cellular mechanism to approve it. She dismissed malnutrition concerns, saying that cows eating slightly less while continuing to gain weight indicates improved feed efficiency, not starvation. An FDA toxicologist noted that residues of Experior in beef pose no risk to humans when the drug is used at approved doses.
The judge did not consider any of the expert testimonies and ruled in favor of the FDA. The Animal Legal Defense Fund is not currently planning to appeal.
Who are animal scientists serving?
Experior belongs to a class of drugs that are called beta-adrenergic agonists (although Elanco classifies Experior as a “beta-adrenergic agonist/antagonist,” a slight departure from the broader classification).
A 2014 study by scientists at Kansas State University and Texas Tech University found that cattle given beta-agonists were 75% to 90% more likely to die than cattle that did not receive the drugs.
There is no official national data on which and how widely feedlots use beta-agonists. But some sources estimate that by 2012, 60% to 80% of cattle in U.S. feedlots were fed one of two beta-agonists: Zilmax, made by Merck Animal Health, or Optaflexx, made by Elanco.
Both drugs have faced controversy. In 2013, Merck stopped selling Zilmax after reports emerged that cattle hooves were coming apart. The drug later returned under stricter use requirements, but its negative reputation and concerns about meat quality limited its appeal. Feedlots increasingly turned to Optaflexx, which contains ractopamine, a drug widely used in hog farming. In 2012, China rejected hundreds of thousands of pounds of U.S. pork after detecting residues of the drug.
Experior, with its environmental claims, has benefited from a more positive reputation. And research published after the drug’s approval gave the drug an additional advantage: studies show that Experior outperforms Optaflexx in promoting growth.
That reputation, as well as the drug’s off-label growth effects, has been bolstered by animal scientists at universities.
“Resistance to change, resistance to technology,” said Ty Lawrence, an animal scientist at West Texas A&M University, addressing a room full of cattle producers in Amarillo, Texas, in June 2025. “If you’re in the cattle feeding business and you’re not feeding Experior, you’re missing an opportunity.”
Ty Lawrence, a West Texas A&M University meat scientist, sits atop a steer weighing more than 4,000 pounds — nearly three times the average weight of cattle before slaughter. Lawrence has promoted Elanco’s Experior at industry conferences and received thousands of dollars in speaking fees from the company. He said the animal belongs to a commercial producer, was not given Experior, and serves as an example of “what is possible in growth physiology.” The image comes from a Lawrence slideshow obtained by Investigate Midwest through a public records request.
But the public university professor did not explain why a drug approved for an environmental purpose is, as he labeled it, a “profit driver” for those who feed cattle. Lawrence also failed to disclose his ties to Elanco, including the thousands of dollars he had received from the company.
Back in 2012, Lawrence was one of the unofficial spokespeople for Zilmax. The Chronicle of Higher Education reported at the time that Lawrence routinely failed to disclose in journal articles that Merck was paying him consultancy and speaking fees. More than a decade later, Lawrence is once again serving as a pitchman, but this time for Experior.
Investigate Midwest obtained email correspondence between Lawrence and Elanco through a public-records request to West Texas A&M University. The emails show that Lawrence received $5,800 from Elanco for a single speaking engagement in 2018.
The emails also offer a behind-the-scenes look at how a 2025 peer-reviewed paper on Experior, which Lawrence co-authored with Elanco scientists, was published in the journal Translational Animal Science. A reviewer for the journal had “major concerns” about what they perceived as gaps in the data and said some passages “read like an advertisement.” The reviewer also challenged the authors’ claim that Experior has “no impacts on mobility,” noting that cattle given the drug appeared to have more mobility issues.
On this last point, one Elanco employee pushed back, writing: “forgive me, sounds like a witch hunt.”
Lawrence did not disclose any conflicts of interest to the Translational Animal Science journal. In an email to Investigate Midwest, Lawrence wrote that he conducts “independent third-party research for Elanco” and cites the paper in the Translational Animal Science as an example. He added that the $5,800 payment he received from Elanco was for a 3-day short course sponsored by the company but not related to Experior. Lawrence did not address questions about his failure to disclose payments from Elanco.
“I do not market Experior to beef producers or processors,” Lawrence added.
Lawrence’s ties to the industry go beyond speaking engagements and his work on Experior. He is also director of the Beef Carcass Research Center at West Texas A&M University, which collects research data for pharmaceutical companies. Elanco has used the center for its own research, paying $42,000 last year to use the center’s facilities and cattle for one study.
According to Lawrence’s resume, also obtained through a records request to the university, the center has generated $3.35 million in revenue. His resume also claims that he has received more than $13 million in “external funding.” In an email to Investigate Midwest, Lawrence said this funding came from various sources, including Elanco, Zoetis, Merck, and the USDA.
West Texas A&M University did not respond to questions about its policies governing potential conflicts of interest and the disclosure of payments.
But Lawrence and the center he leads are not exceptions. Public universities — particularly land-grant universities, which Congress established in the 19th century to serve farmers and advance agricultural research and education — have long maintained close ties with the livestock industry.
Jessica Sperber, an animal scientist who previously worked at the University of Nebraska and now works for Merck, has promoted Experior to cattle producers through talks and educational workshops, including a University of Nebraska workshop titled, “Ca$hing in on Carcass Weight with Experior.” Some of these events were sponsored by Elanco.
“I have never personally received or accepted any monetary payment, honorarium, or other financial compensation from Elanco for conducting research on Experior, presenting research involving Experior, or discussing the product,” wrote Sperber in an email to Investigate Midwest.
As Elanco continues to position itself as part of the “sustainability solution” for the livestock industry, the company has partnered with Frank Mitloehner, an animal scientist and air quality specialist at the University of California, Davis.
In a sit-down interview with Elanco CEO Jeff Simmons, Mitloehner said that feed additives like Experior and Bovaer — a second environmental drug by Elanco that the FDA authorized in 2024 to reduce methane emissions from dairy cattle — will help the industry achieve its climate goals by 2030. Mitloehner also described meeting with legislators to advocate for the treatments. “And our legislature listened. I’m very encouraged by that,” he said.

Industry funding has helped elevate Mitloehner as a public voice on livestock and climate change, according to a 2024 paper by researchers at Yale Law School and the University of Miami.
The authors say his research and outreach have downplayed animal agriculture’s climate impact while promoting industry-friendly solutions and policies. In an interview with Investigate Midwest, Viveca Morris, one of the paper’s authors, noted that the animal drug industry lacks the funding disclosure requirements that exist in human medicine.
“When there’s an exchange of funding, it’s significant, and there has been a recognition in the human medical field that this matters, and that patients and regulators deserve to know,” Morris said. “It certainly seems like it’s past time that the same be applied to animal pharmaceuticals.”
In an email to Investigate Midwest, Mitloehner said that his funding is “diverse,” coming from both the private and public sectors.
“My communications on climate solutions, regardless of the tool, are rooted in the science I have conducted and that has withstood scrutiny,” wrote Mitloehner.
The system rewards drug approvals
Experior entered the market in 2021 but sales did not take off until a few years later.
A turning point came in 2024, when several research papers published in scientific journals highlighted Experior’s growth effects. That same year, the FDA also approved Experior for use in combination with other drugs, like antibiotics, that have “improved feed efficiency” and “increased rate of weight gain” claims on their labels.
Elanco cannot market Experior on its own as a growth promoter. But it can market combination products containing Experior and another drug with growth claims for those benefits. And the post-approval research papers allow scientists like Lawrence and Sperber to promote Experior for its off-label growth effects.
By 2025, the drug was a success. It made $200 million in sales, an increase of 80% from the previous year.
New animal drug applications, including Experior’s, undergo reviews to assess effectiveness, safety, environmental impact, and other areas. In the past, animal drugs, like human drugs, would also be reviewed by an independent advisory committee of experts. But the FDA dissolved its Veterinary Medicine Advisory Committee in 2013.
The former FDA employees who spoke with Investigate Midwest said about 15 to 20 scientists — possibly more — reviewed Experior’s application. They emphasized that the approval of Experior was not the result of a single actor pushing it through.
One of them described a systemic pressure within the agency to approve drugs. He pointed to the Animal Drug User Fee Act (ADUFA), the system enacted in 2003 under which drugmakers pay the FDA millions of dollars each year to supplement the agency’s funding and help it review drugs faster. For fiscal year 2025, the FDA collected $30 million in fees through ADUFA.
The system sets goals for how quickly the FDA reviews applications and what information drugmakers must submit. These terms are renegotiated every five years, with the latest round of negotiations now underway.
At a public meeting in May on ADUFA’s reauthorization, Steve Roach, director of Food Animal Concerns Trust — one of the groups that joined the Animal Legal Defense Fund’s lawsuit over the approval of Experior — called the system “inappropriate.” He argued that it creates a conflict of interest by allowing drugmakers to influence the FDA’s priorities.
“We have this real need for speed when it comes to drug approvals, it’s what everyone’s talking about,” said Roach. “But there seems to be no concern for actually protecting public health.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Commentary: State rules for independent contractors are ‘onerous,’ confusing
description: New state regulations surrounding independent contractors are “onerous” and confusing, argues freelance writer Kim Kavin.
text:
New state regulations surrounding independent contractors are “onerous” and confusing, argues freelance writer Kim Kavin. (Photo by Hal Brown/New Jersey Monitor)Working people in New Jersey are getting squeezed from every direction.
The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, utilities, and almost everything else remains too high. Federal policies like tariffs are making countless goods more expensive. And something quieter but just as consequential is happening in the workplace: Union organizers are pushing policymakers to limit our available pathways to achieve the American dream.
For generations — every generation, actually, since the day the United States was founded — we have all had the option to be our own bosses. George Washington worked for himself as a land surveyor. Alexander Hamilton opened his own shop as a lawyer. The tradition of being able to work in whatever ways work best for us has always been part and parcel of liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
Increasingly, some unionists want a different arrangement: The government should give union organizers unprecedented power to target independent contractors. These unionists want to codify an ever-growing universe of so-called “worker protections” into law that are actually attacks on the ways we can legally earn a living.
That should concern every working person in New Jersey.
One way that unionists are pushing to restrict this freedom right now in our state
is the Department of Labor & Workforce Development’s newly adopted ABC test, which regulators use to determine whether someone should be classified as an independent contractor or a unionizable employee. If an independent contractor can’t pass this ABC test the way the Labor Department is interpreting it, then the company working with the independent contractor is subjected to fines and penalties.
Last year, when the Department of Labor first proposed this rule, the interpretation was so severe that attorneys said it would almost entirely eviscerate anyone’s ability to be an independent contractor at all. They wrote that the ABC test rule posed an existential threat to independent work itself. About 9,500 written public comments were filed, with 99% of them opposed. The only people who testified in support at the standing-room-only public hearing were either on a union payroll or affiliated with organizations that have strong union ties.
The version of the ABC test rule that the Labor Department just adopted is scaled back, but it’s still so onerous that on October 15, the Senate Judiciary Committee spent nearly two hours asking acting Labor Commissioner Kevin Jarvis how anyone can actually pass the test. Democrats and Republicans alike said they were being hammered daily with calls from every conceivable industry — insurance, performing arts, amateur sports — because nobody can figure out what to do.
One senator said he convened a group of accountants to gain some clarity, but they all gave him different answers. Laughter erupted in the chamber when Jarvis couldn’t seem to give a straight answer on how a business trying to comply could get the information required to do so. Yet another senator asked if there was going to be a Division of ABC Test Clarification to help everyone make sense of what’s going on.
New Jersey AFL-CIO President Charlie Wowkanech describes what’s happening with the ABC test as “expanding and protecting the freedom of workers to join unions for a better life.” It’s actually threatening the incomes and chosen careers of our state’s estimated 1.7 million independent contractors to try and give a bigger honeypot of targets to union organizers.
Don’t let the headlines about Uber and Lyft fool you. What’s happening with New Jersey’s ABC test rule is some of the most extreme policymaking in the country. During the public-comment period for the ABC test rule, research that supporters cited raised many questions. The Workplace Justice Lab at Rutgers University used footnotes to cite research that also compares independent contractors to human trafficking, child labor, and workplace violence — literally comparing entrepreneurial effort to violent crime.
These are extreme views. And yet it’s the extremists the Sherrill administration sided with when it defied the public’s 99% opposition and pushed the regulations through. It did so with strong support in particular from Wowkanech and the New Jersey AFL-CIO, which is Jarvis’ former employer. Wowkanech testified during the recent judiciary committee hearing that Jarvis is his “dear friend.”
A basic principle behind New Jersey’s labor and employment laws is as necessary as ever: We all should be able to work in whatever ways work best for us, whether that’s as a union employee, a nonunion employee, an independent contractor, or a combination that includes a side hustle. Especially at a time when it’s increasingly hard to pay grocery and gas bills, everyone should have the freedom to choose any kind of work we want.

title: Florida Department of Veterans affairs wants more money for veteran nursing homes
description: The Florida agency that helps aging American veterans in the state is asking for tens of millions in extra funding in the coming year from the Florida Legislature. The money is needed to help the Florida Department of Veterans Affairs staff and run veterans nursing homes around the state. The budget request suggests the agency […]
text:
The Florida Department of Veteran Affairs wants more money in the coming year to hire nursing staff to care for residents at state operated VA homes. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Florida agency that helps aging American veterans in the state is asking for tens of millions in extra funding in the coming year from the Florida Legislature.
The money is needed to help the Florida Department of Veterans Affairs staff and run veterans nursing homes around the state. The budget request suggests the agency is dealing with a growing population at its locations along with more extensive health care needs for veterans who reside in the homes.
There also continues to be “staff turnover” and ongoing staffing shortages.
“The composition of residents requiring nursing home care has dramatically changed to reflect increasing clinical acuity, fragility and behavioral needs,” the agency noted in its legislative budget request.
Florida agencies were asked last month to submit budget requests. The requests are guidelines for lawmakers to consider when they get down to the business in their 2027 session of creating the next fiscal year budget. They will also be relied on by Gov.-elect Byron Donalds when he submits his budget recommendations next year.
The agency, led by executive director James “Hammer” Hartsell, runs eight nursing homes and one assisted living facility and is funded by a blend of state and federal money. Its budget is nearly $241 million, according to this year’s Appropriations Act, and it has roughly 1,100 beds in its facilities.
The department’s asks include nearly $16.6 million emergency repairs and maintenance at its nine locations, which vary in age from five to 37 years. According to the request, over the past decade the available money has “not been sufficient to fully address the department’s accumulated maintenance, repair and infrastructure needs.”
Moreover, the agency said, it had to put its resources into salaries and staffing needs stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic. That resulted “in capital improvements receiving less attention from 2020 to 2024.”
“The State Veterans Homes have reached a point where extensive capital improvements are required,” the request states.
The agency is also asking for extra money to pay for additional staff in several areas, including services to veterans, as well as bolster those who care for veterans in nursing homes. For example, the department is seeking $6.6 million to make sure they are providing required levels of nursing home care.
“With the approval of this funding, the department will have sufficient budget authority to operate all facilities and fulfill its obligations in a timely manner and to ensure proper supplies are available for the veterans who reside in the State Veterans Nursing Homes,” the request states.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Republicans need to listen to voters, not their loudest voices
description: My grandfather used to tell us, “Sometimes the squeaky wheel gets the grease, but sometimes it gets replaced.” Republicans should consider that as we reflect on Tuesday’s electoral drubbing. For too long, the loudest people in our party have been at the head of the table. They have been bombastic, attention-seeking and consumed with proving […]
text:
(Will Steinfeld/New Hampshire Bulletin)
My grandfather used to tell us, “Sometimes the squeaky wheel gets the grease, but sometimes it gets replaced.”
Republicans should consider that as we reflect on Tuesday’s electoral drubbing.
For too long, the loudest people in our party have been at the head of the table. They have been bombastic, attention-seeking and consumed with proving party loyalty. In Missouri and across the country, voters finally asked what was behind the bravado. The answer was very little. Fed up, voters turned against Republican candidates, delivering what Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called “close to an extinction-level event” for Republicans.
Republicans in Missouri have been tone-deaf to the concerns and frustrations of voters. When Missourians said they wanted access to abortion, Republican lawmakers tried to sell them another ban two years later, this time packaged as a “reasonable” compromise. It didn’t work, and it was insulting. When Missourians approved a higher minimum wage and paid sick leave, the Republican-led legislature repealed the sick leave requirement and eliminated future inflation-based wage increases. Again, tone-deaf and insulting.
Nationally, a party that campaigned on stopping endless wars found itself defending a war with Iran and the higher gas prices it helped cause. Families paying more to drive to work needed leaders who took their frustrations seriously. Instead, they were told the economy was thriving.
Republicans deserved the reckoning they received on Tuesday. Voters are tired of the empty bravado and won’t tolerate policies that ignore their priorities. The question now is whether we’ll learn from it.
I remain a Republican because I believe individual liberty, responsible spending and economic opportunity can help families build good lives. Those principles have long given us a case to make to voters. Now we have to show what they mean in people’s lives.
What does our commitment to families mean for a mother recovering from childbirth who can’t afford time away from work? That question is especially personal to me as I write this while nursing my seven-week-old son. What does economic opportunity mean for parents whose child care costs swallow a paycheck? What does individual liberty mean if we are unwilling to trust women with decisions about their own pregnancies?
Those questions deserve serious solutions that Republicans can and should provide. But that requires us to listen to what families need, even when the answers challenge our party’s preferred policies.
Good policies aren’t worth much if the people who write them can’t get them passed. We have rewarded candidates for sensationalism and treated cooperation as a liability. This election should make us reconsider that approach. We should be confident enough in our ideas to discuss them with people who disagree. Sometimes Democrats will have good proposals. Sometimes Republican perspectives will improve them. And sometimes Democrats will improve Republican ideas. Negotiating those differences is part of the job voters expect our elected leaders to do.
Democrats may very well overplay their hand in the next two years. But Republicans can’t build a comeback by simply waiting for the other party to stumble.
My hope is that Republicans will move toward the middle, giving pragmatic voices a place at the head of the table again.
Republicans have two years to decide what they’ll offer voters in 2028. The people who will decide whether they get another chance care a lot less about party loyalty than many politicians in Jefferson City and Washington do.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska Department of Economic Development staff count continues its unprecedented drop
description: LINCOLN — The number of full-time employees of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development continues to drop, reaching a level this month not seen since the summer of 2020. DED has lost an unprecedented number of staff members over the last year and a half under its latest director, Maureen Larsen, who was appointed by […]
text:
Maureen Larsen, director of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development and former general counsel to the governor, at an inaugural public roundtable of Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen's cabinet. April 20, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The number of full-time employees of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development continues to drop, reaching a level this month not seen since the summer of 2020.
DED has lost an unprecedented number of staff members over the last year and a half under its latest director, Maureen Larsen, who was appointed by Gov. Jim Pillen in July 2025. Before her appointment, Larsen served as Pillen’s general counsel.
According to the department’s interim spokesperson Brennan Hallock, DED had 61.75 full-time employees as of Nov. 10, down from the peak of 115.25 it reached in May 2025. The decimal points represent part-time employees in how the department measures its full-time equivalents.
Last year, DED’s then-spokesperson Justin Pinkerman — who left the department this October — said the downsizing was part of an intentional winding down of pandemic-era programs. Data Pinkerman previously shared with the Examiner showed that DED had 63 full-time staff as of June 30, 2020.
“Governor Pillen’s administration made it a priority to shrink state government, including DED to its pre-COVID size,” Pillen spokeswoman Laura Strimple said in an email. “We have made strong progress toward that goal, while maintaining dedicated public servants in necessary positions.”
Hallock noted that in addition to the 61.75 permanent full-time employees, DED has filled three temporary full-time positions and two temporary part-time positions. The department currently has five active job postings and anticipates more to come.
“When considering the total number of permanent and temporary positions, the total exceeds 63 filled positions,” Hallock said in an email.
Several former DED employees have expressed doubt that the department’s initial reasoning for the downsizing was accurate. Sheryl Hiatt, who worked at DED for 26 years before she retired in June, said the truth could be seen in which employees were leaving.
While some DED divisions that managed pandemic-era projects have retained staff, such as the economic recovery division, Hiatt noted other divisions have been hit harder. She said DED’s housing staff has been hit particularly hard, as well as the data and technology division, which did not have any staff listed on DED’s website as of Nov. 10.
Hallock said the filled temporary positions at DED include data and technology staff.
Hiatt said DED has brought on temporary staff before, but they were rare occurrences to her recollection, and usually were hired in response to an immediate need. She gave the example that DED could bring on a temporary worker to serve as a receptionist, back when DED’s main office had a receptionist.
Hiatt said she believes the current permanent full-time staff level is not enough to offer manageable workloads for DED’s active employees. The last time she said the department was consistently operating at that level was under the leadership of Richard Baier, who served as DED’s director from 2003-2011.
Hiatt said the federal and state programs that DED employees oversee often require long-term commitment, as some come with compliance periods that can last decades. If an employee in charge of one of those programs leaves, that increases the workload of the staff designated to take over, not least because they may have years of work to catch up on, she said.
Speaking from her perspective as DED’s former director of field operations, Hiatt said many of these programs have a major impact on rural communities, both in spurring community development efforts and aiding businesses looking to locate across greater Nebraska.
“You’re basically hurting rural Nebraska with this workload,” Hiatt said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
In a recent survey of DED staff, several employees expressed concerns about growing workloads brought on by the downsizing. Multiple comments noted that most current staff are operating at burnout level.
“There is no way my workload is manageable for anyone. I feel like I am drowning every day,” one respondent wrote.
In a September interview with the Examiner, Larsen said DED was looking to fill some positions, but noted that as some pandemic-era programs have completed, leadership found that some of the workloads remaining from vacant positions did not warrant a replacement.
When an employee leaves DED, Larsen said, leadership talks with the position’s program manager to figure out how to divide the work the employee left behind. She said there are multiple options if an employee feels overworked, noting they can come to her, HR or their division head.
“If you want leaner government, if you want to cut waste and abuse, there’s a way to do it,” said Hiatt, who said she keeps in touch with people still working at DED. “And that’s by analyzing each program and each workflow across the agency, and that’s never been done. They’ll probably claim that they’re doing it behind the scenes, but you can’t do that without walking through that with every program manager.”
Strimple said Pillen has been “a strong champion of Nebraska’s economic development,” and pointed to several examples, including the 6 Regions, One Nebraska initiative, and the governor’s steps to strengthen the Business Innovation Act, opportunity zones and several other efforts.
“Economic opportunity in Nebraska does not depend on bloated bureaucracies,” Strimple said.

title: Commentary: On this Veterans Day, I remember my dad
description: I’m a “Boomer,” a son of parents from “The Greatest Generation.” What I can’t comprehend, the more today’s bad news metastasizes, is how so many people of my generation have desecrated the legacy of their parents’ generation by voting for and supporting Donald Trump and his corrupt oligarchs. Together, they are destroying our 250-year-old but […]
text:
Dr. Fergus Mayer (Photo provided by Marshall Mayer, used with permission).I’m a “Boomer,” a son of parents from “The Greatest Generation.”

What I can’t comprehend, the more today’s bad news metastasizes, is how so many people of my generation have desecrated the legacy of their parents’ generation by voting for and supporting Donald Trump and his corrupt oligarchs. Together, they are destroying our 250-year-old but fragile democratic republic for the exclusive benefit of the obscenely rich.
My dad was born the year Herbert Hoover (both from Iowa) was appointed Secretary of Commerce for Republican Presidents Warren G. Harding and then Calvin Coolidge (he was the Howard Lutnick of his time). In due course, President Hoover ushered in the Great Depression, and my grandfather moved his family to Detroit to find work in the auto industry, only to return home empty handed to work in Iowa’s coal mines. My dad graduated high school and turned a summer job of cleaning up in a slaughterhouse into a year-round job cleaning up in a slaughterhouse.
By the time my dad was old enough to serve, he and his best friend enlisted to fight fascism in World War II. He had good enough eyesight to serve in the Army Air Corps, where he flew—by himself—67 missions in Europe in a P-47 fighter. On his last mission, 81 years ago, he was shot down over northern Italy, was marched to Germany on a broken ankle, and served the last few months of the war in a prisoner-of-war camp. When he was finally liberated, he was down to about half his healthy body weight, had contracted pneumonia, and lived only because he got injections of penicillin in what became the first mass use of the patent-free drug to treat war injuries.
And here I am.
In my father’s memory, I fight fascism, too.
My dad, upon returning from the war, started a family, went to college and became a doctor, thanks to the GI Bill (he got a free education because he was a white male veteran). Like many other WWII veterans, my dad did not say much about his experience in the war, even when asked. Rather, he focussed on his present: his family and his patients, and doing what was right for both. He lived a good long life and made the same possible for those he cared for and loved.
I’ve always considered myself among the luckiest: Born in mid-twentieth century America, straight, white, and male in a suburban ZIP Code. I just want everyone to share in that privilege—a concept that should not be part of any truly political, economic, or social democracy—no matter the accidents of their birth or life. And to think, I almost wasn’t born.
In this election season, I can only image what my dad would be saying about my generation (and our progeny) voting in large enough numbers to elect politicians whose only fealty is to Trump and extreme wealth. May our generation’s children and grandchildren live to be proud of what we do—in the next two years—to save our democracy. Last week was a good start.
Marshall Mayer is an organizer in Montana who has worked to elect economic populists in presidential primaries, including Jessie Jackson, Bernie Sanders, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

title: Commentary: SC soldier recalls her battle from addiction to redemption
description: My name is Willette Alston-Hockaday, and my journey began over 30 years ago, when I was just a young girl who was innocent and full of life. In 1990, I did the one thing I had always dreamed of doing: I joined the U.S. Army. I joined in the summer of 1990 and was scheduled […]
text:
Retired U.S. Army Col. Willette Alston-Hockaday is pictured in her military uniform in winter 2024. (Photo with illustration courtesy of Willette Alston-Hockaday)My name is Willette Alston-Hockaday, and my journey began over 30 years ago, when I was just a young girl who was innocent and full of life.
In 1990, I did the one thing I had always dreamed of doing: I joined the U.S. Army.
I joined in the summer of 1990 and was scheduled to return to Benedict College in Columbia to complete my college education in January 1991.
Instead, I found myself deployed to Saudi Arabia as a 19-year-old private in operations Desert Shield and Desert Storm. It was one of the scariest times of my life. I had no idea what to expect in a wartime environment, and I had no idea what was waiting for me when I returned to the U.S.
In wartime, you share a foxhole with Army comrades, and you depend on each other to protect and defend you in war and in peacetime.
When I redeployed from Desert Storm, I realized that not every Army comrade was there to protect and defend. Upon my arrival back in the U.S., I was excited and overjoyed to be back with family and friends.
I expected to pick up where I left off. I was expected to go back to college and finish my degree.
However, that all changed when I fell in love with one of my Army comrades. Falling in love is supposed to be a beautiful thing, but when crack cocaine enters a relationship, everything changes.
Using crack cocaine, or any drug, was something I thought I would never engage in. Growing up in the small town of Awendaw, where everyone knows everyone, talk of my drug use started to spread like wildfire.
My drug use took over my mind, soul and body. My life was spiraling out of control, and I didn’t know what to do. And if that wasn’t enough, I gave birth to a baby in 1992.
Addiction in the 1990s was different.
I was ashamed and, of course, embarrassed. I struggled with drugs because I couldn’t see myself asking for assistance.
I felt that I could stop at any time. I felt that no one would understand. The fear I felt was undeniable.
I feared losing my son, I feared losing my freedom, and most of all, I feared losing my life.
In the 1990s, struggling with addiction was an awful feeling. I remember being called a crackhead. I remember being judged and ostracized.
My family conducted an intervention, and like an addict, I denied it. I told my family that I was fine and that they were the problem.
That was the turning point in my life. I entered rehab for 30 days and made up my mind that I needed and wanted to change my life for my son.
I had to accept the fact that I was an addict, and I needed to ensure that my son had a mother he was proud of and could depend on.
In January 1994, I decided to go back to college to complete my degree.
My first semester was a struggle because my family worried about my sobriety. At that point, I realized that I had to gain the trust of my family and friends.
I continued to strive for excellence in college and went back to my first love, the Army. I joined ROTC while in college and was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the U.S. Army in 1997.
After commissioning, I learned how to navigate my way in the Army as an officer. I learned how to cope with day-to-day operations and continued to move up in rank.
I had my struggles in the Army, and there were times I didn’t know which way to turn.
I was thankful that the stigma around mental health began to dissipate and service members began to seek treatment. I sought treatment and was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder in 2020.
Today, I have more than 30 years of sobriety.
I retired in 2023, and I am proud of the transition I made from the early 1990s to the present. I believe many veterans still struggle with addiction and PTSD.
However, the difference between the 1990s and the present is that veterans have more access to healthcare and can receive treatment for addiction and PTSD.
Second chances are possible, because your worst chapter does not have to become your identity.
