name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Supreme Court hears Stein’s appeals of laws stripping governors’ powers
description: The North Carolina Supreme Court Tuesday heard two cases concerning Gov. Josh Stein’s powers to make appellate court appointments and fill state commission vacancies.  The Republican-led legislature has worked for years to limit governors’ appointment powers to various boards and commissions. The state Supreme Court’s opinions on these attempts have been mix[...]
text:
The North Carolina Justice Building, which houses the Supreme Court of North Carolina, pictured on June 2, 2026. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) The North Carolina Supreme Court Tuesday heard two cases concerning Gov. Josh Stein’s powers to make appellate court appointments and fill state commission vacancies. 
The Republican-led legislature has worked for years to limit governors’ appointment powers to various boards and commissions. The state Supreme Court’s opinions on these attempts have been mixed. 
One case heard Tuesday was Stein’s challenge of a law requiring that the governor’s appointments to vacant Court of Appeals and state Supreme Court seats be taken from lists compiled by the state Democratic or Republican Party executive committees. The law also requires the appointee to be from the same party as the person who vacated the seat. 
Sarah Boyce, Stein’s general counsel, said the state constitution leaves decisions about those appointments to the governor alone. 
“Once you permit the legislature to insert itself into the process by imposing qualifications, you have taken what the constitution specifically grants the governor and given it to other actors,” she said.
Boyce pointed out that Republican lawmakers themselves said in 2018 that that power rests with the governor. 
In 2018, voters rejected a proposed constitutional amendment to change how judicial vacancies are filled. The wording of the amendment said it would “change the process in which the Governor has sole appointment power,” she noted. 
If the legislature believed that the governor had the sole constitutional authority, what changed between 2018 and now to make legislators think they had the authority to do it on their own, asked  Democratic Justice Allison Riggs. 
Martin Warf, an attorney for the legislature, said there’s no way to know why voters rejected the proposed constitutional amendment because it included other changes. 
The law preserves the voters’ partisan choices for judicial seats, Warf said, and there’s no language in the state constitution prohibiting the legislature from creating a nominating pool. 
In the other case, Stein is appealing a law that cuts his appointments on the Environmental Management Commission, the Coastal Resources Commission, the Wildlife Resources Commission, and the Utilities Commission.
Appeals Court sides with NC General Assembly in latest lawsuit over appointment powers

The governor no longer appoints the chairs of the Environmental Management, Coastal Resources, and Utilities commissions. They are elected by commission members. 
Diminishing the governor’s role inhibits his ability as the state’s chief executive to ensure laws are faithfully executed, as required in the constitution, Stein’s lawyer Eric Fletcher argued. 
Lawyers for legislators and Treasurer Brad Briner, who was given a Utilities Commission appointment, said legislators have the option to take appointments from the governor and distribute them to other members of the Council of State, who are all also members of the executive branch.
Every statutory official swears an oath to follow the law, said Matthew Tilley, the lawyer representing legislators. 
The justices did not indicate when they would rule on the cases. 
Stein is also appealing a recent Court of Appeals decision upholding the law allowing the transfer of Board of Elections appointments from the governor to the state auditor.  The Supreme Court has not yet scheduled that case for oral arguments.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Trump withdraws Rudofsky nomination for federal judge post in Arkansas
description: President Donald Trump nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice and former state Republican Party chairman Cody Hiland to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals Tuesday, withdrawing his nomination of a federal judge he originally named for the post. Trump nominated U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky to the appeals court in August. The federal judge previously [[...]
text:
The exterior of the Thomas F. Eagleton U.S. Courthouse in St. Louis, Missouri on Friday, June 5, 2026. The courthouse includes the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. (Photo by Andrew DeMillo/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Supreme Court Justice Cody Hiland (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
President Donald Trump nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice and former state Republican Party chairman Cody Hiland to the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals Tuesday, withdrawing his nomination of a federal judge he originally named for the post.
Trump nominated U.S. District Judge Lee Rudofsky to the appeals court in August. The federal judge previously issued rulings narrowing the Voting Rights Act and in favor of a state ban on “indoctrination” in the classroom.
Hiland was nominated to the Arkansas Supreme Court to fill a vacancy by Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders in 2023, and was elected to a full term in March.
The nominee swap comes a week after Democrats won control of Congress, raising the odds that Trump nominees will have a more difficult time being confirmed in the Senate next year. If Rudofsky was confirmed to the 8th Circuit bench, it would have created a vacancy in the Eastern District of Arkansas.
Trump previously praised Rudofsky as someone who would be a “rock solid defender of the Constitution,” in a post on Truth Social announcing the nomination. 
Republicans rammed through Supreme Court nominees. Now Democrats will have the votes to stop them

Hiland served as the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas during Trump’s first term in office, and was the prosecuting attorney for Faulkner, Van Buren and Searcy counties prior to that. After leaving the federal prosecutor’s office, he worked for the Arkansas Department of Public Safety and for Sanders’ 2022 campaign. He became chairman of the Republican Party of Arkansas the same year.
Since joining the Arkansas Supreme Court in 2023, Hiland authored an opinion striking down a state law that changed which state courts could hear constitutional challenges.
If confirmed, Hiland would replace retiring Judge Bobby Shepherd, a nominee of former President George W. Bush and father of Republican state Rep. Matthew Shepherd and U.S. District Judge Thomas Shepherd.
Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin said on the social media platform X that Hiland’s experience made him an “excellent choice” for the appeals court.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Independent candidate claims victory in tight Alabama Senate battle
description: An independent conservative candidate claimed victory Tuesday in a tight battle for a northeastern Alabama Senate district, but the Republican incumbent had not conceded as of early Tuesday evening. Independent candidate Jesse Battles said in a Facebook post that he had won the race by 74 votes out of more than 40,000 cast, following the […]
text:
Independent Senate candidate Jesse Battles claimed victory in Senate District 10 in northeast Alabama on Tuesday, but incumbent Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, did not immediately concede, saying he would wait for a recount. (Via jessebattles.com)An independent conservative candidate claimed victory Tuesday in a tight battle for a northeastern Alabama Senate district, but the Republican incumbent had not conceded as of early Tuesday evening.
Independent candidate Jesse Battles said in a Facebook post that he had won the race by 74 votes out of more than 40,000 cast, following the counting of provisional and write-in votes. He posted a photo of Etowah County Circuit Judge Sonny J. Steen administering him the oath of office.
“I’m humbled and honored to serve the people of District 10,” Battles said in a statement. “I look forward to working with Governor-elect Tuberville, Senate leadership, and local leaders across our district to ensure northeast Alabama is the best place to live, work, and raise a family.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Incumbent Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, wrote in a Facebook post early Tuesday evening that he was behind Battles by 72 votes and would wait for an automatic recount in the race.
“Although it would be an uphill climb for us to pull out a win at this point, I remain firm in my belief that every vote needs to be accurately counted,” Jones wrote in his post. “The automatic recount process exists in state law to ensure the integrity of our elections. Our team is waiting on the recount to be completed before making a final statement about the election.”
Multiple messages were sent to Battles and Jones seeking comment. Senate District 10 includes Cherokee and Etowah counties and a portion of DeKalb County.
As of Tuesday afternoon, the Alabama Secretary of State’s website showed Battles leading Jones by 52 votes, 20,341 to 20,289.
Sen. Andrew Jones, R-Centre, looks up to the gallery in the Alabama Senate on March 10, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
Battles originally sought to challenge Jones in the Republican primary for the district, but was removed from the ballot by the Alabama Republican Party in February. According to The Anniston Star, Battles faced allegations that he had done work for former Alabama House Minority Leader Craig Ford, D-Gadsden, who ran against Jones as an independent candidate in 2018.
Battles accused the “Montgomery Establishment” of removing him from the primary, and later gathered enough signatures to win ballot access as an independent.
Jones, seeking his third term in office, faced Alabama Public Library Service board member Amy Minton in the Republican primary in May. He won the party nomination with 8,325 votes (54%) to Minton’s 7,141 (46%).
Jones was one of several Republican candidates targeted by flyers from Alabama Values, a PAC created by former Sen. Del Hill that accused “our so-called conservative leaders” for voting for in-state tuition for immigrants without status. Jones was one of several candidates who later demanded retractions of the claims in the flyers.
Jones, who started the campaign with about $432,000, reported raising $1 million and spending $1.2 million on the race, according to campaign finance reports. Battles raised $142,000 and spent about $135,000.
Jones focused on economic development, infrastructure and improving education on his campaign website. He helped lead efforts in the Alabama Legislature to reduce the state portion of the sales tax on food.
Battles, a small business owner, also highlighted infrastructure and education as priorities. He also said he wants to expand the skilled trades, support veterans and law enforcement, protect people’s Second Amendment right to own a gun.
If the result holds, the Alabama Senate will consist of 24 Republicans, 10 Democrats and one independent. After the 2022 elections, the chamber had 27 Republicans and eight Democrats.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: In eastern Idaho’s Bannock County, officials find 333 uncounted ballots week after election
description: A week after the midterm election, Idaho election officials reported more than 300 ballots went uncounted on election night in an eastern Idaho county. The Office of the Idaho Secretary of State on Tuesday afternoon announced that 333 uncounted ballots had been identified during a post-election review in one precinct in Bannock County. State election […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at Borah High School in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)A week after the midterm election, Idaho election officials reported more than 300 ballots went uncounted on election night in an eastern Idaho county.
The Office of the Idaho Secretary of State on Tuesday afternoon announced that 333 uncounted ballots had been identified during a post-election review in one precinct in Bannock County. State election officials said no outcomes changed once the ballots had been counted. The votes will be added to the state’s election results website Tuesday, officials added.
Election recount planned in North Idaho county that didn’t report 2,300 ballots

“Once again, this demonstrates the importance of the reconciliation process we use to verify election results following every election,” Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican who was reelected as the state’s top election official, said in a written statement. “While I am thankful that these ballots were identified, we will be working to determine why these ballots were not processed on election night and working with counties across the state to reinforce our election processes.”
This is at least the second Idaho county to report it left some ballots unreported in election results after last week’s election. State election officials on Tuesday were overseeing a recount of ballots in North Idaho’s Latah County, after the county reported more than 2,300 ballots went unreported in election results. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
All of the uncounted ballots in Bannock County came from the same precinct, named Pocatello 2, state officials said. The county has 57 precincts.
 The closest race for any races that precinct was voting in, state officials say, is for county coroner, where Republican Torey Danner led independent candidate Wilson Simmons by 4,857 votes. 
The Bannock County Elections office, which features a ballot dropbox, is located on North Sixth Avenue in Pocatello, Idaho. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun)
The precinct also voted in Legislative District 29, where Democrats swept all three seats. But in two of those races, Democrats had led by around 2,000 votes over Republicans, according to election results. The Idaho Office of Secretary of State soon corrected its announcement about the uncounted ballots.
Bannock County Clerk Jason Dixon, the local election official, said in a statement that “this should not have happened.”
“We take pride in Bannock County in the work that goes into running our elections,” Dixon said. “We are working closely with the Secretary of State’s office to ensure full transparency and to determine if additional steps can be taken to ensure this does not happen. I want Bannock County voters to know your votes will count.”
The Idaho State Board of Canvassers, which certifies the state’s election results, is set to meet at 1 p.m. Friday to select counties and precincts that will undergo audits of election results, including hand counts and reviews of reported results.
“We have numerous safeguards in place to verify the accuracy of Idaho’s elections,” McGrane said. “My main focus throughout all of this is to ensure that every single vote is counted and that Idahoans have confidence that their voice is heard.”
The Bannock County Board of Commissioners is set to meet 9 a.m. Thursday to recanvass the election results, including the added ballots. 
The results from last week’s election remain unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which is scheduled to meet Nov. 24.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Voters struggle as ballot deadlines pass in Mississippi Senate race
authors: By Emily Cochrane, The New York Times and Michael Goldberg, Mississippi Today
description: A shuttle on the campus of Toogaloo College transports students to check on their affidavit ballots on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Multiple phone calls. A car pool to the Madison County Circuit Clerk’s Office, where Zemaryiah Johnson had cast an affidavit ballot. And then instructions that she had to go somewhere else entirely, in an adjoining Mississippi county.
All that to ensure that Johnson, an 18-year-old freshman at the historically Black Tougaloo College, would have her vote counted — for Scott Colom, the state’s Democratic candidate for Senate.
“It’s like going back in time,” Johnson said.
The long, slow count in the tight race between Colom and the Republican incumbent, Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, reached a critical deadline on Tuesday, the last day that affidavit ballots could be fixed — a process known as curing — and that mail-in ballots postmarked on Election Day could arrive. Recent days have highlighted the problems and frustrations that Mississippi’s strict election laws can cause in such a tight contest.
Organizers, community leaders and lawyers spent Tuesday scrambling to ensure the final tranche of ballots were in order. By the end of the day, Colom, who would be the first Black senator elected from Mississippi since Reconstruction, led Hyde-Smith by just over 2,600 votes, but an unknown number of affidavit ballots and 2,578 still uncounted absentee-by-mail ballots could still determine the winner.
“Votes should be counted, and that’s all we’re concentrating on today,” Hyde-Smith told reporters on Capitol Hill on Tuesday.
She added: “We’re just looking for the conclusion of our race.”
In Jackson, Colom and his allies have been calling on Mississippi to expand its voting process, by among other things, setting up an early voting period that many other states share. He also questioned whether “there may be some disadvantages to our potential to lead in D.C.,” given that he couldn’t join new lawmakers in orientation on Capitol Hill.
Cortorian Keeton, 22, a Tougaloo senior, managed to resolve his ballot problem. He said he had never seen friends and peers so engaged in the political process. Credit: Blake Barnes / Mississippi Today
Michael Watson, Mississippi’s secretary of state, had “created chaos” with the affidavit rules and should apologize for the delay, Colom said on Tuesday, during a visit to the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office.
Watson said that as of 5 p.m. Monday more than 15,500 affidavit ballots had been processed. Just over three-quarters of them had been accepted, he said. He did not say how many ballots were left.
Mississippi and Alaska are the only states yet to declare a winner in their Senate contests, but Mississippi is drawing closer. State law does not allow for a recount of votes in a statewide election, nor will there be a runoff.
The tussles over affidavit ballots have also drawn attention to a decision from July 2025, when Watson’s office announced a partnership where data from Experian, the credit reporting agency, would be used as part of the agency’s maintenance of the state’s voter rolls.
Under the partnership, some registered voters identified as having a new address were labeled “inactive,” meaning they had to fill out an affidavit ballot if they showed up to vote. On Election Day, some voters — though it was unclear how many — found themselves mistakenly marked as having moved or inactive.
Scott Anderson, an Experian spokesman, said the agency hadn’t worked with Mississippi since early last year, and that the sharing of “supplemental address information” at the time “was not designed or intended to validate voter records.”
Watson defended the affidavit ballot process in a statement on social media last week as “a safety net for errors” during voter roll maintenance that would result in “more accurate voter rolls” and “decrease opportunities for voter fraud.”
Over the last week, affidavit ballots have been processed by hand, as election commissioners checked to see whether each voter was in the system, or if someone had arrived to “cure” a ballot with proper identification. That has created considerable friction.
“Seeing people genuinely have to call every day and have to go up there every day and exhaust their finances with gas and their energy to do things like this — it’s almost like they want people to get tired,” Johnson said.
The process proved especially confounding for many Mississippi college students, including at Tougaloo, which straddles Hinds and Madison counties, two of the state’s largest. The geographic positioning had sowed confusion, since some students lived in one county but tried to vote in the other.
Terry Rogers II, 21, a senior studying political science, drove students in a college van between the two counties, as he wrestled with each student’s particular instructions on where to go to check a ballot.
“Think about how many others did not have the opportunity and have advocates like that,” Rogers said. 
Lyric Wise, 18, a freshman at Tougaloo, said elections officials were sending students around in circles. Wise has already made two trips to the Madison County Circuit Clerk and was set to board Rogers’s shuttle to the Hinds County Circuit Clerk on Tuesday afternoon.
Cortorian Keeton, 22, a Tougaloo senior who managed to resolve his ballot problem, said he had never seen friends and peers so engaged in the political process: “A lot of people mad, a lot of people happy, a lot of people want Mississippi to stay the same and a lot of people want Mississippi to be different,” he said.
But even some organizers who lamented the hurdles for voters basked in the attention of the nation and the pride they said they felt in Mississippi’s civic engagement.
“People are actually looking at Mississippi right now,” said Jada Barnes, the field director for Mississippi Votes Action Fund. Over wings and pizza in the organization’s Jackson office, volunteers spent Monday evening calling voters, checking to see if they had voted using an affidavit ballot or fielding questions about the process.
The state’s voters, she said, “really beat the odds.”
One of those voters, Heather Holland, 28, said that since she got married in 2022, she had cast her ballot several times in Jackson County, a Republican stronghold on the Gulf Coast. But last Tuesday, when she showed up to vote, her registration turned up under her maiden name, requiring her to file an affidavit ballot.
“It could make a difference,” Holland, a Democrat, said on Tuesday. She reached out to volunteers to make sure that her vote had been counted.
On Tougaloo’s campus on Tuesday, Rogers printed off fliers with a QR code that directed students to a state website that allows people to check the status of their ballots. With about 40 fliers in hand, Rogers joined other students who had gathered steps away from the Woodworth Chapel, a haven of the Civil Rights movement where leaders like Medgar Evers and Fannie Lou Hamer had spoken, and opened the driver-side door for the final trip on Tuesday.
His next destination: Jackson State University, another historically Black college where students had reported problems filling out affidavit ballots. More ballots needed curing.

text:
Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, speaks at a signing ceremony for a landmark literacy bill at John W. Rex Charter Elementary in Oklahoma City on April 21, 2026. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The Republican leader of the Oklahoma Senate is poised to stay in his role for another two years.
Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, ran unopposed to be the GOP supermajority’s nominee for the top post. Republican senators chose him to continue as president pro tem in a closed-door caucus meeting Tuesday.
Paxton, who has led the Senate since 2024, must pass a vote by all 48 Oklahoma senators during the Legislature’s organizational day Jan. 5. If elected, he will continue guiding the Senate’s policy priorities and overseeing its operations while working with the state House and executive branch.
Paxton has represented a moderate coalition of the Senate Republican Caucus that held a majority over the far-right Freedom Caucus in recent years. That majority is expected to grow in the next legislative session after some Freedom Caucus senators weren’t reelected this year.
In a statement Tuesday, Paxton said the Senate’s focus “will remain on responsible budgeting, strengthening our economy, improving education and ensuring state government remains accountable to the people we serve.”
“I’m honored to have the continued confidence and support of my colleagues,” he said. “Serving as pro tem is a responsibility I take seriously, and I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together.”
Paxton is an insurance agent, business owner, farmer and rancher, and longtime volunteer firefighter.
He was elected to the Senate in 2016 and has two years left before reaching a 12-year term limit.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska DNR approves scaled-down land transfer to AIDEA for industrial park near Houston
description: The Alaska Department of Natural Resources on Tuesday approved a scaled-down version of a controversial land transfer to a state-owned corporation, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority. According to a final finding and decision published Tuesday afternoon, DNR has approved a plan that would give approximately 6,800 of land for free to the s[...]
text:
This map, published Nov. 10, 2026, shows the site of a land transfer from the Alaska Department of Natural Resources to the state-owned Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority. (DNR graphic)The Alaska Department of Natural Resources on Tuesday approved a scaled-down version of a controversial land transfer to a state-owned corporation, the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority.
According to a final finding and decision published Tuesday afternoon, DNR has approved a plan that would give approximately 6,800 of land for free to the state-owned corporation. That’s less than the 19,500 acres that had been earmarked for transfer in a preliminary July decision.
DNR further said it will impose conditions on the transfer, including the right for local residents to use roads and trails in the area. DNR will also include a reversion clause that returns the land to the state agency if AIDEA fails to develop it.
“DNR has determined that it is appropriate to reduce the conveyance acreage from 19,500 to approximately 6,800 acres, and to modify the arrangement of the subject parcel in a manner that will maintain public access and use of these lands while also incorporating measures intended to mitigate the anticipated impacts of the conveyance,” it wrote in Tuesday’s decision.
After DNR published its decision on Tuesday afternoon, the Beacon emailed AIDEA for its thoughts on the scaled-back approval. The agency has not yet responded.
Explaining its interest in the area, AIDEA said in July that the land could be used for a logistics hub, advanced manufacturing and “scalable data centers.”
“AIDEA proposes to use the conveyed land to establish a multi-use industrial and energy development district for the public purpose and public interest of creating jobs, improving energy reliability, and diversifying the economy,” DNR wrote in Tuesday’s decision.
AIDEA’s initial proposal received a storm of opposition from local residents who rely on trails and roads in the area and harvest timber in the region. Fishermen said they were concerned that development could disturb salmon streams.
The Alaska Legislature held a pair of hearings investigating the legality of the transfer, and a former state legislator filed suit to block it. That suit is still pending.
DNR received more than 2,300 public comments on the transfer, mostly in opposition.
“Reducing the area to 6,800 acres allows the conveyance to alleviate many of the concerns raised during the public comment period,” the agency said in its final decision.
It also said that public reaction caused it to reverse the elimination of the reversion clause, require the protection of salmon streams and mandate public access to roads and trails in the area.
Tuesday’s decision opens a 20-day window for reconsideration, and if someone requests that DNR reconsider its decision, the agency has 30 days to act on that decision.
Any further challenge would have to be filed in the state court system.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Former Arkansas prison system leader says state has infrastructure to address overcrowding
description: Joe Profiri, who was fired two years ago as the head of the state’s corrections department over a dispute with the state Board of Corrections, told lawmakers Tuesday that Arkansas already has the policy infrastructure in place to address persistent overcrowding in its prisons. Profiri, now a senior adviser to Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, […]
text:
Former Arkansas Corrections Secretary Joe Profiri, left, listens as Gov.Sarah Huckabee Sanders talks about criminal justice legislation during a news conference at the State Capitol on March 28, 2023. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)Joe Profiri, who was fired two years ago as the head of the state’s corrections department over a dispute with the state Board of Corrections, told lawmakers Tuesday that Arkansas already has the policy infrastructure in place to address persistent overcrowding in its prisons.
Profiri, now a senior adviser to Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, appeared before the House and Senate judiciary committees as they held the latest in a series of hearings to discuss prison overcrowding.
Arkansas’ growing prison population is driven in large part by high rates of recidivism, according to experts and department data.
It marked Profiri’s first appearance before legislators since 2025. Profiri faced criticism from some lawmakers for not appearing at a hearing last year to discuss Sanders’ proposal for a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County that the governor has since put on hold.
“What it comes back to is based on the scale (of Arkansas’ community corrections system), maybe we need a larger capacity to actually show success,” Profiri said.
The former corrections secretary told lawmakers that the corrections system may need to be “rightsized,” citing the more than 80,000 people who are on some kind of supervision. He said the pieces were in place, but scaling was necessary. 
“You and this body have done an excellent job with legislation over the last, almost four years, in putting all the elements in place,” Profiri said. “At this point it’s largely about executing.”
The prison system needs to become rehabilitative instead of punitive, he said.
Lawmakers have held several meetings since September discussing Arkansas’ prison population, which has grown consistently since the COVID-19 pandemic but has long outstripped the state’s ability to house everyone sentenced. That’s led to a growing county jail backup, where people who have been convicted await an open state prison bed.
Overcrowded: Tighter parole, probation rules set stage for Arkansas prison population increases

The jail backup and prison bed shortage has been the source of clashes between Sanders and the Board of Corrections. Her efforts to open more beds in 2023 while Profiri was still corrections secretary ultimately contributed to the board suspending then firing him, and was the focus of an ongoing legal battle over who controlled the state’s top prison officials. Former Board Chairman Benny Magness said at the time that the prison system was severely understaffed and couldn’t safely open the extra beds Sanders asked for.
Later efforts by Sanders and her allies in the Legislature to approve $750 million in funding for the Franklin County prison project met stiff opposition from a bipartisan coalition in the Senate and from the local community, leaving the project in limbo.
The Joint Performance Review Committee requested Profiri testify during a hearing last year on the prison project and how the site for it was selected — but he didn’t show, frustrating several Republican legislators. The absence led to a failed legislative effort this year to eliminate his advisory position in the governor’s office.

title: Public Service Commission approves NorthWestern Energy, Black Hills Corp merger
description: The Montana Public Service Commission approved the $15.4 billion NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp. merger on Tuesday. The merged company, Bright Horizon Energy, will serve 2.1 million electric and natural gas customers in Montana, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, Nebraska and Wyoming. In a split vote, the PSC supported the deal, with C[...]
text:
Electricity pylons (Photo by Getty Images). The Montana Public Service Commission approved the $15.4 billion NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Corp. merger on Tuesday.
The merged company, Bright Horizon Energy, will serve 2.1 million electric and natural gas customers in Montana, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, Nebraska and Wyoming.
In a split vote, the PSC supported the deal, with Commissioner Randy Pinocci in opposition and PSC President Jeff Welborn a “reluctant” no.
Commissioners Jennifer Fielder, Annie Bukacek and Kirk Bushman voted yes.
Montana is the last state that needed to vote on the deal, announced in August 2025.
Pinocci said he’s worried Black Hills, based in South Dakota, has more to gain from the merger than Montanans, and the deal didn’t address people’s top concern.
“What are we going to do about lowering the rates for the people?” Pinocci said.
But Fielder, who made the motion to approve the merger, said evidence shows the merger will mean “tens of millions of dollars in savings” for the companies.
“Those savings are savings that get passed onto the customers,” Fielder said. “Those are costs the customers will not have to pay.”
The approved order said rates will not increase as a result of the merger.
Most members of the public voiced opposition to the merger prior to the decision, citing concerns about increases in power bills, loss of utility oversight, and subsidizing energy and infrastructure for data centers.
But a couple of representatives from the business community said Montana’s economy needs power, and the merger was important to economic growth.
This story will be updated.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Lawmakers argue about legislative data center memo that one calls ‘a very opinionated piece’
description: A South Dakota state senator employed by a utility company criticized a legislative staff report on large data centers as “very opinionated,” drawing pushback from some fellow lawmakers who said the report fulfilled its purpose. Sen. Steve Kolbeck, R-Brandon, is an executive for Xcel Energy, a multi-state provider of electricity and natural gas. He is […]
text:
Sen. Steve Kolbeck, R-Brandon, speaks on the Senate floor in Pierre on Feb. 11, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)A South Dakota state senator employed by a utility company criticized a legislative staff report on large data centers as “very opinionated,” drawing pushback from some fellow lawmakers who said the report fulfilled its purpose.
Sen. Steve Kolbeck, R-Brandon, is an executive for Xcel Energy, a multi-state provider of electricity and natural gas. He is also a former member of the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission, which regulates investor-owned utilities. 
During a Tuesday meeting in Pierre of the Legislature’s Executive Board, Kolbeck criticized Legislative Research Council staff attorney Rachel Hale’s 17-page “Hyperscale Data Centers” issue memorandum. Kolbeck went on to cast the lone no vote against accepting the memorandum. 
“I was just kind of trying to figure out where LRC staff came up with a very opinionated piece,” Kolbeck said, calling some of the memorandum’s sources “not necessarily factual.”
Data center restrictions signed into South Dakota law after push for incentives failed

He asked whether Hale consulted electric cooperatives, investor-owned utilities or the Public Utilities Commission.
Hale said she had not interviewed stakeholders. The assignment from the board in April was to “summarize the documented effects and challenges, particularly on water and electricity, of hyperscale data centers in other states and those states’ regulatory actions in response,” according to the board’s minutes. Hale’s sources included government publications, academic research, law review articles and news reports.
Kolbeck said he found parts of the report inaccurate, particularly its discussion of potential electricity rate increases. The memorandum acknowledges disagreement over whether data centers increase electricity rates.
Kolbeck said the Legislature had addressed electricity cost concerns earlier this year through Senate Bill 135, which was signed into law.
That law — as explained in the Legislative Research Council memo — requires data centers with peak electrical use of 10 megawatts or greater to cover any costs associated with meeting their power demand, including costs if a data center unexpectedly stops operating. It also bars the state from preempting local laws limiting, banning or regulating data centers. Data center projects additionally have to notify local water providers about their proposed projects, and the providers must determine whether the data center’s projected consumption is compatible with the local water supply. 
The memo also outlines competing research and arguments about data centers. For example, it cites research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory finding that infrastructure upgrades, rather than data centers, were the primary drivers of recent electrical rate increases. It also notes that some states experiencing substantial data center growth experienced declining electricity rates.
The report contrasts those findings with research warning that large data centers can strain electrical grids, require costly infrastructure upgrades and potentially shift expenses onto residential customers.

State House Speaker Jon Hansen, R-Dell Rapids, the House prime sponsor of the new data center law, challenged Kolbeck’s characterization of the report.
“I read this with sort of the eye of trying to make sure that it was just laying out the facts and presented neutrally, and I did think you did a really good job at that,” Hansen told Hale. “So, I just want to push back on some of the criticism that was leveled earlier.” 
House Majority Leader Scott Odenbach, R-Spearfish, called the memorandum a “thorough and dispassionate look” at the issue.
Legislative Research Council Director Doug Decker defended the work, saying the memorandum addressed the assignment lawmakers provided.
“It was a dispassionate presentation of both sides of the issue, and it met the charge that was given,” Decker said. 
Some lawmakers acknowledged that more research could be useful, but Decker said additional questions should be addressed in another memorandum rather than “a criticism of this one.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Providence historic preservation group warns federal bill could limit public’s say in development
description: One of the largest and oldest preservation groups in Rhode Island’s capital city is opposing a sweeping federal permitting bill cosponsored by U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse that proposes changes to the National Historic Preservation Act. The Providence Preservation Society, a citywide advocacy group founded in 1956, says the legislation could undermine the pu[...]
text:
The relocation of railroad tracks near Station Park in Providence in the 1980s underwent federal historic preservation review because of its proximity to the Rhode Island State House, the Providence Preservation Society says. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)One of the largest and oldest preservation groups in Rhode Island’s capital city is opposing a sweeping federal permitting bill cosponsored by U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse that proposes changes to the National Historic Preservation Act.
The Providence Preservation Society, a citywide advocacy group founded in 1956, says the legislation could undermine the public’s participation in local development. The group is also worried that the legislation could do away with the consultations typically undertaken with state and tribal preservation officials concerning projects in their communities.
The preservation society first raised its concerns with Whitehouse in an Oct. 23 letter, followed by similar correspondence to the state’s senior senator, Jack Reed, on Nov. 2. Both messages were received by the senators in advance of Monday’s 73-25 vote that saw the Senate advance consideration, but not final passage, of H.R. 2347 — an unrelated bill already passed by the House that is being used as a vehicle for the senate legislation.
Whitehouse is the top ranking Democrat on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which is chaired by West Virginia’s Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito. The permitting reform legislation is spearheaded by this committee and the Senate Energy Committee, led by Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee and New Mexico Democratic Sen. Martin Heinrich.
Whitehouse and Reed voted to advance the legislation Monday.
The permitting reform bill has some bipartisan support, although it has also faced opposition from some Democrats who have concerns over the bill’s intention of streamlining the approval pipeline for energy-related construction projects.
Permitting overhaul advances in US Senate with tepid bipartisan support

Providence Preservation Society Executive Director Marisa Angell Brown explained in emails to Rhode Island Current that her organization is opposed to the bill for different reasons. 
Revisions made on Saturday axed an earlier provision which would have let the Interior Department take over certain Tribal Historic Preservation Officers’ responsibilities. It also requires federal agencies to conference with local parties consulting on federal construction projects, and would lengthen the period in which local stakeholders can issue a formal objection.
These proposed amendments have not totally soothed her group’s concerns, Brown said Tuesday.
“We have reviewed the amendment, and while there have been a few changes that addressed some of the Tribal concerns, we are still opposed to the bill,” Brown said in an email. 

The Preservation Society is most concerned about proposed changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which outlines the review process federal agencies must undertake when embarking on projects that could affect historic properties. 
Under current regulations, state and tribal historic preservation officials must be consulted before projects begin, and agencies also need to provide a chance for local governments and the public to have their say in the process. These regulations are meant to identify potential harm to historic properties so agencies can avoid, minimize or mitigate the damage and prevent what federal regulations dub an “adverse effect.”
The proposed permitting legislation, Brown said, could overwrite these regulations and leave out comparable requirements for public involvement.
“The bill still does not enshrine in law the public’s ability to substantially inform projects that may take place in their communities,” Brown wrote Tuesday, echoing a concern she had written in an earlier email on Friday: “The bill is silent on if the public must be considered. When the public is allowed to participate, it is only in the form of public comment in a small window of time.”
Brown was also concerned that the revised legislation would narrow just exactly what the federal government defines as an “adverse effect” of a project, noting that the weekend’s revisions “still limit what is recognized as harm or whether harm to a cultural resource/historic property is recognized at all.”
The current set of federal regulations acknowledges outcomes which alter historic properties either “directly or indirectly.” The latter is omitted in the proposed permitting legislation. 
In a statement responding to Saturday’s amendment, the National Trust for Historic Preservation shared similar concerns, writing that the organization “supports efforts to make federal permitting more efficient, predictable, and timely.”
“But efficiency should not come at the expense of meaningful consultation, public participation, Tribal sovereignty, or the consideration of historic properties in federal decision-making,” the statement continued.
U.S. Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse campaigns outside the Mary V. Quirk School in Warren, Rhode Island, on Nov. 5, 2024. (Photo by Ken Castro/Rhode Island Current)
Providence’s history illustrates a reason for concern 
What might change in Providence specifically under the permitting bill, if passed into law?
In her Tuesday email, Brown said she had pondered over the weekend how Providence’s landscape had been reshaped by urban renewal during the 1950s and 1960s. Approximately 9% of the city’s landmass, Brown said, was redeveloped during this time. It mostly affected communities of color. 
“So much of that redevelopment was driven by federal highway construction,” Brown wrote. “The next wave of federal infrastructure projects will likely be tied to green energy — which is so critical — but my fear when I think about the changes underway is that they would pave the way, again, for neighborhoods like South Providence to take the brunt of development as resourced neighborhoods often have access to attorneys to help fight plans while less-resourced neighborhoods are more dependent on regulations like Section 106.”
Rhode Island State Historic Preservation Officer Jeffrey Emidy was not immediately available for comment Tuesday, but his office sent an August statement from Emidy concerning a separate proposal to revise regulations in Section 106. 
Emidy wrote then that his office reviews more than 1,000 federally connected projects annually. Most leave historic properties unscathed, Emidy wrote, noting that the “vast majority of federal projects that occur in Rhode Island do not impact historic properties.”
But consultations remain an important part of the process, Emidy wrote, and involve “assessing and mitigating possible impacts, and suggesting alternatives to avoid adverse impacts.”
One example offered by Brown, although she said it was “long past,” involved the Rhode Island State House itself. The relocation of the train tracks and Station Park — which sit across the street from the State House — were required to undergo an older version of the Section 106 process, Brown said.
Meaghan McCabe, a spokesperson for Whitehouse, said in an email Tuesday that Saturday’s amendment “protects by statute the consultation rights of historic preservation groups and other interested parties.”
Whitehouse also defended the permitting overhaul in a joint statement released after Saturday’s amendments, characterizing the changes as incorporating “the thoughtful feedback we have received.”
“Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs,” Whitehouse said in the statement. 
An explainer on the permitting legislation published in October by the Bipartisan Policy Center, meanwhile, noted that “a Section 106 review can run for years without a fixed end date.” 
“The burden falls hardest on linear infrastructure, which crosses hundreds of miles and dozens of jurisdictions, each with its own preservation office working through a backlog,” the article stated, noting that Section 106 “can add years to a schedule before construction begins” and delay the improvements to grid infrastructure the legislation seeks to expedite.
The legislation remains under Senate consideration before it can head toward a final vote.

name: Maryland Matters
title: High court says Penman cannot serve on Harford Council and work as a deputy
description: A Harford County councilman was removed from office Tuesday after the Supreme Court of Maryland ruled that he cannot be on the council at the same time he's employed as a sheriff's deputy, capping a four-year legal battle with just weeks left in the council's term.
text:
Harford County Council Member Aaron Penman (R) said he was shocked by a Maryland Supreme Court ruling removing him from office because he also serves as a county sheriff's deputy. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)A Harford County council member will leave office weeks sooner than expected, after the state’s highest court ruled Tuesday he cannot simultaneously be on the council while employed as a sheriff’s deputy.
The brief ruling from the Supreme Court of Maryland follows a hearing last week for Republican Council Member Aaron Penman, who has now been removed twice since being sworn in four years ago in an ongoing legal fight over his status..
In a two-page order Tuesday, Chief Justice Matthew J. Fader wrote that the court found “the Harford County Charter bars a deputy sheriff employed by the Harford County Sheriff from simultaneously serving as a Harford County Council member.”
The order removed Penman effective immediately and requires him to pay court costs.
Harford County Executive Bob Cassilly (R), said in a statement that the order “affirmed that Aaron Penman is and has been ineligible for a seat on the Harford County Council due to his simultaneous employment as a sheriff’s deputy, in clear violation of the county charter. Harford, like most Maryland counties, prohibits such dual employment because it creates an obvious conflict of interest for council members charged with oversight of county spending on the sheriffs’ office and other state offices.”
Republican Harford County Executive Robert Cassilly. (File photo by Danielle E. Gaines/Maryland Matters)
Penman said he was shocked by the order.
“I don’t understand it,” he said.
“The sheriff is a self-elected official. He doesn’t answer to the state. He doesn’t answer to the county executive, as it represents salaries, hiring, firings,” Penman said. “But yet, they somehow lump deputy sheriffs in as state employees — that have really no impact on local legislation.
“They say I cannot serve on the council because I’m a state employee, and a state has no input on the local county council, county budget,” he said. “They’re not saying I’m a county employee. They’re saying I’m a state employee, which makes me ineligible.”
The order does not fully explain how the court reached its conclusion or how Penman’s case differs from an earlier case involving Jacob Bennett, the Harford County Council member and teacher who Cassilly unsuccessfully tried to keep from being seated on the council citing the same county charter provision.
A fuller explanation from the court will come later.
Cassilly, in his statement, said the order also effectively invalidates a series of bills sponsored by Penman that include an expansion of the council’s budget powers and changes to the county charter sections regarding eligibility to serve on the council.
The executive vetoed one of those bills last week. A decision on another was expected by Wednesday. With Penman off the council, it is unlikely there are the required five votes to override a Cassilly veto.
Cassilly, in his statement, said Penman “illegally rushed” the bills through the council, and said the court order removing Penman invalidates the bills.
“Those bills have now been invalidated by the Maryland Supreme Court’s ruling that Penman was not a legitimate member of the Harford County Council when he introduced those bills,” the Cassilly statement said.
A Cassilly spokesperson was not immediately able to clarify Tuesday what the executive’s statements mean for the fate of the bills.
The order reverses an Appellate Court of Maryland ruling that cleared the way for Penman to return to the council in June.
Penman’s time on the council was already coming to an end. Because of the ongoing legal case, he did not seek reelection this year, and would have left office on Dec. 7, when the new council is sworn in.
The order issued Tuesday requires Penman to step down immediately.
The courtroom wrangling grew out of a feud between Harford County Republicans including Cassilly, Sheriff Jeff Gahler and Penman, as well as Council President Patrick Vincenti, who unsuccessfully challenged Cassilly in the 2026 primary. The kerfuffle traces back to a dispute over a funding for a training facility for Gahler’s department.
Four years ago, Cassilly refused to swear in Bennett because he was employed as a middle school science teacher in the county school system. The executive said a county charter provision barred county employees from also holding elected office.
The state’s highest court quickly ruled in Bennett’s favor.
Penman’s lawyers argued that the decision in the Bennett case cleared the way for their client to also retain his seat on the council.
Penman lost an early round and was off the council for 18 months before securing an order from the Appellate Court of Maryland. That court in part cited the Bennett decision in overturning a circuit court ruling.
“They’re basically reversing their own opinion and carving out a new path to adversarially affect deputy sheriffs, law enforcement,” Penman said Tuesday.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Limits of South Dakota law on new trials for DNA evidence debated at state Supreme Court
description: An impending South Dakota Supreme Court decision stands between a man who’s spent 42 years in prison for a double murder and his chance to convince a jury he never should’ve been there. The decision and underlying case will offer guidance on how judges are meant to apply a South Dakota law. The statute lets […]
text:
The South Dakota Supreme Court conducts a hearing Feb. 14, 2024, at the Capitol in Pierre. From left are Justices Patricia DeVaney, Janine Kern, Steven Jensen, Mark Salter and Scott Myren. (David Bordewyk/SD NewsMedia Association)An impending South Dakota Supreme Court decision stands between a man who’s spent 42 years in prison for a double murder and his chance to convince a jury he never should’ve been there.
The decision and underlying case will offer guidance on how judges are meant to apply a South Dakota law. The statute lets them grant a new trial if new DNA evidence “would result in acquittal” when considered alongside “all other evidence” in a case.
A Rapid City judge granted 84-year-old George Luna a new trial based on that 2009 law. The Attorney General’s Office appealed, setting up Tuesday’s Supreme Court hearing in Pierre.
Tony Mangan, spokesman for the attorney general, told South Dakota Searchlight that, “to the best of our knowledge,” Luna is the only person to have been granted a new trial based on that law.
Decades of attempts
Luna has maintained his innocence in the beating deaths of his estranged wife and her mother since the crime in 1983, before DNA testing became a common factor in criminal trials. He got a life sentence in 1984. He’d appealed the initial conviction to the state Supreme Court and exhausted his other available appeals by 2004.
Between 2007 and 2015, Luna tried unsuccessfully to force the state to conduct DNA testing on evidence collected in his case, representing himself. 
South Dakota Supreme Court says father doesn’t have a right to police records about son’s death

In 2015, a lawyer for a nonprofit group filed for DNA testing on Luna’s behalf, setting in motion a series of tests that found none of Luna’s DNA on more than a dozen pieces of evidence collected from the crime scene.
The tests also found no conclusive evidence for the presence of DNA from either of the two men Luna’s initial defense team had suggested as possible “third-party” perpetrators. But the results left open the possibility that strands of hair found in one victim’s hand belonged to one of them.
A circuit court judge ordered a new trial in 2023, concluding that a new trial would likely result in an acquittal. The ruling also said Luna would be allowed to present “third-party perpetrator” evidence, which he wasn’t allowed to do in 1983.
In 2024, further DNA testing conducted by the state in response to that ruling showed that the strands of hair belonged to a female, ruling out one of the alleged third-party perpetrators.
A judge reviewed that evidence, but reached the same conclusion on the likelihood of acquittal, once again ordering a new trial. 
State: DNA adds nothing new for jury to consider
Tuesday’s arguments focused largely on the certainty of the circuit judge’s conclusion about the likelihood of an acquittal. 
Luna was convicted based largely on a collection of circumstantial evidence, not physical evidence. That reality played into arguments from both his own lawyer and the assistant attorney general arguing against a new trial.
State’s high court says survival bunker owners can pursue eviction for gun incident

Without DNA evidence to show that another person was present at the crime scene, Assistant Attorney General Matt Templar said, there’s little Luna might be able to offer a new jury.
In 1983, prosecutors pointed to microscopic bits of glass found on Luna’s clothing to say he’d been present at the murder scene, where a window had been broken. They also pointed to what Templar called “incessant threats” by Luna against the victims in the months leading up to the murders. Luna’s alibi — that he was at a Rapid City hotel at the time of the killings — was “shaky,” Templar said.
“You put all of that together, it proves beyond a reasonable doubt that George Luna was the one that committed these murders, not some unknown third-party perpetrator,” Templar told the justices.
Because the DNA evidence shows no proof of a third-party perpetrator, Templar said its existence doesn’t amount to “compelling” proof that a jury would reach a different conclusion.
Defense: New trial warranted
Justice Patricia DeVaney pointed to that issue in her questioning of John Murphy, the Rapid City lawyer who now represents Luna.
To earn a new trial under a law linked to DNA evidence, shouldn’t the chance of success at a new trial “somehow still tie into the DNA evidence?” DeVaney asked Murphy.
Yes, Murphy said, and it does. Early rounds of DNA testing showed that Luna’s DNA wasn’t present on a towel and stain on the sink, where the killer was thought to have cleaned up after the crime. 
The new testing amounts to evidence that “expressly excluded George Luna from being present in the house,” Murphy said.
The DNA law on new trials “mandates an expansive factual review” of an entire case, he said, and that happened before Luna was granted a new trial. The judge’s order was “a 66-page, single-space report with 204 footnotes” on the evidence, he said.
The DNA evidence alone needn’t prove that another person killed Luna’s ex-wife and mother-in-law, Murphy said, for a judge to find “compelling” proof that its existence would swing a jury toward a not guilty verdict.
“The third-party perpetrator issue is kind of a red herring that’s been manufactured by the state, Murphy said. 
In his rebuttal, Templar said the first jury knew that police found none of Luna’s fingerprints at the scene and still convicted him. It’s “not unusual” for police to find no fingerprints or DNA from a suspect, or for someone to be convicted regardless.
“These results,” Templar said, referring to the DNA testing, “do nothing to contradict other credible evidence that supports his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.”

name: VTDigger
title: Burlington City Council confirms Geraci as new police chief with 10-2 vote
description:
“At this moment, I am choosing Burlington, and up to this point, Burlington is choosing me. I couldn’t be more grateful for that opportunity,” Chief Anthony Geraci said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Burlington City Council confirms Geraci as new police chief with 10-2 vote.
text:
Anthony Geraci chats with Burlington City Councilor Allie Schacter, D-East District, after being ratified as the new police chief at City Hall in Burlington on Monday, November 9, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger
BURLINGTON — Anthony Geraci started Tuesday as Burlington’s new police chief amid some concerns about accountability related to a previous position of leadership.
In a 10-2 vote after 8 p.m. Monday, the City Council confirmed Progressive Mayor Emma Mulvaney-Stanak’s appointment of Geraci, with Democratic councilors Becca Brown McKnight, Ward 6, and Evan Litwin, Ward 7, voting no.
The mayor and the majority of the council vigorously defended Geraci’s record and welcomed him on board after the vote. Mulvaney-Stanak, who introduced him to the public at a morning press conference, said the hire is among the most consequential decisions for the city and as mayor.
“Today marks what I hope will be the start of an important new chapter for the Queen City,” she said prior to the councilwide vote. 
Councilor Gene Bergman, P-Ward 2, said he has worked with many chiefs and is confident Geraci will be “an excellent choice.” 
Geraci, 49, appeared in the chamber Monday flanked by his wife and extended family, many of whom he said served in law enforcement, including his father.
He recognized that staffing, recruitment and retention are among the department’s immediate challenges and said he was drawn to Burlington because of a strong sense of community. He thanked the council and the community for the warm welcome.
“At this moment, I am choosing Burlington, and up to this point, Burlington is choosing me. I couldn’t be more grateful for that opportunity,” Geraci said. “Throughout my career, I have embraced leadership challenges, developed people, strengthened organizations, and addressed complex public safety issues. I remain committed to principled leadership and being part of meaningful solutions.” 
He has bought a house in Burlington and will draw a salary of about $185,000 a year for the initial term of his contract, which ends next October, according to city officials.
Council President Ben Traverse, D-Ward 5, who recently announced his campaign for mayor, said the comments of the evening are reflective of a community that cares deeply about the appointment, which he said comes with a mix of skepticism and support.

READ MORE

Traverse voted in favor of the appointment after saying last week that he was undecided.
Geraci, who spent much of his police career in Albany, New York, was hired as police chief in Newburgh, New York, in August 2021 after serving as chief in Watervliet, New York. He left the Newburgh department abruptly in April 2024 amid allegations of workplace discrimination. He then became the director of school safety and security for Newburgh schools but resigned in February 2025, according to News 12 Westchester.
News 12 reported that three female members of the Newburgh Police Department accused Geraci of gender discrimination, retaliation and creating a hostile work environment. It also reported that an independent probe — in which six other department members and Geraci were interviewed — ultimately found the allegations to be unfounded.
Geraci, at that time, said the investigation was closed prior to his departure from the police department. He also said news of the allegations felt “retaliatory in an effort to defame my reputation and tarnish my character.”
Burlington officials have not responded to requests for details of the incidents or the investigation that followed. 
At Monday’s council meeting, Brown McKnight said her decision not to approve the appointment was based on the workplace allegations of discrimination. She also said that no one — not the council, the mayor, the hiring committee or the recruiting professionals — has been able to review the underlying details of the claims.
“I am in no way making a judgment on anything that happened. I cannot do that because I don’t have the facts,” she said. “It could have been nothing, or it could have been something.”
Brown McKnight said she heard about favorable impressions and an agreeable personality. But she also heard about “a toxic workplace and disgruntled women.” As a result, she said, she did not believe that the city had fully vetted Geraci. 
“But that has absolutely not happened, and this is what institutional sexism looks like at every turn — another barrier prevents us from understanding what happened to the women involved,” she said, adding, “I’m really disappointed that our first-ever female mayor has brought forward a candidate with this history.”
Her comments drew the ire of Mulvaney-Stanak, who interpreted the charge as an attack on her integrity. The mayor agreed that gender discrimination claims should not be taken lightly and said, “I have vetted this personally, inside and out.”
“I really want to emphasize that IACP (the International Association of Chiefs of Police) did a deep background check,” she said, which found “no wrongdoing by any policy violation whatsoever.” 

 
Anthony Geraci speaks at City Hall in Burlington on Monday, November 9, 2026. Video by Auditi Guha/VTDigger

The IACP conducted the nationwide search that netted five candidates. Geraci was one of three out-of-state finalists.
City Councilor Melo Grant, P-Central District, who was on the 12-person hiring committee, reiterated that Geraci was deeply vetted in a process that included a polygraph test. She said she was most interested in the fact that he had helped turn around a distressed police department.Geraci restored the police department in Newburgh to full staffing and implemented strategies that led to a 50% reduction in gun violence, according to a Nov. 5 press release from the Burlington mayor’s office. He also replaced an enforcement-focused street crimes unit with a community engagement initiative in Albany that remains active, the release said.
Councilor Litwin’s no vote hinged on what he described as “a failure of the process” that led to the hire. He took issue with the time it took the mayor to begin the hiring process, although former Chief Jon Murad announced his intention to leave early in November 2024, and the length of the process. The position was posted May 18, and the hiring committee was created July 7.
“We received very little substantive updates. There were meetings that seemed quite secretive to me,” he said, adding that councilors did not have a chance to meet the finalists.
The mayor and Melo have pushed back on allegations that the process was too secretive, saying they were following the process and that top hires often have to maintain anonymity until the final stage. 
Geraci thanked Shawn Burke, who has been serving as interim chief since early 2025, and addressed other members of the department and the police union.
“I do not come to this position believing that I will have answers,” Geraci said. “I am prepared to listen, learn and lead. I will advocate for you. I will challenge you. I will support you, and I will work in partnership with you as we design a culture together that is one that is of shared vision and shared purpose.”
He said he hopes to earn the public’s trust through building meaningful relationships and working collaboratively. 
“My wish is to foster a department where community members feel comfortable approaching officers, sharing concerns and asking questions while working together to make Burlington safer,” Geraci said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Official: Moving Arkansas Medicaid expansion enrollees to new program would take more than 6 months
description: Transferring the nearly 209,000 low-income Arkansans on expanded Medicaid to a new health insurance program would take longer than the six months allowed under a temporary extension granted by the Trump administration, the state official overseeing the programs told lawmakers Tuesday. The state asked the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for a [...]
text:
Elizabeth Pitman, Director of the Division of Medical Services for Arkansas Medicaid, addresses the Human Services subcommittee of the House and Senate Public Health committees on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Transferring the nearly 209,000 low-income Arkansans on expanded Medicaid to a new health insurance program would take longer than the six months allowed under a temporary extension granted by the Trump administration, the state official overseeing the programs told lawmakers Tuesday.
The state asked the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for a two-year reprieve in August after the agency verbally denied a five-year extension of the expansion program known as Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME.
The Trump administration notified Human Services Secretary Janet Mann last week that the program will remain in effect until June 30, 2027.
The Department of Human Services wanted a two-year grace period because it would take that long to move the entire Medicaid expansion population to a managed-care program if need be, state Division of Medical Services Director Elizabeth Pitman told the Human Services subcommittee of the House and Senate Public Health committees.
Instituting fee-for-service Medicaid instead would take 12 to 18 months, Pitman said. She reiterated Mann’s past statement that nixing Medicaid expansion completely is not an option.
Arkansas officials confident people on Medicaid expansion will retain health coverage

Republican Rep. Aaron Pilkington, the subcommittee’s House chair, said formulating a new expansion model will be a high priority in the legislative session that begins in January.
Pilkington asked Pitman how many more staff the Department of Human Services would need to hire to conduct fee-for-service Medicaid. Pitman said she was unsure of the need for additional staff but knew the agency would have a higher volume of paperwork to process, such as prior authorizations.
“It’s not necessarily adding new processes,” Pitman said. “It’s just a matter of scaling those up.”
Last year’s federal tax and spending cut legislation known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act requires special Medicaid programs, such as Arkansas’ hybrid expansion, not to cost the federal government more than would be projected without them.
Arkansas’ program uses Medicaid money to purchase private insurance for low-income residents. The first-in-the-nation model was approved in 2013 as an alternative to expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act allows the state to increase its Medicaid reimbursement to the same rate as Medicare. Doing this for a fee-for-service model that covers all 208,837 Arkansans in the current expansion program would save the state between $22 million and $35 million, Pitman said. The same for a managed care model would save the state between $61 and $70 million. Pitman did not give an expected time frame for the projected savings.
Private insurer Centene announced its upcoming withdrawal from the program in July. The company’s three Medicaid expansion plans cover about 70,000 Arkansans, Pitman said, and open enrollment began last week for enrollees to get new coverage starting Jan. 1.
If Centene enrollees do not choose their own Blue Cross Blue Shield insurance plans by Sunday, the Department of Human Services will choose for them, Pitman said.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act put in place work requirements for Medicaid expansion recipients that Arkansas will start enforcing Jan. 1. Negotiations over the future of Medicaid expansion will not impact the work requirements, which apply to able-bodied Arkansans between the ages of 19 and 64, the agency said last week.
The Department of Human Services has been preemptively working to determine Medicaid enrollees’ continued eligibility before the work requirements go into effect. If the agency does not have enough information to make a determination, Pitman said, it will enlist the help of a customer service center that’s in the process of launching after lawmakers approved a three-year, $48 million contract last month.
Starting Jan. 1, the customer service center will reach out to Medicaid enrollees via phone, email or any other means of communication to get any outstanding eligibility information, Pitman said.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Case not dismissed: Doug Carter returns to court for more debate over evidence, DNA testing
description: Doug Carter came to Provo’s 4th District Court smiling big Tuesday morning, but his attorneys were frustrated.
text:
Douglas Carter, a former death row inmate who was recently released from jail after crime scene DNA doesn't match his, appears in court in Provo on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune) Douglas Stewart Carter came to Provo’s 4th District Court smiling big Tuesday, but his attorneys weren’t in the same good spirits. 
They had hoped prosecutors would move to dismiss the murder case against their client Tuesday after DNA analysis revealed that blood from the scene of Eva Olesen’s death in 1985 was not Carter’s. 
Doug Carter, twice sentenced to die, steps out from behind bars in Utah thanks to DNA analysis

The revelation was the basis for prosecutors withdrawing their intent to seek the death penalty against Carter, and for his subsequent release from jail last month after more than 40 years behind bars. 
“That should have been the opportunity to step back and say, ‘Hey, we might have gotten this wrong. We’re going to regroup, but while we regroup, we’re going to dismiss these charges,’” Carter’s defense attorney Neal Hamilton said by phone after the hearing. “There’s no statute of limitation on homicide.”
Utah County prosecutors on Tuesday were not ready to drop the case. They said they want to see results of further DNA testing Carter’s defense team is pursuing to investigate whose blood was found at the scene. They also want a judge to rule on whether a confession Carter’s attorneys say was coerced can still be considered as evidence at a new trial scheduled for next summer. 
Douglas Carter, a former death row inmate who was recently released from jail after crime scene DNA doesn’t match his, appears in court in Provo on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Pool photo by Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune)
Fourth District Judge Derek Pullan took Carter’s motion to suppress the disputed confession under advisement and said he would rule at a later date. 
The Utah Supreme Court had ordered a new trial for Carter last year, citing “intentional misconduct” on the part of investigators and prosecutors and noting a key witness was instructed “to fabricate a statement intended to show that Carter harbored a premeditated intent to commit rape on the night of the murder.”
Carter did not speak publicly about the case then or last month when he left the Utah County Jail wearing an ankle monitor. 
He sported a leather jacket Tuesday, a far cry from the shackles and jail uniform he wore in court for years. He returns to court Nov. 18.
