name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Deluzio urges local police to reject 287(g) cooperation with ICE
description: The study found nearly two-thirds of all ICE detention in the 17th Congressional District occurred in Beaver County, where the sheriff’s department and eight municipal police departments have 287(g) agreements with ICE.
text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and weapon are seen as ICE conducts a vehicle checkpoint on Georgia Avenue on Aug. 30, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Deluzio urged Pennsylvania law enforcement agencies to avoid or rescind agreements to work with federal immigration agents as he presented findings of a study of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in his western Pennsylvania district.
The study found nearly two-thirds of all ICE detentions in the 17th Congressional District occurred in Beaver County, where the sheriff’s department and eight municipal police departments have 287(g) agreements with ICE. 
The portion of Deluzio’s district in Allegheny County saw fewer ICE detentions despite having a larger population and a greater number of foreign-born residents. It also has only one police force, in Springdale, that works with ICE while two others, Coraopolis and Stowe Township, canceled their agreements, the report found. 
“One of the many things that the American people are angry about and pushing back about is Donald Trump’s mass deportation regime and ICE agents abusing American liberties at the president’s direction,” Deluzio said, noting voters spoke clearly against the “chaos and corruption” of the Trump administration in last week’s election.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The review of 209 arrests between Jan. 1 and Aug. 6 also shows most people detained have no convictions or pending charges for violent offenses or otherwise. And it revealed that ICE is hiding data from the public, including why people were detained under 287(g) in places where local police have no such agreement.
“All of us in western Pennsylvania and across the country have the right to clear and complete information about what is happening in our neighborhoods and the departments or agencies funded with public money that are responsible for carrying them out,” Deluzio said.
ICE enforcement around healthcare facilities in Pa. leads to fears about immigrants who need care

Named for the section of the federal Immigration and Nationality Act, 287(g) agreements have police assist ICE in identifying, arresting and removing immigrants. There are 146 local police agencies that have agreements with ICE and the number has nearly doubled in the last six months, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported last week. 
The Pennsylvania State Police does not have an agreement with ICE.
Jaime Martinez, founder and executive director of the immigration rights group Frontline Dignity, noted that behind the numbers the report reveals are Pittsburgh-area residents who have been directly affected by ICE. 
He cited the case of a 13-year-old girl who was detained alongside her  father for several days while family members had no information about their whereabouts. And Martinez described the ordeal of a Pitcairn father who was held while his wife gave birth to their son.
“His 5-year-old daughter was left afraid that her parents might disappear again,” Martinez said, adding that the trauma of seeing a parent detained follows children and families. “These are our neighbors, and the consequences of immigration enforcement extend far beyond the immediate moment of detention.”
Frontline Dignity has trained more than 3,000 people to lawfully recognize, document and respond to immigration enforcement. Through that work, the organization saw what is happening in communities every day and what the government is reporting. 
By comparing what its observers documented and federal detention records, Frontline Dignity identified patterns that demanded further scrutiny, Martinez said. It took its initial analysis to Deluzio’s office, which conducted its own analysis and produced the report. 
Among the report’s other findings:

Out of the 209 detentions, 112 were coded under Section 287(g), meaning local law enforcement was involved.
140 of the 209 people detained had no criminal record or pending charges.
And among the 112 detentions under 287(g), 91 people had no record or pending charges. 

Martinez said the involvement of local law enforcement in immigration enforcement also raises the question of whether police are engaging in racial profiling. He noted that community members have reported police repeatedly stopping white construction vans carrying people to work.
“According to those accounts, individuals have been turned over to ICE without receiving a clear explanation as to why they were stopped,” Martinez said, adding that Frontline Dignity has been unable to confirm the details of every stop. “No one should have to wonder whether the vehicle they drive, or the language they speak, or the color of their skin makes them a target.”
Deluzio added that detentions listed under 287(g) that occurred in municipalities with no agreement should be further investigated to determine which departments and officers were involved. 
“We should know which local law enforcement is engaged in this,” he said. “Are they outside their jurisdiction? Are they patrolling and being pulled away from their municipality, where they have responsibilities in local law enforcement, which again, I think, is the prime job of local law enforcement.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Greater Yellowstone grizzly bear deaths spike past previous record
description: In Yellowstone National Park and areas just outside the park, a record number of at least 81 grizzly bears have died in 2026, mostly at the hands of humans.  That’s according to preliminary data, through Nov. 10, released by the U.S. Geological Survey and a group of researchers that focus on the species across the […]
text:
Grizzly bears in the lower 48 states are federally protected as a threatened species. A new memo from U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik says that endangered animals may be killed as long as the action was not “intentionally directed at a particular animal or animals.” (Photo courtesy of Terry Tollefsbol/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)In Yellowstone National Park and areas just outside the park, a record number of at least 81 grizzly bears have died in 2026, mostly at the hands of humans. 
That’s according to preliminary data, through Nov. 10, released by the U.S. Geological Survey and a group of researchers that focus on the species across the Rocky Mountain region. 
The database, documented by the Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team, lists 84 grizzly mortalities this year, including one death dated to last fall and two live removals of bears sent to zoos. The number is the highest documented known and likely grizzly mortalities in a calendar year on record. 
In 2025, published USGS data listed 72 known or probable grizzly deaths, though the numbers are routinely updated as wildlife managers continue to investigate some incidents.
With two months left in the year, 2026 is at least a 50% increase from the 10-year average of 54 deaths in the region, and a 12.5% jump from the last two years. 
Grizzly bears are classified as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act, though members of Congress have pushed to delist them in recent years. 
 Federal shifts

This summer, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum journeyed to Montana to announce a proposed rule shifting management of grizzly bears from federal to state control, a long-time goal of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming — the three states with the highest grizzly concentrations. 
A population of more than 2,000 grizzlies lives along the Continental Divide, most heavily concentrated in two areas — around Glacier National Park and the Bob Marshall Wilderness area, and Yellowstone National Park. 
Under the proposed rule, grizzlies would remain under threatened status under the Endangered Species Act, but a new tiered system would allow more management authority to state wildlife agencies in the Greater Yellowstone and Continental Divide ecosystems — essentially expanding the allowable killing of bears by wildlife managers. 
The proposed rule would not authorize a hunting season.  
Idaho Gov. Brad Little, Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte, Wyoming Gov Mark Gordon, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announce a rule to shift grizzly bear management toward states. Courtesy photo
Montana’s all-Republican federal delegation and governor have long-supported delisting grizzly bears and support the proposed rule, while wildlife and conservation organizations decried it as a slippery slope to lowering the population. 
Many of those groups raised concerns over the high mortality rate seen around Yellowstone this year as well, saying such an increase in deaths should be a reason to slow down the shift to state management. 
“Record high grizzly deaths show bears need more protection, not less, as they continue expanding their range and attempt to reoccupy the places they once freely roamed,” said Adam Rissien, rewilding manager with WildEarth Guardians. “It is no surprise conflicts are increasing and more grizzlies are getting killed. Bears are having to search for more food in more places because of shorter winters, more severe summer heat and drought, and a steep drop in whitebark pine nuts that they’ve historically relied on for a substantial portion of their fall diet.”
Among the documented mortalities in the Yellowstone area, more than 50 were attributed to humans, including 11 killed by vehicles, two that drowned in a man-made canal, one killed in self-defense and one attributed to a human when a tracking collar was found with no carcass. 
Wildlife agency officials killed 36 “problem bears” that had either killed cattle, damaged crops or become habituated to humans or food rewards. 
“Dead grizzlies are the predictable price of putting more cattle in grizzly country,” said Patrick Kelly, Montana director for Western Watersheds Project. “Livestock conflict has killed more Greater Yellowstone grizzlies this year than any other cause, yet the Trump administration is pushing national forests across the region to restock vacant grazing allotments, and several already have.”
Matthew Gould, the Interagency Grizzly Bear Study Team’s leader, told the Daily Montanan last year that record-high number of bears in the region, and record crowds flocking to public lands, including Yellowstone, create more instances of bears and humans coming into conflict. 
Of the 84 grizzly deaths listed, 15 are still under investigation. 
 In the 406

In Montana, the state department of Fish, Wildlife and Parks has its own grizzly mortality information dashboard, launched in 2024, to track human-caused grizzly deaths. 
FWP said in a news release at the time that the dashboard is part of an effort to increase transparency, educate Montanans on why grizzlies are killed or die when they are currently federally protected, and to prove that the state is ready to manage grizzly bears on its own.
According to the dashboard, there have been 41 human-related grizzly mortalities this year, up from 32 in 2025. Some of those deaths overlap with the data from the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem. 
Similar to that data, the majority of deaths are human-related. 
Eleven recorded deaths were due to vehicle collisions, one was considered self-defense, four a case of mistaken identity, and 15 were conflict management removals.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Prediction market Kalshi registers as New Mexico lobbyist employer ahead of legislative session
description: Amid ongoing litigation with New Mexico pueblos, online prediction market Kalshi has registered as a lobbyist employer ahead of next year’s legislative session.
text:
Kalshi, the online prediction market currently fighting New Mexico tribal governments in federal court, filed Aug. 24, 2026, as a lobbyist employer with the New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Amid ongoing litigation with New Mexico pueblos, online prediction market Kalshi has registered as a lobbyist employer ahead of next year’s legislative session.
According to New Mexico Secretary of State’s Office filings, Kalshi officials registered in late August as a lobbyist employer, which state law requires for organizations or businesses that intend to lobby elected officials or lawmakers. 
The company has not yet hired a New Mexico lobbyist, and its most-recent filings in early October show it has not yet spent any money on lobbying activities in the state. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The filing does not say which issues or legislation the company seeks to influence at the 60-day legislative session beginning Jan. 19. State law does not require lobbyists to disclose that information. 
Blake Bee, Kalshi’s director of state relations, signed the form on the company’s behalf and listed an address that corresponds to a UPS store in Glendale, Ariz. Bee did not respond to Source NM’s phone call seeking comment Tuesday. 
In May, the Pojoaque, Sandia and Isleta Pueblos, along with the Mescalero Apache Tribe, alleged in federal court that Kalshi violates tribal gaming compacts and federal law by providing anyone over age 18 access to sports gambling in New Mexico.
Under existing state gaming compacts and federal law, only people aged 21 and over in New Mexico can place bets on sports in person at tribally owned casinos. The plaintiffs argue that Kalshi is causing irreparable harm to tribal governments, which rely on gambling revenues to fund schools and other services.
Kalshi’s lawyers have countered that the federal Commodities Exchange Act trumps the federal  Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, as well as state gaming compacts, and contends the federal Commodities Futures Trading Commission has sole authority for regulating the platform.
Still, Kalshi has come under increasing scrutiny from state and tribal governments that allege the platform is undermining their gambling laws. Some states have sought to regulate the company’s activities and others have sued it in federal and state court. 
In response, Kalshi, its competitor Polymarket and the Coalition for Prediction Markets have spent at least $3 million on lobbying and campaign contributions across the federal and state levels in recent months, according to an analysis by Open Secrets, a nonpartisan research organization tracking money in politics.
New Mexico tribe and pueblos wrap up case that Kalshi sports betting hurts their sovereignty

In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick did not respond to Source NM’s questions about which legislation or issues Kalshi might seek to influence in New Mexico, or whether it intended to hire a local lobbyist. Instead, she reiterated the company’s contention that New Mexico and other states have no legal authority to regulate it. 
“As a national derivatives market overseen by the CFTC, Kalshi answers to federal law,” she said. “However, states like New Mexico can still play a part within the federal framework.”
New Mexico Rep. Derrick Lente (D-Sandia Pueblo) the chair of the state Legislature’s House Taxation and Finance Committee, attended closing arguments in federal court in September in the plaintiffs’ lawsuit against Kalshi and has been working closely with gaming tribes on the issue. 
He said he’s meeting with the New Mexico Coalition of Gaming Tribes next week to discuss, among other issues, how the Legislature might address prediction markets’ operations.
Leaders of tribal governments in the gaming coalition could not be reached Tuesday. Their lawsuit remains pending in federal court. 
Lente told Source NM on Tuesday that he was not aware Kalshi had registered as a lobbyist employer, but said the news was not unexpected given the proliferation of the markets and amount of revenue they generate. 
“It does not surprise me that they would have some paid lobbyists come through now,” Lente said. “I think the move to online gaming is going to be much more pushed upon states that have withheld for the sake of supporting tribal gaming compacts.”

name: VTDigger
title: Annual count finds slight decline in homelessness in Vermont
description:
While the January 2026 point-in-time count found a modest decrease in the number of people experiencing homelessness overall, it registered a jump in the number of unhoused children and an increase in people without shelter.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Annual count finds slight decline in homelessness in Vermont .
text:
The cold weather shelter at the Miller Center in Burlington in Jan. 2026. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger.
For the second year running, an annual tally found a modest decrease in the number of people experiencing homelessness in Vermont. 
“On its face, this is an encouraging finding. We certainly want to see fewer people experiencing homelessness in Vermont, and any movement in that direction is worth acknowledging,” said Kim Anetsberger, director of the Lamoille Community House and co-chair of the Balance of State Continuum of Care, at a press conference revealing the January count’s results on Tuesday. 
But the tally, designed to be a yearly snapshot rather than a comprehensive census of everyone experiencing homelessness throughout a given year, gives limited insight, she added.
“We think it’s important to exercise caution before interpreting this decrease as evidence that Vermont is making meaningful progress towards ending homelessness,” Anetsberger said.
The yearly point-in-time count is a federally mandated effort to tally each person experiencing homelessness nationwide on a single night each winter. The Vermont count registered 3,286 people in January of 2026, a nearly 3% decline from the 2025 tally, according to a report released Tuesday.
The drop mirrors a national trend: The 2026 count found a more than 6% decrease in homelessness across the country, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said last week. 
In the years following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, Vermont saw a rapid rise in homelessness. That happened as the state experienced skyrocketing housing prices and razor-thing rental vacancies. But that white-hot housing market has now cooled off somewhat, and the state has added more subsidized housing thanks to COVID-era federal aid.   
Travis Poulin, the community action network director for the Champlain Valley Office of Economic Opportunity and co-chair of the Chittenden County Homeless Alliance, said service providers have made some progress in moving unhoused people into homes.
“Our efforts at trying to help people secure stable housing are working – albeit, more slowly than we would like,” Poulin said.
Even as the Vermont count found fewer people experiencing homelessness overall in January, it registered an uptick in the number of people living without shelter – meaning they were sleeping in a vehicle or outdoors. 
The count tallied 284 people experiencing unsheltered homelessness last January, a 5% jump from the year prior, with Chittenden County seeing the largest increase. 
The number of people sleeping outside in the state has more than doubled since before the pandemic, according to previous point-in-time count data. Advocates have blamed that uptick on the ongoing scale-back of the state’s motel voucher program, which has historically provided an option for unhoused people when traditional community-based shelters are full.
This year’s count also found a rise in homelessness among children. The number of unhoused people under the age of 18 jumped by 5% as of the 2026 count. The 667 children identified in the tally represent nearly one in five of all people experiencing homelessness in Vermont.
“Families are increasingly struggling to find housing that is both affordable and large enough to accommodate their households. At the same time, the cost of living continues to rise, and many families simply don’t have the financial resources or cushion to withstand a job loss, unexpected expenses, rent increases, or other crises,” said Taylor Thibault, associate director of homelessness prevention initiatives at Champlain Housing Trust and co-chair of the Chittenden County Homeless Alliance. 
The point-in-time count is generally regarded as a low estimate of the number of people experiencing homelessness. Accurately counting people sleeping outdoors is notoriously difficult, particularly in Vermont’s rural setting, and cold weather might drive people into less visible places or to take emergency measures like pooling funds for a motel room, the report’s authors note. 
And because of HUD’s relatively narrow definition of homelessness, the count does not include people who are couch-surfing or doubling up with relatives. Other tallies of homelessness in the Green Mountain State point to a larger population struggling to maintain stable housing. 
The Vermont Agency of Education counted close to 1,700 students experiencing homelessness in Vermont public schools during the 2024-2025 school year, the latest data available. 
The state’s “Coordinated Entry” system, which homeless service providers use to streamline assistance for unhoused people, registered nearly 4,900 individuals with completed assessments as of October. 
Still, the consistent January count offers a helpful yearly benchmark to track trends over time and understand who is experiencing homelessness in Vermont. 
The 2026 tally found that more than a third of unhoused people in the state report living with a serious mental illness. About 18% of people counted in the survey said they experience substance use disorder. 
The report also shows a persistent racial disparity among people experiencing homelessness in Vermont. The 2026 count found a 9% increase in homelessness among people who identify as Black, Indigenous, and people of color. 
Vermont is making gains in easing homelessness among certain populations, according to this year’s count. The tally found that homelessness among veterans declined by 17%, mirroring national trends in recent years. The number of unaccompanied youth experiencing homelessness also fell.
While the number of unhoused people in the Green Mountain State is comparatively small, the annual point-in-time count has found that Vermont’s rate of homelessness consistently rivals those of states like New York, Oregon and California.
The results come as state leaders are in the middle of overhauling Vermont’s homelessness response system, an effort that began in September and has included further reducing the scale of the state’s motel voucher program. That program provided shelter for the majority of unhoused Vermonters at the time of January’s tally.
“As Vermont continues to implement changes to its emergency housing system, we need to be thoughtful about what happens when shelter resources are reduced or changed without sufficient alternatives available,” said Chad Simmons, director of the Housing and Homelessness Alliance of Vermont.
The report’s authors also called for the creation of more affordable housing options for people with extremely low incomes, a more robust effort to prevent homelessness through rental aid and eviction mediation, and an expansion of behavioral health and supportive services.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC preservationists worry federal permitting bill could make saving historic sites more difficult
description: The bill is intended to speed up permitting processes, but preservation groups are opposed because of concerns about taking away local input.
text:
A trumpeter plays at Florence National Cemetery during a burial service for a skeleton uncovered during an archaeological survey to expand the cemetery on May 16, 2010. (Photo courtesy of Friends of Florence Stockade)Portions of a federal bill meant to speed up permitting could make saving South Carolina’s historic sites more difficult, state preservationists said ahead of an expected vote on the bill this week.
A massive regulatory bill advanced in the U.S. Senate on Monday in a technical vote that sent the proposal to the floor. Advocates for preserving historic sites said a section of the bill could claw back protections written in federal law 60 years ago that require government agencies to consult with local communities before interfering with potentially significant areas.
The bill’s supporters say it will improve efficiency in government permitting, allowing energy-related projects, such as gas plants, oil drilling, and wind and solar projects, to face fewer delays.
“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth,” U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, a West Virginia Republican and the bill’s main sponsor, said in a news release. The three co-sponsors are from New Mexico, Rhode Island and Utah.
Preservation advocates are worried about a section of the nearly 500-page bill that would change the process for deciding when a project affects culturally or historically significant areas.
Under those changes to the 1966 National Historic Preservation Act, federal projects could move forward with little input from surrounding communities, say preservationists opposed to the changes.

“Essentially, the opportunity for public input would be stripped,” said John Sherrer, director of preservation for Historic Columbia.
More than a dozen South Carolina preservation groups signed onto a letter opposing the project, joining more than 600 similar groups nationwide.
What does the bill do?
Under the National Historic Preservation Act, any project using federal money has to go through a review process to make sure changes won’t affect any nearby cultural or historic resources.
That could mean demolishing historic buildings, developing unmarked cemeteries or battlefields, or building projects that conflict with an area’s appearance, said Brian Turner, president of the Preservation Society of Charleston.
In its effort to speed up the permitting process, the bill would remove much of the local input, instead leaving decisions as to whether an area is significant up to the federal agency, said James Stewart, president of the Archaeological Society of South Carolina.

An aerial photo of the Charleston peninsula, with White Point Garden and The Battery at the southern tip, looking up the Cooper River to the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge. (Photo by Vanessa Kauffmann/Courtesy of Preservation Society of Charleston)

The proposal requires input from neighbors only if the project is under “substantial federal control,” which is not defined.
Getting detailed regulations explaining which projects would be covered could take years and introduce confusion into the process, Turner said.
“Our concern is that this defeats the very purpose of the bill, to create so much unpredictability and revision to an existing process,” he said.
When building new projects, federal agencies wouldn’t have to take into account the character of the area, opening up the possibility of creating eyesores in otherwise historic areas, Turner said.
Take, for instance, the sea wall designed to protect Charleston from storm surges and flooding. The city needed help to pay for the roughly $1.3 billion project along The Battery at the southern end of the peninsula. But that doesn’t mean people should have to look at a concrete wall instead of the harbor, Turner said.
“We would expect that the (Army Corps of Engineers), when it comes, doesn’t just design a big concrete barrier around the peninsula but instead makes it more aesthetically arranged with our historic district,” Turner said.
Cutting locals out of the process could mean losing stories federal officials wouldn’t otherwise know about, Stewart said.
“You don’t have the context to say, ‘This is where this important historical event occurred,’” he said.
Preservationists hope SC battlefield’s designation as endangered will boost attention

The changes might also make it so federal officials don’t have to consider portions of sprawling battlefields when building new projects, he said.
Because battlegrounds generally aren’t well-marked, it’s hard to say where an archaeologist might find important artifacts or markers without first doing a survey, Stewart said.
The same is true of many small, historic cemeteries, he said. Sometimes, those types of places remain undiscovered until a project such as a road widening starts and officials uncover remains or artifacts.
Under the proposed changes, “you’re going to have cemeteries and sites that are going to be graded and paved over all over the state,” Stewart said.
How the federal law has been used in SC
During a planned 10-acre expansion of the Florence National Cemetery in 2005, local advocates for historic preservation raised concerns that work might interfere with unmarked portions of a Confederate prison camp.
Under the federal law, state and federal officials organized a survey of the area.
Archaeologists unearthed hundreds of previously unmarked features of the prison camp for Union soldiers, including dropped buttons, fences and poles giving a clearer idea of the stockade’s dimensions, and a human skeleton, said John Andrews, president of Friends of the Florence Stockade.
Without the survey, “those things would have been lost,” Andrews said. “Nobody would have found them, or they would have been ignored.”
Scientists identify a soldier who died in the 1780 Battle of Camden, hold out hope of naming others

Local historical groups buried the skeleton in an unmarked grave, giving respect to the unidentified soldier, Andrews said.
And the findings of the survey helped researchers better understand what might have happened at the stockade, where the Confederate Army held as many as 15,000 captured Union soldiers, thousands of whom died there.
“That information is important to understanding the period and understanding how men on both sides of this conflict lived and how they survived or didn’t survive during that period,” Andrews said.
The Florence stockade isn’t much of a tourist attraction, but it’s still important to save, Andrews said.
“History’s not always pleasant,” he said. “How do you honor those people who died there? You need to preserve that site.”
The recovery of the H.L. Hunley, a Confederate submarine, was also done under the preservation law.
Because the submarine was considered a historic artifact, the Navy had to consult with local partners when moving and preserving the ship to ensure as little damage as possible, according to the Preservation Society of Charleston.
Other examples of where the federal law played an important role include the city of Columbia’s decision in 2021 to raze two crumbling public housing complexes, Gonzales Gardens and Allen Benedict Court, Sherrer said.
The two complexes were among the first public housing complexes in the country, though they had grown dated and dangerous over time. In 2019, two men died of carbon monoxide poisoning at Allen Benedict Court due to a faulty furnace.
Because federal agencies had to give local historians a heads up before demolishing the property, Historic Columbia researchers saved photographs of the complexes, collected stories from former residents, and created a website detailing the history of public housing in the city.
Those sorts of stories, which don’t seem important to outsiders but matter a lot to people in the community, are the ones that might get lost without public input, Sherrer said.
“What if you grew up in an area and that area was totally erased because of some project using federal funds, which you contributed to with your tax dollars, and you had no say-so in that?” he said.
That happened in the early 1950s, after the federal government took 310 square miles from Barnwell, Aiken and Allendale counties to create the Savannah River Plant to produce nuclear materials for bombs.
In 1950, about 6,000 people were given 15 months to evacuate from small towns before they were wiped off the map. About 6,000 graves were also moved. Local officials’ post-Cold War efforts to get some of the land back have failed.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Colom leads Hyde-Smith by 2,604 votes in Mississippi Senate race as final Hinds County tally looms
description: Deputy clerk Devin Black, right, assists Cheryl McGee and Johnny McGee Sr., who came to verify their identification after voting by affidavit on Election Day, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson.
text:
All eyes remained fixated on the Hinds County Election Commission Tuesday, hoping that outstanding ballots from the area could determine the outcome of a nail-bitter U.S. Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. 
The Associated Press late Tuesday afternoon reported that Colom led Hyde-Smith by 2,604  votes with around 97% of the vote counted, but it still has not called the race.   
Tuesday was the deadline for voters who had to cast affidavit ballots on Election Day because of issues with providing valid photo identification to return to their local circuit clerks’ offices and present a valid form of ID to “cure” their ballot. 
LIVE: 2026 Mississippi election results
It was also the deadline for local election officials to receive late-arriving, mail-in absentee ballots that were postmarked by Election Day. 
Counties have until Friday to transmit their official election results to Secretary of State Michael Watson’s office, but officials in Hinds County, the state’s largest county and a Democratic stronghold, are expected to upload the results of their outstanding affidavit ballots on Wednesday, an attorney for the county told Mississippi Today. 
Hyde-Smith and Colom each on Tuesday continued to say they have a path to victory. 
Hyde-Smith, notorious for refusing to answer reporters’ questions in Capitol hallways, returned to Washington on Monday and initially declined to answer questions. On Tuesday she briefly told the media she was “feeling very optimistic” about winning reelection but refused to elaborate on the math behind her optimism. 
Colom, at an event thanking Hinds County Sheriff’s Department deputies, said he believed that once Hinds County reports the remainder of its ballots, it will likely be enough for him to be declared the winner. 
“The reality is she can’t point to a direction where she has a possibility to win, right?” Colom said of Hyde-Smith. “If she thinks she truly has the ability to win, explain how.” 
U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom, center, takes a photo with law enforcement officers after his news conference at the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
As election commissioners across the state continued to process the thousands of remaining affidavit ballots by hand, scores of election attorneys and a coalition of community and advocacy organizations that work on voting rights monitored the process.
Max Meyers, an attorney with the NAACP, said at an event on Monday night that he had not found any major issues with how election commissioners were processing the ballots and that they were continuing to “do their jobs.”
“I haven’t had to send any angry letters, which has been great,” Meyers said. “I haven’t had to set foot in a courtroom, which is lovely.” 
After county officials certify the election results, it’s possible that a campaign or political party could file litigation to contest the results or ask for a recount. 
Mike Hurst, chairman of the Mississippi GOP and general counsel to the Republican National Committee, previously said at a press conference that the party will “fight like hell” to ensure every legal ballot cast is counted and is prepared to “avail ourselves of every legal resource” available.
Colom said that Hyde-Smith needs to “accept the will of the voters,” but he’s also prepared to litigate.  
It’s unclear how litigation would play out. Mississippi has no recount law, and there is no clear process spelled out in state law for someone to challenge the results of a general election for a state office.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: LEAP District land purchase faces pushback over company’s ties to nuclear power development
description: A California company’s plans for a medical radiopharmaceuticals plant in the central Indiana LEAP District is facing questions over whether it could possibly open the door for a nuclear power generation site.
text:
Rachel Wolverton, of Protect Pike Township, carries signs protesting the LEAP District ahead of a State Budget Committee touching on the controversial development on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)A California company’s plans for a medical radiopharmaceuticals plant in the central Indiana LEAP District is facing questions over whether it could possibly open the door for a nuclear power generation site.
A contract between the Indiana Economic Development Corp. and a subsidiary of Oklo Inc. for land purchases lists several possible uses for the site near Lebanon, including “nuclear power generation, radioisotope production, research and development.”
Democratic legislators challenged an IEDC official during a State Budget Committee meeting Tuesday over the company’s intentions during discussion of the agency’s request for $20 million toward expanding the LEAP District by 185 acres for the project.
Indiana Economic Development Corp. Senior Vice President Mark Wasky (Provided by IEDC)
Mark Wasky, the IEDC’s senior vice president, told the committee that discussions with Oklo had “focused on radioisotopes,” which are medications that contain a small amount of a radioactive substance.
That did not satisfy Democratic legislators about the future options for the company that describes itself on its website as an “advanced nuclear technology company developing fast fission power plants” along with “building a domestic supply chain for critical isotopes and advanced nuclear fuel recycling capabilities.”
“Can you look us in the eye and say that you’re not going to come back over here and tell us that there will be nuclear generation discussion by that project that could feed into data centers into the LEAP project?” asked Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis.
Wasky replied that nuclear power plants had not been discussed with the IEDC.
“I can’t say today whether or not those conversations may occur in the future, but we have not had any conversations about building power to serve the data center within the LEAP District,” Wasky said.
A few LEAP District opponents protested outside Tuesday’s committee meeting. The district aimed at attracting high-tech businesses now spans some 6,700 acres and has faced persistent public criticism as the state has poured about $1 billion into its development.
Wasky said Oklo’s project would still need to gain approval from Lebanon city and zoning officials before proceeding with construction.
But Rep. Ed DeLaney, D-Indianapolis, criticized what he described as insufficient public disclosure about the development proposal, which was listed on the Budget Committee’s agenda as “Project Phoenix.”
Bigfoot Metals IEDC agreement
 
“This is not what people would call a confidence building method and that’s a real problem,” DeLaney told Wasky. “We need confidence in the IEDC.”
Santa Clara, California-based Oklo did not immediately comment to the Capital Chronicle about its plans for the Indiana site.
The Budget Committee voted 4-1 to approve the IEDC’s request, with support coming from Sens. Ryan Misher, R-Mishawaka, and David Niezgodski, D-South Bend; Rep. Jeff Thompson, R-Lizton, and State Budget Director Chad Ranney.
Rep. Greg Porter, D-Indianapolis, voted against approval, joining the objections from Qaddoura and DeLaney, who are non-voting members of the committee.
Porter said he saw no harm in waiting until the committee’s next meeting in December to take action for greater transparency.
“I’m asking that we stop this or slow it down,” Porter said. “They can come back and look at it again.”

name: VTDigger
title: A broken heart, and a strong backbone
description:
Vietnam veteran Garry DuFour discusses the archive he built, its significance, and why forgetting is the true enemy.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A broken heart, and a strong backbone.
text:
Veterans’ Advocate Garry DuFour examines a 1980s map that details the number of Veterans Administration locations available in each section of the country. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Vermont News and Media

This story by Danielle M. Crosier was first published in the Bennington Banner on Nov. 9, 2026.
PAWLET — In 1968, Garry DuFour was drafted into a war that he strongly opposed. More than half a century later, he has found that he never stopped serving. Disillusioned from the start, DuFour’s service became a private life dedicated to investigation, public action, and revealing the truth behind lies and cover ups. And, in the process, he has devoted himself to preserving the accounts of veterans who, he believes, were ignored and mistreated at the hands of his government. 
Now, after many years of heart and back trouble, DuFour is confronting a question that worries him deeply — his own looming mortality, and who will care for the archives and the truths that he has amassed when he is gone?
The skeptical soldier
Before Garry DuFour became a keeper of other veterans’ stories, he was a young man who did not want to go to war. Drafted into the Army in 1968, despite opposing the Vietnam War, DuFour said that he only ever wanted one thing — to go to Canada and marry his girlfriend. Instead, he did his due diligence and stepped up to serve.
Even today, the futility of the war still hangs heavy on him, “Vietnam was a lie,” said DuFour. “We didn’t belong there. It was a civil war.”
Serving with the 101st Airborne in Vietnam and earning a Bronze Star, DuFour said that he learned to rapidly adapt to military life, but he never lost his skepticism. That persistent instinct to think and to question what powerful institutions say — and to ask what happened to the people expected to obey — would shape nearly all of his later work. 
DuFour’s story is not only about what he says he found in veterans’ records; it is also about why he kept looking — it is about the fact that the people behind those records were still alive, still struggling, and often still trying to be believed.
From Washington to veterans’ accounts
After returning from Vietnam, DuFour’s path led to Washington, D.C. Working in the U.S. Senate Committee on Veterans Affairs, and later as a national correspondent for the Stars and Stripes National Tribune, DuFour said that he was appointed as an adviser in the Agent Orange lawsuit distribution process. And — that started it all.
The documents that he had organized in piles in his living room — letters, credentials, clippings, and congressional materials — span those years and more. They trace a life that moved from military service into the work of reporting on, and advocating for, those who served. Over the years, DuFour’s advocacy developed across multiple subject areas, including Agent Orange, LSD trials, and “atomic veterans” (service members involved in nuclear weapons testing), and DuFour said that he first encountered information on “atomic veterans” while working with veterans’ correspondence.
“I was shocked when I found out about them,” he recalled. “I didn’t know a darn thing about it [before that].”
What began as a shocking secret turned into a long effort to gather and to preserve — and later, to validate — as the government denied that the events had ever occurred. DuFour said that he read mail that had been directed to the committee, copied the records, and kept the veterans’ letters. He described making copies of official documents that detailed the testing in Washington and carrying them out of the Capitol, slid beneath the front of his shirt as he came and went throughout the day. “I knew it was so hot,” he said of the material that he held close to his chest. To DuFour, it was proof.

DuFour explains his shock at the revelation, and his efforts and desire to secure the evidence. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Vermont News and Media

Then, he said, he put the papers away for 32 years. When he brought them out again, he began contacting television stations and veterans, “I knew I had some hot stuff,” he said, shaking his head. “These men — so many men.” 
He picked up a book and began flipping through the pages of testing sites, dates, and details. He pointed to the numbers — 1047 “volunteers” observed Operation Teapot, with 24 listed as “troop participation” — Shot “Wasp” on February 18, 1955, with a 1 kt explosion; Shot “Turk” on February 22, 1955, with a 43 kt explosion; Shot “Moth” — and more. That was just three pages in a thick binder of nuclear tests. And DuFour hung his head, adding that a longtime friendship had developed with one of the service members involved in this testing — Hank Bolden.
DuFour’s sense of purpose is plain in the way that he spoke about the work that he has done to provide evidence to the veterans whose stories have not been believed. 
“Atomic Veterans — my baby,” he said, holding the book and placing a hand on yet another stack of files and correspondence. Firmly, he believes that this matters — still. The papers that he has amassed are not simply a collection to him. They are a way to reveal what was hidden, and ensure that what was experienced remains visible — and a way, he believes, to challenge accounts that minimized what veterans went through while they served.

DuFour points to one of the items that he has in his archives, recalling a conversation that he had with the service member standing on the far left. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Vermont News and Media

The archive — and what DuFour believes that it shows
The collection in DuFour’s home is crowded across tables and seating areas and during the interview he moved from one document to another — the volume that he called the “Bible” of U.S. nuclear testing, survey materials, veterans’ letters, government records, and even newspaper clippings.
DuFour, placing a hand once again on the “Bible,” said that the volume of documents details more than 2,000 U.S. nuclear tests that utilized the “volunteer” efforts of about 250,000 soldiers, as well as some civilians. 
He pointed to materials that, in his view, show gaps in protection, monitoring, and accountability — including the limits of dosimeter badges and the failure to account for some forms of exposure — and DuFore repeatedly made the case that the archives matter. They are a historical record. They are accessible to the public, through him. They detail a system of abuse of power. They are proof of what was initially a cover-up. And, they serve as a reminder of a lesson that should not be repeated.
DuFour’s collection also includes records related to Agent Orange. DuFour pulled out a congressional update, and pointed to a paragraph — one that he said he wrote, based on his own work with veterans. The passage describes veterans reporting indifferent treatment during examinations, and concerns that physicians did not know what to look for. One veteran, the text says, feared retaliation for participating in a simple survey.
In his work gathering physicals and working with surveys that were distributed through veterans’ organizations, DuFour said that the records contain reports of symptoms and medical problems. The value of those materials, he suggested, is not that every document answers every question. It is that they preserve what veterans reported, and how they were treated when they sought help.
Identifying a pattern of institutions failing to protect veterans, or take their accounts seriously, DuFour’s collection indicates that there was a purposeful effort to bury the truth and deny medical coverage to damaged veterans. 
For DuFour, the larger pattern is a failure to value the people asked to serve — and, afterward, to listen to them. He believes the documents help to establish a history that could otherwise be denied or forgotten. Asked what he had uncovered, he answered, “The trend is — look what happened, and look what they did.” He then described the letters as testimonials of those trying to document their own service and its consequences. 
“I have so many letters here from veterans saying, ‘This is what I did. This is what it did to me,’” he said. “And — there’s the evidence.” 
DuFour is clear that not every case that he has documented could be considered deliberate experimentation. 
When asked whether examples such as asbestos and lead exposure meant veterans were treated as guinea pigs (as he had earlier defined those who participated in atomic testing), he called some situations “severe carelessness.” 
The distinction matters. His archive covers different events, different risks, and different claims — and each requires its own evidence. What connects them for DuFour is a concern about whether the people in uniform were valued and protected, and whether anyone listened when they said something had gone wrong.

DuFour spoke about the Agent Orange survey that was distributed and collected at VA sites across the country. Many of his tallies from those surveys were collected and saved in his archives, keeping the recorded answers alive and available to those interested in finding out more about the veteran experience. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Vermont News and Media

A friend on the phone
That concern became tangible when DuFour reached for his phone, and called his friend Hank Bolden. He placed the phone on speaker, and introduced the atomic veteran that he had known for years. Bolden described his own account of being taken to a Nevada test site without knowing what would happen, and of later struggling to prove that he had been there at all — and that the test had been a reality, after his and other’s military records had been lost. 
DuFour prompted Bolden to tell his story, and he listened as Bolden described what he remembered — and answered questions that were posed. The conversation was not only an interview between a reporter and a source; it was also a call between two old friends.
“I’ll see you again,” DuFour called out, at the end of the call, and the two exchanged pleasantries with a commitment to catch up again soon.
That exchange carried the human stakes of DuFour’s work. Behind the documents are the military personnel who served under orders, suffered real consequences as a result, lived with uncertainty about their health, went uncovered for medical care, and sometimes had to assemble their own proof. 
Behind DuFour’s archive are real-life relationships that were built by years of sharing those accounts. The work could be defined as an act of defiance, but it is also an act of care — of listening, of remembering, and of refusing to let someone’s experience become a forgotten page.
A heart that has been broken, and restarted – again and again
DuFour’s own body has become another reminder of how fragile time can be. He described a serious heart episode in 2023, noting, “I died, and they brought me back.” Later, he confided that he had undergone 33 cardioversions, in all, and he spoke about mortality without pretending that it frightened him, “After all this, I am not scared to die,” he said. 
One thought, though, does trouble him — what will happen to the research that he has amassed?
“That worries me — that does worry me,” DuFour said, adding that he has no family left. He brought up the name of another friend — a newer acquaintance than Bolden, and one who has made it a point to secure the stories of veterans. He is hoping that this individual might now help him preserve and organize the larger collection — and this was a possibility, not a settled plan. However, it serves to illustrate his concerns.
The worry is understandable. DuFour has spent years trying to keep other people’s histories from disappearing. Out of sight, afterall, is out of mind. Now, he is given very real thoughts as to who will keep his story — and his work — alive.
What survives — and the larger arc of his quest
DuFour’s story holds two kinds of human nature in tension. There is the harm he believes that institutions have inflicted or failed to prevent, and there is the loneliness of veterans who have had to make themselves heard. But, there is also persistence — veterans who kept writing, a friend who kept listening, and one man who gathered paper after paper because he believed that the stories presented were too valuable to let go unheard.
DuFour’s life has been devoted to speaking up for those who felt silenced and invaluable — a life of questioning the integrity of the very authority that we all live under. However, an even deeper and unanswered question still lingers, and it is this — what makes a patriot? With the very definition of the word, three core principles emerge — a personal devotion to one’s country, the belief that one must stand ready to defend its constitutional values and the wellbeing of its citizens, and the trust and hope for continued constructive improvement. 
DuFour wants young people considering military service to be careful, be knowledgeable, and be politically engaged, “Be careful who you’re voting for,” he said. The message beneath that advice is perhaps more broad — service carries obligations that do not end when a person leaves the military. Care, accountability, and a trustworthy record are an integral part of that trust, and administrations and their policies are built out of individuals.
With several titanium reinforcements, DuFour has a strong backbone, but his archive is not self-preserving. It needs care, it needs tending and organizing, and it needs people who are willing to examine it. The documents that he has amassed may help to tell the story of what happened to veterans in the past, but its value is in ensuring that this type of situation does not happen again in the future. 
For DuFour, this involves the willingness of an administration that does not fear accountability, and DuFour’s account of administrations is a personal and politically critical view that has been shaped by his work with veterans and their records. He described some changes in Washington as affecting his own career, and judged administrations by what he believed they did — or failed to do — for veterans.
DuFour’s comments suggest that his view of administrations is tied to a continuing question — whether veterans are protected during service, believed when they report harm, and cared for afterward — and he described collecting records and veterans’ accounts to preserve what he believes institutions have overlooked.
Across the administrations that he discussed, his account combines personal experience with more inclusive judgments — a political change that cost him his Senate job, a law that he saw as important progress, and a continuing worry that veterans’ needs can be subordinated to political priorities. 
His archive — as he describes it — is his effort to keep those experiences and questions from being truly lost, as a human life is not disposable. It is of value, and it has meaning.
A heart can falter, DuFour knows. The work that he has built is an effort to make sure that the record does not.

The archives amassed by Veterans’ Advocate Garry DuFour is vast and telling. Photo by Danielle M. Crosier/Vermont News and Media

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV House, Senate Democrats want AG opinion on Auditor Hunt’s actions after WV Watch investigation
description: Democratic lawmakers in the House and Senate have jointly requested that West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey issue an opinion on whether state Auditor Mark Hunt followed the law in executing deeds for delinquent tax properties.
text:
The West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)Democratic lawmakers in the House and Senate have jointly requested that West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey issue an opinion on whether state Auditor Mark Hunt followed the law in executing deeds for delinquent tax properties.
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey. (Office of the Attorney General JB McCuskey photo)
In their request, the House and Senate Democratic Caucuses cited a recent West Virginia Watch investigation showing that Hunt personally signed nine tax deeds last year for a friend, who is also an employee of the auditor’s office. 
Hunt signed the deeds after the deadline mandated by state code. 
“The State Auditor’s Office exists to root out corruption, not to practice it,” the House and Senate Democratic Caucuses wrote in their request on Tuesday. “Thousands of tax deeds pass through that office every year, and the Auditor’s handling of these deeds jeopardizes the appearance of an office that is meant to protect property rights and that must not be rigged for political insiders. 
“The Legislature should seek the opinion of the Attorney General to determine whether or not the Auditor has operated within the bounds of state law.”
Under state law, only the Senate President and Speaker of the House can request a formal opinion from the attorney general. Democratic lawmakers have asked Senate President Randy Smith, R-Preston, and House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay, to deliver their request to the Attorney General’s Office. 
“This is not a partisan concern,” Democratic lawmakers wrote. “The 2022 tax-sale reforms were written carefully to protect West Virginians from losing their homes and land without due process. The Auditor’s handling of these tax deeds raises questions about what the law requires, and the Legislature should seek the advice of the Attorney General.”
Democratic members in the House and Senate want McCuskey’s formal opinion on several issues, including whether Hunt had the authority to execute deeds. State law says that the deputy land commissioner — not the auditor — is supposed to sign those deeds. 
McCuskey was also asked to weigh in on Hunt signing the deeds after the statutory deadline.
The nine deeds signed by Hunt went to MAPA LLC, a landholding company incorporated under Patricia Johns, the wife of Robert Johns. 
Hunt confirmed that Robert Johns is an employee of the auditor’s office and his work includes consulting on land issues. Democratic lawmakers want the attorney general to determine if it was inappropriate for Robert Johns to purchase land while working for the state auditor. 
Democratic lawmakers also want to know if there are any remedies available for affected property owners in West Virginia who could have been impacted by Hunt’s actions. 
Prior to becoming attorney general, McCuskey served as state auditor from 2017 to 2025 prior to Hunt assuming the role.
McCuskey has informally responded to Hunt’s allegations that McCuskey left the state’s land division in disarray, thus prompting Hunt to step in and personally sign deeds to get things in order.  
“Claims that the land division was left in disarray do not match the facts of eight years of positive reform and success,” McCuskey wrote in a statement to reporters on Monday.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Revenues still surging in CT, opening options in new budget
description: Connecticut’s coffers can expect an extra $1 billion in revenue over the next two-year budget cycle, according to the latest projections.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont will have extra help managing state finances to start his third term, even as lawmakers seek more dollars for cities and towns, education, childcare and middle-class tax relief.
Citing strong income, business and sales tax receipts, Lamont’s budget staff and the legislature’s nonpartisan Office of Fiscal Analysis said Connecticut’s coffers can expect an extra $1 billion over the next two-year budget cycle.
Those same trends also mean the current fiscal year can expect more than $750 million in additional revenues, according to the new consensus revenue forecast. And state coffers — already on pace for a robust finish — now are on pace for a $2.65 billion surplus on June 30, the second-largest financial cushion in state history.
In the context of a state budget that spends more than $28 billion annually, having $340 million extra next fiscal year and another $690 million in 2028-29 appears modest.
But the latter figure exceeds the extra investments in town aid and affordable childcare officials made last summer and hailed throughout the just-completed state campaign season as transformative.
And because Connecticut is on pace now for its largest surplus since the $4.3 billion windfall recorded in 2022 — when Connecticut received billions in federal pandemic grants — lawmakers also could carry some of this year’s surplus into the next biennial budget to open more spending and tax-cutting options.
Still, Lamont was restrained Tuesday in his assessment of the revenue growth.
“These latest revenue projections reinforce the progress Connecticut has made,” Lamont said late Tuesday afternoon. “Over the past eight years, we have strengthened our fiscal foundation and built an economy that attracts innovative companies, supports good jobs, and helps communities and schools thrive. Connecticut is on a stronger path, and I am confident we can keep building on that momentum.”
His budget director warned the good news is not a license for legislators to spend.
“These projections are estimates and should be viewed with care,” said Office of Policy and Management Secretary Josh Wojcik, who added that the results, while encouraging, also are subject to federal policy decisions and a volatile global economy.
Investment-related tax receipts continue to grow
Much of the projected growth comes from two sources: capital gains and other investment earnings from wealthy Connecticut households, and payments from certain business partnerships that are not major corporations — a category that includes hedge funds.
Analysts now say these two categories will generate an extra $500 million this fiscal year, beyond what the administration projected last month, thanks to a robust stock market. They also upgraded forecasts for these sources by $223 million for next fiscal year and $415 million for the second half of the next biennium.
Analysts also foresaw steady growth in the sales tax, Connecticut’s second-largest revenue engine after the income tax. Though receipts are matching projections this fiscal year, they should climb by nearly 3% in each of the next two, approaching $5.9 billion by 2029.
Competition for surging revenues is fierce
How much of this revenue will be invested in programs or used to fuel tax cuts hinges on one key question: Will the governor and the legislature’s new Democratic super-majority revise the caps that have blocked much spending and forced huge surpluses since 2017?
Lamont, a fiscal moderate, has allowed mostly temporary cap workarounds and exceptions over the past two years. But many Democratic legislators want ongoing reforms and have a long list of potential uses for those extra dollars.
For example, officials have invested an average of $356 million over the past two years to expand affordable childcare, and many want another similar payment made next summer.
The governor and legislators carved out a one-time spending cap exception to expand municipal aid by more than $280 million this past July and will be looking for options to sustain that assistance in each of the next two fiscal years.
State officials still have $263 million in a special response fund they created to mitigate big cuts to federal human services programs. But those dollars are expected to be exhausted over the next year, backfilling Medicaid and other healthcare program cuts. Lawmakers may be looking to dedicate more state funds to this effort.
A citizens’ assembly organized by the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities has challenged the governor and legislature to shift billions of dollars in special education costs off struggling local school districts and into the state budget.
And the private, nonprofit agencies that deliver the bulk of state-sponsored social services to clients with disabilities and those suffering from mental illness or addiction insist they lose hundreds of millions yearly because state payments have lagged inflation for decades.
In addition, many legislators and policy groups insist Connecticut must cut state taxes further to assist low- and moderate-income households. Lamont and lawmakers face appeals from coalitions seeking to create new income tax credits for households with children and for renters.
Most legislative leaders still were reviewing the revenue projections late Tueday afternoon.
But House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford, whose caucus has pushed hard for deep state tax cuts for the middle class in recent years, said that has become an imperative both parties cannot ignore.
“I think, universally, people ran on the notion of affordability and the things that are making Connecticut unaffordable,” said Candelora, whose caucus pitched hundreds of millions in relief last April, chiefly by reducing income tax rates. “We have a problem that has to be addressed. We’ve got to provide tax relief for the residents.”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont can’t build its way to affordability
description:
Every acre of open land lost to development makes Vermont less special, not less expensive.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont can’t build its way to affordability.
text:
Dear Editor,
Act 250, now maligned by builders, real estate agents and financiers, has kept unmitigated growth and sprawl at bay in Vermont for years. It was enacted by people who wanted to keep the natural beauty of Vermont’s woods, fields and open spaces protected from the wanton destruction of urban growth and capital greed.
And it worked. 
But the Vermont of half a century ago is gone. The idyllic, romantic view of old rural Vermont has somehow persisted while our towns have become cities and suburbs and our state population has grown nearly 50%. That’s a lot of growth. So much that our infrastructure and resources struggle to keep pace. And during that time, nothing got more affordable. The narrative that municipal sprawl and population growth are our salvation is an oft-repeated story from real estate agents, business associations and chambers of commerce who put money in and want money out. It’s a marketing campaign by Let’s Build Homes and the Vermont Business Roundtable, posing as community outreach and nonprofits with endorsement from the University of Vermont Health system. 
It’s false, and it’s why Vermont is in trouble.

READ MORE

Both Vermont and the world have changed, as has the economy: Vermont is no longer commercially isolated from its neighbors or the Northeast corridor as it was 50 years ago. The gig economy pushes air traffic, employment and urban money through the state. Vermont is a destination for all sorts of recreation, activities and lifestyles. Seeing Vermont as precious, many visitors long to own a piece of the state as seasonal getaways or weekend retreats. They seek the woods, the trees and clean waterways and all the natural things that make Vermont, Vermont. Outside money and urban privilege have been — and will always be — a threat to Vermont’s rare natural beauty.
And anything rare or precious is ultimately going to come with a higher price. You can’t stop or force revaluation on a desired commodity using the precept of “fair and equitable” because they aren’t making more of it. But you can devalue it.
Cut down trees, eliminate forests and kill wildlife. Build shopping areas and residences on every open field, turn towns into cities. If you want Vermont’s growth to equate with sprawl, it will lose its pristine value, demoted to the same suburban malady as Massachusetts and New Jersey. But don’t expect affordability; just like those citified centers, growth has never reduced taxes or made them more affordable. Ask your neighbors, as many of them came from there.
Unmitigated growth won’t fix affordability, nor will it reduce taxes or school budgets by one penny. It will simply erode the natural splendor of Vermont and devalue it. Don’t let rallying memes and slick marketing pitches conflate housing, growth and population with affordability. Vermont needs economic growth and revitalization, not a population explosion or a new high-rise. We need to grow quality, not quantity.
Wiley SearlesColchester, Vt.
