name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Abdul El-Sayed’s Michigan miracle
description: The conventional wisdom is that Michigan Senate-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s midterms victory was unremarkable given that he “only” won by 7 points in a purple state, while Democrats won by 14 points nationwide, and “underperformed” Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson by 2 points. To the contrary, I believe that El-Sayed’s victory was both remarkable and historic given [...]
text:
Vote Abdul poster in Ann Arbor. August 2, 2026 | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceThe conventional wisdom is that Michigan Senate-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s midterms victory was unremarkable given that he “only” won by 7 points in a purple state, while Democrats won by 14 points nationwide, and “underperformed” Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson by 2 points.
To the contrary, I believe that El-Sayed’s victory was both remarkable and historic given the unprecedented obstacles that he had to overcome to become the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate.
El-Sayed had to survive a months-long, vile and dishonest, smear campaign orchestrated by a sitting president and echoed by his sycophants. President Trump sneeringly called Abdul a “communist,” a “terrorist sympathizer,” and/or “a jihadist lunatic who hates our country” in practically every speech and social media post over the last two months of the campaign. It was the most brutal and bigoted presidential assault on a political candidate in modern American history.
His Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, never disavowed the naked bigotry, and claimed that El-Sayed “believes America deserved 9-11.”  He repeatedly fabricated allegations about the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, and Hezbollah, and, at their last debate, showed how low he would go by asking “are you for America, or are you for these terrorists groups?”
Trump invokes anti-Muslim rhetoric to attack El-Sayed at Michigan rally supporting Rogers, James

To my knowledge, not a single national or Michigan Republican had the basic human decency to call for an end to the shameful lies and smears.
El-Sayed also had to overcome an obscene amount of outside PAC spending by right-wing billionaires. In the August Democratic primary, AIPAC and corporate PACs spent over $60 million to defeat Abdul and support his primary opponent, Haley Stevens. This obliterated the all-time record for the most PAC money in a Democratic congressional primary. El-Sayed refuses corporate PAC money, and was outspent by about 10-to-1 in the primary despite outraising Stevens among individual donors. The PAC dollars were exclusively devoted to deceptive ads designed to impugn Abdul’s character. Tellingly, no major Democratic leaders objected to this attempt by right-wing PACs to buy a Democratic primary.
In the general election, Rogers was supported by over $170 million of PAC spending (most from Elon Musk, AIPAC, and the MAGA PAC), about twice the outside spending for El-Sayed (all of which came from the Senate Democratic PAC and issue-oriented groups). Again, El-Sayed outraised Rogers from small donors, but was outspent by about 2-to-1.
Another major challenge was that El-Sayed faced a state Democratic Party that was almost universally united behind his primary opponent, Haley Stevens. Governor Gretchen Whitmer, retiring Senator Gary Peters, Attorney General Dana Nessel, and ex-Senator Debbie Stabenow all endorsed Stevens, along with many other state and local party officials. To their credit, Senator Elissa Slotkin, Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, and Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson chose to stay neutral and let voters decide.
The weekend before general election day, Haley Stevens reneged on her earlier endorsement of El-Sayed and endorsed Mike Rogers. This backfired by finally coalescing the state party establishment behind Abdul.
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), center left, speaks during a press conference supporting U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, center right, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Finally, there was a double standard in mainstream media coverage of the Michigan Senate campaign. The media scrutinized and parsed not only every phrase that El-Sayed uttered over the last 20 years, but also statements by distant relatives with whom he never lived and twitch streamers who generate attention by being provocative. But the media did not apply the same level of scrutiny in pressing Mike Rogers to explain how he and his wife made millions of dollars after leaving Congress, why he flip-flopped to support election denialism, or why he employed a white supremacist as a campus organizer.
The media obsessively parroted the Rogers’ campaign talking points that El-Sayed was struggling with both Jewish voters statewide and Black voters in Detroit. The debate within the Michigan Jewish community was in fact real and newsworthy, but the electoral relevance was greatly exaggerated given that Jews represent only about 1.5 percent of Michigan voters. While there are many more Black voters, the “concerns” turned out to be wishful thinking by the Rogers campaign as El-Sayed captured over 90 percent of the Black vote in Detroit. Yet the media barely reported on the incredible success of the El-Sayed campaign in shifting large numbers of young, unaffiliated, and Arab-American voters to his side which led to his comfortable victory margin.
The simplistic claim that Abdul El-Sayed’s victory was much more expected than Democratic victories in, say, Mississippi or Texas, falls apart in view of the massive challenges that dwarfed those faced by any other Senator-elect in the country. He and his grassroots campaign met the moment, as did the decent people of Michigan, who rejected the presidential smears, the big money PACs, a hostile state party bureaucracy, and a biased mainstream media, to deliver one of the greatest political stories in Michigan, and American, history.

name: VTDigger
title: Kid Governor shows our future voters that their voices matter now
description:
More than 2,000 Vermont fifth graders are casting ballots this month for classmates whose platforms include housing, mental health and addiction.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Kid Governor shows our future voters that their voices matter now.
text:
This commentary is by Sarah Copeland Hanzas, Vermont’s secretary of state. 
Think of a problem that’s too big for you to solve alone. One that requires bringing people together and participating in collective action to propose solutions. This is really the crux of civics and democracy. It’s the question I pose to Vermont’s students whenever I visit classrooms, and some of those students are answering it on a public stage right now — fifth graders, to be exact.
Vermont’s Kid Governor program is in its second year. Founded in 2015 by the Connecticut Democracy Center, the program has spread nationwide, offering fifth grade teachers a free toolkit for teaching about state government, voting and the power of civic participation. This education is not just theory but also practical. Students identify an issue they’d like to address and then run in primary elections within their schools. They develop a three-point campaign platform to earn their classmates’ votes. This develops their critical thinking, research and public speaking skills. Seven finalists are chosen from the top candidates at participating schools. Those finalists then create short campaign videos that explain and advocate for their platform. Classrooms across the state view those videos, and then all the fifth graders vote. It’s an authentic election, tallied by my office, with tangible and relatable stakes.
The other six finalists don’t miss out; they form the Kid Governor’s cabinet. All seven students work together to advance their platforms, with help from my office and organizations throughout Vermont.
Last year we weren’t sure what to expect but were amazed when 65 schools and over 1,000 fifth graders participated. This year — right now — more than 2,000 fifth graders are voting to elect their Kid Governor and his or her cabinet.
What are these 10- to 11-year-olds running for? More recess? More candy in school lunches? Try again. Last year’s Kid Governor, Roslyn Fortin, of Highgate Elementary, won on a platform addressing homelessness. Her cabinet ran on issues including youth mental health, healthcare access, bullying and healthier school lunches. This year’s platforms are housing, mental health, bullying, drug abuse and addiction, and climate change. In other words, these kids are tackling the same issues as legislators six times their age.
There are many things I love about this program. I love students learning about civics and democracy. I love the enthusiasm and pride with which entire schools and communities band together to support their candidates. Even better, I love seeing a student in one corner of the state cheering for the election victory of a student who goes to school hours away, whom they’ve never met, but whose platform and candidacy resonated with them.
When I speak with Vermont students, I make a point of emphasizing that even if they aren’t a high school senior casting a ballot in our elections, student voices are crucial at both the state level and in their local communities. Communities rally around their youth, supporting their passions and learning from their concerns. A legislative truism is that our youth are the future, and that means when the future calls, emails, writes you a letter or travels to Montpelier to advocate, you’d better listen.

READ MORE

Vermont’s middle and high schoolers certainly aren’t too young to advocate for their concerns and make change. The Kid Governor program shows that our elementary students are ready to step up too, given the opportunity. By learning how government works, organizing together and experiencing voting firsthand, Vermont’s fifth graders are setting a foundation for lifelong civic engagement. We are at a moment when civics matters. It is not expected that we agree on what the issues are or how to solve them, but civics is about how to have those conversations. It’s the work of elected leaders like me, but it is also the work of every Vermonter, even if they are 10 years old.  
In 2025, my office helped administer a statewide Youth Civic Health Survey to find out how engaged young Vermonters are. One question asked: “When you turn 18, do you plan to register to vote?” Fewer than 60% said yes. The goal of Kid Governor is to inspire Vermont’s youth to be forever voters. Pam Letourneau-Fallon, a teacher at St. Johnsbury School who helped us bring the Kid Governor program to Vermont, said it best: “This is not a pretend election. The stakes are high. Their platforms will become a reality. … I can’t see any of these students not voting in elections moving forward. They’re invested.”
The week of Nov. 16, we’ll announce this year’s Kid Governor and their cabinet. In January, they will be sworn in at an inauguration ceremony at the Statehouse, and then they get to work, advancing their platforms to make the changes they want to see in their communities and our state. I hope you’ll join me in helping them do so. And let them inspire you to take action — big or small — on the problems you are concerned about.

title: Senators question North Dakota judge pick Axt on experience, 2020 election, Jan. 6
description: North Dakota’s top appeals attorney faced questions from U.S. senators Tuesday about his experience and views on the 2020 election in his confirmation hearing for a federal judgeship. State Solicitor General Phil Axt sat with three other nominees before the Senate Judiciary Committee. President Donald Trump announced Axt’s nomination in August for the U.S. d[...]
text:
North Dakota Solicitor General Philip Axt argues on behalf of the state before the state Supreme Court on Dec. 18, 2023. At left is Justice Jerod Tufte. (Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s top appeals attorney faced questions from U.S. senators Tuesday about his experience and views on the 2020 election in his confirmation hearing for a federal judgeship.
State Solicitor General Phil Axt sat with three other nominees before the Senate Judiciary Committee. President Donald Trump announced Axt’s nomination in August for the U.S. district judgeship previously held by Dan Traynor, who was confirmed earlier to the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals.
U.S. Sens. John Hoeven and Kevin Cramer, both R-N.D., introduced Axt. They praised his military experience, West Point and Yale Law School background and legal acumen.
“He’s got the finest academic accolades and accomplishments, but he’s a guy that served our country in battle, won the Bronze Star, and now he’s our state solicitor general. Now that’s pretty fantastic experience for a U.S. district court judge,” Hoeven said.
Trump to nominate top North Dakota appeals litigator to be federal judge

Axt began as solicitor general in 2023 under North Dakota Republican Attorney General Drew Wrigley. Axt has defended various state laws in high-profile cases before the state Supreme Court, including North Dakota’s bans on abortion and gender-affirming medical treatments for kids. As recently as last month, he successfully urged the court to deny a petition seeking to throw out the potential election wins of four legislative candidates.
Axt gave a short statement to the panel in which he recognized his family and thanked several state officials, including Wrigley.
“I would not be here were it not for the trust that he was willing to place in me and in my work product and in my legal judgment and in the responsibilities he’s entrusted me with these last several years,” Axt said of his boss.
Chair Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, asked Axt what has prepared him as solicitor general to preside over cases in North Dakota. 
Axt said he has overseen most of the state’s high-profile court cases over the last few years, appeared in more than 100 cases and argued many of them in state and federal court. 
“One thing I’ve learned through that experience is you can tell when the court has put in the effort and the time to really understand the best version of the arguments that are at issue,” Axt said. That is something he would strive to do, if confirmed, he said.
Ranking Member Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., hammered on the perceived inexperience of Axt and other nominees for a lifetime appointment.
Axt said he was not a lead or co-counsel during trials, and generally tries to avoid trial. Most of his cases involved constitutional issues or interpretation of state laws, he said. He also said he has supervised trial teams, developed legal strategies and witnesses and argued certain motions.
Durbin said to the nominees, “I think it’s unfortunate. You are talented in certain areas, but a lifetime appointment for a federal district trial judge, I just don’t see how you put it together.”
Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said some judicial nominees of Democratic presidents had no experience as a judge at any level or as “a judge at the fair’s pie contest.”
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., asked the nominees who won the 2020 election and whether the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021, frequent questions Democrats ask of Trump nominees.
Trump lost the 2020 election to Democrat Joe Biden. Trump’s supporters rioted and broke into the Capitol on the day Congress met to certify the election results, clashing with law enforcement officers and temporarily halting the proceedings.
Axt said he agreed with a fellow nominee’s answer that Biden “was certified the winner of the 2020 election,” and said “I condemn the acts of violence on that day” in 2021. 
The Senate Judiciary Committee did not take immediate action on the nominations.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: High court axes Oklahoma Legislature’s efforts to overhaul initiative petition process
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – The Oklahoma Supreme Court on Tuesday tossed out a controversial law that made it more difficult for Oklahomans to get their issues on the ballot. In a 5-4 ruling, the state’s high court found that Senate Bill 1027, passed into law in 2025, violated the U.S. and Oklahoma Constitution, was legally void […]
text:
The Oklahoma Supreme Court chamber is pictured Dec. 7, 2023. (Photo by Carmen Forman/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – The Oklahoma Supreme Court on Tuesday tossed out a controversial law that made it more difficult for Oklahomans to get their issues on the ballot.
In a 5-4 ruling, the state’s high court found that Senate Bill 1027, passed into law in 2025, violated the U.S. and Oklahoma Constitution, was legally void and lacked enforceability.
Instead of severing the offending portions of the law and letting the rest remain, Oklahoma’s high court tossed out the entire statute.
Sen. David Bullard, R-Durant, and House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, were the authors. 
Hilbert said the law protected the integrity and fairness of the initiative petition process.
“We encourage the state to appeal this decision and continue defending the Legislature’s authority to establish reasonable safeguards for this important process,” Hilbert said. “The fight to uphold the integrity of Oklahoma’s initiative petition process is not over.”
Bullard declined to immediately comment, saying he wanted to read the opinion. 
Senate Bill 1027 was among a number of recently passed laws that made it more difficult for people to use the initiative petition process to collect signatures to get issues on the ballot. 
The law put caps on how many signatures could be collected by county. For a change in state law, it limited the number of signatures that could be gathered to 11.5% of the number of votes cast in the county during the most recent general election for governor. For a constitutional change, it was 20.8%.
It also sought to put more restrictions on signature collectors and to control the wording contained in a petition’s description.
The signature restriction caps pose broad First Amendment problems and do not accomplish the stated goal of rural participation, the court ruled.
Despite the state Constitution guaranteeing all registered voters the right to sign initiative petitions, the law prohibited them from signing the petition once the cap is met, the court said.
“Never before have legal voters been outright prohibited from signing an initiative or  referendum petition,” the court said. “In short, this Act severely disenfranchises voters in all 77 counties.”
The court noted that the Legislature’s caps would disproportionately harm rural residents living in less populated counties because a fewer number of people would be eligible to sign petitions than in more populated urban areas. The high court said it would result in fewer petitions being circulated in rural areas.
The new law’s restrictions on the wording of the petition’s gist, or description at the top of the signature page, also violated the First Amendment, the court ruled. 
The court found the requirement to be prior restraint, a type of government censorship that attempts to prohibit free speech ahead of time.
The law’s ban on incentive-based compensation, such as pay based on collected signatures, is unconstitutional, the opinion said, adding that the defendants failed to justify the burden.
The court found that the law’s prohibition of contributions from certain entities restricted political speech.
Requiring petition circulators to disclose if they are being paid and by whom also violates the First Amendment, the court ruled.
It found that the law’s requirement that circulators be registered to vote in Oklahoma violated the First Amendment. 
The U.S. Supreme Court had previously ruled unconstitutional a similar effort in Colorado to require that state’s signature collectors to be Colorado residents, Oklahoma’s Supreme Court said. 
Justices James Winchester, James Edmondson, Douglas Combs, Noma Gurich and Richard Darby voted to find the law unconstitutional.
Chief Justice Dustin Rowe, Vice Chief Justice Dana Kuehn, Justice John Kane and Special Justice James R. Huber dissented. Justice Travis Jett recused.
The now defunct law was passed after citizens successfully used the initiative petition process to expand Medicaid, legalize medical marijuana and implement criminal justice reform, all issues lawmakers declined to pursue.
Amber England, CEO of Strategy 77, worked to get Medicaid expansion on the ballot.
She said the new rules meant only the wealthiest interests would be able to reach the ballot.
“Having led ballot campaigns across Oklahoma for years, I’ve seen what voters can do when they’re trusted to fix what the Legislature won’t,” she said. “I’ve seen what happens when politicians try to manipulate the process and take power out of the hands of the people. Today’s ruling means Oklahomans keep the one tool that works when their government doesn’t.”
Senate Minority Leader Julia Kirt, D-Oklahoma City, was among those voting against the measure.
“This ruling puts power back where it belongs – with the people,” she said.

text:
The screenings will run from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute in Newark and Wilmington Hospital. Appointments are encouraged, but walk-ins will be accepted as part of National Lung Cancer Screening Day, according to ChristianaCare.   Image provided by ChristianaCare.
Nov. 14 appointments highlight how annual low-dose CT scans can help eligible current and former smokers detect cancer before symptoms appear
ChristianaCare will offer lung cancer screenings Saturday, Nov. 14, in Newark and Wilmington, encouraging eligible adults with a history of smoking to take a step that could detect the disease when treatment is more effective.
The screenings will run from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute in Newark and Wilmington Hospital. Appointments are encouraged, but walk-ins will be accepted as part of National Lung Cancer Screening Day, according to ChristianaCare.
The effort addresses a challenge with lung cancer: People can feel healthy while the disease develops. Screening is designed to find cancer before symptoms appear, giving patients and their medical teams an opportunity to begin treatment earlier.
“Screening gives us the opportunity to detect lung cancer at an earlier stage, when treatment is often more effective and outcomes can be significantly better,” said Dr. Thomas Schwaab, the Bank of America Endowed Medical Director of the Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute, in ChristianaCare’s announcement.
The screening uses low-dose computed tomography, commonly called a low-dose CT scan, to create detailed images of the lungs with a small amount of radiation. Patients lie on a table while the scanner takes images. The scan itself takes only a few minutes and does not hurt, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
ChristianaCare says the screening takes less than 15 minutes to complete, with results typically provided through the referring health care provider within one to two weeks.
Who qualifies for screening?
The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommends annual low-dose CT screening for adults ages 50 through 80 who have at least a 20 pack-year smoking history and either currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years.
A pack-year measures smoking exposure over time. Smoking one pack a day for 20 years, or two packs a day for 10 years, equals 20 pack-years.
ChristianaCare’s announcement also lists not having received a lung CT scan within the past 12 months among its screening criteria. A navigator can help residents review their smoking history and determine whether screening is appropriate.
Screening involves potential benefits and risks. The CDC notes that scans can produce false-positive findings that lead to additional testing, detect cancers that would never have caused illness and expose patients to radiation. Patients should discuss those considerations with their health care provider.
Understanding coverage and cost
Insurance coverage requirements can differ from clinical screening recommendations. Medicare Part B, for example, covers annual lung cancer screening for eligible adults ages 50 through 77 who meet its smoking-history requirements, have no signs or symptoms of lung cancer and receive a provider’s order. Patients pay nothing when the provider accepts Medicare assignment.
ChristianaCare says its lung screening navigators can help uninsured or underinsured patients explore available resources and understand their options. Residents with coverage should confirm their plan’s requirements before their appointment.

title: Trump administration wants to trim BLM process behind Rock Springs Resource Management Plan
description:
“The current planning process is too slow, too complicated and weighed down by outdated requirements,” BLM Director Steve Pearce said. Conservationists are skeptical.
The post Trump administration wants to trim BLM process behind Rock Springs Resource Management Plan appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The Department of the Interior is proposing updates to the regulations that govern Bureau of Land Management land-use planning, three years after a management planning process for 3.6 million acres of public land in southwestern Wyoming fueled a political firestorm. 
The proposals aim to update a decades-old set of regulations by cutting unnecessary red tape, improving coordination with state and local governments and hastening decision-making for public lands across the country, according to an announcement from the department. 
“The current planning process is too slow, too complicated and weighed down by outdated requirements,” BLM Director Steve Pearce said in the announcement. “These proposed changes would help the BLM make decisions more efficiently, reduce costs for taxpayers and improve coordination with the people and communities that rely on public lands.”
To conservation organizations, however, the changes would hinder public input and weaken what they consider to be a vital tool for protecting resources, the Area of Critical Environmental Concern designation. 
“The administration’s new proposed rule on BLM land-use planning grievously limits public input and critically undermines the agency’s ability to conserve naturally or culturally significant places,” Wyoming State Director for The Wilderness Society Julia Stuble said. “It is another clear attempt to put politics over people and ensure top-down directives override local community input.”
The proposed changes are available for review in the Federal Register. The public can comment through Jan. 11. 
The rules would impact BLM field offices nationwide. There’s no indication the furor surrounding Wyoming’s Rock Springs resource management plan revision influenced the proposal. 
A crowd of people came to a BLM open house in September 2023 to learn about the controversial Rock Springs Resource Management Plan drafts. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
But for many state residents, the contention elevated a document once synonymous with a dry and tedious process — a resource management plan — into a household term. More than 15 years after officials embarked on its rewrite, the Rock Springs field office resource management plan update is yet to be finalized.
Land-use blueprints
The BLM manages more than 245 million acres, the most of any federal agency. The land is concentrated in the West, including Wyoming, where the agency oversees 18.4 million acres of public surface land — about one-third of the state.
The agency manages for multiple uses including recreation, mineral leasing and grazing. It also uses various designations, including Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, which are lands deemed to require special management to protect important values and resources from irreparable damage.
BLM field offices rely on resource management plans to guide the management of their particular zones. These documents act as blueprints, identifying areas that can be drilled, grazed, recreated on or protected. 
The creation of a finalized resource management plan entails a regulated series of steps like public scoping periods, public comments, resource inventories and exhaustive environmental impact statements. That process is what the agency is considering changing. 
The BLM first adopted its land-use planning regulations in 1979. The rules have been updated twice since then. The latest proposed updates would “update planning terminology, eliminate duplicate requirements and simplify parts of the planning process that have become unnecessarily burdensome over time,” according to the Interior Department. 
Pronghorn and a drilling rig in western Wyoming. (Wyoming BLM)
The proposed changes include many tweaks, revisions and deletions. Among them: 

Redesignate the section titled “Environmental Impact Statement” to “Environmental compliance,” and remove language in the section that requires the BLM to prepare an environmental impact statement every time it develops or revises a plan. 
Amend the public participation guidelines to: remove a requirement to publish notice in the Federal Register at the initiation of the planning process; remove a 30-day public comment period on any significant changes made to a proposed plan prior to issuing a decision; and remove the 90-day public comment period requirement for all draft land use plans, revisions, and amendments supported by environmental impact statements. 
Remove “burdensome” requirements in the existing regulations for Areas of Critical Environmental Concern. These include the existing requirement for the identification of Areas of Critical Environmental Concern in a draft land-use plan, the associated 60-day comment period and the existing requirement for a Federal Register notice publication.

These changes aim to achieve a more efficient and accessible process by cutting red tap and improving coordination with state and local authorities, according to the Interior Department. 
“Public lands are set aside for the benefit and use of the American people,” Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said in a release. “They should be managed by the people closest to the land, not held back by outdated bureaucracy in D.C.” 
But Stuble with the Wilderness Society said the proposals would actually do the opposite by shutting down public input opportunities — including shortening the governor’s review period. 
“This is the type of top-down political over-reach that Wyomingites routinely reject,” she said. 
What happened in Wyoming
In August 2023 the BLM released a long-awaited Rock Springs field office draft resource management plan. Its release followed more than a decade of scoping, inventories and stakeholder meetings aimed at updating the original plan — which was signed in 1997. 
The area the plan would oversee is enormous — 3.6 million acres of public lands and 3.7 million acres of federal mineral estate in southwestern Wyoming, including the vast Red Desert, the prized hunting grounds of the Greater Little Mountain Area and several ungulate migration corridors.
Yufna Soldier Wolf at the White Mountain Petroglyphs in October 2022. The rock panels were one stop on a tour of Indigenous resources in the Red Desert. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile) 
The 2023 draft plan drew intense backlash. The draft’s conservation-heavy “preferred alternative” sparked outrage over stricter limits on energy extraction and expansions of protected areas. Critics lambasted the plan as an instrument that would kill the area’s economy and close off much-loved areas to outdoor recreation. Anger and misinformation — including erroneous information accidentally disseminated by the BLM itself — characterized the packed meetings that immediately followed. Some 35,000 comments poured in during the extended public comment period.
Amid that extended comment period, Gov. Mark Gordon announced the formation of a gubernatorial task force, tapping the University of Wyoming’s Ruckelshaus Institute to facilitate stakeholder conversations. The intent was to hammer out recommendations supported by all the interests represented — everything from trona mining to oil and gas, conservation and hunting.
The 11 members reached consensus on more than 100 recommendations for the BLM. The agency finalized the plan’s 550-page record of decision in December 2024, but nine months later the agency announced it would be amending the plan. When it made that announcement, the BLM said it would “review and revise” the plan to ensure it complies with several executive orders issued under the Trump administration, including Unleashing American Energy and Reinvigorating America’s Beautiful Clean Coal Industry.
Though BLM-Wyoming Acting State Director Kris Kirby told WyoFile in December the agency would have amendments signed by October, the plan has yet to be finalized.

November stakes races, dining and casino entertainment offer reasons to make an evening of a trip to the track
DOVER, Del. — Hawaiian Warfare extended his winning streak to eight races Nov. 5 at Bally’s Dover, adding another victory to a season that has already included a sweep of his Delaware Standardbred Breeders’ Fund series at Harrington Raceway.
For fans following the 2-year-old pacer — and residents looking for a different kind of evening out — the victory comes during a November schedule featuring major stakes races and opportunities to combine a visit to the track with dinner and entertainment.
Driven by Michael Cole, Hawaiian Warfare led throughout his $20,000 breeders’ fund preliminary, finishing in a career-best 1:53.2 and defeating See Jack Run by 2¼ lengths. Erin Neilson trains the gelding for owner and breeder Forrest Bartlett.
Favorites also won the other two opening-round divisions for 2-year-old male pacers. He’s Soaring, driven by Ryder Skinner for trainer Jason Skinner, beat Earl’s Watching in 1:54.3. Aeneas, driven by Montrell Teague for trainer Jamie Sullivan, defeated Bootcamp Baby in 1:54.4.
A full November racing calendar
Bally’s Dover’s 83-day season opened Nov. 2 and runs through April 1, 2027. Live racing takes place Monday through Thursday, with the first race at 4:30 p.m. There is no live racing on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 26.
Remaining November dates, beginning Nov. 10, are Nov. 10-12, Nov. 16-19, Nov. 23-25 and Nov. 30.
The month includes several significant events. The Matron Stakes for 3-year-old trotters and pacers are scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 12. Progress Pace eliminations follow Thursday, Nov. 19, ahead of the $300,000 final Wednesday, Nov. 25.
Delaware Standardbred Breeders’ Fund championship races for 2-year-olds, each carrying a $110,000 purse, are scheduled during Nov. 19-25. Those championships provide another milestone in the series featuring Hawaiian Warfare, although his next appearance will depend on published entries.
Making an evening of it
The late-afternoon start gives visitors an opportunity to watch racing and include dinner or other entertainment during their visit.
Dining choices include Italian dishes at Jerry Longo’s Meatballs & Martinis, Asian cuisine at Macau Kitchen and steak and seafood at Royal Prime Steakhouse. Restaurant schedules vary: Jerry Longo’s lists Monday and Thursday dinner service among its operating days, Macau Kitchen serves dinner Tuesday through Saturday, and Royal Prime opens Wednesday through Sunday.
Wednesday, Nov. 25, offers a particularly convenient combination. The Progress Pace program begins at 4:30 p.m., and DJ Ray Dr is scheduled at Círculo Lounge at 8 p.m. Visitors can plan around both, although the racing program may still be underway when the music begins.
Círculo, a rotating lounge overlooking the casino floor, also lists Thursday night football viewing at 8:15 p.m. Other November entertainment includes a comedy show Nov. 14 and Best Kept Soul on Nov. 28, both at 8 p.m. Those Saturday events fall outside the regular live racing schedule.
Visitors can also find free racing programs, entries, results and replay links through Bally’s Dover’s racing website. Simulcast wagering on races from other tracks continues year-round.

title: Do North Carolinians have an appetite for impeachment? Here’s what a new poll finds.
description: A week after the 2026 midterm that saw Democrats winning control of both the U.S. House and Senate, a new Elon University poll finds support for the idea of impeachment. The survey of 800 North Carolina adults was conducted before the Nov. 3rd election and released Tuesday. It was fielded by YouGov and has a […]
text:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Capitol Hill on July 21, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)A week after the 2026 midterm that saw Democrats winning control of both the U.S. House and Senate, a new Elon University poll finds support for the idea of impeachment.
The survey of 800 North Carolina adults was conducted before the Nov. 3rd election and released Tuesday. It was fielded by YouGov and has a margin of error of +/-4.03%
Nearly half of those surveyed – 47% – said they would react either “very” or “somewhat positively” if the U.S. House of Representative passed articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump. On the other end of the spectrum, 26% said they would respond “very negatively” or “somewhat negatively” to a possible Trump impeachment.
“I think in some ways, the resounding rebuke of the midterm elections may have even pushed those numbers up higher,” said Husser.
Husser said while the poll did not ask people follow-up questions about why they might want to see President Trump impeached, an open-ended question in the survey found a substantial number of respondents concerned about corruption, protecting democracy, and making sure elections are fair.
“I do think that this impeachment question is very much tied into the sense of negative partisanship that we have going on in the United States today,” Husser told NC Newsline.
Whether Democrats decide to pursue a third Trump impeachment with their newfound power in 2027 remains to be seen.  But this week saw U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and member of the House Judiciary Committee, filing articles of impeachment targeting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Massie maintains Hegseth abused his powers as defense secretary, implemented unlawful strikes against Iran, and ignored laws to minimize civilian casualties.
On Tuesday, Hegseth called the impeachment articles “a farce” and a “political spectacle.”
Defense Secretary Hegseth calls impeachment push a ‘farce’ as US House heads toward vote

Hegseth’s fiery rhetoric has done little to win over the public. Forty-six percent of North Carolinians surveyed in the Elon poll disapproved of Hegseth’s job performance, compared with 27% who approved and 28% who were unsure.
Among Democrats, 72% disapproved, compared with 58% of Independents who disapproved and just 13% of Republicans.
“When the baseline for Hegseth in a swing state like North Carolina is 27%, that means he does not have robust support,” said Husser. “Even among Republicans in North Carolina, only 61% approve of Hegseth.”
Husser said public opinion on Hegseth could fall even lower depending on what is revealed in an impeachment investigation.
“What matters is the opinion of U.S. senators, and how they respond will really be the most important thing going forward for Hegseth,” said Husser.
Outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis has made his disdain for Hegseth clear in recent weeks,calling his vote for Trump’s choice for Secretary of Defense in 2025 the “biggest regret of my career.”
U.S. Senators Thom Tillis and Ted Budd (Photos: Senate.gov)
Senator Ted Budd, R-NC, has not openly criticized Hegseth. But in October, Budd expressed reservations aboutHegseth’s plan to cut 20% of the nation’s senior admirals and generals.
“I certainly want to see his rationale in detail, and I don’t have that yet,” Budd told The Hill.
Husser said it’s a difficult lift to remove any cabinet official. The U.S. House would need only a simple majority to impeach Hegseth, but in the Senate, it would require a two-thirds majority or 67 votes to convict him.
“Typically, what we would see is that the president or the cabinet official relent at some point and say, ‘Okay, we’ll pick another person.'” said Husser. “We may not see that. We saw Hegseth digging in very deeply, saying that he’s not going anywhere.”
Husser said that Trump’s support for Hegseth could shift as he weighs public opinion and lessons from a bruising midterms for Republicans.
“He still cares a lot about his legacy, and he cares about getting things done over the next two years,” said Husser. “So, if a budget can’t get passed for the Department of Defense because of Hegseth being at the top, we might see President Trump responding differently than he has already.”
Source: Elon University Poll

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Another normal year expected for Bristol Bay sockeye salmon, Alaska biologists say
description: Alaska fishery biologists expect next year’s run of sockeye salmon in Bristol Bay — site of the world’s largest sockeye runs — to be about normal. The forecast for 2027, released by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game last week, estimated a return of 49.31 sockeye salmon in the coming summer season. That would […]
text:
Spawning sockeye salmon returning from Bristol Bay swim in 2013 in Lake Clark National Park and Preserve's Tazimina Lake. (Photo by D. Young/National Park Service)Alaska fishery biologists expect next year’s run of sockeye salmon in Bristol Bay — site of the world’s largest sockeye runs — to be about normal.
The forecast for 2027, released by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game last week, estimated a return of 49.31 sockeye salmon in the coming summer season. That would support a harvest of 33.97 million fish, the department forecast said.
The forecasted totals are about normal compared to the last 20 years, and would follow another normal run this year, when 45.7 million sockeye returned to the bay. But it would be 31% larger than the long-term average dating back to 1963, according to the department.
This year’s forecast, like others produced by the department, includes a range of uncertainty. The run could be as low as 35.47 million and as high as 63.14 million fish, according to the department.    
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

Estimating future salmon returns “is inherently difficult and uncertain,” the department forecast said. Over the past two decades, the forecasts have underestimated actual runs by an average 13%, though there have been occasions when the forecast total was higher or almost exactly the same as the actual run total.
The tendency to underestimate run sizes is partly related to some outlier years when runs hit record high or near-record highs, said Fish and Game Area Biologist Stacy Vega. The model that the biologists use in their forecasts does not fit very well when there are super-large runs, as has been the case in some recent years, Vega said by email.
Forrest Bowers, director of Fish and Game’s Division of Commercial Fisheries, concurred with that assessment.
“There is considerable uncertainty inherent in forecasting salmon returns and in periods of strong productivity it is common to see realized returns greater than the preseason forecast,” he said by email. “This is the situation we have been in with Bristol Bay sockeye salmon for over a decade.”
Once the fishing season is underway, the department is able to manage based on actual numbers of fish and catches, making the preseason forecast less important, he said.
The preseason forecast for 2026, however, turned out to be nearly spot-on once the actual run materialized. The department had a mean preseason forecast of 45.32 million fish for the sockeye run, just slightly lower than the actual return to the bay.
“We did get very close with last year’s forecast, which is always nice,” Vega said.
The accuracy was helpful to the industry, Bowers said.
“The fishing industry relies on our forecast to plan for tender vessel needs and placement, shipping containers, and processing worker staffing and an accurate forecast helps maximize the value of the harvest,” he said.
The fishing industry strives to have estimates as early as possible, even if they are preliminary estimates that precede the department’s official forecasts. To help with its planning, the industry uses estimates of not just the size of runs but the size of individual fish.
The total catch this year was 30.1 million fish. Thanks to significantly higher per-pound prices, fishers earned more money on this year’s total catch than they did in 2025, when they harvested 41.2 million sockeye out of a run totaling 56.7 million fish, according to the department.
The Alaska Department of Fish and Game’s annual observed total run of sockeye salmon in Bristol Bay compared to preseason total run forecasts from 2027 to 2026, with the just-released forecast for 2027. Error bars represent the ranges of uncertainty used in the department’s forecasts. (Graph provided by the Alaska Department of Fish and Game)

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Transgender victims of violence memorialized, Democrats say they’ll pass anti-discrimination bill
description: Advocates, officials and lawmakers gathered in the Capitol Tuesday to honor transgender and gender-diverse victims of violence ahead of the Transgender Day of Remembrance, which is widely recognized on Nov. 20.
text:
Amy Santiago speaks at the Capitol in Harrisburg on Nov. 10, 2026 (photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)If you are experiencing thoughts of suicide, please call or text 988 to be connected to a crisis counselor free of charge 24/7.
Speaking in the East Wing rotunda of the Capitol Tuesday, Amy Santiago said she had tried to get her teenage child help, but struggled to find a therapist appointment on their health plan in Bradford County.
“Auggie wanted to make changes in the world,” she said. “He made people feel like they belonged. He built people up, always. He’s such a special person.”
But in October, they took their own life, roughly two months before they were scheduled to begin therapy. Their photo was one of dozens placed in the Capitol Tuesday to memorialize the 55 known transgender and gender-diverse people who lost their lives to violence or suicide in America last year. Four of them were in Pennsylvania.
“Auggie was also just beginning to come out as a trans person,” Santiago said. “Online, he had a community of friends and supporters who knew her as Cass. Thank you for loving her. We didn’t get to know her yet.”
Santiago was joined by advocates, officials and lawmakers who gathered in the Capitol Tuesday to honor transgender victims of violence ahead of the Transgender Day of Remembrance, which is widely recognized on Nov. 20.
A memorial in the Capitol in Harrisburg for transgender victims of violence (photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
According to Ashleigh Strange, the executive director of the Governor’s Advisory Commission on LGBTQ affairs, the number of recorded deaths in America is likely an undercount, as well as the global tally of 297.
“The numbers tell the story of a population in crisis, particularly for trans people of color who are targeted more often,” they said. “As a trans and nonbinary person, I am always sad to be a part of these events, but I’m proud to be a part of this community.”
The event was attended by lawmakers like Reps. Dan Frankel (D-Allegheny), Tim Briggs (D-Montgomery), and Jessica Benham (D-Allegheny), co-chair of the Pennsylvania LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, spoke.
Rep. Ismail Smith-Wade-El (D-Lancaster), Benham’s co-chair, spoke.
“I often say that we as legislators hand off our job to take care of the commonwealth of Pennsylvania to a variety of other people and organizations,” he said. 
But he recalled how, in his first year as a lawmaker, six young transgender people died in Lancaster County. 
“It became clear that there are some things that we simply cannot afford to hand off, and that we must take responsibility for as legislators ourselves,” Smith-Wade-El said. “We are here because we are committed to making sure that Pennsylvania as a commonwealth – a place that we call home – is safe, dignified, compassionate and free for all of its residents, particularly for our trans young people.”
In each of the last two legislative sessions, the Democrat-majority House has passed a bill called the Fairness Act, which would update the state Human Rights Act to explicitly provide protections from discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity or expression.
Beth Rementer, a spokesperson for House Democrats, said the bill would be a priority when the new session begins and Democrats have majorities in both the state House and Senate.
Savannah Thorpe Capizzi, a spokesperson for Senate Democrats, said the bill would be prioritized in the upper chamber as well, where Democrats will have a new majority next year.
Asked if Gov. Josh Shapiro would support the bill, a spokesperson pointed to a recent statement where Shapiro said Democrats would soon outline an agenda, which would contain numerous bills that have earned support in the House, but stalled in the Republican-controlled Senate.
“As a parent and as a person, I tried to be supportive, but that wasn’t enough. I’m not sure what would have been enough,” Amy Santiago said. “I do know that we as people — everybody — we need community, we need support, we need freedom, we need kindness and we need love.”

name: VTDigger
title: Why do only 2 health insurers sell plans on Vermont’s exchange?
description:
“Insurance is a game of large numbers, and we don't have those numbers,” said the commissioner of the Department of Financial Regulation, pointing to the state’s lack of scale.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Why do only 2 health insurers sell plans on Vermont’s exchange?.
text:
Left: BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont headquarters in Berlin in Oct. 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger. Right: A building for the MVP insurance agency on State Street in the downtown section of Schenectady, New York, captured Oct. 2, 2020. Photo by Tyler A. McNeil via Wikimedia Commons.
Over the weekend, Andrew Garland, an executive at BlueCross and BlueShield of Vermont, found himself at Home Depot staring down the array of tools that “all seemed to do the same thing,” he said. DeWalt? Milwaukee? 
It’s a version of the choice the more than 60,000 Vermonters who buy their insurance on the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace are making this fall, as open enrollment gets underway. Vermonters have until Dec. 28 to sign up for 2027 plans and until Dec. 15 to sign up for coverage that begins on Jan. 1. Though the marketplace hosts an array of options, they notably come from only two insurers: BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont and MVP Health Care.
So why is that? And how unusual is Vermont in having so few insurers in the marketplace? Is the fact that there are so few marketplace insurers what drives the high premiums Vermonters pay for marketplace plans? And is it really such a bad thing to have so few options?
For a state that prides itself on its exceptions from the norm, Vermont is not alone in having only two insurers who chose to do business on the marketplace here. Seven other states, plus Washington D.C., have only two insurers participating in the individual health insurance marketplace, according to the health policy group KFF.
Still, the Green Mountain state remains exceptional in other ways: experts point to a handful of uniquely Vermont conditions that make the marketplace undesirable for new entrants. Namely, the extremely small population of the state, the regional monopolies of the state’s hospitals and the high costs of care. 
“I think number one is the size of our market,” said Kaj Samsom, the commissioner of the Department of Financial Regulation, which regulates health insurers in Vermont. 
“Insurance is a game of large numbers, and we don’t have those numbers,” he said. 
BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont CEO Beth Roberts agrees: “When you look at the size of our market here in Vermont — of individuals and small groups who purchase insurance — the market is small. Two carriers is likely the exact right size for a small market,” she said.  
Vermont’s marketplace, Vermont Health Connect, is the state-managed exchange for people to buy health coverage even if they do not qualify for federal Medicare (which is for those over 65 or with certain health conditions) or for the state-federal Medicaid (which is for certain low income levels) or have an employer-sponsored plan available to them. 
A smaller market is a more volatile one, where only a handful of big claims can destabilize just how much an insurer needs to pay out vs. how much it can keep in reserves, as was the case in 2024 when BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont saw claims significantly higher than expected and paying them out dug deep into the insurer’s reserves. 
Insurers talk about risk in terms of the pool —  who pays premiums into it and who needs to pull money out of it for care. The larger the pool, the more diluted the risk. 
“When you fragment it too many times, it actually doesn’t help stabilize the pool. To get to a stabilized pool, each insurer has to have a critical mass of people in that pool to stabilize those premiums. And so, to just think about carving that up further amongst more and more payers… it goes out of line with the market size,” Roberts said. 
Though insurers and regulators have actuaries to predict what a given year’s claims might look like and how much revenue an insurer needs to raise through its premiums, predicting health outcomes “has an inherent amount of uncertainty that is hard to to quantify,” Samsom said.
And despite the best laid plans, marketplace plans historically lose money. For every dollar marketplace insurers collect in revenue, they lose a dollar and one cent paying out claims. 
“There’s very little opportunity to even break even,” Samsom said, let alone for an insurer to add to its reserves. 
All of this comes down to the cost of the claims the insurers have to pay out, said Owen Foster, who chairs the Green Mountain Care Board, which also regulates the ACA marketplace plans. The way he sees it, three main factors drive the high charge to insurers: that’s how much care people use, where they get the care — for instance, if they get an MRI in a less expensive, standalone imaging clinic or a more pricey hospital — and just how much the price of the service actually is. 
“If they want to make a margin, the insurance companies need enough money at the end of the  year after they pay all the claims to have some money in the bank,” Foster said. Historically, they have not.
In most of the state, people have one real option for local hospital care. These “regional monopolies” over care, as Samsom calls them, have limited insurers’ ability to negotiate on how much a hospital charges them. And, at the same time, Vermont has few options for less expensive care outside of a hospital — such as an independent imaging center or stand-alone surgical center. 
“The cost of care just eats up so much of the available resources, right?” Garland, the BlueCross executive, said. “We find ourselves just scrapping for any strategies we can to help bring that cost down or find ways to cover more services that folks need. There is no margin for margin. The cost of care is just demanding so much money right now.”
Insurers in Vermont have network adequacy requirements that mandate them to include local providers, which, with many regions having only one main hospital, means insurers cannot simply walk away from a hospital that does not want to negotiate on prices.
“In another state they could,” Mary Block, the Department of Financial Regulation’s deputy commissioner, said, explaining a situation where a city might have more than one major hospital. “That leverage doesn’t exist for the insurers (here).” 
Absent market pressure, the Green Mountain Care Board, which sets marketplace premium increases, fills the void.
“What I think the care board has effectively done in the last two (or) three (years) is put some pretty clear motivation on the hospitals to think differently about negotiations,” Samsom said. He described the effective pressure that the care board has put on insurers to pull down their premiums (and on hospitals to pull down their prices) which has contributed to more robust contract negotiations, such as the contract BlueCross BlueShield and University of Vermont Health inked for 2026 that was credited as one of the driving factors behind its significantly leaner budget for this coming fiscal year. 
Still, Vermont has some of the highest premiums in the nation for younger people purchasing plans on the Affordable Care Act marketplace, according to a KFF comparison of plans for 40-year-olds across the country. 

READ MORE

Yet, as the rest of the country watches steep increases in premiums — with the national average rate for a benchmark marketplace plan increasing 13% for 2027 and 26% for 2026 — Vermont has drastically curbed increases for its marketplace plans, with BlueCross BlueShield of Vermont’s individual plans set to increase 2.2% and MVP’s increasing 3.9% for 2027. This year marks some of the smallest increases in premiums that Vermont’s marketplace has seen. But monthly base rates — without any federal or state subsidy assistance — range from over $800 for a bronze plan to nearly $16,000 for a silver plan (which in Vermont are more expensive than gold-rated plans).
“We’re nothing but a proxy for ensuring Vermonters can afford healthcare,” Foster said. “If they want to say the regulatory pressure is too much, I think what they’re really saying is Vermonters should be paying us more.”
Regulation is a fine balance, though, Block said. Vermont is “unlike any other state,” in how much regulation its marketplace insurers are subject to, she said. It can act to further dissuade new insurers from entering Vermont’s market. It would, Roberts acknowledges, be much less administrative time and expense to have to report to one state regulator than both the care board and the Department of Financial Regulation.
But the regulation alone is not what’s driving insurers’ losses in an expensive healthcare environment.  
“I don’t want to sit here and blame the care board and their rate reductions,” Samsom said. “Even without the pressure from the board reductions, they still lose money.”  
Competition of the two insurers does also work to drive some price reductions, Samsom added. It can act as a disincentive for them to buffer their rate too much and can drive each insurer to negotiate a better contract with the hospital, Samsom added.   
As the insurer’s actuaries build their rate, they’re thinking how much do we expect to pay for care? Samsom explained. It’s a calculation of utilization and price — and the insurer has more control over prices. 
“Price is what you’re negotiating with the providers on (every year) and you want to do better in that negotiation than your competitor,” he said.
Without that competition, Samsom warns that too much of that volatility inherent to insurance would concentrate into one insurer. Though there is no indication that MVP, nor BlueCross, are going anywhere, having only one insurer on the marketplace would introduce new vulnerabilities. 
“Their share would increase but their vulnerability to financial distress would go up quite dramatically,” he said, “Given how volatile that market is, they are doubly at risk of the type of claim surge and solvency concerns we saw two to three years ago.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Why do only 2 health insurers sell plans on Vermont’s exchange?.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Ole Miss students and parents call for accountability after viral racist incident
description: University of Mississippi students on campus, Thursday, March 26, 2026, in Oxford.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Some University of Mississippi students and parents are calling on officials to address concerns about campus climate and culture after a video showing white students making racist gestures outside a Black student’s apartment went viral. 
Parents have emailed Chancellor Glenn Boyce and other university leaders calling for the students to be suspended or expelled. Other social media commenters have pointed to Ole Miss’ history of racism, while students have demanded a thorough investigation. 
They’ve also expressed outrage and disappointment about the latest incident. 
Kristina Pluta of Utah, whose son Jansen is a sophomore at UM, said she felt shocked and disgusted when she first saw a video of the incident on Instagram Saturday night. Racism and hatred are learned behaviors that can be unlearned, she said. 
“There has to be consequences and the university should hold the students’ behavior accountable,” said Pluta, who is white. 
The University of Mississippi in Oxford, Monday, Dec. 1, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I just hope the girls that did it will be able to learn from this experience. I want them to grow beyond their ignorance and prejudice that informed their behavior.” 
On Friday night, a doorbell camera recorded three young white women making ape-like gestures and noises as they walked past Ole Miss student Jakiyra Metcalf’s apartment door. Metcalf posted the video on TikTok and tagged the university in the caption with the question, “what do we have to say about this??”
By Tuesday, the TikTok video had more than 12.6 million views, about 1 million likes and more than 37,000 comments.
It has drawn national media attention and sparked outrage and criticism over the apparent use of the racist trope and behavior at the university. The university has tried over the last several decades to distance itself, amid fits and starts, from a history of racism.
Metcalf could not immediately be reached for comment.
Alaina Kunes, one of the students identified making gestures in the video, issued a statement Tuesday apologizing for the incident. She said she didn’t know the race of the students in the apartment.
University leaders have said they’re investigating the incident. Shawnboda Mead, UM’s vice chancellor for student affairs, condemned the behavior in a statement published Sunday.
The incident has contributed to many students feeling “unwelcomed and unsafe,” Demetrick Stringer Jr., president of the university’s Black Student Union, said in a statement released Sunday. In addition to an investigation, he called for campus officials to support the affected students and make stronger efforts to educate students about the university’s values. 
“We believe this moment calls for education,” Stringer wrote. “The students involved are new to our community and we encourage the University to strengthen how first year students are introduced to the University creed and its commitment to respect for the dignity of each person, so that no student has this experience again.” 
Taylor Winfield, a senior multidisciplinary studies major, said the incident also prompted criticism from social media commenters of Black students who chose to attend Ole Miss rather than one of Mississippi’s historically Black universities. 
Students walk near Vaught-Hemingway Stadium on the campus of the University of Mississippi, Thursday, March 26, 2026, in Oxford. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Winfield said Black students have a place at Ole Miss and can help change campus culture by being a part of it. 
“It’s been a great place for us,” said Winfield, who is Black. “No matter the situation, it’s still our home.” 
But for Kierah Robinson, a junior political science major, the university’s response doesn’t fully address Black students’ concerns. 
The students targeted by the gestures shouldn’t have to question their safety and comfort in their own home, she said. Robinson identifies as Black. 
“The psychological feeling of not feeling safe or feeling like you belong in the spaces you have a right to occupy is a form of racial violence,” Robinson said. 
The university should be transparent about its investigation and any disciplinary process while maintaining privacy limits, she said. 
The incident cannot be separated from the university’s history of racism, Robinson said. 
That history includes a riot in 1962 when James Meredith attempted to enroll and students’ pro-Palestinian demonstrations in 2024, when counter-protestors shouted racist remarks such as “hit the showers” and “your nose is huge.”   
University officials should engage with Black students about what it would take to make them feel safer and more welcomed on campus, she said. While the university has taken steps to address its past, Robinson said that progress doesn’t mean the work is finished. 
“We can care deeply about our school and still hold it accountable,” Robinson said. “Racism exists everywhere and wanting better for institutions means being willing to challenge it at the same time.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Commentary: Veterans Day: A monumental occasion in Utah
description: Six months ago, Utah and the rest of the nation observed Memorial Day. On that solemn occasion we paid tribute to service members who did not make it home alive. On Veterans Day, we honor military personnel who did return home safely. Some of those who served, however, sustained inconspicuous injuries that have affected their […]
text:
The Utah Agent Orange Memorial is pictured on Oct. 9, 2026.
(Photos courtesy of Hannah Smalling, Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation board member)Six months ago, Utah and the rest of the nation observed Memorial Day. On that solemn occasion we paid tribute to service members who did not make it home alive.
On Veterans Day, we honor military personnel who did return home safely. Some of those who served, however, sustained inconspicuous injuries that have affected their lives ever since. 
In the Beehive State and elsewhere, the day includes parades and other events that convey our tremendous gratitude to veterans who have helped preserve a way of life Americans have treasured for over 250 years. 
Veterans Day owes its origin to the aftermath of the First World War (1914-1918). According to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, its observance began on Nov 11, 1919, one year after WWI, and was originally known as “Armistice Day.” Armistice Day became an official U.S. holiday in 1938 and was renamed Veterans Day in 1954.
Throughout the entire length and breadth of Utah, meaningful activities will take place on Veterans Day and the following weekend. One of the most significant of those events is planned in the city of Sunset near Hill Air Force Base.
On Veterans Day weekend, a monumental celebration in Sunset will commemorate the construction of one of the most unique and profound veterans memorials ever built in Utah.
The Utah Agent Orange Memorial was completed in early October and its official dedication is scheduled for Nov. 20. On that historic occasion, Utah will became the latest state to pay tribute to veterans exposed to toxic chemicals in Vietnam and elsewhere with a fitting and rather conspicuous monument.
At 10 feet high, 8 feet wide, and almost 2 feet thick (excluding its base and cap), the memorial is an impressive structure. In addition to vast dimensions, its orange color makes it strikingly apparent in the landscape of Sunset Veterans Park. 
Some of the memorial’s other distinctive features include a giant-sized Orange Heart Medal on its front and an image of an Air Force C-123 aircraft spraying Agent Orange etched in stone on its back.
With such extraordinary characteristics, the Agent Orange Memorial is undoubtedly fated to become one of the most renowned landmarks in the entire Beehive State. I can hardly imagine otherwise. 
Its immense appeal will likely attract visitors who travel to the Hill Aerospace Museum at Hill Air Force Base. Another nearby attraction is the replica of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Layton, which honors wartime casualties.
The dedication ceremony for the Agent Orange Memorial will represent the culmination of a formidable project that began about three years ago in Davis County.
Compelled by Agent Orange related health issues and the staggering death toll that hazardous defoliant was causing, Vietnam veteran Larry Kerr established the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation.
With Larry as its chairman, the foundation set out to build a monument recognizing victims of Agent Orange and similar toxic herbicides, educate future generations about the use of those chemicals, and provide a place for reflection.
Over a period of time, the organization’s mission evolved to include recognition of Gulf War and post-9/11 era veterans exposed to toxic chemicals as well.
The memorial was designed to be a proper tribute that helps ensure the sacrifice of Utah veterans is preserved long after their heroic battle with illnesses caused by toxic chemicals is over.
Accomplishing the task of building the memorial took a great deal of dedication and tenacious effort. Those attributes are exemplified by zealous members of the Utah Agent Orange Veterans Foundation and ardent supporters of the organization’s mission.
The valuable support of individuals who helped transform a dream into a reality has come from all corners of Utah and beyond, showing the monument’s symbolism strikes a chord with Americans regardless of where they live. 
Foundation Board of Directors member Hannah Smalling vividly demonstrated the prevailing relevance of the Agent Orange Memorial at its groundbreaking ceremony in the fall of 2025.
In a teary-eyed speech, Hannah described how her father, Vietnam veteran Robert Smalling, had been struggling with serious health problems caused by his exposure to Agent Orange.
Hannah’s heartwrenching description aptly illustrated the memorial’s profound significance. Very soon that meaningful, majestic, and timeless tribute will take its rightful place in Utah’s storied history.
