name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson gets $64 million federal grant to hire more police, boost anti-crime surveillance
description: Mayor John Horhn, far left, poses with members of the Jackson Police Department and a nearly $64 million dollar check presented to the city by the U.S. Department of Justice at City Hall as part of the Model Cities Initiative, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche presented Jackson Mayor John Horhn with a symbolic $64 million check Monday, possibly giving Mississippi’s capital city a surge of funding to hire more police officers, rebuild its forensic lab and expand drone surveillance of suspected criminals and abandoned properties.
Under Jackson’s form of government, the city council must now decide if it will accept the money. Council members authorized the Jackson Police Department to apply for the U.S. Department of Justice’s new Model Cities initiative grant earlier this year.
The Jackson City Council earlier this year authorized the police department to apply for the grant. Under Jackson’s form of government, the council must now decide if it will accept the money. 
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche presented Jackson Mayor John Horhn and Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney with a $64 million check after a press conference announcing the city as one of four recipients of the U.S. Department of Justice’s Model Cities Initiative grant. Credit: Molly Minta/Mississippi Today
Horhn heralded the potential investment, saying at Monday’s press conference at City Hall that Jackson “is dealing with scarce resources.”
“We are ideas rich and we are money poor,” Horhn said. 
The mayor’s comment drew chuckles from state officials, including Gov. Tate Reeves, whose presence at City Hall is a rare sight. Reeves, a Republican, has sometimes clashed with leaders of the Democratic-led city over policing.
“Today is a good day for the people of Jackson, which means today is a good day for the state of Mississippi,” Reeves said. “And, also, today is a bad day for the criminals who wish to do us harm.” 
Blanche said the widespread support among state officials for Jackson’s application is why the Justice Department selected the city out of 47 applicants. He said the money would become available early next year and that residents would see results “almost right away.”
“You’re going to have more cops on the street, and the cops on the street will be working with better equipment, better technology and better information,” Blanche said. 
In its grant application, JPD wrote that it hoped to use the federal money to expand its network of cameras housed at the Real-Time Command Center and create a database linking 911 calls to abandoned properties in the city. 
Taken together, Police Chief RaShall Brackney said these efforts will reduce violent crime “before it arrives” in Jackson.
“We have to change the conditions” that foster violence, the chief said. “Not simply manage the consequences.” 
Hours before the press conference, the ACLU of Mississippi released a statement saying the partnership could trample civil liberties. 
In an email, Candi Richardson, the ACLU of Mississippi’s communications director, expressed worry that Horhn and other Jackson officials were too trusting of the Trump administration in respecting the rights of Black Jacksonians, low-income communities, immigrant families and unhoused individuals.
“The more likely outcome: The Trump administration will hijack this funding to increase control of Jackson law enforcement agencies and communities and push its ideological obsession, racism, and approach of loyalty over law,” Richardson wrote. 
Horhn previously told Mississippi Today that he had not heard concerns from any constituents about a potential federal takeover of the Jackson Police Department. 
Two residents of the Jackson metro area whose family members had been killed spoke at the press conference in support of the grant.
Violet Horne, who lost two sons to gun violence in 2024, said she hoped the grant would lead Jackson to “a chapter where jurisdiction and boundaries do not become barriers to justice.” 
In addition to Jackson, the Justice Department also awarded grants to Baton Rouge, Louisiana; Jacksonville, Florida; and St. Louis.
Unlike other federal law enforcement grants, the Model Cities Initiative will be administered through a “cooperative agreement,” giving the DOJ an active role in implementation. The grant requires participating cities to comply with certain Trump administration priorities, including immigration enforcement and efforts to ban homeless people from sleeping in public.
Voting rights demonstrators gathered near the Hinds County Courthouse in Jackson, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Chanting from the unrelated protest prompted a press conference on the federal government’s Model Cities Initiative to be moved inside City Hall. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
That is why the initiative has proved controversial in other Democratic-led cities, including Charlotte and New Orleans. 
During the press conference, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward alluded to controversies in cities that ultimately decided against applying for the grant, saying that “public safety is not controversial.”
Another concern from civil liberties advocates: The Justice Department has touted its Memphis Safe Task Force as a prototype for the Model Cities Initiative grant. In one year, officers working under the task force fatally shot four people and made more than 23,000 arrests, mostly for nonviolent offenses following traffic stops conducted on one in three residents. 
In a letter supporting the grant application, Horhn wrote that Jackson had seen “meaningful reductions in homicides and other violent crime” under Brackney. 
However, statistics show otherwise. By Aug. 3, the date on the letter that Horhn submitted to the federal government, 54 homicides occurred in Jackson. During that same period in 2024, the city had 44 homicides in Jackson, according to WLBT’s Homicide Tracker. 
“That’s not what we looked at,” Blanche said. “What we looked at is, do we have motivation and commitment from leadership that we can work together?” 
JPD’s grant application sought $125 million over three years. The department proposed to use most of the money to create a specialized gun-crimes unit focused on “repeat shooters.” 
“We cannot arrest our way into community stability,” Brackney said. “We cannot technology our way into trust.”
The press conference was scheduled to be held on the steps of City Hall, but officials moved it inside because of an unrelated demonstration by voting rights advocates chanting “count every vote” outside the Hinds County Courthouse.

description: Farmers had a slow start to harvest in Iowa following an abnormally wet September that kept combines parked. The first week of November was also unseasonably wet, leaving farmers less than two days suitable for field work, according to the latest crop progress and condition report. The weekly report, published by the U.S. Department of […]
text:
A farmer works in a field near Cambridge, Iowa on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Farmers had a slow start to harvest in Iowa following an abnormally wet September that kept combines parked. The first week of November was also unseasonably wet, leaving farmers less than two days suitable for field work, according to the latest crop progress and condition report.
The weekly report, published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture marked 72% of Iowa corn acres had been harvested as of the Nov. 2 through Nov. 8 reporting period. The five-year average pace shows normally 89% of corn acres have been harvested by this reporting period. 
Soybeans, on the other hand, are just slightly behind the five-year average, with a reported 93% of acres harvested.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said in a news release that dry weather in the upcoming forecast should give farmers a “good opportunity to make another strong push toward wrapping up harvest.”
“A wet start to November slowed harvest progress across Iowa, but cooler and drier conditions over the weekend helped get combines rolling again,” Naig said in a statement. “Soybean harvest is nearing completion, and farmers continue to make steady progress on the remaining corn crop.”
State Climatologist Justin Glisan reported that the statewide average precipitation for the reporting period was 1.47 inches, which was more than triple the normal precipitation average for the period. 
Glisan reported most of the rain events hit at the beginning of the week, with high precipitation amounts, more than three inches at some stations, reported Nov. 4. 
“More than 250 stations reported at least an inch with a statewide average of 1.24 inches,” Glisan wrote of the Wednesday night storms in his weekly weather report. 
Topsoil moisture rated 27% surplus during the reporting period, according to USDA, and subsoil moisture condition rated 18% surplus. 
In addition to above average precipitation, Glisan reported higher than normal temperatures during the reporting period. The statewide average temperature of 49.5 degrees Fahrenheit was nearly 8 degrees above the normal.
The warmer, wetter weather conditions are consistent with forecasts from climatologists following “super” El Niño conditions at the equator. 
According to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet, soil temperatures across the state are in the low 50s and upper 40s, as of Monday.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas lawmakers plunge ahead with unproven IT system despite huge risks
description: House Majority Leader Chris Croft, an Overland Park Republican, asked peers on the Legislative Coordinating Council to move ahead with implementation of a new bill-writing software system ahead of the 2027 legislative session in January. In this image from March 24, 2025, Croft speaks to peers in the House. (Photo by Grace Hills/Kansas Reflector)
text:
House Majority Leader Chris Croft speaks on March 24, 2025, while House Speaker Dan Hawkins sits behind him. (Grace Hills/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The Kansas Legislature’s bipartisan leadership committed to implement an unproven bill-writing software system despite skepticism the private contractor might not deliver a workable platform for start of the 2027 session.
The contractor hired four years ago to replace the state’s antiquated system for drafting, proofing and publishing bills was showered with criticism from the Legislative Coordinating Council long before missing the revised January 2026 deadline for completion. The LCC’s frustration continued to mount this year, but Senate and House leaders sensed they were in too deep to refuse the go-live order sought by Propylon.
Altaf Uddin, chief information technology officer for the Legislature, recommended lawmakers move ahead despite risks of a meltdown. He emphasized it was a “hard decision for all of us.”
“There is no option here,” said House Majority Leader Chris Croft, an Overland Park Republican. “We spent a ton of money on this thing, waited a long time and you’re telling us to leap. You’re pushing us off at the same time. It’s just disappointing that this is where it’s come.”
The Republican-dominated LCC gave its approval on condition the existing bill-drafting system was ready if Propylon didn’t meet the objective. The LCC also approved a request to hire a business system analyst to work with Propylon on behalf of the Legislature so attorneys responsible for crafting bills no longer had to devote so much time to troubleshooting with Propylon.
Overall, the Legislature has spent approximately $8 million on development of the bill-writing system. The original completion date was June 2025, but that slipped six months to January. During 2026, testing revealed defects in the new Computer Assisted Legislative Information System, otherwise known as CALIS.
Uddin promised Propylon would deliver the minimum functionality required to process bills by the end of November.
“While operationally viable,” Uddin said, “this is really not the polished product.”
Gordon Self, who manages the Legislature’s bill-writing office, said everyone at the Capitol should appreciate the complexity of adopting a new system. He requested patience with legislative staff when problems emerged. He insisted the old system remain available as a backup because of the potential of system failure.
Rep. Blake Carpenter, the Derby Republican likely to seek appointment as House speaker, said there was no going back on this IT project.
“I don’t have a whole lot of faith right now,” he said. “Only in government can we spend millions and millions of dollars — I can see why the taxpayers are frustrated, right? In business, if you do that, you’re out of business. We can’t really go backwards, but we’re taking a massive risk going forward. We’re left with an impossible choice at this point.”
Senate Majority Leader Chase Blasi, R-Wichita, said he was disturbed neither bill writing system would be available for use by legislators until early December. The old system can’t be rebooted until approximately Dec. 2, while the new system wouldn’t be online until Dec. 7.
That would leave one month for Kansas lawmakers to get professional assistance on drafting and tweaking bills ahead of the Jan. 11 launch of the 2027 session.
“People are very upset,” Blasi said. “I think that’s incredibly undemocratic, frankly. People have been robbed of the opportunity to draft legislation.”
Meanwhile, the LCC put off until December the selection of a contractor to deliver to the Legislature a system for tracking the evolution of bills in the House and Senate. Five companies were chosen as finalists, but realignment of House leadership prompted a decision to postpone awarding of the contract.
While leadership of the Kansas Senate could remain as it was in 2026, the election of House Speaker Dan Hawkins, R-Wichita, to the job of state insurance commissioner and the reelection defeat of Croft meant the newly elected 125 members of the House would be responsible for selecting new leadership. LCC agreed not to make a contract decision before gathering feedback on bidders from new Republican leaders in the House.

title: You can support affordable housing in NC by drinking beer
description: The N.C. Housing Coalition is partnering with Vermont-based Lawson’s Finest Liquids to raise money for affordable housing through the craft brewery’s “Good Brews for a Cause” initiative. The coalition will receive a portion of the sales from every Cosmic Shift IPA — a limited seasonal release brew — sold in North Carolina. The proceeds will […]
text:
(Photo: Courtesy Lawson's Finest Liquids) The N.C. Housing Coalition is partnering with Vermont-based Lawson’s Finest Liquids to raise money for affordable housing through the craft brewery’s “Good Brews for a Cause” initiative.
The coalition will receive a portion of the sales from every Cosmic Shift IPA — a limited seasonal release brew — sold in North Carolina. The proceeds will support the coalition’s effort to ensure every North Carolinian has a “home in which to live with dignity and opportunity.” Artisan Beverage, the local distributor of Lawson’s Finest brews, will match the brewery’s donations.
Stephanie Watkins-Cruz (Photo: Greg Childress/NC Newsline)
“At the Coalition, we believe that everyone has a role to play in addressing our housing challenges, and we’re excited to see Lawson’s Finest Liquids bring another example of creative collaboration for a good cause to life,” said Stephanie Watkins-Cruz, the coalition’s director of housing policy. 
The Good Brews for a Cause initiative focuses on creating special limited release beers and small-batch collaborations that are specifically brewed to raise funds for causes the company cares about. Each beer benefits specific nonprofit organizations that are working to uplift its community.
“Good Brews for a Cause grew out of a simple idea: brew great beer and use it to do good,” Sean Lawson, founder of Lawson’s Finest Liquids, said in a statement. “Cosmic Shift has allowed us to take that idea even further, turning this brew into a way to support organizations doing meaningful work across our distribution footprint.”
Lawson’s Finest expanded this year’s initiative across 12 states to partner with 13 nonprofits and 19 wholesalers to address the affordable housing crisis. Its employees said in a companywide survey that affordable housing is a top concern.
Low-income renters in North Carolina far outnumber affordable housing units   

“North Carolina Housing Coalition really rose up for a level of interest to us because of that ability to have a more widespread impact by focusing on the advocacy of legislation that can help more people get access to housing, the ability to buy a home, the ability to have a home that’s safe for their families,” said Carra Cheslin, social impact manager at Lawson’s Finest.
The nonprofits chosen to partner with the brewery this year are engaged in developing and managing affordable homes, providing emergency shelter and housing assistance and advocating for more equitable housing policies.
“We’re really excited to get to support awesome organizations like NC Housing Coalition to try to address that, and also bring more awareness to our beer drinkers about the issue of affordable housing,” Cheslin said.
Last year, Cosmic Shift raised $36,436 for 10 nonprofits across nine states. The theme was healthy communities. 
The brewery and coalition held a celebration at Beer Study in Durham last week for the North Carolina launch. Two more events are planned for this month, one on Nov. 17 at YIMBYTOWN 2026, 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. at Transfer Co. Food Hall in Raleigh, and another Nov. 19 from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. at Carolina Beer Temple in Matthews.

name: VTDigger
title: Montpelier has its long-awaited housing blueprint for Country Club Road
description:
DEW Properties plans to build roughly 108 housing units in its initial phase. Residents won’t move in for several years.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Montpelier has its long-awaited housing blueprint for Country Club Road.
text:
An overhead rendering of a housing development project proposed by DEW Properties for the Country Club Road property in Montpelier that would incorporate townhomes and smaller buildings.

MONTPELIER — Four years after buying a 138-acre former golf course to help solve its housing crisis, Montpelier finally has its most detailed development blueprint to date for Country Club Road.
Under a non-binding letter of intent approved unanimously by the Montpelier City Council, developer DEW Properties has proposed building an initial 108 housing units on roughly 20 buildable acres along the site’s lower ridge.
The agreement represents the most concrete vision produced for the Country Club Road property since city voters authorized its purchase in 2022.
“We were just eager to get involved if they wanted us involved,” Robert Wells, development coordinator for DEW Properties, told VTDigger Monday. “So happy that the (selection) process is done now, and we can get started.” 
Shovels aren’t set to hit dirt until around 2028, though, Wells said. The city and the company are waiting on a market evaluation, determining whether or not the project’s size and timeline are feasible for Montpelier. 
The letter of intent serves as a placeholder, solidifying the city’s choice for a development firm as it awaits the evaluation process before executing a formal development agreement. This process allows either party to walk away if financial terms cannot be reached.
While the city’s municipal schedule originally targeted October 19 for executing a final development agreement, the City Council did not vote to approve the preliminary letter of intent until October 14. 
DEW Properties, based out of Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont, previously built the housing above the Transit Center in Montpelier and worked on Barre City Place.
The development project has long-been controversial. And unclear. The initial $2 million bond vote to purchase the property in 2022 was met with questions about property taxes and affordability. A citywide vote passed narrowly, 1,205-1,021.  
The real estate development and property management service DEW Properties was selected from a pool of four New England-based developers who had submitted proposals, responded to questions and attended interviews with the city since December 2025. 
But by July, the City Council’s Country Club Road subcommittee had narrowed the search down to DEW Properties and Chinburg Properties. 
After requesting secondary proposals from DEW and Chinburg, the subcommittee opted to recommend DEW Properties. 
Reasons for the endorsement included development that “best balances housing production with preservation of the site’s natural and recreational assets” and “a phased approach that aligns infrastructure investments with market demand,” according to the council’s decision memo.
The subcommittee’s vote for DEW Properties in July was “pretty much a unanimous” one, Alfano said, as DEW “took an extra step” in their second proposal. “They were extraordinarily conscientious about answering our questions,” he said.
DEW Properties expects to have the market study’s results back by the end of the year, which will impact planning and budgeting, Wells said. 

An overhead rendering of a housing development project proposed by DEW Properties for the Country Club Road property in Montpelier that would incorporate townhomes and smaller buildings. 

A poor finding would likely require making cost, material or timeline adjustments, Alfano said, before signing a development agreement, locking the relationship in. 
“Nothing’s ever impossible,” Wells said. “I would say it just gets more challenging, and we’re pretty good at figuring out challenges.”
Major legal, financial and regulatory hurdles still remain before any construction can begin.
DEW Properties and the city still await the results of the market study. Construction costs, local buyer demand and price absorption must be feasible, or the proposed layout could be modified or abandoned entirely.
Montpelier is projected to spend $8 million on infrastructure to bring water, sewer and road improvements to the site. The city has secured grant funding, including a $3 million Northern Borders Regional Commission grant, to cover the bill, according to the city’s Planning Director Mike Miller. 
Finally, the property must undergo environmental cleanup to address historical golf course pesticide contamination, complete local zoning reviews and clear state Act 250 land-use permitting before work can begin. Wells said he expects this to take between four and 12 months. 
“This is a fairly large project for Vermont, so we wanted to give an adequate timeline for that permitting, due diligence and feasibility aspect of the project.”
Country Club Road units are expected to open to occupants in 2029 or 2030, Wells said.

title: From classroom to Congress, Cyril Jefferson is bringing his public service to Washington
description: HIGH POINT, N.C. — Before Cyril Jefferson ever considered a career in public office, he worked with students whom he believed deserved better than the circumstances they were born into. As a music teacher, he saw students who were academically gifted, ambitious and supported by their families. He also saw others growing up in historically […]
text:
Cyril Jefferson previously served as the mayor of High Point before being elected to North Carolina's 6th Congressional District. (Photo: Cyril Campaign Website) HIGH POINT, N.C. — Before Cyril Jefferson ever considered a career in public office, he worked with students whom he believed deserved better than the circumstances they were born into.
As a music teacher, he saw students who were academically gifted, ambitious and supported by their families. He also saw others growing up in historically marginalized neighborhoods that lacked investment.
Jefferson, who spent years working in education and youth development, said those experiences shaped his understanding of government’s responsibility to create opportunities for people.
“Talent is universal, but opportunity is not,” he said, quoting a saying that has always stayed with him.
That’s what helped motivate Jefferson to run for Congress after serving as High Point’s first Black mayor, a seat he won in 2023. 
Democrats appear to win the NC House majority and gain seats in the Senate

Last Tuesday, he defeated Republican incumbent Addison McDowell in North Carolina’s 6th Congressional District, part of a “blue wave” that flipped six congressional seats held by Republicans. 
He’ll be one of the youngest members of Congress at just 34 years old. 
Taking kitchen table issues to Washington
Jefferson acknowledged that he wasn’t sure about the outcome when he entered the race. He believed he could win, but knew unseating an incumbent in a district drawn to favor a Republican was a challenge.
He credited volunteers, donors and voters across the district, as well as the enthusiasm surrounding Democratic candidates at the top of the ticket, for helping make the victory possible.
On the campaign trail, Jefferson said affordability was a common thread in conversations with voters, particularly as families struggle to keep up with rising costs. He criticized the Trump administration’s tariffs and the decision not to extend Affordable Care Act subsidies, arguing that federal policy decisions have contributed to financial pressures facing households.
He also pointed to concerns about artificial intelligence and the growth of data centers, saying residents want to better understand how emerging technologies could affect their jobs and communities.
Jefferson said he intends to request a seat on the House Committee on Science, Space and Technology, arguing that Congress needs to take a more active role in regulating artificial intelligence. “When the folks who lead AI are saying to you that we need to put guardrails up, well, that’s just a clear sign,” he said.
Beyond economic issues, Jefferson said government accountability and reform will be central to his work in Congress. He supports banning stock trading by members of Congress and the executive branch. He’s also interested in campaign finance reform and limiting partisan gerrymandering. 
“If you get government reform right, then you can change the motives and change the incentives for your levers of government,” he said.
Patrick Harman serves on the High Point City Council and worked directly with Cyril. (Photo: Harman Campaign Website)
Patrick Harman, a High Point City Council member who has known Jefferson since 2018, said his commitment to community development has been evident throughout their work together.
Harman pointed to Jefferson’s involvement in Thrive High Point, an initiative focused on expanding opportunities for minority entrepreneurs. Jefferson helped initiate the effort following the 2020 murder of George Floyd, working with High Point University and local organizations to move the project forward.
Harman described Jefferson as a collaborative leader to his fellow council members.
“He’s a good listener,” he said. “He’s very accepting of everybody’s points of view. He knows the issues and is always willing to dive right into them.” 
Harman said he hopes Jefferson brings that approach to Washington, along with the values that motivated him to enter public service.
“He’s serious about all of this,” he said. “ It’s not just some casual thing for him. He’s doing it for all of the right reasons”

text: WASHINGTON — Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer Monday welcomed 11 newly elected Senate Democrats at the U.S. Capitol, following midterm elections in which his party flipped both chambers in Congress. “Last week the American people put Donald Trump and the GOP on blast,” Schumer, a New York Democrat, said on the Senate floor. “Americans pulverized the red wall and for good reason. Americans want a government that recognizes and responds to their needs and Democrats are ready to deliver.”  Joining Schumer for a brief press event in his office were Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, Roy Cooper of North Carolina, James Talarico of Texas, Juliana Stratton of Illinois, Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Josh Turek of Iowa, Adam Hamilton of Kansas and Troy Jackson of Maine. While Schumer is currently the Senate Democratic leader, he’ll have to run again next month to keep his leadership position. Several of the incoming Senate class also broke barriers. Pappas will be the first openly gay elected senator,  El-Sayed is the first Muslim senator and Minnesota voters made Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan the first Native American woman senator. She could be joined by Alaska Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, an Alaska Native whose Senate race is still too close to call. By the 120th Congress in January, Democrats will have 54 senators, potentially 56 if Peltola and Mississippi Democratic candidate Scott Colom win their races, in which votes are still being counted.Colom could become the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era if he defeats GOP incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Lawsuit challenges Landry-backed ‘lightning’ speed approval for data center power projects
description: A group of Louisiana landowners and community advocates are suing the Louisiana Public Service Commission over its procedure to fast-track large utility projects in the name of economic development. It comes as regulators are poised to give expedited approval to a power project linked to the massive $50 billion Meta Hyperion data center campus in Richland Pa[...]
text:
From left, Louisiana Public Service Commissioners Foster Campbell, Mike Francis, Jean-Paul Coussan and Eric Skrmetta during a Feb. 19 PSC meeting. (Photo credit: Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)A group of Louisiana landowners and community advocates are suing the Louisiana Public Service Commission over its procedure to fast-track large utility projects in the name of economic development. It comes as regulators are poised to give expedited approval to a power project linked to the massive $50 billion Meta Hyperion data center campus in Richland Parish.   
The lawsuit, filed Monday with a state court in Baton Rouge, lists the Louisiana Landowners Coalition, Louisiana Citizen Advocacy Group and Save My Louisiana as plaintiffs.
The plaintiffs claim the Public Service Commission violated rules in the Louisiana Constitution by not giving public notice before it adopted the “Lightning Speed Initiative” in December 2025. The policy change speeds up the regulatory approval process for utility projects linked to major investment in the state.
According to the lawsuit, the agenda for the meeting where the initiative was approved did not adequately explain the policy changes commissioners were considering, and the revised rules have never been placed “in the books.”
“The Louisiana Constitution requires the Public Service Commission to be transparent with the public when it tries to change its rules. It didn’t do that here,” William Most, a New Orleans attorney representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview Monday.
The Public Service Commission’s procedural change followed an executive order from Gov. Jeff Landry, issued in September 2025. It directed governmental bodies to ensure certain large-scale economic development projects earmarked as state priorities “receive focused attention and coordinated support across state government.” 
At the time, the governor said the existing regulatory approval process for major utility upgrades, which could take several months, put Louisiana at a distinct disadvantage for attracting major business investment to the state. 
Landry has long been bullish on data center development in Louisiana, despite growing bipartisan skepticism and voter opposition over the projects. The governor recently called for relabeling data centers as “digital factories.” 
Most said the Lightning Speed Initiative keeps “everyday” utility customers out of the loop on decisions that could impact their monthly bills.   
“Generally, utilities have to show their work to the [Public Service] Commission that they are seeking low-cost options for projects, and that’s an important requirement to keep electricity rates low for ratepayers,” he said. “The Lightning Directive allows some utilities to skip that in certain contexts.”
Entergy Louisiana has submitted an application to state regulators to build around $14 billion in energy infrastructure for Meta Hyperion, though many of its details have been kept confidential. Such documents can be kept under seal or redacted under PSC rules when commissioners deem they contain “sensitive” information. 
The plan has been the subject of challenges from groups such as the Alliance for Affordable Energy and Union of Concerned Scientists, which have submitted testimony to the Public Service Commission alleging lack of transparency from Meta and Entergy. 
The commission is scheduled to consider Entergy’s application at its Dec. 8 meeting. 
Meta and Entergy have said Louisiana utility customers will not bear the costs of powering the data center. Their respective leaders signed ratepayer protection pledges in March at the White House, and Landry issued another executive order in June in response to growing concerns that data centers planned for Louisiana would lead to higher utility bills.
Critics of the pledges and executive order have pointed out they are not legally binding, meaning average utility consumers could still be forced to foot the costs of powering data centers in Louisiana.
The groups behind the lawsuit share the common thread of private property rights. 
The Louisiana Landowners Coalition was founded by LaSalle Parish cattle farmer Dustin McAnn specifically to oppose Entergy’s use of eminent domain to acquire property to provide power to the Meta Hyperion data center campus. Save My Louisiana was launched by property owners opposed to eminent domain for the purposes of carbon sequestration, and the Louisiana Citizen Advocacy Group is an independent group chiefly known for its conservative constitutional stances.    
Most has also sent a letter on behalf of the consumer nonprofit Alliance for Affordable Energy to the Public Service Commission’s executive council, Kathryn Bowman, with an argument similar to the one he made in the lawsuit. The alliance is not involved in the case. 
In a written response to Most’s letter, Bowman said commissioners did not violate its rulemaking procedures when it adopted the Lightning Directive.  
“The utility still bears the burden of proof throughout the proceeding that the generation is in the public interest and is at the lowest reasonable costs,” Bowman said in the letter.
She also maintains the vote on the policy change was “properly noticed” on the commission’s agenda, and that public comment was allowed at the meeting when it was approved.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Winter is coming. So are deeper electric bill discounts for low-income Rhode Islanders
description: Marissa Diakite can’t seem to catch up. First it was electricity bills for the Pawtucket apartment she shares with her mom. The costs kept rising even as she worked more – and was home less – to try to make ends meet, she said. Now, Diakite has debt from months of partially unpaid electric bills. […]
text:
A new discount program modeled on other states including Connecticut and New Hampshire will curb monthly electric bills for eligible Rhode Island Energy  customers. (Photo by Janine L. Weisman/Rhode Island Current)Marissa Diakite can’t seem to catch up.
First it was electricity bills for the Pawtucket apartment she shares with her mom. The costs kept rising even as she worked more – and was home less – to try to make ends meet, she said.
Now, Diakite has debt from months of partially unpaid electric bills. And the other costs: rent, gas, student loans, even internet, are becoming harder to manage.
“For a while I went without wifi because it was too much of a luxury,” the 26-year-old CNA said in an interview Monday. “I portion all my food. But I’m starting to fall behind more.”
She is not alone. More than 114,000 Rhode Island Energy customers were behind on their electric bills, owing a combined $172.9 million in debt as of September, according to company filings with state regulators. 
Recognizing the financial strain facing customers — and cutting into its own pockets — the state utility supplier is set to launch an expanded discount program for low-income customers starting in January. The Enhanced Electric Discount Rate approved by state regulators in August reimagines an existing, two-tier discount program by concentrating the bulk of the savings for the lowest income, and most vulnerable, customers. The resulting five-tier program, modeled after offerings in other states including New Hampshire and Connecticut, aims to curb monthly electric bills such that eligible customers spend no more than 3% of their income on electricity costs. 
“There’s a lot of talk about affordability right now, and these enhancements provide real solutions for income-qualified customers by making sure their discount is directly tied to their financial circumstances,” Greg Cornett, Rhode Island Energy president, said in a statement on Monday.
The largest savings will be for people who earn at or below 50% of the federal poverty level: up to $7,980 for one person, or $16,500 for a family of four. For that income bracket, company discounts will cover 75% of monthly electric bill costs. The discount level decreases as income rises, with the smallest discount, of 10%, available to individuals whose earnings are between $23,940 and $39,900, or $49,500 and $82,500 for a family of four.
Most of the 33,000 Rhode Island Energy customers already enrolled in the existing, smaller program will automatically receive the enhanced discounts once the new program begins, said Carrie Gill, Rhode Island Energy’s head of electric regulatory strategy. 
However, some customers may be asked to verify certain personal information like names, addresses, and income to continue receiving discounts. For those people, notices are already in the mail, Gill said in an interview Monday.
Widening the net
Gill also hoped a wider public outreach campaign about the enhanced discounts would increase participation. Company analysis shows that just 25% of the customers who qualify for existing discounts participate in the reduced rate program, potentially because the discount is so small that some customers decide it’s not worth it, Gill said.
“We do think we will see increased enrollment because discounts are more meaningful for folks and because we’re doing this outreach,” Gill said.
She declined to share a projection on enrollment, saying it would be premature.
Also too early to predict are the potential returns for Rhode Island Energy. The company expects to spend $22.7 million in the enhanced discount program — 3.5% more than its existing discount offerings — according to analysis by Roger Colton, a consultant for the Rhode Island Division of Public Utilities and Carriers. But Colton also pointed out in regulatory filings that the net cost to Rhode Island Energy may actually be a savings, since more customers will be able to pay their bills, in turn reducing money on debt collection and shutoffs.
Gill agreed.
“If there are fewer arrears, there’s less expenses on collections,” she said.
But again, potential positive returns won’t materialize right away.
“Payment is a behavior and behavior changes take time to go through,” Gill said.
For people like Diakite, relief can’t come soon enough.
“It adds a lot of mental stress when you see all the bills compiling,” she said. “Trying to balance everything is getting kind of ridiculous.”
For some, it comes too late. More than 4,000 Rhode Island Energy customers had their electricity shut off as of September for unpaid bills, just under 1% of the 466,000 customers, according to company filings. That’s 33% more than in September 2025, when pandemic-era protections preventing utility shutoffs were still in place.
Those protections ended in May, leading to a sharp rise in utility shutoffs and calls for assistance to nonprofit and advocacy groups like United Way of Rhode Island and the George Wiley Center.
A seasonal moratorium on shutoffs began Nov. 1, keeping customers with unpaid bills in light and heat through May 1. But Camilo Viveiros, lead organizer at the George Wiley Center, remained worried for the thousands of customers whose age, health and financial circumstances put them at risk when the moratorium ends next spring.
Especially as energy prices continue to rise, driven by global unrest and limited supply, potentially making the enhanced discounts not as helpful, Viveiros noted.
“We still need more protections,” he said, naming more flexibility in repayment for customers facing serious medical conditions, and a hot weather-specific shutoff moratorium as important measures. “As is often the case, you win incremental victories and you continue to push for more.”
Cornett in a statement credited advocates for helping shape the upcoming discount program, which achieves the same objectives as the long-desired Percentage of Income Payment Plan program available in a dozen other states.
The tiered-income policy has been a perennial proposal at the Rhode Island State House, introduced every year for at least a decade but stalled amid industry opposition and competing legislative priorities.
The Public Utilities Commission authorized Rhode Island Energy to roll out the new discount program in January, but does not set a specific date. The start date will depend on extenuating circumstances, like another historic blizzard requiring emergency storm response, Gill said.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Opponents of South Dakota court consolidation say move would harm rural access to justice
description: The South Dakota Supreme Court heard concerns Monday at the Capitol in Pierre from people who said the proposed merger of two western judicial circuits could leave rural communities behind.  The proposal would combine the state’s 4th and 7th Judicial Circuits into a single 12-county 4th Circuit headquartered in Rapid City, reducing the number of […]
text:
The Pennington County Courthouse and jail complex in Rapid City is pictured in June 2023. A proposal from the state Unified Judicial System would consolidate two western South Dakota judicial circuits into one headquartered in Rapid City. (Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Supreme Court heard concerns Monday at the Capitol in Pierre from people who said the proposed merger of two western judicial circuits could leave rural communities behind. 
The proposal would combine the state’s 4th and 7th Judicial Circuits into a single 12-county 4th Circuit headquartered in Rapid City, reducing the number of judicial circuits in South Dakota from seven to six.
The 4th Judicial Circuit encompasses the northwestern part of the state, including Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties. 
The 7th Judicial Circuit includes the southwestern corner: Custer, Fall River, Oglala Lakota and Pennington counties. 

A map shows South Dakota’s seven judicial circuits. The Unified Judicial System is proposing merging the 4th and 7th circuit courts in western South Dakota. (Courtesy of the Unified Judicial System)

State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn told justices more than 90% of court business in the affected counties occurs in just Pennington, Meade, Butte and Lawrence counties. He said the merger would allow the courts to share personnel and resources more effectively, and eliminate duplicate positions. 
“It’s an important process, even if it’s a hard process,” Sattizahn said. “We need to position and ensure that our courts are stable and responsive and can move forward to the needs that we foresee.”
The Unified Judicial System estimated efficiencies from the consolidation would allow it to “repurpose” three positions, avoiding a $300,000 state funding request to add those positions. 
However, speakers at Monday’s hearing raised concerns about access to courts in rural communities.
Attorney Lora Waeckerle, of Black Hawk, said the merger could worsen staffing challenges and questioned what she called a lack of detailed implementation planning. The merged circuit would have the second-largest population and largest geographic footprint of any in the state, and the second-largest caseload. 
“No matter how dedicated our clerks and court reporters are, regularly traveling three and a half hours from Rapid City to McIntosh is simply likely not to occur,” Waeckerle said. “And I believe that the major concern of individuals is that there will be fewer in-person judicial services if this proposal is granted.”
4th Circuit Judge Eric Strawn said specific inefficiencies justifying consolidation have not been identified. 
“It’s kind of fighting smoke,” he said. “I have asked. We have tried to seek out what the actual harm is.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Shane Penfield, the state’s attorney for multiple 4th Circuit counties, said combining rural counties with Pennington County could diminish rural residents’ influence in judicial elections. He also raised concerns about impacts on communities within the Standing Rock and Cheyenne River Sioux reservations.
“Not only does it affect the ability of tribal members to choose who their state court judge should be,” he said, “but it also, ultimately, could change how justice is delivered.”
South Dakota Supreme Court Chief Justice Steven Jensen said the court must balance its responsibility to maintain access to justice in every county with its obligation to operate efficiently and spend taxpayer dollars responsibly.
The justices did not announce a decision Monday. Jensen said the court will issue a written order addressing the proposal, but provided no timeline. If approved, the consolidation could take effect at the beginning of 2027.

title: Voter turnout in Colorado midterms outpaces 2022, but falls short of 2018
description: As of Monday, about 67.3% of registered voters in Colorado participated in the 2026 midterm elections last week, outpacing participation in the 2022 midterms, but falling short of turnout in 2018.  County clerks had processed 2.76 million ballots from Colorado voters as of Monday, according to the secretary of state’s office.  In 2022, a little […]
text:
An election judge sorts through ballots on Election Day last week at the Douglas County clerk and recorder’s ballot processing center in Castle Rock. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)As of Monday, about 67.3% of registered voters in Colorado participated in the 2026 midterm elections last week, outpacing participation in the 2022 midterms, but falling short of turnout in 2018. 
County clerks had processed 2.76 million ballots from Colorado voters as of Monday, according to the secretary of state’s office. 
In 2022, a little more than 66% of active registered voters cast a ballot, while in 2018, nearly 75% did. Participation this year is higher among unaffiliated and Democratic voters than in the 2022 midterm election, while Republican voters lag behind 2022 turnout. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
More than 77% of Colorado’s active Democratic voters participated in the 2026 midterm elections, which resulted in a “blue tsunami” in the state and nationally. Almost 61% of active registered unaffiliated voters, Colorado’s largest voting bloc, cast a ballot. Slightly more than 73% of active Republican voters did so. 
About 95% of all ballots returned were mail ballots. 
Nearly 600,000 voters between the ages of 18 and 34 voted in 2026. According to New Era Colorado, a nonprofit that encourages young people to engage in the political process, 48% of young voters in Colorado participated compared to 45% in the 2022 midterms. 
“Young people turned out with a vengeance this year to fight back against the wealthy and secure a future where all Coloradans can thrive, not just a select few,” Christina Soliz, executive director of the New Era Colorado Action Fund, said in a statement. “We have a vision for Colorado where young people can thrive and share in abundance.”
Voters age 35 and older outpaced participation from young voters, though. Nearly 900,000 voters between the ages of 35 and 54 voted, and more than 920,000 voters between the ages of 55 and 74 voted. 
The Front Range is home to most voters who participated in the election. El Paso County has the highest voter turnout, with over 326,000 voters, followed by Denver and Jefferson counties at about 316,800 and 316,100, respectively. 
The secretary of state’s office will continue to send out daily turnout reports through Thursday.

text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks at the Department of Health and Human Services in Washington, D.C., in December. The agency on Monday announced Oklahoma's most recent award for investing in rural healthcare. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — The federal government awarded nearly $227.1 million to Oklahoma to invest in programs that strengthen rural healthcare, according to the state health department. 
The allocation, which is up by nearly $4 million over the year prior, will help fund 29 programs in Oklahoma that range from expanding training for doulas and community health workers to growing rural residency programs and telehealth. 
Oklahoma, which has some of the nation’s worst health rankings, received one of the largest awards in the second year of the Rural Health Transformation Program, trailing Texas, Alaska, Montana and California, according to a news release. 
“Receiving our budget period two award reflects the tremendous work of our partners throughout the state and our shared commitment to transforming rural healthcare,” said Oklahoma Commissioner of Health Keith Reed. 
Congress allocated $50 billion to the rural health fund as part of the Big Beautiful Bill, which was passed in 2025, to be appropriated across a five year span. Each year, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services are responsible for allocating $10 billion between all 50 states. 
This marks the second budget period of the program, which stretches from Oct. 31 Oct. 30, 2027. 
During the first award period, Oklahoma was allocated $223.5 million for rural health programs. 
Also part of the Big Beautiful Bill, Congress also slashed future Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over 10 years. 
The bulk of the changes are scheduled to begin rolling out in 2027 and run through 2029. They are expected to lead to staffing and service cuts at hospitals, officials estimated last year. The impact will be worse for rural Oklahomans who already have to travel further for healthcare. 
The Rural Health Transformation Program was added to the bill at the tailend of negotiations and was intended to mitigate the impact of these Medicaid cuts on rural areas of the country. 
All 50 states submit annual reports to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to prove they’ve made progress on the program’s initiatives and provide accountability for taxpayer dollars, according to a news release. 
Half of the $10 billion is divided equally between all 50 states each year, according to a news release. The other $5 billion is allocated based on factors like a state’s rural population and healthcare facilities, initiatives within the state’s plan or policy actions. 
While the program has five overall goals – make rural America healthy again, sustainable access, workforce development, innovative care and tech innovation – each state can tailor its programs to the needs of its rural communities.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Report: CT’s budget safety net is growing as other states’ shrink
description: A Pew report says CT's reserves are more than 40% greater than the national median, even though CT has redirected funding to bolster programs.
text:
Despite redirecting state budget surplus money to bolster childcare, municipal aid and federal human services programs under the knife, Connecticut still boasts one of the most robust emergency reserves in the nation, according to a new analysis from The Pew Charitable Trusts.
And while many states’ rainy day funds are declining, Connecticut’s continues to grow, despite a struggling economy.
When the last fiscal year closed on June 30, the median state had enough reserves to run for 47.9 days, Pew analysts wrote, citing data from the National Association of State Budget Officers. That’s down from 49.1 days following fiscal 2025 and 54.5 days after 2024.
“Although rainy day fund levels are still high compared with before the [COVID] pandemic, policymakers are navigating sluggish tax collections, growing spending pressures and decreased aid from the federal government,” wrote Pew staffers Justin Theale and Page Forrest.
But despite those trends, Connecticut’s state government could operate for 68.6 days on the nearly $4.5 billion it held on June 30, eight days longer than its surplus operating capacity two years ago.
That’s more than 40% greater than the national median and ranks 11th highest among all states. Connecticut’s $4.5 billion represents 18% of annual operating expenses, the maximum allowed by state law.
“Families set aside money for emergencies so that an unexpected expense doesn’t force difficult budget choices. State government should take the same approach,” Gov. Ned Lamont’s budget spokesman, Chris Collibee, said Friday.
States chiefly tap their rainy day funds during a recession or other severe economic downturn, using those saved dollars to temporarily replace eroding tax receipts and spare key programs such as health care and education from deep cuts.
“This [budget reserve] gives residents and businesses greater confidence that their state will be there to help protect essential services when they need it,” Collibee added.
While nearly all states have exhausted the billions in American Rescue Plan Act funds Congress awarded them in 2021 to recover from the pandemic, Connecticut also continues to impose aggressive budget caps that have forced surpluses averaging $1.8 billion, more than 8% of annual operating expenses, since 2017.
Those surpluses initially built a miniscule reserve into a record-setting one, but they mainly have been used to shrink the Connecticut’s hefty pension debt, a $30 billion-plus problem that still drains resources from other programs. About $11 billion in unfunded liabilities has been eliminated since 2020 because of surplus alone.
Connecticut could accommodate those surpluses more easily when it was awash in federal pandemic grants, which could be spent outside of the traditional budget process and replace much of the savings forced by fiscal caps.
But as those grants dwindled in recent years, Connecticut legislature’s Democratic majority has pressured Lamont to redirect some of that savings to respond to several issues.
Acknowledging a dearth of affordable childcare program slots statewide, the governor and lawmakers have invested $712 million in potential surplus over the past two years into a childcare expansion program.
Another $550 million was set aside to bolster federal human services programs cut by Congress and President Donald Trump.
And more than $280 million went to cities and towns this past summer to help communities avert property tax increases.
Lamont, a fiscally moderate Democrat, initially had been reluctant to modify budget caps and savings efforts.
But House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, brokered a compromise in 2024. Connecticut would shift some potential surplus to protect key programs, but it also would increase its maximum allowable rainy day fund from 15% of annual operating expenses to 18% to guard against future recessions.
Ritter has predicted legislators will look to make more adjustments to budget caps over the next two years, with changes depending heavily on whether Washington continues its present course of cutting human services funding and aid to states.
But he also said lawmakers also want to continue to pay down pension debt at a healthy pace, though not as aggressively as they did during the early 2020s, while continuing to invest more in education, affordable childcare and municipal aid.
“Nobody is opposed to paying down pension debt,” he said. “The question is to what degree.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC Senate Democratic leader sees a path to bipartisanship next year
description: Sen. Sydney Batch, a Wake County Democrat and the leader of her caucus in the North Carolina Senate, may have one of the most challenging jobs in the General Assembly next year. She’ll likely be balancing the expectations that come from Democrats being able to pass anything they wish in the House with the reality […]
text:
N.C. Senate Democratic Leader Sydney Batch, D-Wake, speaks to members of the media after Senate session on June 10, 2026. (Photo: Claire Michal/NC Newsline)Sen. Sydney Batch, a Wake County Democrat and the leader of her caucus in the North Carolina Senate, may have one of the most challenging jobs in the General Assembly next year.
She’ll likely be balancing the expectations that come from Democrats being able to pass anything they wish in the House with the reality that the Republican-majority Senate, where she serves, can scuttle all of it.
“We’re living in a world where nothing’s going to get done unless we get Republican support,” she said, “so people need to temper their expectations.”
Democrats will control the state House next year for the first time since 2010. Democratic leader Robert Reives, D-Chatham, is expected to become House Speaker. But Republicans will hold a majority in the Senate, albeit a slim one, with 26 seats to the Democrats’ 24, according to unofficial election results. One race could still be subject to recount.
Divided control could be a recipe for gridlock, but Batch sees an opportunity for bipartisan accomplishments. 
“It is going to be a challenge with us being at 24, but I do think that with every challenge comes a great opportunity for us to be able to finally sit down, reset in the Senate, and work with whoever ends up being their leader, to make sure that we can be an example here in North Carolina of a chamber that can govern in parity.”
Republican Sens. Jim Burgin of Harnett County, Ralph Hise of Mitchell County, Brett Jackson of Sampson County, and Todd Johnson of Union County are vying to succeed Senate Leader Phil Berger of Rockingham County, who lost his primary. 
Batch said she didn’t have a preference about who succeeds Berger.
NC Democrats will have more power next year, but must first face a GOP-controlled lame duck session

She said she has good relationships with many Senate Republicans, and will respect the decision they make about who will lead them.
“I will be more than happy to work with them to pass legislation,” she said. 
Batch has served nearly three terms in the Senate. She has also served one House term. She’s been the Senate’s Democratic leader for one term.
Democrats have seen most of their proposals dashed against the rocks of Republican legislative majorities for the past 16 years. Some of those doomed ideas have had widespread support from Democrats in both chambers. Some of those ideas still won’t get past a Republican Senate. 
Likewise, if Senate Republicans want their bills passed, they’ll have to work with House Democrats, she said. 
Batch said she’d like the legislature for the next two years to focus on making healthcare more affordable, to talk about housing affordability, and address returning academic freedom to higher education.
Some issues in the legislature already have bipartisan support, but have died in battles between House and Senate Republicans. For example, bills that would limit sales of edible hemp products to adults have passed the House and Senate, but the chambers have not been able to agree on details. 
This is an example where the Senate being closely divided will matter, she said, because some Republicans will want to work on a bill that can pass both chambers.
With the potential for a closely divided Senate comes the speculation that a Republican will change parties. That would essentially give Democrats a majority because Democratic Lt. Gov. Rachel Hunt can break tie votes. 
Batch said she has not spoken to any Republican about switching parties. 
“Any of them want to change and be in our party — more than happy,” Batch said. “But it will not be because I ask, and it certainly won’t be because I’m offering them anything for it.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Mirror’s P.R. Lockhart selected for New America Foundation reporting fellowship
description: Lockhart, CT Mirror’s economic development reporter, was selected to participate in New America and Work Shift’s new Future of Work Reporting Fellowship.
text:
P.R. Lockhart, The Connecticut Mirror’s economic development reporter, was selected to participate in New America and Work Shift’s new Future of Work Reporting Fellowship. 
Lockhart joins a cohort of 11 early to mid-career reporters who will study how education, workforce development and the innovation economy intersect, as well as the impact these convergences have on people. They are the first group to participate in the program.
Lockhart will focus on Connecticut’s recent investments in building out a quantum computing sector, exploring how those efforts play out for communities most in need of economic development. 
“It’s the job of journalism outlets like ours to keep tabs on whether this big bet pays off — and for whom,” said Erica E. Phillips, The Connecticut Mirror’s state policy editor. “I’m thrilled that P.R. will have support from New America’s Future of Work fellowship to dig into this reporting so we can hold state leaders accountable.”
New America is a public policy think tank that researches U.S. and global systems. The Future of Work reporting fellowship is part of New America’s Future of Work and Innovation Economy initiative, which studies policy solutions at the intersection of workforce, economic development and emerging technology ecosystems. The stories produced will illustrate how technological change is impacting communities across the nation. 
The reporting fellowship is also launched in partnership with Work Shift, an independent news site covering education, work and economic opportunity. New America’s experts and Work Shift’s editors will provide professional development, funding, communications and strategic support to each fellow.
The Future of Work Reporting Fellows will produce stories from 10 regions across the country, including Connecticut, Wisconsin, North Carolina, Florida, Pennsylvania, Colorado and more. Newsrooms represented include The Guardian, Open Campus and others.

title: Republicans’ Utah House supermajority still on track to break as counting continues in tight races
description: A couple of the closest Utah House races have flipped again as more votes are counted, with Democrats leading in what are currently Republican-held seats. If results stand, House Republicans’ supermajority is still set to break, with the GOP losing 16 seats. As of Monday, Republicans had 45 seats, Democrats had 28, and unaffiliated candidates […]
text:
Charice Nauman gathers sorted ballots at the Salt Lake County Government Center on Tuesday, Nov 3, 2026. (Photo by Marco Lozzi for Utah News Dispatch)A couple of the closest Utah House races have flipped again as more votes are counted, with Democrats leading in what are currently Republican-held seats.
If results stand, House Republicans’ supermajority is still set to break, with the GOP losing 16 seats. As of Monday, Republicans had 45 seats, Democrats had 28, and unaffiliated candidates were poised to take two districts, according to the firm Morgan and May. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Morgan Republican Rep. Tiara Auxier is trailing Democrat Zane Woolstenhulme, who as of Monday had received 51.49% of votes in House District 4, representing areas in Rich, Morgan and Summit counties. Woolstenhulme is ahead by 565 votes.
Auxier wished Woolstenhulme well on a social media post Sunday and said that while this may be the end of her term in the Utah House, she will continue her public service efforts.
“Serving reinforced my belief that government works best when it remembers who it works for,” Auxier wrote. “I love the people of this district. You represent some of the very best of Utah, and it has been a privilege to serve you.”
Democratic candidate Celeste Johnson is also ahead in the race for House District 59, a seat vacated by Republican Rep. Mike Kohler, who did not seek reelection this year. Johnson had received 50.89% of the votes tallied by Monday, leading Republican Luke Searle, who got 49.11%, a 322-vote difference.  



Let us know what you think...


 


However, a Republican candidate has taken over the lead in the race for District 48’s seat, left open by Herriman Republican Rep. Doug Fiefia, who has won a seat in the Utah Senate. Jake Hunsaker, a Republican, had 51.03% of votes on Monday, 298 more than Democratic candidate Benyde Walker.
“Things are looking up, but the county still is counting a handful of provisional ballots, absentee ballots, and there are some ballots coming in as well,” Hunsaker said on Monday on his Instagram account. “We don’t believe those are going to be statistically significant, but we’re being patient, and we’re not counting any chickens before they hatch, and we’re riding the ride alongside you. So my hope is we get more information from the county today, and we will be able to make some decisions about what the next steps look like in this race.”
In the Senate, incumbent Emily Buss, the sole Forward Party lawmaker in the state, is still behind Republican challenger Brooks Benson by a tight margin. Benson is leading with 50.81% of votes in the race for Senate District 11, representing areas in Tooele and Utah counties. That’s 512 more votes than what Buss had claimed. 
Election results are not official until county and state canvasses are completed on Nov. 23.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Feds launch investigations into Albuquerque, Santa Fe schools’ gender identity policies
description: The U.S. Department of Education announced Monday that it launched investigations into the Albuquerque and Santa Fe Public School districts, alleging their gender-identity and expression policies violate federal family education and privacy law.
text:
The U.S. Department of Education announced investigations into the Albuquerque and Santa Fe Public Schools’ gender identity policies on Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Patrick Lohman/Source NM)The U.S. Department of Education announced Monday that it launched investigations into the Albuquerque and Santa Fe Public School districts, alleging their gender-identity and expression policies violate federal family education and privacy law. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The federal agency instructed its Student Privacy Policy Office to investigate whether policies regarding student gender identity at the Albuquerque and Santa Fe public school districts violate the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment, according to a news release.
Specifically, the U.S. Department of Education alleges that a district social worker with the Albuquerque Public Schools was “prevented from sharing ‘gender identity’ information with parents,” due to APS’ non-discrimination rule regarding gender identity and expression, which mandates that schools use a student’s chosen name and directs schools to separate a student’s preferred name and gender in informal records, while referring to their legal name in permanent records that are made available to parents. 
In an emailed statement, APS Senior Director of Communications Martin Salazar responded to the allegations: “APS policies and procedures adhere to FERPA guidelines. We have been notified of the investigation and will respond through the appropriate channels.”
The ED and U.S. Department of Justice sent letters on Oct. 5, 2026, to all state Attorneys General, pointing them to recent federal guidance and expressing “concerns about their school districts’ lack of compliance with these federal laws regarding mental health screenings conducted in schools.”
The New Mexico Office of the Attorney General confirmed receipt of the letter to Source NM.
In addition, the ED says it has received reports from parents in Santa Fe who alleged that “the school district utilized ‘gender support plans’ without their consent or knowledge.” The ED cited a form titled “Name and Pronoun Info Sheet” that asks students what they’d like to be referred to in class. The form, the ED says, explicitly states that the teacher will keep what the students filled out confidential from parents. 
Neither SFPS spokesperson Tara Melton nor SFPS Board President Kate Noble immediately responded to SourceNM’s phone call and email seeking comment Monday afternoon. 
Since taking office last year, President Donald Trump has signed numerous orders targeting transgender rights.
“Policies designed to conceal or hide the most sensitive information about a child’s well-being not only violate federal law but also educators’ moral obligation to let parents be the first decision-makers in their child’s lives,” U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement. “We will vigorously investigate these allegations and hold districts accountable to bring parents out of the dark.”
The news release also says the department is taking action against two Pennsylvania school districts, and partnering with the U.S. Department of Justice in one instance for an enforcement action. 
This is a developing story and may be updated.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana reports results from its first-ever sport alligator hunting season
description: Sport hunters bagged more than 1,800 alligators during Louisiana’s new recreational hunting season, the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries announced Monday.
text:
An alligator basking in the sun at Jean Lafitte National Park in Jefferson Parish. (Louisiana Illuminator file photo)Sport hunters bagged more than 1,800 alligators during Louisiana’s new recreational hunting season, the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries announced Monday. 
The monthlong season, which the Louisiana Legislature established during its spring session, ended Oct. 31. Gov. Jeff Landry lauded the campaign, in which 3,600 hunters participated, as a wild success. 
“With more than 3 million alligators in our state, this was an exciting opportunity for families to enjoy our Sportsman’s Paradise,” Landry said in a news release. “We can’t wait to bring it back next year.”
The state set a maximum of 10,000 alligators for its first recreational hunting season. State residents had to hold a standard hunting license and obtain an alligator hunting permit through a lottery in order to bag a reptile. Non-Louisiana residents were also able to participate as long as they accompanied a state hunter with a recreational permit and acquired the necessary $150 out-of-state license.
Sen. Robert Allain, R-Franklin, authored the bill that created the recreational hunting season, which overlapped with the commercial season. Commercial hunters began taking gators in early August in the state’s eastern zone and early September in the western zone. Both commercial seasons last through Dec. 31.   
Before the sport hunting season existed, anyone who wanted to hunt gators for fun in Louisiana’s public waters and wildlife management areas needed tags from a state-licensed commercial hunter, who typically harvests the reptiles for their hides and meat.
The state’s 2,900 licensed commercial hunters get tags for every gator they are allowed to harvest, with the number they are issued based on the property where they hunt and the local gator population. 
Wildlife officials and conservationists have celebrated the establishment of an alligator sport hunting season as a sign of success for the species. Once listed as federally endangered, the wild alligator population in Louisiana has risen from 100,000 to more than 3 million over the past 50 years, according to the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries. 
Officials rescued the species by limiting the taking of alligator eggs, and they encouraged farming to help boost its numbers in the wild.

title: Former POW Ralph Galati to headline Delaware Veterans Day ceremony
description: Annual New Castle observance will focus on service and sacrifice, with Vietnam veteran who endured 406 days in captivity delivering keynote address NEW CASTLE, Del. — Delawareans will gather Wednesday at the Delaware War Memorial Plaza to honor the men and women who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces, with former Vietnam War prisoner of war Ralph Galati de[...]
text:
Hosted by the Delaware Department of Veterans Affairs and Delaware Commission of Veterans Affairs, the ceremony is intended to recognize veterans from across Delaware and the generations of Americans whose military service has helped preserve the nation’s freedoms. created on 11/9 by using AI
Annual New Castle observance will focus on service and sacrifice, with Vietnam veteran who endured 406 days in captivity delivering keynote address
NEW CASTLE, Del. — Delawareans will gather Wednesday at the Delaware War Memorial Plaza to honor the men and women who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces, with former Vietnam War prisoner of war Ralph Galati delivering the keynote address.
The annual Veterans Day ceremony begins at 10:30 a.m. Nov. 11 at the memorial plaza, 163 Cherry Lane in New Castle.
Hosted by the Delaware Department of Veterans Affairs and Delaware Commission of Veterans Affairs, the ceremony is intended to recognize veterans from across Delaware and the generations of Americans whose military service has helped preserve the nation’s freedoms.
Galati brings to the ceremony a story of combat, captivity, resilience and decades of continued service to fellow veterans.
A Philadelphia-area native and graduate of St. Joseph’s University, Galati was commissioned into the U.S. Air Force in 1970 and earned his flight wings the following year. He became a weapons systems officer aboard the F-4 Phantom and served as a laser-guided bomb lead and forward air controller while stationed at Ubon Royal Thai Air Force Base in Thailand.
On Feb. 16, 1972, Galati and his pilot were shot down over North Vietnam. Galati was captured and taken to Hanoi, where he remained a prisoner of war for 406 days.
He was released March 28, 1973, as part of Operation Homecoming, which returned hundreds of American prisoners of war from Southeast Asia.
Galati has described captivity as long periods of uncertainty and isolation punctuated by fear. During a 2014 visit to Dover Air Force Base, he told service members that training, faith, trust and reliance on fellow prisoners helped sustain him during his imprisonment.
His military decorations include the Silver Star, two Bronze Star Medals with Valor, two Purple Hearts, multiple Air Medals and the Prisoner of War Medal. His Silver Star recognized his actions as an F-4 weapons systems officer on the mission during which he was shot down.
After returning home, Galati continued serving in the Air Force as a flight instructor, curriculum developer and member of the Secretary of the Air Force’s legislative liaison staff at the Pentagon. He completed active duty in 1978 and later served in the Air Force Reserve.
His commitment to veterans continued long after his military career ended.
Galati spent 28 years with IBM before retiring in 2007. He later served as veterans liaison for Delaware County, Pennsylvania, and founded the Office of Veterans Services at St. Joseph’s University, where programs included assistance and entrepreneurship training for veterans. He remains involved with veterans organizations, including the Delaware County Veterans Memorial Association.
His appearance in New Castle comes more than half a century after his captivity and provides a personal connection to the purpose of Veterans Day: remembering not only those who fought in America’s wars, but everyone who accepted the obligations and risks that come with military service.
Veterans Day traces its roots to the end of World War I, when fighting stopped at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918. Originally observed as Armistice Day, the holiday was renamed Veterans Day in 1954 to honor American veterans of all wars and all eras of service.
Unlike Memorial Day, which specifically honors those who died while serving the country, Veterans Day recognizes all who have served in the nation’s armed forces.
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs describes the purpose of the day as honoring veterans for their patriotism, service and willingness to sacrifice for the common good.
Wednesday’s ceremony will include state and federal officials, but its central focus will be Delaware’s veterans and the experiences represented by Galati and other former service members in attendance.
The Delaware Department of Veterans Affairs and Delaware Commission of Veterans Affairs also work year-round to help veterans and their families obtain benefits and services, including disability compensation, employment and housing assistance.

When: 10:30 a.m. Wednesday, Nov. 11
Where: Delaware War Memorial Plaza, 163 Cherry Lane, New Castle
Keynote speaker: Retired U.S. Air Force Capt. Ralph Galati, Vietnam War veteran and former prisoner of war
Who may attend: Veterans, military families and members of the public
