title: North Carolina’s governor celebrates huge milestone for Meals on Wheels
description: Gov. Josh Stein was on hand Monday as Meals on Wheels delivered its eight millionth meal in Forsyth County. The recipient was Ben Briggs, a 105-year-old retired science teacher who relies on the nonprofit to deliver meals to his home. In North Carolina 13.9% of seniors, more than 341,000 older adults, face food insecurity. Stein […]
text:
North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein visits with 105-year-old Ben Briggs (center) and his family in Forsyth County on Nov. 9, 2026. Stein helped Meals on Wheels deliver its eight millionth meal in the county. (Photo: Office of Gov. Josh Stein.) Gov. Josh Stein was on hand Monday as Meals on Wheels delivered its eight millionth meal in Forsyth County. The recipient was Ben Briggs, a 105-year-old retired science teacher who relies on the nonprofit to deliver meals to his home.
In North Carolina 13.9% of seniors, more than 341,000 older adults, face food insecurity.
Stein said rising grocery prices leave too many North Carolinians like Briggs wondering where their next meal may come from.
“Delivering eight million meals is an incredible milestone,” said Stein in a statement. “I am grateful to the Meals on Wheels and Senior Services team and every volunteer who connects people to the food they need.“
The Stein administration has focused on hunger-related issues for much of the past year with the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill, which cut food benefits and instituted work requirements to qualify for them.
Last month, the governor sent a letter to congressional leaders and the North Carolina congressional delegation, urging them to repeal the work requirements because they could put 90,000 North Carolinians covered by SNAP at risk of losing that benefit.
Statewide, more than 1.2 million North Carolinians rely on SNAP to purchase groceries.
Starting next October, states will also be required to pay a portion of the SNAP benefit costs based on their payment error rate.
“We know that in North Carolina, the costs of H.R. 1 implementation will fall heavily on already-strained county budgets, and counties may need to cut other services to make up the shortfall,” Stein wrote in the Oct. 13 letter.
In July, the comprehensive state budget Stein signed included more than $9 million to support food banks and North Carolina farmers.
Hunger crisis widens in North Carolina as food banks face more demand, federal cuts

Stein also used Monday’s meal delivery to announce that the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services will relaunch a streamlined Healthy Opportunities Pilot (HOP) program in early 2027. The program will deliver weekly healthy food boxes to high-need NC Medicaid Managed Care recipients across three pilot regions through June 30, 2027.
The initial pilot program was suspended in July 2025 because of a lack of additional funding by the North Carolina General Assembly, where some Republican leaders were skeptical about the program’s impact. However, a study this year by the Sheps Center at the University of North Carolina found the pilot program resulted in fewer emergency department visits and reduced healthcare costs by an average of $164 per month for N.C. Medicaid beneficiaries.
“By focusing on food insecurity, we are keeping our highest-risk neighbors healthy at home and proving that proactive nutrition is one of the most effective tools we have to keep people out of the hospital,” said NCDHHS Secretary Dev Sangvai in a statement.

name: California
title: Los Ángeles tuvo su peor año de mosquitos en esta década. El fenómeno de El Niño podría empeorar aún más la situación
description: California está registrando el mayor nivel de actividad del virus del Nilo Occidental en cinco años. El próximo año podría ser peor.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Cuando las temperaturas superan los 70 grados, unas diminutas partículas del virus del Nilo Occidental comienzan a replicarse rápidamente en el intestino de los mosquitos Culex , que luego salen a la caza de su próxima “comida de sangre”, inyectando saliva cargada de virus en sus presas cuando se alimentan de ellas.
 Este año, el verano y el otoño cálidos y húmedos de California propiciaron la mayor actividad del virus del Nilo Occidental en cinco años. Hasta el 6 de noviembre, el virus había enfermado gravemente a 528 personas y causado 32 muertes, según el Departamento de Salud Pública de California.
 La mayoría de las personas infectadas nunca presentan síntomas, pero aproximadamente 1 de cada 5 puede desarrollar fiebre, dolor de cabeza y dolores musculares. En el caso de los pocos afectados —1 de cada 150— la situación se agrava: el virus puede llegar al cerebro, causando inflamación, problemas neurológicos e incluso la muerte. No existe cura, solo atención médica de apoyo.
 El sur de California fue la zona más afectada por las infecciones, y el condado de Los Ángeles concentró más de la mitad de todos los casos humanos notificados.
 Los residentes de la zona pronto podrían notar una disminución en la presencia de mosquitos, ya que las noches más frescas ralentizan tanto su reproducción como la propagación del virus. Sin embargo, los expertos siguen preocupados por lo que sucederá después, dado que el cambio climático y los fenómenos meteorológicos extremos crean las condiciones propicias para un aumento de las enfermedades transmitidas por mosquitos, especialmente en las zonas costeras y las llanuras aluviales.
 “Todos tenemos miedo del próximo año”, dijo Paula Macedo, presidenta de la Asociación de Control de Mosquitos y Vectores de California. “Con la cantidad de actividad que ya hemos visto este año y con el pronóstico de que será un año de El Niño, todos nos estamos preparando”.
 Que el próximo año traiga alivio o un nuevo repunte depende de una compleja combinación de aves, mosquitos y condiciones climáticas que incluso los expertos tienen dificultades para predecir. 
Costa de California corre el riesgo de un aumento de las enfermedades
 En septiembre, una tormenta cálida azotó las regiones costeras e interiores del sur de California. Los extremos del huracán Marie dejaron caer una pulgada y media de lluvia en gran parte del oeste de Los Ángeles; el centro de la ciudad batió el récord de precipitaciones de 1965. En los días siguientes, las temperaturas alcanzaron los 104 grados Fahrenheit, y las mínimas nocturnas no bajaron de los 77 grados Fahrenheit.
 Los mosquitos proliferaron en los días siguientes. Según el Distrito de Control de Vectores del Condado de Los Ángeles, las lluvias arrastraron los tratamientos antimosquitos de más de 4.800 kilómetros de desagües pluviales subterráneos.
 “Una de las principales fuentes de mosquitos Culex son nuestros desagües pluviales subterráneos”, dijo Susanne Kluh, la gerente general del distrito. “Allí abajo la temperatura ronda los 22 grados Celsius y hay humedad todo el año”. 
 Los bañistas permanecen de pie en medio de una densa humedad mientras el huracán Marie avanza, el lunes 7 de septiembre de 2026, en Huntington Beach, al sur de California. (Foto AP/Ethan Swope)
 El distrito trata los desagües pluviales mensualmente, pero con larvicida. Tras ser arrastrados al mar, las poblaciones de mosquitos se dispararon. En un momento dado de este verano, Kluh afirmó que más del 70 % de los mosquitos capturados para su análisis portaban el virus del Nilo Occidental. Ese porcentaje ha disminuido en las últimas semanas hasta aproximadamente un tercio.
 Las investigaciones sugieren que el cambio climático aumentará el riesgo de transmisión del virus del Nilo Occidental en la costa del sur de California. Un estudio dirigido por la Universidad de California en Berkeley, basado en datos del área de Los Ángeles recopilados entre 2006 y 2016, identificó un punto de inflexión preciso: cuando las temperaturas promedio se mantenían por debajo de los 21 °C, la probabilidad de que el virus se transmitiera a los mosquitos era mucho menor, y cuando superaban los 23 °C, aumentaba considerablemente. Las temperaturas más altas también se asociaron con un mayor número de infecciones en humanos.
 La costa de Los Ángeles se encuentra justo en ese límite. Las temperaturas promedio en verano rondan entre los 60 y los 70 grados Fahrenheit, y un ligero aumento de unos pocos grados puede hacer que se superen. Eso es precisamente lo que ocurrió este año.
 “Cuanto más tiempo se mantengan esas temperaturas adecuadas, mayor será la probabilidad de que se produzcan casos en humanos”, afirmó Tristan Hallum, director científico del Distrito de Control de Mosquitos y Vectores del Valle de San Gabriel.
 El virus se propaga en un ciclo complejo impulsado por aves, mosquitos y las condiciones climáticas. Una mosquita que se alimenta de un ave infectada puede ingerir el virus e infectar posteriormente a otras aves y, en ocasiones, a humanos. Sin embargo, las aves que han sido infectadas previamente y han sobrevivido desarrollan inmunidad al virus del Nilo Occidental, y su sangre ya no contiene el virus que los mosquitos puedan consumir.  
 Esa inmunidad tiende a generar un ciclo natural de actividad del virus del Nilo Occidental de tres a cinco años, lo que significa que Los Ángeles, el condado de Orange y otras áreas con muchos casos podrían tener un respiro el próximo año, pero otras partes del estado siguen siendo vulnerables. 
El virus prolifera durante condiciones climáticas extremas
 Los meteorólogos federales pronostican una probabilidad superior al 90 % de que se produzca un fenómeno de El Niño muy intenso este invierno, lo que aumenta las probabilidades de fuertes lluvias, especialmente en el sur de California. Esto preocupa a los funcionarios de salud pública y control de vectores: si las inundaciones persisten hasta la primavera a medida que suben las temperaturas, la población de mosquitos podría proliferar.
 Esto ya ha ocurrido antes. En 2023, las fuertes lluvias e inundaciones llenaron la cuenca del lago Tulare, que llevaba mucho tiempo seca en el Valle Central, sumergiendo vastas extensiones de tierras agrícolas y reactivando los humedales. El lago se mantuvo durante aproximadamente un año, alterando temporalmente los patrones y el comportamiento de las aves migratorias; además, creó un hábitat ideal para los mosquitos Culex, especie autóctona del estado.
 Ese año, las autoridades sanitarias registraron 433 casos humanos de virus del Nilo Occidental.
 La sequía también importa, y de una manera paradójica. En 2014 y 2015, más de 1600 personas contrajeron el virus del Nilo Occidental durante algunos de los años más secos registrados. 


 Protégete del virus del Nilo Occidental. 
 Según los funcionarios de salud pública estatales y los expertos en control de vectores, tomar precauciones sencillas puede reducir el riesgo.

 Vacía el agua estancada en el jardín al menos una vez por semana. Los principales culpables son los platos de las mascotas, los platillos de las macetas, los juguetes de los niños, los bebederos para pájaros y los escombros.
Trata las fuentes de agua permanentes, como los pequeños estanques, con larvicidas . Algunos distritos de control de vectores suministran peces mosquito.
Utiliza un repelente con ingredientes activos registrados por la EPA, como DEET, picaridina o aceite de eucalipto limón.
 Si vas a pasar tiempo al aire libre entre el anochecer y el amanecer, usa camisas de manga larga y pantalones largos.
Informa sobre aves muertas, en particular cuervos, cornejas y arrendajos californianos, al departamento de salud en westnile.ca.gov/report .

Conoce los síntomas: Busca atención médica si presentas dolor de cabeza intenso, rigidez en el cuello, confusión o debilidad muscular, especialmente si tienes más de 60 años.


 “Una hipótesis es que las condiciones secas propician un mayor contacto entre aves y mosquitos debido a la escasez de agua en el paisaje”, dijo Chris Barker, profesor de la UC Davis que estudia las enfermedades transmitidas por mosquitos y ayuda a dirigir el programa estatal de vigilancia del virus del Nilo Occidental.
 Según Barker, dado que el virus del Nilo Occidental depende de una combinación variable de aves, mosquitos y condiciones climáticas, los casos no aumentarán de forma constante año tras año a medida que el clima se calienta. En cambio, los fenómenos meteorológicos extremos —tanto inundaciones como sequías— generarán más años con las condiciones propicias para los brotes, lo que dificultará la lucha contra el virus.
 “El cambio climático tiene el efecto de inclinar la balanza un poco más en nuestra contra”, añadió. 
Los expertos buscan una vacuna
 No existe una vacuna para protegerse contra el virus del Nilo Occidental. Aaron Brault, un destacado experto e investigador del virus del Nilo Occidental de los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades, afirmó en un correo electrónico que Estados Unidos necesita una.
 “A pesar de que el virus del Nilo Occidental ha sido una causa importante de enfermedad en Estados Unidos durante más de 25 años, nuestro conjunto de herramientas es limitado”, dijo Brault.
 Los CDC solo aceptaron preguntas por escrito y no pusieron a Brault a disposición para una entrevista.
 El uso de repelentes y mangas largas ayuda a disminuir el riesgo, pero la gente suele ignorar estas medidas, dijo Brault, y esas medidas “no han reducido adecuadamente el número de casos o muertes por el virus del Nilo Occidental en los Estados Unidos”.
 Los CDC están explorando nuevas formas de combatir el virus del Nilo Occidental y fomentando el desarrollo de una vacuna, nuevos tratamientos y mejores pruebas de diagnóstico, pero es una labor ardua. Los brotes del virus del Nilo Occidental son impredecibles, lo que dificulta la realización de los grandes ensayos clínicos que requieren las vacunas.
 “Los virus a veces nos desafían, especialmente a quienes intentan predecirlos”, dijo Barker.
 El cambio climático agrava esa incertidumbre y dificulta aún más la labor de quienes intentan mantener baja la población de mosquitos. 
El control de vectores se enfrenta a nuevos desafíos y a una financiación limitada
 Los distritos de control de vectores de California gastan millones cada año en la captura y eliminación de mosquitos. Los residentes financian este trabajo localmente mediante impuestos sobre la propiedad, que suelen oscilar entre 4 y 10 dólares anuales, según la Asociación de Control de Mosquitos y Vectores de California. La aparición de nuevas plagas y las temporadas de mosquitos más largas dificultan su labor.
 Es probable que los mosquitos que más molestaron y de los que se rascaron los residentes del sur de California este año no fueran el mosquito Culex , portador del virus del Nilo Occidental , sino una especie invasora llamada Aedes aegypti .
 Las especies nativas de mosquitos Culex pican entre el anochecer y el amanecer y prefieren las aves a los humanos, aunque también pican ocasionalmente. En cambio, el mosquito Aedes, de rayas blancas y negras, caza durante el día y se alimenta principalmente de sangre humana. No transmite el virus del Nilo Occidental, pero puede propagar otras enfermedades infecciosas como el dengue, el zika, la chikungunya y la fiebre amarilla.
 El mosquito Aedes también es más difícil de controlar. Se reproduce con tan solo una cucharadita de agua, y sus huevos pueden sobrevivir meses de sequía , reviviendo cuando regresan las lluvias. Algunos distritos de control de vectores en California han gastado cientos de miles de dólares liberando mosquitos Aedes machos estériles para reducir la población total de mosquitos, lo que disminuye la capacidad de combatir los mosquitos Culex .
Los desastres pueden agravar la situación. El incendio de Eaton, que destruyó 9,000 estructuras en 2025, dejó tras de sí 1,400 piscinas con agua estancada.
 “Con el tiempo, el presupuesto se ha visto muy reducido debido a la necesidad de responder a estos mosquitos adicionales y a otras causas”, dijo Macedo, de la Asociación de Control de Mosquitos y Vectores de California.
 La ley estatal limita la cantidad que los gobiernos locales pueden recaudar por estos servicios, aunque algunos distritos de control de vectores han consultado a los votantes para solicitar más fondos.
 Aun así, Macedo afirmó que ningún presupuesto puede cubrir todos los patios traseros.
 “No podemos entrar en todas las propiedades. No podemos tratar todos los focos de mosquitos”, dijo. “Necesitamos que la gente entienda cómo pueden prevenir esta situación”.
 Este programa cuenta con el apoyo de la Fundación de Atención Médica de California (CHCF), que trabaja para garantizar que las personas tengan acceso a la atención médica que necesitan, cuando la necesitan y a un precio asequible. Visite www.chcf.org para obtener más información.

name: California
title: ‘Un dolor desgarrador’: Familiares de las víctimas indignados por la decisión de Newsom de conmutar penas de muerte en California
description: Las familias de las víctimas de presos condenados a muerte reaccionan ante la decisión del gobernador de California, Gavin Newsom, de conmutar sus sentencias por cadena perpetua.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Han vivido los peores horrores que una familia puede soportar, y se les prometió que sus seres queridos asesinados recibirían justicia mediante la ejecución. Sufrieron años, si no décadas, de apelaciones y audiencias en las que se vieron obligados a escuchar una y otra vez los relatos gráficos de las muertes violentas de sus seres queridos.
 Observaron cómo los tribunales —y luego el gobernador Gavin Newsom— suspendían las ejecuciones. La última se llevó a cabo en 2006, antes de que fuera elegido, a pesar de que los votantes de California habían reafirmado repetidamente su apoyo a la pena de muerte durante los últimos 50 años.
 Y el jueves se enteraron de que Newsom, en uno de sus últimos actos como gobernador, había conmutado las penas de muerte por cadena perpetua para cada uno de los 548 asesinos condenados a muerte.
 “No se trata solo de números en un documento legal”, dijo Sandy Friend, cuyo hijo de ocho años fue violado, torturado y asesinado por un hombre condenado a muerte. “Cada caso deja una familia atrás. Cada caso tiene la historia de un final horrible y violento para un ser querido. Borrar todo eso con un simple trazo de pluma, sin considerar los detalles ni mirar a los ojos de las familias, era completamente impensable”.
 En una carta abierta sobre las conmutaciones de penas, Newsom afirmó que la decisión fue una de las más difíciles de su carrera, “no porque dude de su necesidad para nuestro estado, sino porque sé que su anuncio puede traer a la memoria recuerdos dolorosos para las familias de las víctimas”.
 El Tribunal Supremo de California tendrá que aprobar las conmutaciones de penas para unos 400 presos que fueron condenados por múltiples delitos graves.
 Tras el anuncio de Newsom, CalMatters habló con Friend y otras dos personas cuyos seres queridos fueron víctimas de asesinos californianos condenados a muerte. Sus reacciones oscilaron entre la aceptación y la furia. 
La madre de un niño pequeño siente un dolor desgarrador
 El 16 de mayo de 1996, Michael Lyons, de ocho años, caminaba de regreso a casa desde su escuela primaria en Yuba City cuando Robert Boyd Rhoades lo agarró y lo llevó en coche a un lugar apartado a lo largo del río Feather.
 Rhoades violó y torturó al niño durante las siguientes 10 horas.
 Cuando los detectives encontraron su cuerpo, estaba desnudo de cintura para abajo y llevaba puesta la camiseta de Batman cubriéndole la cabeza. Según Friend, la madre del niño, había recibido entre 70 y 80 puñaladas.
 Cuando Friend fue a ver el cuerpo, los investigadores solo le permitieron ver su rostro y una mano. “Pude ver esas marcas de raspaduras, esas heridas de cuchillo, en su carita”, escribió en un ensayo publicado en el sitio web de la Fundación Legal de Justicia Penal. “Esa imagen será para siempre la última imagen de su hermoso rostro que veré jamás”. 

 Foto familiar de Michael Lyons. Foto cortesía de Sandy Friend.

 En mensajes de texto enviados el viernes a CalMatters, Friend calificó la decisión de Newsom como una traición a todo lo que ella y las familias de otras víctimas han pasado.
 “Siento un dolor profundo que me desgarra el alma y una rabia inmensa por dentro”, dijo. “Luchamos por la justicia, y ahora un hombre ha anulado las verdaderas sentencias de estos monstruos en un instante, igual que los monstruos que arrebataron las voces de nuestros seres queridos y los silenciaron”.
 Una amiga comentó que le preocupa que Rhoades pueda quedar en libertad algún día, a pesar de la insistencia de Newsom en que estos asesinos nunca lo harán.
 Su experiencia reciente la lleva a creer que esas preocupaciones son válidas.
 Fue apenas en diciembre pasado cuando Rhoades, ahora de 73 años, vio rechazado su último intento de reducir su condena.
 Rhoades intentó utilizar una ley que Newsom firmó en 2021 que permite a los reclusos solicitar la reducción de ciertas sentencias, una de las varias leyes que la Legislatura y los votantes de California han aprobado a lo largo de los años para aumentar las oportunidades de libertad condicional y liberación anticipada.
 La familia de Michael salió victoriosa, pero fue una experiencia dolorosa. Una vez más, Friend y los seres queridos de Michael tuvieron que volver a los tribunales para revivir los peores días de sus vidas.
 “Era un niño pequeño. Era mi hijo”, dijo Friend. “Tenía voz, y esa voz merecía ser escuchada, al igual que las voces de los cientos de otras víctimas y sus seres queridos”. 
Una hermana afligida no le guarda rencor al gobernador
 La hermana de LaVerne Brison, Cynthia Annette Johnson, fue una de las 14 víctimas del violador y asesino en serie Chester Dewayne Turner, que aterrorizó el sur de Los Ángeles en las décadas de 1980 y 1990.
 Turner se aprovechaba de mujeres vulnerables en el Corredor de Figueroa, una zona tristemente célebre por la prostitución, el consumo de drogas y los delitos violentos durante las epidemias de crack. Los detectives encontraron el cuerpo de Johnson, de 30 años, en febrero de 1997 en Green Meadows, una localidad cercana.
 Brison, una enfermera jubilada de 75 años que ahora vive en Georgia, dijo que no guarda rencor a Newsom por su decisión. Jamás imaginó que Turner sería ejecutado en vida.
 “No culpo a Newsom”, dijo. “Al fin y al cabo, él lo heredó. Si él no hubiera hecho nada, ¿qué iba a hacer el siguiente gobernador?”.
 Tiene sentimientos encontrados respecto a la pena de muerte. 
A la derecha, Chester Dewayne Turner y su abogado, John Tyre (a la izquierda), escuchan mientras un jurado sentencia a Turner por cargos de asesinato en el Tribunal Superior de Los Ángeles, el 15 de mayo de 2007. Turner fue declarado culpable del asesinato de 11 personas a lo largo de más de una década. Foto de Francine Orr-Pool, Getty Images.
 Ella sabe lo imperfecto que puede ser el sistema judicial. Según el Los Angeles Times , otro hombre fue acusado inicialmente del asesinato de Johnson antes de ser exonerado. Finalmente, Turner fue vinculado al asesinato de Johnson mediante pruebas de ADN.
 “Yo era enfermera. Salvé vidas. No creo en matar”, dijo Brison. “Pero hay gente que se lo merece. Y él es uno de ellos”.
 Cuando terminaba con sus víctimas, Turner arrojaba sus cuerpos como si fueran basura. Una de las víctimas de Turner fue encontrada en un baño portátil.
 Brison dijo que conoce a otras personas en su misma situación que han pasado sus vidas llenas de dolor, rabia y frustración mientras esperaban durante años la ejecución del asesino de su ser querido.
 Ella no es una de ellas.
 Brison dijo que prefiere imaginarse a Turner, que ahora tiene 60 años y está recluido en la prisión estatal de California, en el condado de Los Ángeles, pudriéndose en una celda, cuando piensa en él.
 “Prefiero no perder el tiempo con él”, dijo. “No dejo que invada mis pensamientos. No vale la pena. De verdad que no vale la pena”. 
“Habría sido un padre espectacular”
 Phyllis Loya, una exabogada de 78 años, está furiosa con Newsom por faltarle el respeto a la memoria de su hijo y por añadir más trauma a todo lo que ella y las familias de otras víctimas han sufrido. “Fue una decisión política deliberada, y le importa un bledo lo que les pase a las víctimas”, dijo. “No quiere nuestra opinión. No quiere escuchar nuestras historias. No quiere tenernos en cuenta”.
 Su hijo, Larry Lasater, de 36 años, agente del Departamento de Policía de Pittsburg, recibió la llamada el 23 de abril de 2005 para que estuviera atento a dos sospechosos armados que acababan de robar una sucursal bancaria dentro de un supermercado. Los agentes avistaron el coche robado en el que huían e intentaron detenerlo. El vehículo se estrelló. Los dos sospechosos salieron del coche y huyeron corriendo por un sendero.
 Lasater y otros agentes persiguieron a los sospechosos. Uno de ellos se escondía entre la maleza, armado con una pistola Glock de 9 mm.
 El sospechoso, Alexander Rashad Hamilton, de 18 años, disparó cuatro veces, dos de los disparos alcanzaron a Lasater. Hamilton continuó disparando contra otros agentes hasta que se le acabó el cargador del arma antes de entregarse. En la audiencia de sentencia, Hamilton dijo que no le importaba ser condenado a muerte. No mostró interés en escuchar a la familia de Lasater y le dijo al juez: “Déjeme seguir mi camino”, según informó el San Francisco Chronicle.
 Hamilton tiene ahora 39 años y se encuentra recluido en el Centro Correccional Richard J. Donovan en San Diego.
 Lasater dejó una esposa que dio a luz a su hijo dos meses y medio después de su muerte. Loya dijo que su hijo dedicó su vida al servicio de los demás y de su país.
 Su voz temblaba mientras describía cómo su hijo, reservista de la Infantería de Marina estadounidense, se había ofrecido voluntario para liderar a los Marines en su antigua unidad de tanques en Irak poco antes de su muerte. “Era un hijo maravilloso, un hermano estupendo, un nieto estupendo, y habría sido un padre espectacular”, dijo ella.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico US Sen. Heinrich urges Senate passage of permitting reform bill amid ongoing opposition
description: U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Monday urged his Senate colleagues to pass his bipartisan permitting reform bill, even as tribal coalitions, environmental advocates and members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation dismissed new amendments to the bill as insufficient.
text:
U.S. Sens Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) held a news conference Nov. 9, 2026, urging fellow senators to advance their permitting reform bill despite ongoing environmental and tribal group opposition. (Screenshot courtesy U.S. Senate Energy Democrats) U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) on Monday urged his Senate colleagues to pass his bipartisan permitting reform bill, even as tribal coalitions, environmental advocates and members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation dismissed new amendments to the bill as insufficient. 
Over the last month, Heinrich has presented the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, of which he is a lead sponsor, as a way to hasten the approval of renewable energy developments, bring down utility costs and hold data centers accountable for their electricity needs. 
But the bill has drawn widespread criticism, particularly from environmentalist and tribal organizations, who say its provisions will also enable new fossil fuel projects and cut tribes out of the regulatory process. They are urging the bill’s sponsors to wait until January — when a new Congress convenes with Democratic majorities in both chambers — to consider the legislation
Faced with mounting criticism, Heinrich and other cosponsors on Saturday introduced more than 70 pages’ worth of amendments to the sweeping permitting reform bill, including those that aim to restore tribal input on federal decisions regarding whether energy developments harm traditional or cultural sites. 
But tribal groups, including the All Pueblo Council of Governors in New Mexico, said the amendments fall short and the bill could still fast-track projects New Mexico Pueblos adamantly oppose, including a uranium mine seeking federal permits near Mount Taylor, an area deemed sacred to many Indigenous peoples.
“We are profoundly disappointed and frustrated,” Council Chairman Joey Sanchez said in a statement Sunday about the amendments. “Despite the concerns we relayed, both the Tribes and the Public are still not part of the process.”
Heinrich, in a news conference Monday morning in Washington, D.C. alongside fellow sponsor U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), said the amended bill “means that mandatory tribal consultation is now built into every single step” of the federal government’s historic preservation reviews.
Heinrich also said the nation can’t wait any longer for the bill’s many provisions to go into effect, including those that could save ratepayers money on their utility bills. He said voters who cast ballots in the Nov. 3 midterm elections largely did so out of concerns over rising prices.
“That message that the people sent was pretty clear,” Heinrich said of the midterm election results. “They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable, and that’s precisely what this permitting reform bill will do.”
President Donald Trump over the weekend also signaled his support for the bill, saying in a social media post that it will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families.” 
The U.S. Senate is scheduled to take its first procedural vote later Monday, a vote that opens the door to floor amendments and a final vote, before it would, if passed, head to the U.S. House of Representatives.
In the House, U.S. Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández and Melanie Stansbury, both  New Mexico Democrats, held a news conference with environmental advocates and tribal representatives last week to express opposition to the bill. Stansbury, in a statement to social media Sunday, urged the bill’s sponsors to reconsider taking the bill to a vote before January. 
“This is a bill that has had no public process, no hearings, and which Trump bragged himself last night he’d use to push through pipelines and data centers,” she said. “Especially in light of last week’s historic election, we’re asking the Senate to take a beat.”
Where the remaining members of New Mexico’s congressional delegation stand on the measure remained unclear Monday. 
Adán Serna, spokesperson for U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján told Source NM in an emailed statement Friday that the senator was awaiting updated bill text to review before he took a final vote. Serna did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Monday.
Jake Morel, a spokesperson for U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), told Source NM on Friday in a text message that Vasquez declined to comment on where he stands on the permitting reform bill.

name: California
title: Gavin Newsom busca vaciar el corredor de la muerte y conmuta las sentencias de cientos de presos
description: El gobernador Gavin Newsom conmutó las sentencias de muerte de 548 presos estatales, afirmando que "el asesinato sancionado por el Estado es incompatible con los valores de California". Los defensores de los derechos de las víctimas criticaron su decisión.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
El gobernador Gavin Newsom conmutará las sentencias de muerte de 548 personas , vaciando el corredor de la muerte de California por primera vez desde que el estado llevó a cabo ejecuciones por ahorcamiento a finales del siglo XIX.
 Se trata de un hecho trascendental en la historia de la pena capital en Estados Unidos : estos presos representan más de una cuarta parte de los reclusos condenados a muerte en el país.
Esta es una decisión sobre la que Newsom, un opositor de larga data a la pena de muerte, se ha expresado en términos profundamente personales. En 2019, poco después de asumir el cargo, decretó una moratoria sobre las ejecuciones y posteriormente desmanteló la cámara de ejecución en la prisión estatal de San Quentin. Esto ocurrió tan solo tres años después de que los votantes rechazaran una propuesta para abolir la pena de muerte y, en su lugar, aprobaran una para acelerarlas. En aquel entonces, el gobernador afirmó que no podía ser responsable de la muerte de otra persona.
 “Tras casi 30 años en el cargo, he llegado a comprender los límites de lo que el gobierno puede lograr con justicia”, escribió Newsom en una carta del jueves dirigida a “todos los californianos”. “Tomo esta medida porque creo firmemente que el asesinato sancionado por el Estado es incompatible con los valores de California, socava los cimientos de nuestro sistema legal y nos menoscaba a todos”.
 Su decisión, que ya se anticipaba, ha suscitado duras críticas en las últimas semanas por parte de grupos de víctimas, que argumentan que contradice la postura de los jurados y jueces que han ratificado las sentencias de muerte, así como la de los votantes que han respaldado esta práctica.
 “No creo que él ni ninguna otra persona deba anular la sentencia dictada por un jurado y ratificada por un juez debido a sus creencias o sentimientos personales”, declaró la semana pasada Topo Padilla, presidente de Crime Victims United.
 Desde 2024, el corredor de la muerte se ha convertido en un lugar simbólico. Los presos varones fueron trasladados de sus celdas individuales en San Quentin y distribuidos entre otros 24 centros penitenciarios . Veinte presas condenadas a muerte fueron trasladadas ese mismo año a la población general del Centro Penitenciario Femenino de California Central. 
El patio de la prisión estatal de San Quentin el 26 de julio de 2023. Fotografía de Samantha Norris, CalMatters.
 Incluso antes de la moratoria de Newsom en 2019 , habían pasado más de diez años desde que el estado ejecutara a alguien. Su sucesor, el gobernador electo Xavier Becerra , se ha comprometido a extender la moratoria cuando asuma el cargo. Sin embargo, un reciente intento fallido de ejecución en Tennessee y la sugerencia del gobierno de Trump de realizar ejecuciones televisadas han reavivado el debate nacional sobre la pena capital.
 No es inusual que los gobernadores o presidentes conmuten sentencias al dejar el cargo. El entonces presidente Joe Biden conmutó las sentencias de 37 de los 40 condenados a muerte a nivel federal en 2024. La decisión de Newsom destaca como el mayor acto de clemencia masiva en la historia de Estados Unidos, según el Centro de Información sobre la Pena de Muerte.
 Esto ocurre mientras decide si se postulará a la presidencia una vez que termine su mandato a finales de año. Junto con otras medidas emblemáticas de Newsom, como su temprano reconocimiento del matrimonio entre personas del mismo sexo cuando era alcalde de San Francisco en 2004, podría reforzar su posición entre los demócratas como un actor audaz que impulsa causas liberales, al tiempo que le acarrea críticas del centro y la derecha, así como de los defensores de una política más dura contra el crimen.
 Los grupos contrarios a la pena de muerte ya han publicado un anuncio que cita a Martin Luther King Jr. y elogia la decisión de Newsom como “basada en la justicia, guiada por la conciencia y tomada con valentía”. Dan Newman, estratega demócrata que trabaja con esos grupos y también asesora a Newsom, afirmó que el gobernador tomó la decisión sin consultar a su equipo político y que Newsom desconocía la existencia del anuncio.
 La mayoría de las decisiones que Newsom tomó el jueves requerirán la aprobación judicial. Para aquellos condenados por múltiples delitos graves —casi 400 presos—, cuatro de los siete jueces de la Corte Suprema de California deberán dar su visto bueno a las conmutaciones de penas.
 Anne Marie Schubert, directora ejecutiva de la Fundación Legal de Justicia Penal y exfiscal, prometió que su organización impugnaría las conmutaciones propuestas por Newsom ante la Corte Suprema estatal. Afirmó que las familias de las víctimas no fueron notificadas de dichas conmutaciones.
 «Me parece atroz, irrespetuoso y la violación más grotesca de los derechos de las víctimas que jamás haya visto», declaró Schubert. «Hay 548 personas en el corredor de la muerte. Eso representa nada menos que 548 familias que han sido destrozadas por lo que estas personas les han hecho a sus seres queridos».
 Newsom declaró que quienes recibieron sentencias conmutadas no podrán acogerse a las nuevas normas de conmutación y revisión de sentencias de la Junta de Audiencias de Libertad Condicional. Esto aborda algunas de las preocupaciones que los fiscales, los grupos de víctimas y los defensores de la pena de muerte habían expresado antes de la decisión de Newsom: que quienes fueran condenados a cadena perpetua pudieran tener la oportunidad de ser liberados posteriormente.
 “Estos delincuentes morirán en prisión, pero no a manos nuestras”, escribió Newsom.
 En su carta, afirmó que la decisión es una de las más difíciles de su carrera, “no porque dude de su necesidad para nuestro estado, sino porque sé que su anuncio puede despertar recuerdos dolorosos en las familias de las víctimas”. Añadió que, tras reunirse con ellas a lo largo de los años, consideró conmutar solo algunas sentencias, pero que “intentar distinguir entre delitos y delincuentes para la clemencia crearía inadvertidamente dos clases de víctimas de asesinato: aquellas cuyos perpetradores merecen la pena de muerte y el resto”. 
Última ejecución en 2006
 California no ha ejecutado a ningún preso desde que Arnold Schwarzenegger fuera gobernador. Tookie Williams en 2005 y Clarence Ray Allen en 2006 fueron los últimos en morir ejecutados en San Quentin.
 Newsom heredó un sistema penitenciario muy diferente al de Schwarzenegger, caracterizado por una población reclusa en rápido descenso. Hasta el momento, ha ordenado el cierre de cinco prisiones, incluyendo un centro en Norco que fue clausurado en octubre, y ha transformado San Quentin en un centro de rehabilitación.
 Natasha Minsker, exdirectora del Centro de Defensa y Políticas de la Unión Estadounidense por las Libertades Civiles de California, afirmó que la pena de muerte es ahora un tema olvidado en la política californiana. «Me sorprende que, cuando hablo con los legisladores y les pido que se opongan a ella, me digan que no tenemos la pena de muerte en California», declaró.
 Mary McComb, la ex defensora pública del estado, dijo que desde su primer caso defendiendo a un hombre con discapacidad intelectual acusado de un delito capital, ha encontrado una razón moral para oponerse a la pena de muerte.
 “Siempre se puede tener esperanza, pero sin las conmutaciones, no siempre está garantizado que los gobernadores sigan teniendo el valor de (mantener una moratoria)”, dijo McComb.
 Según un estudio de la Universidad de Miami sobre las condenas a muerte en California entre 1987 y 2019, la persona con mayor probabilidad de ser condenada a muerte es una persona negra o latina que asesina a una persona blanca. El estudio también reveló que las disparidades raciales eran bastante consistentes en todos los condados de California, aunque los jurados de algunos condados eran más propensos que los de otros a dictar una sentencia de muerte.
 Según el estudio, el condado de Riverside impone una proporción desproporcionada de las sentencias de muerte del estado.
 “Si bien las diferencias porcentuales reales que se describen aquí son pequeñas dada la rareza de las sentencias de muerte, la magnitud de las disparidades (geográficas) entre los condados es convincente y apunta claramente a varios ‘puntos críticos’ de sentencias de muerte con sesgo racial, especialmente en el condado de Riverside”, escribió el autor del estudio, Nick Petersen.
 Ese estudio y otros que hallaron disparidades raciales en las condenas a muerte fueron citados por la defensoría pública estatal, que en 2024 presentó un recurso de amparo ante el fiscal general Rob Bonta, solicitando que el estado dejara de aplicar la pena de muerte en los tribunales o de llevar a cabo las ejecuciones.
 Una persona destacada presentó un escrito en apoyo de esa causa: Gavin Newsom.
 “California no es inmune a la influencia perniciosa del sesgo racial en la aplicación de la pena de muerte”, escribió Newsom en el informe de 2024. “El sistema de pena capital del país está intrínsecamente ligado al legado de la esclavitud y el terror racial”. 
 Legado de asesinatos infames
 Las conmutaciones de Newsom afectarán a presos condenados por algunos de los asesinatos más notorios del estado, entre ellos Richard Allen Davis, cuyo asesinato de Polly Klaas, de 12 años, conmocionó el Área de la Bahía en la década de 1990; Charles Ng, condenado por matar a 11 personas en las estribaciones de Sierra Nevada en la década de 1980; y Scott Peterson, cuyo asesinato de su esposa Laci Peterson en Modesto acaparó los titulares de la prensa sensacionalista.
 En una entrevista previa al veredicto, Marc Klaas, padre de Polly Klaas, declaró que la posibilidad de la conmutación de penas le causaba una profunda preocupación. En 1993, Davis secuestró a Polly mientras ella celebraba una pijamada con amigas en Petaluma y la estranguló. Tenía antecedentes penales, y el caso marcó el inicio de una era de sentencias más severas para los delincuentes y llevó a los políticos a impulsar la ley de los “tres delitos”. 
 Marc Klaas, padre de Polly Klaas (a la derecha), abraza a su esposa Violet a las afueras del Tribunal Superior del Condado de Santa Clara en San José, el 31 de mayo de 2024. Un juez se negó a revocar la sentencia de muerte contra Richard Allen Davis, quien en 1993 secuestró y asesinó a Polly Klaas, de 12 años. Foto de Nic Coury, AP Photo.
 Tras años de apelaciones, Klaas dijo que, en el momento de la moratoria de Newsom, ya había perdido la esperanza de que Davis fuera ejecutado algún día.
 “Pero seguía convencido de que él y los demás estarían en el corredor de la muerte de por vida”, dijo. “Es tan desalentador. Me hace sentir fatal y revive todos mis sentimientos personales”.
 El caso de Davis es uno de los que Newsom está presentando ante la Corte Suprema para su aprobación.
 La hermana de Polly opina diferente. En un comunicado emitido el jueves, afirmó que antes creía que Davis merecía la pena de muerte, pero que llegó a comprender que su asesinato no contribuirá a su recuperación ni a la seguridad pública.
 “El sistema les dice a los sobrevivientes que la ejecución es importante para nuestra sanación. No lo es. Es una distracción de lo que realmente necesitamos”, dijo Jess Nichol.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawmakers aim to turn social media settlement funds into mental health support for Michigan youth
description: With Michigan set to receive a sizable amount as part of a settlement agreement between 50 states and territories and Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, two state lawmakers are looking to use those funds to bolster Michigan’s youth mental health efforts. In August, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced the state would […]
text:
Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey MonitorWith Michigan set to receive a sizable amount as part of a settlement agreement between 50 states and territories and Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, two state lawmakers are looking to use those funds to bolster Michigan’s youth mental health efforts.
In August, Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced the state would receive at least $171 million, following allegations that Meta had intentionally designed its apps with addictive features, harming young people and misleading the public about the safety of its platforms.
To ensure the settlement funds are reinvested in youth mental health efforts, state Reps. Julie Rogers (D-Kalamazoo) and Mike Mueller (R-Linden) have proposed legislation to create the Youth Social Media Settlement Fund within the Michigan Department of Treasury.
“For years, parents, educators and health professionals have raised concerns about the toll social media can take on our children’s mental health,” Rogers said in a statement. “Now, these companies are facing legal consequences, and Michigan stands to recover millions of dollars. We have a responsibility to make sure that money goes toward helping our young people, giving them the care, support and opportunities they need to lead healthy lives.”
If House Bills 6463 and 6464, sponsored by Rogers and Mueller, are signed into law, this new trust fund would receive money from social media-related lawsuits and settlements. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services would use that fund to distribute grants for youth mental health services, crisis intervention, after-school programs, mentoring and other evidence-based programs. 
The package also includes statewide planning and annual reporting requirements to ensure the funds are used as the Legislature intended.
“The funds made available through this settlement should be invested in solutions that address the growing mental health challenges facing our communities,” Mueller said in a statement. “As technology continues to rapidly evolve, we must ensure our efforts keep pace with the challenges our children face and provide them with the resources and support they need to thrive.”

Roger Arthur BrookwellJune 7, 1949 – November 4, 2026Worland, WyomingShared by: Bryant Funeral HomeRoger Arthur Brookwell, 77, passed away on November 4, 2026, at The Billings Clinic, surrounded by the people he loved most.
Roger was born on June 7, 1949, in San Francisco, California, to Nick and Gertrude (Brady) Brookwell. He grew up in San Francisco, where he graduated from high school before attending college. His education was interrupted when he was drafted into the United States Army on May 18, 1971. Roger served as an infantryman in Vietnam, earning the National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Vietnam Campaign Medal with 1960 Device, and Army Commendation Medal. He was honorably discharged on February 11, 1973.
Following his military service, Roger traveled to Worland, Wyoming, to visit his sister, Pam. He quickly took a liking to the small-town atmosphere and decided to make Worland his forever home. He began working in construction, helping build the Coors plant and several homes throughout the community, including the house he would eventually call his own.
Roger went on to spend much of his working life serving the people of Worland and Washakie County. He served as mayor of Worland for 4 years and spent 23 years in law enforcement with 12 years at the Worland police department and 11 with the Washakie County sheriff’s department. Roger took his responsibilities seriously and believed his job was to stand up for people. He wasn’t afraid to speak his mind or fight for what he believed was right.
It was his work in law enforcement that led him to the love of his life, Barbie Wessel. In the late 1990s, Roger responded to a 911 call Barbie had made on behalf of her grandmother. Being the thorough officer he was, Roger made sure to stop by several more times over the following weeks, just to check on Barbie, of course. Eventually, he worked up the nerve to ask her on a date. He packed a picnic, and by the end of the evening, he had earned a goodnight kiss. That was all it took. The two spent the next 25 years deeply in love.
When Roger and Barbie became a family, he welcomed her two boys, Clinton and Austin, as his own. To the boys, Roger was their dad, regardless of what any paperwork said. Making it official took longer than they had hoped, but on Roger’s 70th birthday, the boys gave him a gift he would never forget. They presented him with their legal adoption papers, making him their dad on paper, just as he had always been in their hearts.
Roger could be a little rough around the edges, and those who didn’t know him might have mistaken his serious exterior for a cold personality. His family and friends knew better. Underneath that tough exterior was a softhearted, emotional man who loved deeply. He was never one to turn down a tight hug or a kiss from his bride, and he treasured time spent with his grandchildren, especially when he could sneak them a few jelly beans.
When he wasn’t working or spending time with family, Roger enjoyed playing racquetball, fishing, and watching WWE wrestling. He rarely missed a match on television.
Roger loved his family and his country and his determination stayed with him until the very end. During his final days at the hospital, he told the nurses he wasn’t going anywhere until he got to see his kids and grandkids. After they had the opportunity to be with him and give him one last kiss, Roger passed peacefully, with the people he loved by his side.
Roger’s family will always be grateful for the love he gave so freely and the family he helped build. More than anything, they want to thank him for choosing them, and loving them without him, they wouldn’t be where they are today. Without him they wouldn’t be Brookwells.
Roger was preceded in death by his parents, Nick and Gertrude Brookwell.
He is survived by his loving wife, Barbie; sons, Clinton (Ashley) Brookwell and Austin (Jacy) Brookwell, both of Worland; grandchildren: Truex, Brexon, Lincoln, and Braylee; sister, Pam (Dan) Arps and sister-in-law, Trich (Brad) Leban.
A celebration of life will be held at 2:00 PM on Friday, November 20, 2026 at Zions Church with family friend, Josh Hansen and Rev. James Byers officiating.
Online condolences may be made at Bryant Funeral Home.








Christina Lara ContrerasJanuary 25, 1982 – November 5, 2026Worland, WyomingShared by: Bryant Funeral HomeChristina Lara Contreras, 44, passed away on November 5, 2026, at Billings Clinic Hospital following a courageous battle with leukemia.
Christina was born on January 25, 1982, in Lubbock, Texas, to Jessie and Marianna (Lopez) Gomez. In her early twenties, she traveled to Worland, Wyoming, to visit her grandmother, Esperanza. During that visit, Esperanza introduced Christina to Felipe Lara Contreras, and the two were immediately drawn to each other. Their first date was simple, Felipe took her to Taco John’s for a burrito, followed by a trip to the park where they could sit and get to know each other. Apparently, a burrito and a little conversation were all it took. The two fell in love and spent the next 20-plus years building a life together.
Christina brought five children into their relationship, and Felipe welcomed each of them as his own. Together, they welcomed one more child, completing their family of eight. Christina worked hard to provide for her family, holding jobs at Subway, Beehive Homes, the nursing home, IGA, and Blair’s. She was willing to do whatever needed to be done to make sure her family was taken care of.
When she wasn’t working, Christina enjoyed crafting, gardening, and cooking. She was an excellent cook and had a creative side that often kept Felipe guessing what he might come home to. She loved rearranging and redecorating the house, especially when he wasn’t there to see the changes being made. Christina could look at something most people would throw away and find a way to make it beautiful. Old tires, for example, became colorful flowerpots after a little cutting, painting, and imagination.
Christina was a girly girl who loved to sing and could happily spend hours getting ready. She enjoyed making things look nice, whether it was her home, her garden, or herself. She was also a woman of strong Catholic faith, which was an important part of her life.
Those who knew Christina knew how much she was willing to give to others. She was strong, generous, and always willing to help, even when she had very little to give herself. She loved her family deeply and worked hard to make a home for the people she cared about.
Christina was preceded in death by her uncle, Abel Flores, and granddaughters: Katalina Ramon and Talia Ramon.
She is survived by her loving husband, Felipe; grandmother, Esperanza Flores of Worland; sons, Andrew Gomez, Danny Ramon, and Joey Ramon, all of Worland; daughters, Veronica Gomez of Worland, Estria (Faith) Gomez of Dallas, Texas, and Aveliena Lara of Worland; and grandchildren, Jonathan, Khristinah, Aleena, Lily, and Miguel.
A Mass of Christian Burial will be held 10:00 AM, Tuesday November 10, 2026 at St. Mary Magdalen Catholic Church with Father Robert Rodgers officiating. In lieu of flowers, the family would greatly appreciate donations to offset the cost of funeral arrangements. Please make checks payable to Bryant Funeral Home and send to PO Box 524 Worland, Wyoming 82401. You may also donate online at Bryant Funeral Home.

Patricia Ann Weaver Hardeman1931 – October 20, 2026Location: Jackson, WyomingShared by: Grand Teton Funeral HomePatricia Ann Weaver Hardeman was born in Ohio, raised in California, and lived the life she loved in Wyoming. She passed away peacefully on October 20, 2026. She was 95.
Pat was born in 1931 to Frank and Maurine Weaver in Columbus, Ohio. Within six months the family was heading west to California to help Frank’s Uncle John on his citrus ranch. Frank and Maurine’s second daughter, Elizabeth (Betty), arrived in 1932. Pat fondly recalled her time on the ranch with her family. She remembered Uncle John as extremely hard of hearing, holding a horn up to his ear so people could speak into it. It was here that her love of animals grew. She loved riding her little horse Poncho, always had a dog, and helped her family raise Siamese cats. It was also at a young age that Pat decided to go into medicine. She remembered strategically placing one of her dolls in the driveway of the family home on Pepper Drive, so that it would be run over by a car and she could see how the eyes worked.
Pat attended San Diego State University, completed her nursing training at Huntington Memorial Hospital in Pasadena, and graduated from the University of Southern California in 1954 with a Bachelor of Science in Nursing. It was during this time that Pat met her lifelong best friend, Marian DiStefano Taylor. The girls stayed and worked at Huntington Memorial Hospital for two more years.
In 1955 Pat and Marian decided to take a vacation to the X Quarter Circle X Ranch owned by Marvel and Irwin Lesher and Uncle Jimmy Manges. Pat likely talked Marian into this vacation, since she had already been to the ranch in high school while working as a nanny for a five-year-old boy. Like many visitors, Pat fell in love with the people and the unmistakable beauty of the Jackson Hole Valley. It wasn’t too long after this vacation that Pat and Marian decided to move. In 1956 Pat and Marian were hired as RNs at a little log-cabin hospital in Jackson, Wyoming, known as St. John’s.
With the help of Marian’s dad, they purchased a Ford station wagon and loaded it with their belongings. Sparks flew as they pulled out of the driveway and started off on their new adventure. They traveled first north to Canada, then south to drop off their belongings in Wyoming, and finally to the East Coast. The girls kept a diary of their travels, and reading the entries brought their children great enjoyment and lots of laughs.
They had many fun memories of working with Dr. MacLeod and Dr. Elmore. At this tiny hospital they needed to be jacks of all trades. They assisted in the OR, ER, OB and went on house calls with the doctors. They would often giggle at the tight ship that was run by the head of nursing: staff were not allowed to use hospital napkins if they brought their lunch from home.
An invitation to dinner from Becky and Roy Chambers led to Pat meeting a tall, handsome, and charming cowboy named Earl Hardeman. He would always say, “They hit it off pretty well.” Earl was also known to tell people that when he saw Pat effortlessly pick up a 50-pound bag of dog food, he knew she would be good on the ranch. They married in 1960 at the Chapel of the Transfiguration with a view from the altar of the mountains she had first fallen in love with. Earl had an interest in becoming an auctioneer, and so part of their honeymoon was spent in Indiana so that Earl could attend Auctioneering School, while Pat went to the movie theater, the only place in town with air conditioning.
Pat gave up her nursing career to become a ranch wife, but never stopped being a nurse. Earl knew it was a bit of an adjustment for her and would tell the story about being on the tractor behind the house at the Hardeman homestead north of Kelly and looking up to see Pat waving a gun at him. He joked that he thought she had snapped, but the truth was that she had spotted a bobcat and wanted to get his attention.
Together they raised two children, Robert and Heidi. Robert Earl (Rob) arrived prematurely in 1962. Before Heidi Lyn arrived in the winter of 1965, Earl moved Pat and Rob to town to stay with family, fearing that Heidi would also come early. She didn’t, but there was a big snowstorm and Earl had to ski out of the ranch to Kelly and then drive to town. Pat and Earl enjoyed working together and raising their family.
The family moved to Wilson in 1967. Pat placed great value on both faith and family. She enjoyed working alongside Earl and his family. She helped with branding, gathering, vaccinating, and doctoring any sickly animal. It wasn’t unusual for a sick calf to be in the house being warmed and bottle fed by Pat. She raised chickens and pigs. She separated the milk and made fresh butter for her family. At butchering time, Pat would make the most delicious liver and onions. She drove a buck rake in the hay field and helped gather firewood in the fall. Pat cooked countless meals and served innumerable cups of coffee to friends and neighbors. She was an amazing ranch wife.
Pat enjoyed supporting Earl in all of his many community activities including 4-H Livestock Auction, Jackson Hole Cattle and Horse Association, Boy Scout Elk Antler Auction, Jackson Hole Outfitter, Trout Unlimited, Ducks Unlimited, and serving as a rodeo announcer. She was the wife who worked alongside her husband, quietly supporting him and happily watching him in his element. Pat did the same for her children, fully supporting them in all of their pursuits from 4-H to sports. She spent a lot of time sitting in the bleachers, smiling and enjoying her children’s interests.
During this time, Pat also pursued her own interests. She enjoyed being part of the Jackson Hole Cowbells and Wilson Homemakers, serving as a leader of the Wilson Hoofbeats 4-H Club for many years, sitting on the C.C. Mosley Scholarship Committee, and helping with Quilting in the Tetons. She loved to read, try new recipes, knit, and sew. Pat always had a strong faith and cherished her time attending First Baptist, Wilson Community Church, or services online.
When the grandchildren started to arrive, it was love at first sight. G-ma, as she was known, truly enjoyed spending time with each of them and hearing about all of their adventures and accomplishments. John, Hailey, Matthew, and Gracie were blessed to have such an amazing Grandma. John recalls going on a walk with her and her telling him about the cattails. She asked if he wanted one, and he couldn’t believe his eyes when she pulled out a pocket knife to cut one down for him. He said, “Right then and there I knew how cool my G-ma was.” Hailey fondly remembers helping her G-ma make the bed, a task where nothing was left to chance. G-ma had even marked the exact folds and sheet placement with a pen. After all, there was a right way to make a bed and G-ma made sure it was perfect every time! Matthew says he always loved how G-ma lit up every room she was in and whenever she saw him, he could feel how much she loved him, even when he was telling jokes that were not that funny. Gracie still gets a good laugh from the time G-ma was serving them Kool-Aid but forgot to add the sugar. Even great cooks can have a bad day.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Pat moved to Washington State to live with Heidi and her boys. She enjoyed her time there, but soon became homesick for the place she had called home for so many years. In September 2024, she moved into Sage Living Center. On her first day, Elaine Luton and Stephanie Brown immediately welcomed her. It was such an amazing coincidence that Elaine was there. Elaine had been Pat’s closest neighbor when Pat first married Earl and moved to Kelly. Pat thrived at Sage. She loved riding the trishaw bike, going river rafting and making a few ski runs in the winter of 2025–26. Pat loved book club, music, art, current events, and winning at bingo, and she especially loved any activity with the preschool students.
Her family is thankful for the long, wonderful life Pat had as a mom and G-ma. They are thankful for her examples of faith and strength. They are thankful for the importance she put on hard work and honesty. They are thankful to be part of the love story between Pat and Earl. They are thankful that God answered one of her last prayers: to pass peacefully in her sleep.
Pat was preceded in death by her parents, Frank and Maurine Weaver; her sister, Betty Causey; and her tall, handsome, and charming cowboy, Earl.
She is survived by her children, Rob (Abbey) Hardeman and Heidi Hardeman Hopkins; her grandchildren, John Hopkins, Hailey Hardeman, Matthew Hopkins, and Gracie Hardeman; and many nieces and nephews who all loved their Aunt Pat.
A celebration of Pat’s long, lovely life will be held in the summer of 2027.








Luella “Kathleen” (Trumbull) HoweOctober 15, 1933 – October 31, 2026Greybull, WyomingShared by: Haskell Funeral HomeIn Loving Memory of Luella Kathleen Howe – Known and loved as Kathleen
Kathleen was born on October 15, 1933, in Emblem, Wyoming, to Adrian Chester Trumbull and Marguerite Myrtle Barbee. On October 31, 2026, at the age of 93, the Lord called Kathleen home to heaven.
On July 12, 1952, Kathleen married the love of her life, Walter Clarence Howe of Shell, WY. Together they shared 74 wonderful years of marriage, building a life filled with love, commitment, family, and faith. Their marriage was a testament to devotion and the enduring bond of two people who shared a lifetime together.
Kathleen and Walter were blessed with four children: Adrian Clarence Howe, Elaine Kathleen Howe, Jerry Walter Howe, and Larry Lee Howe. Their family experienced the heartbreaking loss of their son Jerry Walter Howe at the young age of seven, a loss that remained forever in their hearts.
Family was the center of Kathleen’s world. She especially loved bringing everyone together and took great joy in hosting large family gatherings on Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New Year’s. Those gatherings were about much more than a holiday meal; they were about family, sharing stories, laughter, making memories, and keeping loved ones close.
Kathleen spent her entire life in the Big Horn Basin of Wyoming; a place she proudly called home. It was there that she built her life, raised her family, formed lifelong friendships, and created countless memories that will be cherished for generations. Throughout her working years, Kathleen held several jobs in the Big Horn Basin. She worked at a furniture and appliance store, a local bakery, and a clothing and variety store before eventually retiring. Through her years of hard work, she made many memories and connections within the communities she called home.
Kathleen was blessed with 7 grandchildren, 5 step grandchildren, 13 great-grandchildren, 10 step-great-grandchildren, and 4 step-great-great-grandchildren, all of whom brought her tremendous joy and pride. Her love for her family was evident in the time she spent with them and the importance she placed on keeping family connections strong.
Her faith was also an important part of her life. Kathleen was very active in the Presbyterian Church in Greybull, Wyoming, where she shared in the fellowship of her church family and remained devoted to her faith in the Lord. She was a member of Lewisia Chapter #16 in Basin, WY.
Kathleen will be remembered as a devoted wife, loving mother, grandmother, great-grandmother, great-great-grandmother, and faithful servant of God. Her life was rooted in family, faith, hard work, and the traditions that brought generations together.
Although her passing leaves a tremendous void in the hearts of those who loved her, there is comfort in knowing that her earthly journey is complete and she has been welcomed home by her Heavenly Father. We find peace in the promise of eternal life and the hope of one day being reunited again. Kathleen’s life was a blessing, her memory a treasure, and her love will remain forever in the hearts of her family.
Kathleen was preceded in death by her parents, Adrian Chester Trumbull and Marguerite Myrtle Barbee; her brother, Rollin Trumbull; her son, Jerry Walter Howe; her son-in-law, Ronald Huff, and granddaughter in law Tiffany Huff. Her brother Sidney Trumbull passed away three days after her passing.
She is survived by husband Walter Howe, brother William Trumbull, Adrian Howe and wife Susan, Elaine Huff, Larry Howe and wife Tawny, grandsons Travis Howe, Timothy Huff, Anthony Huff, Trenton Howe, granddaughters Destinee Edison, Shawndra Garido, Brittney Howe-Rivera, step-grandsons Nicholas Bracken, Jeremy Bracken, step-granddaughters Samantha O’Hara, Nicole Roberts, Tiffany Rauff, 23 great-grandchildren, and 4 great-great-grandchildren.
In lieu of flowers, the family requests a loving memory donation in Kathleen’s name to the Greybull Community Church in care of GCC, P.O. Box 484, Greybull, WY 82426

Judy ParkerAugust 13, 1941 – November 6, 2026Cody, WyomingShared by: Ballard Funeral HomeJudy Kay Parker was born on August 13, 1941, in Billings, Montana, and passed away on November 6, 2026, in Cody, Wyoming surrounded by the love of her family.
Judy shared a beautiful life and a lasting love with her husband Don. Their love story began at the Yellowstone County Fair in August of 1959. It didn’t take long for them to know they had found something special. Just two months after meeting, they were engaged, and on February 13, 1960, they were married. Together, they built a life filled with love, family, and countless memories.
After the birth of their son Jerry, Judy and Don moved to Cody, Wyoming, where they raised their two boys, Jerry and Tony, and made a home filled with family, love, and traditions.
Judy was one of the most loving and kind women you could ever meet, but she was also known for being stubborn and strong-willed. Throughout her life, she faced many health scares, meeting each challenge with a strength and determination that defined her. She was a fighter, and her strength was an inspiration to those who loved her.
Above all else, Judy loved her family and friends. Her greatest joy was spending time with those she loved, especially her great-grandchildren, who held an extra-special place in her heart. Whether gathered outside in the summer time watching the kids play, sharing stories, or simply enjoying one another’s company, those moments meant everything to her.
Judy loved cooking with her family, and her homemade ravioli will surely be remembered and missed by everyone lucky enough to have enjoyed it. She also earned the unofficial family title of professional dishrag maker, knitting countless dishrags over the years. These little handmade treasures were more than just useful gifts; they were pieces of her love, care, and the time she spent thinking of her family.
Judy was also a devout Catholic, whose faith was an important part of her life. She rarely missed a weekend Mass, and her faith remained a constant throughout her journey.
Judy is survived by her loving husband of 66 years, Don; her two sons, Jerry and his wife, Karen, and Tony; her three granddaughters, Heather and her husband, BJ, Amanda and her husband, Jesse, and Miranda; and her great-grandchildren, Jace and his wife, Maya, Kian, Parker, Tenley, Landyn, Aubree, Kaitlee, and Nolan. She also leaves behind her great-great-grandchild, McCoy, who represents another beautiful generation of the family she loved so dearly.
She was preceded in death by her parents, Butch and Lydia Wadsworth; her sister, Norma Pelo; and her twin sister, Jill, who passed away when they were just three years old.
Judy leaves behind a family who will forever cherish her love, her strength, her laughter, her cooking, and all the little things that made her who she was. From homemade ravioli to countless knitted dishrags, she found ways to show her love that will continue to be felt for generations.
Her hands may no longer be busy in the kitchen or with knitting needles, but the love she put into everything she did will never be forgotten.
She was deeply loved, fiercely strong, and one of a kind. Her legacy lives on in the family she built, the traditions she passed down, and the countless hearts she touched.








Raymond Albert SarclettiAugust 11, 1938 – October 30, 2026Manila, UtahShared by: Vase Funeral HomeIt is with heavy hearts that we announce the passing of Raymond Albert Sarcletti, who passed away at his home in Manila, Utah, on October 30, 2026, at the age of 88.
Ray was born on August 11, 1938, in Rock Springs, Wyoming, to Albert and Margaret Sarcletti. A proud Wyoming native, he devoted much of his life to the community and state he loved so dearly.
Ray married the love of his life, Billie Dee Willis, and together they began building their family while he attended the University of Wyoming. He graduated in 1960; an accomplishment made all the more remarkable by the fact that he and Billie were already raising three young children while he pursued his education. Together, they raised five children and shared 66 wonderful years of marriage.
For many years, Ray owned and operated Yellowstone Wholesale in Rock Springs, becoming a familiar face and an integral part of the community. His dedication extended well beyond his business. He generously gave his time to numerous boards, committees, and community projects, always striving to make Rock Springs and the state of Wyoming better places to live.
Ray had a genuine love for his community and the people who made it special. Whether supporting the Shriners’ mission, attending the horse races, or enjoying the excitement of pig wrestling, he was always in the middle of the action. Ray had a natural gift for connecting with people. It seemed he knew everyone, and everyone knew Ray. A gifted storyteller with a quick wit and wonderful sense of humor, he could bring laughter to any gathering.
His dedication to public service eventually led him to the Wyoming Legislature, where he proudly served in both the Wyoming House of Representatives and the Wyoming Senate. It was yet another chapter in a lifetime of service to others.
After many years of hard work and community involvement, Ray and his beloved wife, Billie, retired to Manila, Utah where they made their home overlooking Flaming Gorge. There, they enjoyed a quieter life surrounded by the beauty of nature. Their home welcomed not only family and friends but also the many cats, dogs, deer and other wildlife that found their way into their lives.
Above all else, Ray was a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His greatest legacy was the family he loved, the friendships he cherished, and the many lives he touched.
Ray was preceded in death by his wife of 66 years, Billie Dee Sarcletti; his parents, Albert and Margaret Sarcletti, his sisters, Lucille Cooper and Diane Jenson; and his grandson, Daniel Sarcletti.
He is Survived by a sister, Margee Matthews and his five children; Rae Eileen Baasch and her husband, Darrell; Albert Sarcletti and his wife, Vickie; John Sarcletti; Christine Smith; and Vincent Sarcletti.
He is also survived by his grandchildren: Jerod Sarcletti, Stefane Sarcletti, Heath Aragon and his wife, Andee, Joseph Aragon, and Aaron Sarcletti: along with his great-grandchildren: Josiah, Jonas, Ashley, Felicia and Ryan.
Ray lived a full and meaningful life, filled with love, laughter, hard work, and service. He leaves behind treasured memories and lasting legacy through his family, his friends, and communities he helped shape.

A Vigil Service with Rosary will be conducted at 4:00 p.m. Thursday, November 12, 2026 at the church. Graveside Services and Interment will be conducted at Rest Haven Memorial Gardens.
