name: Kentucky Lantern
title: PACs spent millions to sway voters in competitive Kentucky House and legislative seats
description: In an unusually expensive race in a Central Kentucky U.S. House District, a Democratic PAC, Kentuckians Not Corruption, spent millions in cash on ads supporting now Congressman-elect Zach Dembo as a way to offset spending by President Donald Trump’s political arm.  By the general election, independent expenditures from PACs, or political action committees, b[...]
text:
Democrat Zach Dembo celebrates after his Kentucky Sixth Congressional District win against Ralph Alvardo, at the Central Bank Center in downtown Lexington, Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Brian Simms for Kentucky Lantern)In an unusually expensive race in a Central Kentucky U.S. House District, a Democratic PAC, Kentuckians Not Corruption, spent millions in cash on ads supporting now Congressman-elect Zach Dembo as a way to offset spending by President Donald Trump’s political arm. 
By the general election, independent expenditures from PACs, or political action committees, ballooned to just over $14 million in the 6th Congressional District, federal finance records showed last week. The PAC spending in the 6th dwarfed all other general elections in Kentucky this cycle.

Kentuckians Not Corruption had about $2.3 million in expenditures. Of that, $1.5 million was spent against Alvarado and about $750,000 in favor of Dembo. The PAC was officially formed in mid-August. 
In favor of the ultimate winner Dembo, PACs in total spent about $1.4 million on ads supporting him and $3.8 million on ads opposing him. For Alvarado, PACs spent $3.8 million on ads backing him and $4.5 million on ads to oppose him. 
Kelsey Coots, a general consultant with Blue Dot Consulting which worked with KNC, told the Kentucky Lantern the PAC came together as a way to counter Republicans’ resources in the district. 
“Zach was an outsider. He’d never been an elected official, and so he was going to be spending all the time introducing himself. And we had a feeling that, of course, the Republican side, specifically Trump’s No Going Back PAC would be in the fight, and so we had a conversation about how we could support the Democratic side in the race,” Coots said. 
PACs that backed Alvarado included No Going Back, which is connected to Trump’s political team and spent more than $5 million in the 6th Congressional District. Of that $2.5 million was in support of Alvarado and $2.5 million against Dembo. 
PACs cannot coordinate with candidates on election messaging, but Coots said PACs can strategize messaging by paying attention to what campaigns and other PACs are doing. Other pro-Dembo PACs involved in the 6th included Gov. Andy Beshear’s In This Together and the House Majority PAC, which supported electing Democrats to flip control of Congress. Coots said polling showed corruption in politics and affordability were top concerns of voters this cycle. The Republican side of PACs “did not have an answer to that” which moved voters this time, she added. 
“(PACs) can be messengers for things that maybe a candidate wouldn’t say. In our instance, we wanted to talk about corruption. We know that that is the issue that’s number one on Kentuckians’ minds, and there was a lot to talk about in that 6th Congressional District race.”
Days ahead of the election, PACs began pushing ads about third-party candidates in the race. No Going Back spent more than $50,000 on mailers and texts opposing Independent Jay Bowman and the Kentucky Party’s Pete Lynch. 
A mysterious group that suddenly popped up in October, Our Heritage Matters, spent nearly $220,000 between Oct. 21 and Nov. 3 propping up Bowman. The New York Times reported the group also spent money on ads in favor of third-party candidates who were seen as spoilers for Republicans in states like Colorado and North Carolina. 
As for the general contests in Kentucky’s other five congressional districts this year, a PAC called Save America Freedom spent about $35,000 supporting Republican Congressman-elect Ed Gallrein in the 4th District and a Planned Parenthood Alliance PAC spent $2,600 in support of Democratic U.S. Rep. Morgan McGarvey in the 3rd Congressional District. 
Legislative races
According to state campaign finance records, PACs spent more than $1.8 million on General Assembly races ahead of the November election. About $1.1 million in ads supported and opposed 46 House candidates and nearly $650,000 on six Senate candidates, with a chunk of that going to suburban Lexington and Louisville districts. 
The biggest spender on statehouse races was the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition, with about $876,000, or about 48% of all legislative PAC spending. 

The group spent about $800,000 opposing House Democratic candidates. In Jefferson County races, that includes more than $186,000 against Suhas Kulkarni, who defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Ken Fleming in the 48th House District and more than $250,000 against Tim Hall, who defeated Republican Rep. Susan Tyler Witten in the 31st House District. 
The coalition also spent $96,000 against Democratic Rep. Adam Moore, who ended up defending his seat in the 45th House District in Central Kentucky against former Republican state Rep. Killian Timoney. 
In the week before the election, the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition spent $35,000 backing Republican House Whip Jason Nemes and about $9,500 supporting Rep. Daniel Fister, of Versailles. Fister won reelection Tuesday, but Nemes lost to Democrat Jennifer Hardin. 
For the Senate, the Commonwealth Conservative Coalition spent nearly $74,000 opposing Sarah Sarah Cole McIntosh, who ended up defeating Republican Sen. Julie Raque Adams in the 36th Senate District in Jefferson County. 
Americans for Prosperity spent more than $130,000 supporting Republican House candidates and more than $67,000 in favor of Raque Adams. 
Raque Adams also had more than $188,000 in support from GOPAC. The Kentucky Chamber Advocacy Committee spent nearly $46,000 on support for Republican Senate candidates, including Raque Adams, and nearly $87,000 backing Republican House candidates. 
The Republican State Leadership Committee spent about $154,000 on the 36th Senate District race. 
National Association of Realtors Fund spent more than $65,000 on Raque Adams and $30,000 supporting Witten. 
NRA Political Victory Fund spent $1,120 on Republican House candidates and $1,110 supporting Sen. Lindsey Tichenor in the 6th Senate District, who later lost to Democrat Christan Furman. 
Planned Parenthood Action Kentucky spent about $26,000 supporting Democrats and opposing Republican candidates in the House. The group also spent nearly $300 supporting Democratic Sen. Karen Berg in the 26th Senate District in Jefferson county. 
Protect Freedom PAC spent about $91,000 supporting Tanner Hesterberg and Marianne Proctor in the House and more than $45,000 supporting Tichenor. 
Yellowbanks Political Action Committee spent nearly $3,400 supporting Democrats in the House and $1,100 for Vicki Quisenberry against Republican Sen. Gary Boswell, of Owensboro, in the 8th Senate District.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi awarded $205M for second year of federal rural health program
description: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz speaks speaks during an event on health care affordability in the Oval Office at the White House, Thursday, April 23, 2026, in Washington.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi will receive nearly $205 million for the second year of a national program that aims to improve rural healthcare, federal officials announced Monday. 
The state’s total award for the 2027 fiscal year is about $1.2 million less than its first-year award announced last December for the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program, though its amount exceeded the award made to the average state. 
Awards were made to all 50 states as part of the $50 billion federal investment in rural healthcare. Like last year, Texas and Alaska received the largest shares of funding, while Connecticut and New Jersey received the smallest amounts. 
“Rural Americans have life expectancies three years shorter than their urban peers, but President Trump’s Rural Health Transformation Program is funding the historic investments necessary to close that gap,” said Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “States have already put these resources to work bringing better care closer to home for their rural communities, and CMS looks forward to helping them build on that progress in the coming year.”
The $50 billion funding program was tacked on to President Donald Trump’s tax-and-spending law passed in July 2025, which is expected to result in significant reductions in federal Medicaid spending in rural areas. Congressional Republicans added the money for rural health to soften the blow associated with those cuts. 
Rural areas are expected to face an estimated $137 billion in cuts to federal Medicaid spending over 10 years, meaning Rural Health Transformation Program funds will offset roughly a third of those cuts, according to analysis from KFF. 
Changes to federal Medicaid payment rules are expected to reduce net payments to Mississippi providers by about $100 million annually beginning in July 2028, according to the Mississippi Division of Medicaid’s strategic plan published in July.
Half of the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program funding is to be distributed evenly among all states with approved applications over five years. Awards for the other half of the funding are informed in part by states’ progress implementing their approved plans, according to CMS.
A federal annual report showed that Mississippi had committed over $94 million in program funding as of July 31, including assessments of the state’s rural healthcare and emergency medical services capacity, and grants for technology upgrades, telehealth and facility improvements. Over $10 million was obligated for program operations. 
Gov. Tate Reeves in October announced $32 million in grant awards for healthcare workforce development and psychiatric emergency services.
The state closed applications last week for a statewide health information exchange to allow health care providers to securely share patient information and coordinate care. A vendor has not yet been announced. 
The state is seeking applications for small rural providers to adopt or replace electronic health records, and for innovative pilot programs to improve healthcare.

text:
The offices of the West Virginia departments of Health, Health Facilities and Human Services are located on Capitol Street in Charleston, West Virginia. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)The state of West Virginia will get more than $200 million dollars during the second year of a federal grant program aimed at improving rural healthcare.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services on Monday announced $10 billion in Rural Health Transformation program grants to all 50 states for 2027. West Virginia will receive $202,081,355 in year two, CMS announced.
“President Trump made a historic investment in rural America, and HHS is putting those resources to work in every state,” U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. said in the news release Monday. “This next $10 billion will expand access to care, strengthen the rural health workforce, improve prevention and help states build solutions that fit the needs of their own communities. 
“We are giving rural America the resources and flexibility to build stronger health systems that deliver better care and better outcomes,” he said. 
The federal program aims to “transform the existing rural healthcare infrastructure and build sustainable health care systems that expand access, enhance quality of care, and improve outcomes for patients.” The program was part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which made historic cuts to healthcare and food assistance. 
The state received about $199 million from the program in 2026. 
The state Department of Health said last week it had obligated all of the 2026 funds, despite an October federal report that said as of July West Virginia hadn’t reported any of its Rural Health spending to CMS. 
“The CMS report reflects a snapshot ending July 31 and does not represent where the program stands today,” Gailyn Markam, director of communications for the state Department of Health, wrote in an email last week to West Virginia Watch. She added that the state had $4.3 million in administrative obligations as of July 31, including contracted implementation support. 
“From the beginning, West Virginia took a deliberate approach,” Markham wrote. “Rather than simply transferring large sums between government agencies or through intermediaries to meet obligation requirements, we prioritized direct agreements with the healthcare providers, vendors and community organizations responsible for carrying out the work.
“That approach required more contracting and coordination upfront, but it provides greater accountability and ensures funding is tied to specific projects, deliverables and results,” she said. “We have now made more than 140 awards and agreements across our seven initiatives, with approximately 90% of those awards going to West Virginia organizations.”
Under Gov. Patrick Morrisey’s plan for the program, schools, libraries and other community institutions in rural West Virginia would be outfitted for use in telemedicine. The state also plans to use the funding to address the state’s healthcare worker shortage by recruiting high school students to healthcare careers, adding healthcare faculty at regional and technical colleges and using financial incentives to attract and keep providers in rural areas. 
Morrisey has announced several awards for the funding, including opening a freestanding birthing center to address complex labor and delivery births, strengthening mental health and recovery services, expanding breast cancer screenings, helping people in recovery get back to work, expanding care for patients with chronic health conditions, helping rural hospitals address staffing shortages and more.

title: Number of plaintiffs in vaccine rule challenge grows by two
description: An administrative judge has denied the DeSantis administration’s request to limit the number of plaintiffs in the administrative challenge to its proposed rules to eliminate a requirement that children receive four vaccines before entering daycare or school. Over objections from the Department of Health, administrative law judge W. David Watkins is allowing [...]
text:
A four-day hearing in the rule challenge over daycare and school vaccine requirements begins Dec. 14. (Photo by kali9/Getty Images)An administrative judge has denied the DeSantis administration’s request to limit the number of plaintiffs in the administrative challenge to its proposed rules to eliminate a requirement that children receive four vaccines before entering daycare or school.
Over objections from the Department of Health, administrative law judge W. David Watkins is allowing the Florida Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians Services to intervene in the consolidated administrative challenge.
A four-day hearing has been scheduled in Tallahassee starting Dec. 14.
Attorneys for DOH unsuccessfully argued the organizations lacked standing and shouldn’t be allowed to intervene. The attorneys were successful in their request that they groups’ standing be somewhat limited and they not be allowed to “unduly delay the proceedings or final hearing.”
Attorney Christopher Nuland, representing the organizations, was pleased with Watkins’ decision.
“We certainly want and deserve a seat at the table,” Nuland told the Phoenix Monday.
Nuland maintains that if Watkins rules in favor of the DOH, the rule could go into effect before Gov. Ron DeSantis leaves office in January.
‘Ambitious’ timeline means DeSantis could pass new vax rules before he leaves office

The consolidated challenge takes aim at the DeSantis administration’s efforts to amend longstanding public health rules that require children to be immunized for haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), and pneumococcal conjugate.
The Florida Academy of Family Physicians, physician Danielle Carter, and three individuals identified only by their initials filed one administrative challenge. A second challenge was filed by Kimberly Thorpe and her two minor children, plus Genevieve Rahmouni and her minor son. Both cases involve medically fragile children.
Both groups argue the DeSantis administration didn’t follow proper rulemaking procedures and that the DOH overstepped its legislative authority.
Ladapo: Eliminating vaccine mandates isn’t about science, it’s about parents’ rights

During a public hearing on the proposed rule changes, DOH Secretary and State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo said the state isn’t pursuing the changes out of fear or concern about the vaccines, but rather to put parents in charge of their children’s healthcare.
The proposed rule change would not affect vaccine mandates for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, and tetanus, all of which are required by statute.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Democratic Party calls for immediate investigation of Auditor Mark Hunt
description: The West Virginia Democratic Party is calling an immediate investigation into the actions of State Auditor Mark Hunt after he signed documents that state law.
text:
West Virginia Auditor Mark Hunt, a Republican elected in 2024, is under scrutiny for personally signing tax deeds for a friend. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Democratic Party is calling for an immediate investigation into the actions of State Auditor Mark Hunt after he signed documents that state law.
A West Virginia Watch investigation published Sunday found that Hunt, elected in 2024, personally signed nine tax deeds between March and June 2025.
State law governing the sale of delinquent tax properties, meaning properties lost because the owner didn’t pay their taxes, states that the deputy land commissioner — not the auditor — is supposed to sign those deeds. 
On Monday, West Virginia Democratic Party Chair Mike Pushkin said an independent investigation should be launched into Hunt’s activities.
“The State Auditor’s Office handles approximately 17,000 property deeds a year. Mark Hunt personally signed nine of them, and every single one benefited a company connected to his longtime friend and employee, whose wife also contributed to his political campaigns,” said Pushkin in a news release. “ … That raises an obvious question: Why did Mark Hunt single out these nine deeds for his personal attention?” 
Pushkin said the allegations demand action from Gov. Patrick Morrisey.
“Has Gov. Morrisey directed anyone in his administration to examine these allegations? Has he requested an independent investigation? If not, why not? Does his commitment to rooting out government corruption end when the questions involve a fellow Republican?” Pushkin questioned. 
He also called for reaction from Attorney General JB McCuskey, House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and Senate President Randy Smith.
Hunt defended his signature on the documents, saying that his role as auditor gives him the authority to sign them.  
“The deputy commissioner works under and through me and through my authority,” Hunt told West Virginia Watch last week. “It would be foolish to think that the commissioner’s boss couldn’t sign the same deed, or any other matter in the office … I can sign whatever I need to sign to make the office work.” 
Hunt also pointed to a different piece of state code to support the practice he said he only did for Robert L. Johns.
Pushkin called for an independent review of Hunt’s handling of delinquent property tax transactions, his office’s relationships with private purchasers of tax-delinquent property, and any potential conflicts of interest involving employees, contractors and political contributors.
On social media, Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, said that Hunt “ignored state code to provide a significant financial benefit to his associate.”
“That is a clear violation of the law. Based on this evidence alone, Mark Hunt should resign immediately,” Leavitt posted Sunday on X.
In late October, Brad McElhinny of WV MetroNews reported that the Auditor’s Office was served a federal grand jury subpoena. Hunt said no one has talked to him about the federal probe and provided no further comment. 
Hunt previously served in the state Senate from 2022 to 2024.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas Legislature’s leaders balk at shrinking their 4.4% salary hike to 1%
description: Kansas Legislature's leaders stall attempt to roll back 4.4% raise for House and Senate members to the 1% boost given other state employees.
text:
Sen. Tim Shallenburger, a Baxter Springs Republican, attempted to convince other leaders of the Kansas Legislature to support a recommendation the 4.4% raise scheduled for House and Senate members be reduced to the 1% granted other state workers. This image of Shallenburger was taken April 6, 2023, on the Senate floor. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Leaders of the Kansas Legislature blocked a proposal to slash to 1% the scheduled pay raise for House and Senate members so their increase matched the percentage they granted to thousands of other state government workers.
The decision by the Legislative Coordinating Council, a bipartisan panel of House and Senate brass, left in place the 4.4% boost in compensation for the state’s 165 legislators.
Senate Vice President Tim Shallenburger, a Baxter Springs Republican, said it would be unfair for the Legislature to reward itself a raise more than four times greater than what the 2026 Legislature allocated for rank-and-file employees. His proposal to limit the raise for legislators to 1% was rejected by the LCC on a 3-3 vote with two members absent.
“I have a little heartburn recommending a 4% pay increase for legislators,” Shallenburger told his LCC colleagues. “I think we should send this signal that we think that if 1% is good enough for employees, it’s good enough for us.”
Voting for the motion were Shallenburger, Senate Majority Leader Chase Blasi, R-Wichita, and House Minority Leader Brandon Woodard, D-Lenexa. The LCC members against the motion were House Speaker Dan Hawkins, R-Wichita, House Speaker Pro Tempore Blake Carpenter, R-Derby, and House Majority Leader Chris Croft, R-Overland Park. Senate President Ty Masterson, R-Andover, and Senate Minority Leader Dinah Sykes, D-Lenexa, were absent.
Carpenter, who voted against the proposal, said he was torn between the idea of bringing equivalency to taxpayer-funded raises for legislative and executive branch employees and endorsing a recommendation that might not be compliant with state law.
“I think there are a lot of individuals within our bodies that agree with the principle overall,” he said. “My fear, though, is that we’re getting ready to take action that we don’t know all the legal ramifications and consequences of.”
Under the defeated proposal, the LCC would strike from the state budget the funding required to make legislative salary adjustments above 1%. The LCC would further recommended the House and Senate take up a bill affirming reduction of the legislative salary enhancements due to take effect in January. It would be up to the 2027 Legislature to make a final decision.
Gordon Self, who leads the Legislature’s Office of the Revisor of Statutes, told the LCC on Friday that he was skeptical the council had authority to tinker with legislative compensation.
“On the spot, I can make a strong argument that you can’t,” Self said. “That would be a question that would need to be fully addressed as we move forward.”
In April, Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly attempted to use her veto power to persuade the 2026 Legislature to improve upon the pay raise granted executive branch employees. She had advocated for a 2.5% pay hike for these workers, but the Legislature approved a 1% increase.
Kelly’s tactic was to veto the Legislature’s entire operating and salary budget in pursuit of a compromise, but the House and Senate overrode her veto.
Kelly’s veto was denounced by Carpenter as the work of a “dictator,” while Blasi said the governor was operating as if she were a “queen.”
Members of the Legislature receive about $58,000 annually in the form of salary and per diem compensation. They benefit from $6,000 per year allocated for official mailing privileges. And, they can participate in a retirement program that calculated benefits as if they were were employees making $90,000 per year.
The 2023 Legislature adopted a bill creating the Kansas Legislative Compensation Committee. The commission was responsible for drafting a plan that would improve legislative salaries. After multiple meetings, the commission proposed base raises for House and Senate members of more than 90%. The commission also developed a system allowing for annual adjustments to legislative wages based on a rolling three-year average of Kansas personal income.
The 2024 Legislature wasn’t required to vote in favor of the commission’s recommendations for the plan to be implemented. The House and Senate could, however, vote to reject the plan. No action was taken by the Legislature, so the new compensation system was automatically adopted.
Meanwhile, raises for about 35,000 Kansas executive branch employees remained at the whim of politicians in the form of appropriations bills considered by the House, Senate and governor.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hinds County on pace to finish Mississippi Senate count Monday, upload Wednesday
description: Affidavit and absentee ballots are being processed by election officials, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Hinds County Election officials are on pace to finish counting affidavit ballots in Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race by the end of Monday, and expect to upload results on Wednesday, an attorney for the county told Mississippi Today.
The results in Mississippi’s most populous county and a Democratic stronghold could cement the outcome of the Magnolia State nail-biter between Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom. The narrow margin between Hyde-Smith and Colom has already shocked many across the nation, but it has remained too close to call since Election Day. Colom led by nearly 2,600 votes with nearly 1 million votes cast and thousands yet to be reported.
Hinds County early Monday still reported about 7% of the vote outstanding, as officials there and in other counties continue processing affidavit ballots.
Tony Gaylor, an attorney for the Hinds County Board of Supervisors, said counting most affidavits would likely conclude on Monday. But voters who had issues with their IDs have until 5 p.m. Tuesday to “cure” their ballots with the circuit clerk.
The commission then will refer the ballots to the Hinds County Resolution Board, which makes determinations on affidavit ballots after initial eligibility checks.
Hyde-Smith and Colom
“I think by the end of the day they’ll probably finish counting the affidavits,” Gaylor said. “They won’t be uploaded until Wednesday, when the (Hinds County) Resolution Board has the final count.”
The resolution board will “go over all of the accepted affidavits,” and the accepted ballots will be added to the vote tally. After that happens, Gaylor said, the commission would likely be able to upload results.
READ MORE: DeSoto County, a Republican stronghold, key to Scott Colom’s midterm election performance
READ MORE: Turns out, Mississippi voters were paying attention in the Colom, Hyde-Smith Senate race
Under state law, counties have until Nov. 13 to certify their election results. A legal challenge could then ensue if one of the campaigns challenges accepted ballots, a potentially messy process that could entail filing lawsuits in separate county courts. 
The fundraising arm of the Senate Republicans has demanded election officials around the state separate and preserve affidavit ballots. Democratic election lawyers and voting rights advocates have said they are confident Colom will win and called for affidavit ballots to be reviewed in public.
Mississippi has a “bottom-up” system of election administration, where 82 county circuit clerks and election commissions are responsible for processing their own affidavit and absentee ballots.
Voters who cast affidavit ballots only need to return to their local circuit clerk’s offices if they experienced voter ID issues at their polling place so that they can present a valid ID.
Hyde-Smith had not published a statement since Friday and has not done a public event since her election night watch party, in which she all but declared victory. On Friday, she vowed to “see this through to the very end!”
Since election night, Colom has travelled the state thanking supporters and promoting local businesses.
“We’re confident that once every lawful vote is counted, he’ll be Mississippi’s next U.S. senator,” said Gerard Henderson, Colom’s campaign mananger, in a statement on Monday. “Thank you to everyone who got us here and believes Mississippi Matters!”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: ICE detained her for 55 days. Now she wants to help others
description: Armelle Bondonga Bradshaw said she felt betrayed when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained her on Aug. 12. ICE agents took Armelle into custody when she and her husband Terrance voluntarily appeared for what was supposed to be a final interview for Armelle’s marriage-based green card. After 55 days in detention, Judge Tanya Walton Pratt […]
text:
Armelle Bondonga Bradshaw, with husband Terrance and their son, left, speaks about her recent ordeal in ICE detention. (Photo by Bonnie Jean Feldkamp for Kentucky Lantern.)Armelle Bondonga Bradshaw said she felt betrayed when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained her on Aug. 12.
ICE agents took Armelle into custody when she and her husband Terrance voluntarily appeared for what was supposed to be a final interview for Armelle’s marriage-based green card. After 55 days in detention, Judge Tanya Walton Pratt ordered Armelle to be released. The government failed to meet its burden of proof to justify keeping her detained. She was being kept unnecessarily separated from her family.
I sat in Armelle and Terrance’s living room once again. The last time I visited their home, I listened to her distraught husband tell me their love story. This time, I listened to Armelle while her son toddled around, happy to be near his mama again.
“I grew up here, you know?” Armelle said. She arrived in the United States from the Democratic Republic of the Congo with her family when she was just 8 years old. As a high schooler, Armelle helped found an organization called The Future Ancestors, raising money for nonprofit organizations in Kentucky while mentoring young people and working alongside her high school teacher. Armelle went on to graduate college, get married and start a family. She even returned to her high school as a substitute teacher.
As her immigration case moved through America’s complicated system, Armelle reached what should have been the final step toward her green card. Instead, ICE detained her. So yeah, Armelle felt betrayed. Not by her community, but by the United States government.
Her community mourned her absence. People sent letters to Armelle in jail, delivered meals to her husband and son and raised money for her legal fees. Not every ICE detainee has such support. In that regard, Armelle knew how fortunate she was to have a community fighting for her.
“The only thing I had to worry about when I was in jail was to keep my head straight,” she said. “The community fought for me to come home, and Terrance was fighting for me to have a home to come back to.”
Even still, detention was hard. It was loud, cold and she had no privacy. She had to ration toilet paper and pay for every phone call. After spending her first 48 hours in the “drunk tank,” where an inmate taunted her about being deported, Armelle was moved to a pod with other immigrants. There, she felt camaraderie. They prayed together and comforted one another.
It was there that Armelle first met Amina Seck, a Kentucky State University basketball player who was detained at the airport while traveling with her team. They leaned on one another in detention, reminding each other when the day felt particularly dire that “God is good.”
Then Armelle and Amina were both moved into the general population jail, though they had not been charged with crimes. Immigration violations are civil, not criminal.
“I sat in jail over paperwork,” Armelle said.
But Armelle still believes her detention served a purpose. Without it, the world might not have learned about Amina Seck. Kentucky State had not spoken publicly about its basketball player’s situation. Amina was injured, in pain and needed surgery. Armelle urged her legal team to help Amina. They did. Even while fighting for her own release, Armelle fought for someone else, too.
Then, 55 days after ICE took Armelle into custody, she heard the words she longed for.
“Bondonga, Bag and Baggage.” The officer said, using a phrase that meant Armelle was being released and should collect her belongings.
“I literally ran,” Armelle said. She grabbed her Bible and her three journals and left the rest.
It was Tuesday, Oct. 6, and just like when she was detained, her release came out of nowhere and it happened fast.
Divine timing is a curious thing. Terrance had injured his hand and taken the day off of work, so he was available to drive to the jail when Armelle was released.
Later that same day, Amina Seck’s bond was set and she was released two days later.
I asked Armelle how she was settling in back at home. The first couple of nights were “kind-of crazy,” she admitted. Someone’s touch would jolt her awake, only for her to realize it was her husband or son by her side. After two months of “sleeping with one eye open,” it was hard for her to let go of that hypervigilance.
But she feels good. She said, “I’m, just, ready to get back to, like, life.”
Armelle keeps the television off, enjoying the quiet time with her husband and son. She’s not venturing out much either. ICE detained her once when they shouldn’t have. “What’s not to say I walk across the street and they try to do it again,” she said.
Her journey is not over. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has approved Terrance and Armelle’s marriage-based petition, but Armelle still must complete the process to obtain her green card. She is working with her attorneys on next steps.
Detention might have shaken Armelle, but she wants people to know that it did not break her. It has lit a new fire under her to continue advocating for others.
“I was so blessed,” she said about the way her community stood up for her.
Armelle went to jail fearing what the government might do to her, but  she came home thinking “how many other people could we help?”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Ex-prosecutor becomes NJ’s new lieutenant governor
description: Shirley Emehelu, a former prosecutor who worked with the governor in the New Jersey U.S. Attorney's Office, was sworn in as lieutenant governor on Monday.
text:
Shirley Emehelu, right, a former prosecutor who worked with the governor in the New Jersey U.S. Attorney's Office, was sworn in as lieutenant governor on Monday. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Shirley Emehelu, a former state and federal prosecutor and a longtime friend of Gov. Mikie Sherrill, was sworn in as the state’s new lieutenant governor Monday.
The appointment, which the state constitution empowers Sherrill to make unilaterally, fills the vacancy created by the resignation of Dale Caldwell, who stepped down in September after internal investigators said he had violated state ethics rules and made inappropriate sexual comments. Sherrill had already tapped Emehelu to succeed Caldwell as New Jersey’s secretary of state.
“Back in September, I said I wanted a partner in government who would represent my administration and the people of New Jersey with honor and integrity,” Sherrill said in Trenton Monday. “I found that partner in Shirley, a leader with an exceptional track record of doing right by people.”
NJ governor warns gas companies of sanctions for importing Russian diesel

New Jersey Supreme Court Chief Justice Stuart Rabner swore Emehelu in Monday morning.
Emehelu is a prosecutor of long experience. Before joining the Sherrill administration as acting comptroller — a position she ceded when she became acting secretary of state — Emehelu was the New Jersey executive assistant attorney general, the third-highest post in the state’s prosecutorial office.
Earlier, she headed the asset recovery and money laundering section of the New Jersey U.S. Attorney’s Office. Her nine-year tenure with the U.S. Attorney’s Office intersected with Sherrill’s own.
Emehelu has also worked as a defense attorney in the private sector.
“As lieutenant governor, I look forward to working alongside Gov. Sherrill and these dedicated public servants to make life more affordable, expand opportunity for all our communities, especially in helping the governor meet the goals of the Black agenda and help all our kids, including mine, build a bright future here,” Emehelu said.
The New Jersey Constitution does not require the Senate to approve when the governor makes an appointment to fill a vacancy in the lieutenant governorship, and it permits the governor to appoint their deputy to head one of the state’s chief departments without Senate confirmation.
That means Monday’s appointment also makes Emehelu secretary of state, the fifth lieutenant governor in state history, and the first immigrant to hold the latter position.
Sherrill said she did not set out in search of a woman to replace Caldwell.
“I didn’t have a preconceived notion that I needed to have another woman serving here. I felt like, as governor, I had that handled,” the governor said to chuckles from an audience that included most of her cabinet.

name: National
title: Low-level arrests are rising despite national crime declines
description: Arrests for low-level offenses, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased nationwide in 2025, even as violent crime continued to decline, according to a new analysis of federal data. The analysis, which was released in late October by the criminal justice advocacy organization FWD.us, found that arrests for vagrancy, an offense often associated with [...]
text:
A homeless encampment under a bridge includes a tent and bags of belongings in Paterson, N.J. Arrests for vagrancy, an offense often associated with homelessness, rose 44% between 2024 and 2025, according to a new analysis by advocacy group FWD.us. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Arrests for low-level offenses, including vagrancy and drug possession, increased nationwide in 2025, even as violent crime continued to decline, according to a new analysis of federal data.
The analysis, which was released in late October by the criminal justice advocacy organization FWD.us, found that arrests for vagrancy, an offense often associated with homelessness, rose 44% between 2024 and 2025, while arrests for marijuana possession increased 6% and possession of other drugs rose 3%.
Arrests for immigration violations nearly tripled, rising 188% between 2024 and 2025, amid President Donald Trump’s crackdown on illegal immigration. The increase continued into 2026, with an average of 36,093 arrests per month through July — nearly four times the monthly average in 2024, according to the report.
The findings point to a shift toward more aggressive enforcement of lower-level offenses, particularly in states that have rolled back major changes to their criminal legal systems in recent years, according to the analysis. 
Violent crime in US fell at record pace in 2025

Voters in nearly a dozen states also backed tougher approaches to crime in this year’s midterm elections, approving statewide ballot measures that impose stricter penalties for certain offenses or tighten bail restrictions.
“There is at this point plenty of time to choose a different path from this one and to kind of redirect ourselves,” said Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us.
The increases in arrests for low-level offenses also come as arrests for more serious offenses, including homicide, robbery and burglary, continue to decline, mirroring broader national crime trends.
Some of the sharpest increases in arrests for low-level offenses were concentrated in a handful of states.
Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada accounted for more than half of the nationwide increase in vagrancy arrests. FWD.us linked the trend in part to the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in City of Grants Pass v. Johnson, which gave local governments greater latitude to enforce restrictions on sleeping outdoors.
Meanwhile, California and Oregon, which rolled back portions of earlier progressive drug policy changes in 2024, experienced increases in arrests for drug possession offenses other than marijuana. Those arrests rose 24% in California and 39% in Oregon.
In 2025, Black people were arrested for marijuana possession at more than four times the rate of white people. From 2024 to 2025, arrests of Black people rose nearly 10%, accounting for 83% of the national increase and 45% of all marijuana arrests in 2025.
But the analysis does not establish that the policy changes caused every increase in arrests or determine whether greater enforcement improved public safety.
The organization warned that continued growth in low-level arrests could reverse years of progress in reducing incarceration and racial disparities, particularly as states reconsider criminal justice policies amid ongoing debates over crime and public safety.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico judge finds state education reform plan deficient, additions due in 2027
description: A New Mexico judge recently ruled that the state’s plan to address the landmark Yazzie/Martinez education equity lawsuit is deficient, and ordered the state education department to supplement the plan by March 2027.
text:
First Judicial District Judge Matthew Wilson found the New Mexico Public Education Department’s action plan to address Yazzie/Martinez reform deficient on Nov. 2, 2026. He ordered the education department to supplement the plan by March 2027. (Photo of Mayfield High School in Las Cruces photographed in September 2026 by Leah Romero for Source New Mexico)A New Mexico judge recently ruled that the state’s plan to address the landmark Yazzie/Martinez education equity lawsuit is deficient, and ordered the state education department to supplement the plan by March 2027. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a Nov. 2 order, First Judicial District Judge Matthew Wilson found that the New Mexico Public Education Department’s remedial action plan, which addresses equitable education reform for at-risk students, is not comprehensive because it fails to address all previous judicial orders. Wilson also identified gaps in the action plan, including inadequate plans to address class sizes, textbook funding and summer school programs. 
Wilson’s ruling came in response to objections filed earlier this year by several organizations, including the New Mexico Center on Law and Poverty and Transform Education NM, that requested the court order PED to rewrite the plan the department submitted last November. 
Although Wilson agreed with plaintiffs that the plan is not comprehensive, the court did not grant the plaintiffs’ request that PED completely rewrite the plan to include stakeholder input. Instead, the court ordered PED to file a supplement by March 25, 2027. The additional materials must succinctly connect its remedial action to every constitutional violation in past court orders and provide ways to assess if remedial actions are successful. 
Both PED and plaintiffs in the case found reasons to commend Wilson’s decision.
In an emailed statement, PED spokesperson Janelle Taylor García said that the education department “welcomes” the order, “which upholds the department’s Action Plan and confirms that the state is on the right path to meet its obligations to New Mexico’s students.”
In regard to the required supplement to the plan, PED sees the order “as a valuable roadmap that provides greater clarity to the department in its work. The court said it is confident the PED can complete this supplement, and we share that confidence,” García said. 
PED, she said, “remains fully committed to delivering an excellent education for every New Mexico student, especially those the original case was brought to serve. This ruling allows us to keep moving that work forward.”
Alisa Diehl, a New Mexico Center on Law and Poverty attorney representing the plaintiffs, told Source NM that Wilson’s order “confirms what we’ve been saying for a year now, which is that PED’s plan still doesn’t fully address what the courts require” and falls short in connecting its solutions with “actual steps that will lead to an education system that our children are entitled to.” 
While the court agreed with plaintiffs that the PED plan is insufficient, it did not require the state to work with plaintiffs or stakeholders on its supplemental plan. “We remain concerned that another version that’s produced by the agency without the expertise and input necessary to develop many solutions isn’t going to produce the changes that we need,” Diehl said. 
The lawsuit has been a watershed moment in education in New Mexico. In 2018, a district court determined New Mexico had violated its constitutional duty to provide a sufficient education to its students, particularly Native American and low-income students, English language learners and students with disabilities.
In 2025, Wilson found that PED hadn’t complied with the 2018 court ruling and ordered the education department to file a remedial action plan to fulfill its constitutional obligation to provide education support for all students. 
The latest ruling comes as Gov.-elect Deb Haaland prepares to take office next year, which education advocates say creates an opportunity for New Mexico to take a different approach and include further collaboration between stakeholders and PED. 
“We have so much to offer the next administration in terms of scholarship, analysis and lived experience from the ground and classrooms,” Loretta Trujillo, executive director of Transform Education New Mexico, told Source NM. “So it would be really important for the next administration to really partner with us.”
The sentiment was echoed by Regis Pecos, co-founder of the Tribal Education Alliance, who said extending the timeline to March to supplement the plan “allows for the opportunity for more collaboration with new leadership at the PED under Gov.-Elect Haaland.” 
Pecos said Haaland’s past comments, in which she called the plan inadequate and said she would bring the plaintiffs and tribes to the table, make him “hopeful” going forward. 
“This has to be a collaborative effort,” Pecos said. “My optimism comes from Haaland’s comments while campaigning. That’s a fundamental change toward finally ensuring New Mexico fulfills its constitutional obligations.”

text:
The University of Northern Iowa will use grant and matching dollars to purchase a machine teaching cluster for computer science students. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The University of Northern Iowa will soon offer students access to secure virtual environments with the goal of allowing them to explore hands-on tools and projects simply and safely.
The Cedar Falls university announced in a news release Monday it has received a $294,000 grant from the Roy J. Carver Charitable Trust — an amount matched by the university to purchase a “modern virtual machine teaching cluster.”
“I’m thankful to the Roy J. Carver Charitable Trust and to UNI for providing the matching funds to buy this cluster,” said principal investigator and computer science professor Sarah Diesburg in the release. “It’s going to drastically expand learning opportunities for students through a wider variety of hands-on activities.”

The cluster creates computing environments disconnected from other university systems for safety, the release stated, while housing five virtualization servers, a dedicated storage server and backup server for students in the university’s computer science department.
Training that students will be able to complete will include building network infrastructure, practicing offensive and defensive virtual security measures, setting information technology services and more. The release stated students will also be able to access virtual desktops with software and tools curated by their instructors, simplifying the process to get students set up with important course resources.
As the cluster is browser-accessible, the release stated online learners will have the same opportunities for hands-on experiences as in-person students. According to the release, as many as 180 undergraduate students will benefit from the cluster, which will be piloted in spring 2027 and implemented across different courses in the next academic year.
“We think it’s important for students to practice what they learn in the most realistic way possible,” Diesburg said. “This cluster will allow them to do that.”

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming trona workers demonstrate amid pending layoffs: ‘Lives are at risk here’
description:
WE Soda plans to reduce its workforce from about 850 to 500 over the next two years due to a flood of Chinese soda ash derived from trona.
The post Wyoming trona workers demonstrate amid pending layoffs: ‘Lives are at risk here’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Trona workers and their spouses, children and more than 100 community members protested at the break of dawn Monday to show support for 350 WE Soda employees facing layoffs. “Lives are at risk here,” a union representative told WyoFile.
“What we would like to see is the mines stay open,” United Steelworkers Local 13214 President Marshal Cummings said. “And if we’re going to go to solution [mining] that we do it in slow waves through attrition so that it doesn’t completely demolish the community.” 

Trona workers and supporters gather early Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, outside the WE Soda Westvaco trona mine and soda ash processing plant in Sweetwater County following the recent announcement that 350 jobs will be cut over the next two years. (Stan Blake)
London-based WE Soda announced Wednesday it will convert its Westvaco underground mining operation to in-situ solution recovery, a less labor-intensive drill-and-pump method that, over the two-year transition, will result in a 41% workforce reduction. The shift is necessary, the company says, due to crushing global market forces driven by a flood of cheaper soda ash — the product derived from trona — from China.
The operational shift will also reduce soda ash output as WE Soda strategically pulls back from the global market to focus on customers in North America, it said. Soda ash is used in glass manufacturing, in cleaning products and in water treatment, among other things.
Layoffs are expected to begin in January and continue over a two-year period, the company said.
The company appears willing to cede Wyoming’s 14% of the global soda ash market, Cummings said, at the expense of a workforce that drives the economy in southwest Wyoming. The union is also pressuring Wyoming’s congressional delegation to take action, he added.
One of WE Soda’s primary soda ash processing facilities lights up in southwest Wyoming. (WE Soda)
“I hope that they understand that lives are at risk here,” Cummings said. “And this is so much more than just a paycheck, because people’s futures are shattered — on a scale that Wyoming hasn’t seen very often.”
The demonstration was timed to show support to fellow workers on their way to work a shift at the Westvaco operations. Protesters lined a frontage road leading to the mine, lit a burn barrel for warmth and chanted “union strong.”
One child was pictured holding a sign that said, “I don’t know what a ‘layoff’ is, I just know my daddy is sad.”
“I think it was 21 degrees [Fahrenheit],” said Stan Blake, a former Wyoming legislator and Green River mayor-elect. “We wanted to show the people going in on the buses that, you know, we’re there, we’re willing to help out.”
“This is a gut punch,” Blake added. “I’d even call it a sucker punch because it came out of nowhere, as far as I know.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Citizen’s Assembly report, the good the bad and the ugly
description: If Connecticut is serious about fixing its property tax crisis, it must put public education at the center of the equation.
text:
I’d like to begin by thanking the 100 volunteers for all their hard work and taking on a thankless task.

Joseph Sokolovic

The Connecticut Citizens’ Assembly released its long-awaited final report on property tax reform. I believe this citizen-led attempt to fix Connecticut’s most notoriously broken system was taken on in good faith. It brought together a diverse group of residents in an attempt to bypass legislative gridlock, their charge was to solve the crushing property tax burden that drags down the majority of our municipalities, strains our homeowners, and starves our children of a decent education.
The report contains genuine breakthroughs —solutions that public education advocates and local leaders have championed for over a half a century. But beneath those noble intentions lies a deeply flawed financial structure that threatens to leave our most marginalized communities, and our public school classrooms, worse off than before.
If we are going to evaluate the Citizens’ Assembly recommendations honestly, we need to look at the full picture, The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly.
The good: recognizing inflationary concerns, mandates and PILOTS
Let’s start where the report does well. For far too long, state government has passed the buck to local taxpayers through unfunded mandates and stagnant aid formulas. The Assembly rightly addresses several of these core structural inequities:
Tying Education Cost Sharing (ECS) to Inflation (Proposal B): For over 13 years, the ECS foundation amount was flat-funded at $11,525 per student, while educational costs have soared past $17,000. Unfortunately the Assembly didn’t touch upon this number but wisely suggested that the formula increase annually alongside the Employment Cost Index, this is a rising tide that will float most if not all school districts.
State-Funded Special Education (Proposal F): Municipalities currently carry the lions share $3.26 billion in annual K-12 SPED costs, approximately two-thirds through local property taxes. The proposal rightly states special education is a constitutional duty of the state, removing a massive, unpredictable burden from city operating budgets.
Mandate Protection and PILOT Reform (Proposals A, G, & H): Delaying state mandates by 12 months, while not perfect is a start, establishing independent mandate oversight, will be helpful but does not call for an outright ban on unfunded mandates.
Revaluating tax exemptions for massive non-profit institutions directly targets the structural drain on urban tax bases. Fiscally distressed host cities that shoulder massive, tax-exempt regional footprints are finally acknowledged. Unfortunately, I see no mention of fully funding the PILOT program in order to make municipalities whole.
The bad: Siphoning state revenue for the few over to the many
Where the report begins to unravel is in its regressive local revenue redistribution scheme, specifically Proposal E, which seeks to share restaurant and hotel tax revenues with host municipalities.
On its surface, letting towns keep local hospitality tax dollars sounds quire reasonable. In practice, it creates a massive “winner-take-all” system that starves the state as a whole.
Proposal E pulls $200 million annually out of the state’s General Fund at a time when state fiscal analysts project structural deficits beginning in FY 2028.
Tax dollars follow commercial and hotel density. Under this plan, just 10 municipalities—wealthy corporate hubs like Greenwich and Stamford, airport hosts like Windsor Locks, and casino towns —will capture the vast majority of the revenue. Meanwhile, over 50 smaller or less commercial towns will receive less than $50,000 a year.
Take Greenwich versus Bridgeport. Greenwich, with a luxury hotel footprint and high-end dining, stands to gain over $3.5 million annually. While Bridgeport with few hotels will be lucky to clear half that, even when major waterfront developments like Steelpointe Harbor fully materialize, the addition of a single extended-stay hotel barely moves the needle against Greenwich’s multi-million dollar windfall.
By carving out $200 million from the statewide pool to enrich a small handful of commercial hubs, Proposal E takes public dollars meant to benefit the entire state and hands them to the privileged few.
The ugly: the public education lock-out
The most concerning aspect of the Citizens’ Assembly report is not just where money is taken from, but how it is statutorily locked up.
Read the fine print of Proposal E carefully: the municipal share of meals and hotel tax revenues “would be dedicated to public safety and public works.”
Let that sink in. While our urban priority school districts face multi-million dollar structural deficits, forcing local boards of education to cut reading specialists, eliminate librarians, art programs, and support staff —the report would explicitly forbid a single cent of this new $200 million revenue stream from going toward public education.
This creates a perverse dynamic inside city halls across Connecticut:
City departments receive dedicated new revenue for paving roads and funding police departments, while local boards of education remain trapped relying on stagnant property tax bases. City councils, pointing to the new state tax relief for municipal services, will face immense political pressure to flat fund education or have to raise revenue elsewhere.
Add to this Proposal J (Interstate Tolls), which generates an estimated $950 million annually but statutorily directs those dollars to transportation infrastructure and motor vehicle tax offsets, and a disturbing pattern emerges: Roads, bridges, and police departments receive guaranteed, dedicated funding streams, while public school classrooms are left to fight for scraps under state spending caps.
Where do we go from here?
The Citizens’ Assembly proved that Connecticut hungers for change. Their calls to fully fund special education, index school aid to inflation, and put the brakes on unfunded mandates, echo the historic battle cries of advocates. These proposals deserve full advocacy efforts and support.
However, lawmakers cannot accept this report blindly. Any regressive tax reform package that drains $200 million from the General Fund to enrich ten commercial hubs, while barring public schools from accessing those funds, is not equity; it is a downward redistribution of wealth that leaves our children behind.
If Connecticut is serious about fixing its property tax crisis, it must put public education at the center of the equation. We must demand that new revenue streams support educational equity rather than widening the racial funding gap which stands at $1.25 billion and growing.
The choices we make in the upcoming legislative session will make or break the current and future generations of children. It is time to fix the bad, throw out the ugly, and build a system that works for every student and taxpayer in our state.
Joseph Sokolovic is Vice Chair of the Bridgeport Board of Education. The opinions expressed here are his alone.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ congresswoman-elect pledges to fight Trump plan for Roxbury migrant jail
description: Rebecca Bennett, who will soon represent Roxbury in Congress, said she plans to fight the Trump administration's plan to put a migrant jail there.
text:
Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett (D) speaks during her victory party in Bridgewater on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Three days after voters in the reliably Republican township of Roxbury supported Democrats in the midterm elections, New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport told a federal judge that the Trump administration for the first time confirmed to state officials that it plans to move forward with a controversial migrant detention center in the Morris County town.
The news brought fresh condemnation from Rebecca Bennett, a Democrat who was elected last week to represent the 7th Congressional District, which includes Roxbury. Bennett, who unseated GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. in the state’s most closely watched House race, blasted the feds for proceeding with the “unwanted” jail despite opposition, and she vowed to work with Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) and state and local lawmakers to fight it.
“Since February, I’ve stood with local residents, including Roxbury’s Republican-led town council, against Trump’s plan to open an ICE detention center in Roxbury,” Bennett said in a statement. “This week, voters spoke loud and clear: Washington should be focused on lowering costs, ending corruption, and making sure that everyone feels safe in their community.”
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security in February purchased the Roxbury site, a 470,000-square-foot warehouse it wants to convert into a processing center for detained migrants, for $129 million. The Sherrill administration and Roxbury’s GOP-leadership sued in March to stop the plan, and in May succeeded in putting a temporary hold on it. The Trump administration has gone back-and-forth in subsequent court filings about whether the plan is moving forward.
New Jersey Attorney General Jen Davenport told Judges Jamel K. Semper and James B. Clark III, in a status report filed Friday night, that the Trump administration “advised Plaintiffs for the first time that DHS had decided to proceed with pursuing a detention facility at the Roxbury site.”
Homeland Security officials also have acknowledged that they used the warehouse parking lot twice in September to process people that immigrants agents had arrested, Davenport added. Such conduct “raises concerns about DHS’s willingness to skirt the boundaries” of the May court order that put a temporary pause on their detention center plan.
The plan was a campaign issue in Bennett’s bid to unseat Kean, with Bennett criticizing Kean for staying largely silent on the president’s push to place a migrant detention center in the 7th District. It may have helped move Roxbury, a Republican stronghold, to the Democrats’ column on Election Day.
Bennett won 51% of Roxbury’s vote this year, compared to 48% for Kean. Two years ago, Kean won the town with 58% of the vote. Roxbury, which voted for President Donald Trump during all three of his White House bids, also voted narrowly last week for U.S. Sen Cory Booker (D) over Republican challenger Justin Murphy. When Booker last sought reelection in 2020, most Roxbury voters cast ballots for his Republican opponent.
Republicans make up 38% of Roxbury’s nearly 19,000 voters, compared to Democrats’ 26%, with unaffiliated and third-party voters comprising the rest, registration data shows.
