name: Mississippi Today
title: Auditor Shad White announces run for Mississippi governor
description: State Auditor Shad White speaks during the Neshoba County Fair in Philadelphia, Miss., Wednesday, July 31, 2024.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi state Auditor Shad White on Monday announced that he will seek the Republican nomination for governor in 2027, calling himself a pro-Trump candidate who will “shut down Jackson’s Good-Old-Boys Club.” 
The announcement comes after White said repeatedly over the past year that he was considering a run for the state’s top job. White was set to kick off his campaign at an in-person announcement in Laurel, and published a video in which he vowed to bring down a network of government insiders. 
“There might be two parties in Jackson, but there’s only one good-old-boys club,” said White. “They tried to ban my office from even looking for government waste. As governor, I’m shutting the whole rotten system down.”
White joins a growing Republican primary field to replace term-limited incumbent Gov. Tate Reeves. That field now includes Attorney General Lynn Fitch, Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson and former House Speaker Philip Gunn.
Other Republicans considering entering the race for governor include Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann, former U.S. Rep. Gregg Harper, and billionaire businessman Tommy Duff.
On the Democratic side, Priscilla Williams Till, a civil rights advocate and distant cousin of Emmett Till, has entered the race along with Ivana Williams, a former Mississippi Highway Patrol trooper who is suing over her termination.
In an interview with Mississippi Today ahead of his announcement, White said his campaign would focus on addressing household costs by cutting fraud, waste and abuse in state government. And he didn’t back away from his support of President Donald Trump, whose popularity has soured nationally, costing down-ticket Republicans in the midterm elections. 
“As long as you are willing to take on that (good-old-boys) club and do what is best for the people of Mississippi,” White said. “I think that will have broad appeal, and I think you can absolutely both energize the people who voted for President Trump two years ago and win a general election in Mississippi.” 
A native of Sandersville in Jones County, White is a former Rhodes Scholar and graduate of the University of Mississippi and Harvard Law School. 
His career in state government began when he served as director of policy to then-Lt. Gov. Phil Bryant in 2011. In 2018, Bryant appointed him state auditor to replace Stacey Pickering, and White won the office unopposed in 2019 and was re-elected in 2023. He also serves as an attorney in the Mississippi National Guard and was recently deployed to the Middle East for several months. 
White’s tenure as auditor has largely been defined by his role in investigating the state’s TANF welfare scandal, the largest public fraud scheme in state history. That ignited a legal battle with former NFL star Brett Favre, a close friend of Donald Trump Jr., who sued White, alleging defamation over comments White made in a book he wrote about the scandal and in media interviews.
White has filed a countersuit asking a court to require Brett Favre to repay welfare funds, but White’s authority to do so was later contested successfully by Fitch, an issue that could arise on the campaign trail. 
Republican candidates running for governor in Mississippi appear to have been working hard to win over Trump and his supporters, often in strikingly similar terms. 
Some political observers and conservative commentators have wondered whether White’s battles with Favre could cost him Trump’s endorsement, but White has said his relationship with the administration remains strong.
Alex Meyer, a former White House official for President Donald Trump, is set to host a fundraiser in Oxford for White on Wednesday. 
While many polls indicate Trump’s approval rating has cratered, his endorsement is still considered a powerful factor in Mississippi Republican primaries. 
White has earned a reputation for a brand of pugilistic politics, whether it was trading barbs with a Democratic lawmaker at a public hearing or threatening to sue a former Republican lawmaker at another. 
Meyer previously told Mississippi Today he thinks that style could help White win over Trump’s base.
“Shad has a lot of the energy that I see in the Republican primary electorate in Mississippi, and across the country. They’re looking for someone who will go to war and will fight for them,” Meyer said.
White has over $3.8 million in cash on hand, leading a fundraising battle that is sure to accelerate before the Aug. 3 primary.
White’s announcement comes as Mississippians are waiting to see who won the nail-biter U.S. Senate race between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom. Colom has been leading as final votes are counted, and his potential victory has been a political earthquake in ruby red Mississippi, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1982. 
The results have stunned the nation, and could result in more investment and attention from national Democrats. White said it shows candidates must be focused on reigning in consumer costs. His pitch will be to target fraud in state government and use savings for tax relief, including lower car tag fees and grocery taxes, continued phase-out of the state income tax and property tax freezes.
“I think if you’re running for governor or really any other state office, it is clear that it’s incumbent on you to have a very clear plan about how to help normal working families,” White said. “That’s the stuff that we have to start talking about and execute to give voters faith that we understand what they are going through every single day.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Commentary: Time for justice and accountability
description: After this past election, we have the opportunity to avenge Minnesotans we lost and bring justice and accountability.  I distinguish avenge from revenge — the latter being a bloodlust, and often selfish. To avenge is to punish the evildoer in pursuit of justice for the wronged.  U.S. Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan will avenge Minnesota by “ripping ICE […]
text:
Carrie Rainey sticks her "I voted" sticker to the memorial for Alex Pretti during the midterm election in south Minneapolis Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Pretti was shot and killed by federal agents in January.(Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)After this past election, we have the opportunity to avenge Minnesotans we lost and bring justice and accountability. 
I distinguish avenge from revenge — the latter being a bloodlust, and often selfish. To avenge is to punish the evildoer in pursuit of justice for the wronged. 
U.S. Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan will avenge Minnesota by “ripping ICE apart,” the vetoes be damned.
Justice is the legal, moral application of due process to avenge for criminal acts. Black and brown Minnesotans, both citizens and undocumented, deserve justice for how this federal administration has attacked their security and livelihoods, tearing apart families and sending Minnesotans to countries and continents they have never been to.
Yes, Democrats have a 100-day agenda and tsunami mandate to undo the harms of this federal administration. End the war. Roll back all the tariffs and restore Congress’ sole authority to tax. Restore funding for food benefits like SNAP and WIC, after cuts hurt working families and strained food banks across the country. Reverse cuts to Medicaid and ACA subsidies which ended coverage for disabled people and made health care coverage unaffordable for millions of families by raising premiums by at times hundreds of dollars a month.
In Minnesota, Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar has promised to prioritize passing and signing comprehensive gun safety reform, the U.S. Supreme Court be damned. Nothing will bring back State Rep. Melissa Hortman and the victims at Annunciation, but a DFL trifecta can ban weapons of war from being used to murder more Minnesotans.
But let us be absolutely clear. When Minnesotans like Flanagan say we will “avenge Minnesota,” they mean we will investigate, prosecute and bring to justice the agents of the federal administration who contributed to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and harmed all of us in ways large and small. The sacrifices of Good, Pretti, and countless others will not be forgotten. They will not have died in the snow, blood in ice crystals, and buried in the earth for us to take half-measures and let killers go free.
My sources in state government say that part of the reason why it took just days to bring charges against Derek Chauvin for the 2020 murder of George Floyd compared to nearly a year for the killers in 2026 is because Chauvin was a local cop. To charge two federal agents on state murder charges is nearly unheard of, and retribution from the Trump administration is a concern.
After the midterms, Trump and Vance are in full retreat. They are blaming each other. Bring the charges. Bring justice to Minnesota.
We have a great task before us. The late Sen. Paul Wellstone taught us that politics was the practice of improving people’s lives and that we can make what was once impossible, possible through organizing neighbors around common values. Flanagan will now hold the Wellstone seat in the U.S. Senate. Minnesota and every neighborhood across this country has sacrificed. We donated to friends and family to stretch the food budget. We delivered diapers and baby formula to families we didn’t know because we recognized their humanity. When there was a blood emergency, we donated blood in the bus parked by the grocery store because somebody, somewhere needed that blood.
The day after the election, Gov. Tim Walz quietly visited the memorials to Good and Pretti in south Minneapolis. He said on social media that he was “inspired to see all those who showed up to pay their respects and leave an ‘i voted’ sticker.”
He added: “We have not forgotten. Accountability is coming.”

name: California
title: Crypto, Meta money lifts new Democrats to CA Capitol
description: Happy Monday, California. We have new election results for you today, including good news if you wanted more business-friendly, centrist Democrats in the Capitol. Of course the progressive wing of the Democratic Party can celebrate Jane Kim’s election to state insurance commissioner. The nation over the weekend continued to absorb Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commuta[...]
text:
Lawmakers on the Assembly floor at the state Capitol in Sacramento on April 29, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Happy Monday, California. We have new election results for you today, including good news if you wanted more business-friendly, centrist Democrats in the Capitol. Of course the progressive wing of the Democratic Party can celebrate Jane Kim’s election to state insurance commissioner.
The nation over the weekend continued to absorb Gov. Gavin Newsom’s commutation of death sentences, and our Ryan Sabalow connected with several victims’ families who felt blindsided by the decision.
Read on for more on those stories as well as to learn why El Niño has L.A. worried about an epic mosquito infestation. Eeeeeeeeeeeek! 
While spending by billionaire Elon Musk and others to thwart a national Democratic blue wave failed, the very rich had more success in California to ensure that more moderate Democrats will take office in the state Legislature, writes CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe.
At least nine Silicon Valley-backed Democrats will be going to the Capitol after Big Tech companies and investors spent a total of at least $50 million on their races generally to the disadvantage of candidates who were perceived as further to the left. That includes Assemblymembers-elect Mark Pulido, Andrae Gonzalez and Annalisa Perea; and Sen.-elect Scott Sakakihara, a former executive for Palantir Technologies.
Grow California, an independent expenditure committee principally funded by cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen and venture capitalist Tim Draper, spent $24 million backing moderate Democrats over more left-leaning Democrats. California Leads, funded mostly by Meta and Google, spent $17 million. 
Together, the groups made up 30% of all independent expenditures on legislative races during a record year for political spending.
Though Grow California and California Leads say they are not advocating for any issues in particular, another super PAC funded by Meta, known as META California, explicitly supports tech-friendly candidates who are receptive to artificial intelligence.
In addition to the state’s legislative races, billionaires and business interests poured huge money into stopping Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire tax, which voters are poised to reject, as well as the passage of Prop. 42, which bans any new wealth tax and is on track to pass. Combined with money in support of another anti-tax proposition, the opponents spent $316 million to achieve their policy goals.
Meanwhile, proponents of tech regulation are raising alarm over the outpouring of new political spending by tech interests. Catherine Bracy, the chief executive of TechEquity Collaborative, said the spending underscores Silicon Valley’s increasing influence in California lawmaking.
Read more.
Other election updates: After more counting over the weekend, California voters officially rejected three more ballot measures: Prop. 41, which would have imposed limits to certain new state taxes; Prop. 43, which would have made it harder to pass citizen-driven local tax measures; and Prop. 45, which would have lifted some environmental review requirements for building homes.
Voters also elected Jane Kim as insurance commissioner and Democrats Sally J. Lieber and Tom Umberg to the State Board of Equalization.



More ways to get CalMatters: We have an app, available for iPhone and Android. You’ll get a notification each morning about the day’s top stories, and you’ll be the first to know about breaking news. We can also send you text alerts on our latest investigations, political coverage and more. Sign up here.

Other Stories You Should Know


SoCal braces for El Niño mosquitoes


A southern house mosquito in 2022. Photo by Lauren Bishop, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention




A muggier, hotter summer led to more mosquitos carrying West Nile, with lethal consequences for Californians, reports CalMatters’ Kristen Hwang.
As of Nov. 6, the virus has seriously sickened 528 people and killed 32 others in California. The balmy weather resulted in the most West Nile activity in five years. 
Los Angeles County accounted for more than half the cases in 2026. Most people infected don’t get sick, but about a fifth of folks feasted on by the insects develop fevers, headaches and body aches.
And while cooler climates may offer a respite, experts worry 2027 will continue the onslaught of menacing mosquitos due to the effects of El Niño. If floodwaters persist into spring as temperatures rise, mosquitoes could boom.Read more.



CalMatters sues Shasta County over elections-related subpoena


Shasta County Clerk and Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis stands next to a lock and seal securing election ballots in a room at an elections office in Redding on Sept. 17, 2026. Photo by Salvador Ochoa for CalMatters




CalMatters and Shasta Scout are suing Shasta County over its refusal to comply with a public records request to release a federal subpoena served after the county’s outgoing elections chief questioned the integrity of the 2026 primary election.
The suit argues that the public has a compelling interest to know “whether any such (federal) investigation is motivated by well-grounded allegations of wrongdoing” or whether the probe is based on no credible evidence and instead intended to “sow unwarranted doubts about elections.”
After the June election, Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis drew the attention of the Trump administration by claiming ballots looked, felt and smelled funny. In September Curtis told several media organizations he received a federal grand jury subpoena related to the ballots, and that FBI agents arrived at a county elections office to inspect the ballots.
CalMatters and Shasta Scout sought copies of the subpoena, but the county rejected the request.
Read more.



And lastly: Some families furious with Newsom’s death row decision


Sandy Friend (left) and another mother of a murder victim comfort each other after a news conference in Sacramento on April 11, 2019. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo




Family members of victims are split in their reaction to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s death row commutations last week. While some do not hold enmity towards the governor, others are furious. Sandy Friend is the mother of Michael Lyon, an eight-year-old who was raped and murdered in 1996 by Robert Boyd Rhoades. Upon news of Newsom’s decision, Friend said she felt “a deep, soul-hurting pain.” Read more from CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow.






California Voices
As L.A. prepares for the 2028 Olympics by constructing new stations and rail lines, I hope that the workers whom the city relies on also get better access to reliable and safe transportation, writes Shanice Joseph, an L.A.-based writer and Watts native.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: What does a blue wave mean in Massachusetts?
description: It's a wrap on elections in Massachusetts, and the Democrats have kept a hold on almost all their levers of power in the state. But there was still plenty of controversial policy for voters to weigh in on. This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporter Jennifer Smith talks with Talia Lissauer of the Berkshire Eagle and Ella Adams of the State House N[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Jennifer Smith
Guests: Talia Lissauer of The Berkshire Eagle; Ella Adams of the State House News Service








WITH THE DUST settled on Election Day, Democrats kept a hold on almost all their levers of power in the Bay State, and the congressional delegation is heading toward several powerful leadership positions. And there was plenty of controversial local policy voters weighed in on.  
This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporter Jennifer Smith talked with Talia Lissauer of The Berkshire Eagle and Ella Adams of the State House News Service about election week, starting with the late-breaking result on a measure to relax single-family zoning.  
Most of the state’s regional centers voted in favor of Question 7, which would have lowered square footage requirements to build single-family homes, though it applied only to areas with sewer systems and therefore would have excluded much of the state. Lissauer noted that many small Berkshire County towns voted against the question, which ultimately would not have affected them. 
“We really need more housing over here,” she said, and there are local efforts to increase the housing stock. As for the urban-focused ballot measure, “a lot of people said that this really was a good start, but there just wasn’t much of a cost-benefit here that would make sense. I was not expecting it to be as close as it was, especially out here, because I was thinking it was going to be a ‘no.’” 
The far western parts of Massachusetts featured few competitive races. Even with nine ballot questions, voters and activists told Lissauer that they would have liked a busier ballot with fiercer competition to represent the region. 
Much of the action down-ballot was on the South Coast, with a number of Democratic flips of Republican seats and one long-held blue seat going red. 
“I think, at the statewide level, everyone expected the blue to remain,” said Adams. But in some more purple districts in southeastern Massachusetts, there were murmurs from both parties that “there are certain races that they’re keeping an eye on, that maybe are closer than they anticipated them to be or, as the days went on, that this might actually end up flipping.” 
One race is still in limbo, with a Democrat up by fewer than 100 votes in the Republican-held Second Plymouth House District.  
On the episode, Smith, Lissauer, and Adams dig into the slew of ballot questions (1:00), the largely foregone conclusions on congressional races and statewide offices (17:30), and the few flips of the cycle in state legislative races (24:30).

name: Mississippi Today
title: Turns out, Mississippi voters were paying attention in the Colom, Hyde-Smith Senate race
description: Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
For closing in on a decade, all a Mississippi Republican candidate needed was an endorsement from Donald Trump and to run ’round parroting the red-meat social phobias he peddled.
No need to propose any real policy. 
No need to push back against anything Trump did or didn’t do –  even if it hurt Mississippi – or anything he said, no matter how awful. 
Heck, no need to really campaign very hard. A blessing from Trump and pledge to blindly follow him was a Willy Wonka golden ticket for a Mississippi Republican politician.
Until it wasn’t.
On Tuesday, Nov. 3, the law of political gravity reasserted itself in Mississippi, for Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
As final votes trickle in, she’s still trailing Democratic challenger Scott Colom, and her defeat looks likely, although, in true Trump fashion, Mississippi GOP leadership has vowed to “fight like hell” as final vote counting is done, whatever that means. Hyde-Smith herself, as she is wont to do, has gone to ground, not been seen in person since election night.
Win or lose, Mississippi voters sent Hyde-Smith and state Republican leaders some messages:
Turns out you can’t just go along without a peep with tariffs, trade wars, shooting wars and big beautiful bills that hammer Mississippians in their pocketbooks and take away access to health care.
Turns out you can’t hide from constituents and back-home media, going for years without holding town halls, granting only the rare, curated interview with friendly media and making a few social media posts. An occasional breakfast at Mama Hamil’s with local Republican leaders and politicians is not constituent outreach.
Turns out saying Mississippians have “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about the exorbitant price of beef you helped bring about is not good messaging. (See also, Marie Antoinette.)
Turns out heavy-handed purges of voter rolls expected to thwart the other side can come back and bite Republicans in the butt.
Turns out threats of Trump-led redistricting, a thinly veiled attempt to suppress Democratic voters, can drive turnout of the very voters you plan to suppress. (Note to state Legislature: RAFO, redistrict and find out. You really sure you want to make districts a little more competitive right now in an attempt to gerrymander the maps overall for Republicans? See also, Texas.)
Turns out complacency, and abandoning the principles your party once espoused about government spending, national debt and free markets, will eventually turn off some of your Republican base, even in Mississippi. 
Turns out a last-minute Trump rally, held in an area you already have sewn up, doesn’t do much good. It might even drive turnout for your opponent.
Turns out you might have to actually campaign, even if you’re a Republican incumbent, to get reelected in Mississippi. (See also, Thad Cochran, 2014.)
And it turns out, you might have to actually do your job in Congress, particularly the part about being a check on executive power and corruption.
It appears it will take a few more days, and counting a few more votes to determine whether the big blue national wave also engulfed Mississippi. But it certainly lapped at its shores at a minimum.
Turns out, Mississippi voters have been paying attention.

name: Nevada Current
title: Lombardo, Wolfson, McMahill likely to be grilled in Ponder lawsuit, says lawyer
description: The attorney who filed a federal lawsuit on behalf of a woman who alleges she was repeatedly sexually assaulted by Hope for Prisoners’ founder Jon Ponder while in the state’s custody says he intends to depose Nevada’s top law enforcement officials to learn what they knew about Ponder and when. “We certainly intend to depose […]
text:
Jon Ponder, Hope for Prisoners founder, at a court hearing in early October, 2026. (Photo: Dana Gentry/Nevada Current)The attorney who filed a federal lawsuit on behalf of a woman who alleges she was repeatedly sexually assaulted by Hope for Prisoners’ founder Jon Ponder while in the state’s custody says he intends to depose Nevada’s top law enforcement officials to learn what they knew about Ponder and when.
“We certainly intend to depose all board members and any public officials who had knowledge of the systematic sexual abuse that was allowed to continue within Nevada Dept. of Corrections by Mr. Ponder and Hope for Prisoners,” attorney James Beckstrom said via email when asked if he expects to depose District Attorney Steve Wolfson and Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill, who were board members in 2020, and Gov. Joe Lombardo, who was sheriff at the time. 
The Current was first to report that the Hope for Prisoners board of directors was advised by its attorney in the summer of 2020 to terminate Ponder following an investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct.  
The board ignored the recommendation after President Donald Trump’s surprise pardon of Ponder at the 2020 Republican National Convention, according to a letter to the board from member Kristina Wildeveld, who resigned when the board took no action. 
Latin Chamber of Commerce President Peter Guzman introducing Gov. Joe Lombardo at an election watch party in Clark County Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo: Dana Gentry)
Other members of Hope for Prisoner’s board in 2020 included former Gov. Robert List, Latin Chamber of Commerce president Peter Guzman, who introduced Lombardo at his election night gathering Tuesday, and former Metro Asst. Sheriff Todd Fasulo, who served as chairman of the board.  
The Current reached out to the former board members and Lombardo, but did not hear back. 
Beckstrom represents a former Nevada inmate who is identified as RS in a federal civil rights lawsuit filed Oct. 29. She alleges that Ponder used his influential relationships to gain access to her and others, and coerced her into engaging in sexual acts by promising contact with her children. 
“There is nothing I wouldn’t do to see my children,” RS later said, according to the lawsuit. 
RS asserts she was directed by Ponder to perform oral sex in his office, that he arranged chairs at the Jean prison “church” service so he could touch her out of the view of the camera, and that he took her inside a storage closet at the prison to kiss her. 
The suit alleges Ponder violated RS’ constitutional right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment, including sexual abuse by those with authority over her. 
There is no cap on monetary judgments against the state for civil rights claims. 
RS is also one of seven alleged victims in a 25-count grand jury indictment handed down in September against Ponder. The charges include four counts of sexual assault that each carry a potential life sentence. Other charges include kidnapping and unauthorized contact with inmates. 
Ponder has been released from the Clark County Detention Center on $400,000 cash bail, which was reduced from $1 million in October by Judge Ron Israel. 
His attorney, Robert Draskovich, has filed a motion to withdraw from the case, noting Ponder’s case originated in Justice Court but was transferred to District Court following the indictment, and Ponder is no longer able to retain him. 
‘A prolific sexual predator’
The criminal allegations in the indictment against Ponder, a three-time convicted bank robber and domestic abuser, span 11 years — from 2015 through this year. 
“The stark reality is that Jon Ponder is a prolific sexual predator,” prosecutor Michelle Fleck said at the October hearing to lower Ponder’s bail.
Metro, under Lombardo’s watch, forged a community partnership with Hope for Prisoners and hosted its monthly graduations at LVMPD headquarters, as well as an appearance by Trump. 
As governor, Lombardo has supported additional state funding for the organization, which also receives federal funds. 
In 2020, Metro denied the Current’s request under the Nevada Open Records Act for Wildeveld’s letter, which was sent to McMahill at his Metro email address. Wolfson, the D.A., denied the same request for the letter, which was sent to his county email.  
Metro and the D.A.’s office claimed the letter was sent to the officials in their personal, not official capacities, and therefore not subject to the Open Records Act. 
In 2022, the Current asked Lombardo to look into the department’s denial. He later said he was unable to release Wildeveld’s correspondence.
Lombardo has remained silent when asked if Metro conducted its own investigation of Ponder in 2020. When the allegations resurfaced in a 2024 lawsuit, Lombardo, who had become governor, again would not respond.
NDOC recently denied the Current’s request for communication between the governor’s office and the department regarding Ponder, asserting the records may be used as evidence in the criminal case and could “undermine the constitutional rights of a defendant to a fair trial.”
Other board members, citing confidentiality requirements, have refused to comment in the last six years, but will likely be required to comply with a subpoena for deposition, says attorney Lisa Rasmussen, who has sued the state over inmates’ civil rights violations. 
“Whatever was board confidential business is so out there in the media now that invoking confidentiality is just not going to work,” she said.
In addition to Ponder and HFP, the federal suit names two prison officials, Jennifer Nash and William Reubart. 
“You have to sue them individually under the theory that they’re acting under the color of their authority,” says Rasmussen. “You can add the state, but it’s not necessary.”
Attorney General Aaron Ford, who defeated Lombardo in the race for governor last week, will likely be required to file an initial response to the lawsuit on behalf of NDOC, which his office represents. 
The bulk of defending NDOC will eventually fall to Attorney General-Elect Nicole Cannizzaro, a former prosecutor under Wolfson.
Ford has called Ponder’s alleged crimes “appalling, and I’m praying for the victims to receive the full measure of justice.”
He said it’s “crucial for more information to come to light, not just about what Ponder was doing, but about who knew about it and failed to stop it. There are allegations that Wolfson and Lombardo may have known about it, but that’s for an investigation to uncover.”
The suit alleges Ponder was permitted to bypass security restrictions at Nevada prisons.
NDOC spokeswoman Teri Vance said Ponder had limited access “equivalent to that of other NDOC hired contract employees,” and added NDOC “maintains strict policies and procedures governing visitors to its facilities. Protocols are in place to ensure compliance with these requirements and to review adherence to applicable policies and procedures.”
Vance did not address the allegations that prison officials Reubart and Nash were aware of Ponder’s alleged acts, but did not report it, as required under the the Prison Rape Elimination Act.
When Jean Conservation Camp officers complained about Ponder’s behavior, Reubart and Nash overrode their concerns and told them to stop treating Ponder like an inmate, the suit alleges.
Reports of sexual assault or harassment by a staff member against an inmate in Nevada prisons average about 27 a year. In the last five years the Nevada Office of Inspector General investigated 136 reports and substantiated 14 cases. 
The lawsuit says emails likely exist detailing the concerns raised by officers, and the case should be easy to substantiate, says Rasmussen. 
“I think there’s an awful lot of evidence against Jon Ponder,” she said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: GM’s former factories are attracting data center developers as redevelopment continues
description: General Motors’ historic 2009 bankruptcy was so massive that it’s taken 15 years for a real estate trust to clean up and sell the hundreds of buildings and thousands of acres of land across 14 states that GM left behind.  And the work isn’t done yet.  Bruce Rasher is Racer Trust’s redevelopment manager. Rasher, who […]
text:
Former GM Lansing Plant 6 property. It's among properties being marketed by  Revitalizing Auto Communities Environmental Response, or RACER, for industrial uses including for data centers. (RACER photo)General Motors’ historic 2009 bankruptcy was so massive that it’s taken 15 years for a real estate trust to clean up and sell the hundreds of buildings and thousands of acres of land across 14 states that GM left behind. 
And the work isn’t done yet. 
Bruce Rasher is Racer Trust’s redevelopment manager. Rasher, who has led the property sales effort since the trust was established by the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in 2011, said the remaining properties should be sold within the next three years. 
RACER stands for Revitalizing Auto Communities Environmental Response. At its inception, RACER was one of the largest holders of industrial property in the United States. 
I asked Rasher if he thought it would take so long to close this chapter in what was the biggest industrial bankruptcy in U.S. history, an event that shook the economies of Michigan and much of the manufacturing-dependent Midwest. 
“I’ve been so focused on the mission I really didn’t think about it,” said Rasher, a former mayor of Marshall. “Some properties take a long time before they sell.” 
GM’s bankruptcy reorganization was highly controversial because it was financed by a nearly $50 billion taxpayer bailout through the federal Troubled Asset Recovery Program. TARP also saved a dying Chrysler, which filed for bankruptcy a month before GM. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bankruptcy split the automaker into two companies: “new” GM, which continued as an ongoing concern, and “old” GM, which consisted of unwanted property transferred to RACER. 
A Gallup poll at the time found 51% of Americans opposed the auto bailouts. GM was derisively called “Government Motors” for years. 
Mitt Romney, a former U.S. Senator from Utah and a Michigan native, famously wrote in the New York Times in 2008 that the federal government had no business bailing out GM and Chrysler. 
But without federal aid, GM and Chrysler might have failed, wiping out more than a million U.S. jobs, according to a forecast by the Center of Automotive Research in Ann Arbor. 
Racer Trust was allocated $500 million from TARP for the massive environmental cleanup required before many of GM’s former factories and land could be sold. 
The trust is responsible for monitoring, groundwater treatment and environmental stewardship of some of the more heavily contaminated properties for 100 years, Rasher said. 
Another $250 million was granted for other costs of selling the properties. Proceeds from the sales go to offset about $100 million in RACER costs that TARP didn’t cover, Rasher said. RACER doesn’t disclose sale prices of its properties. 
The former Buick City complex in Flint now contains the Flint Commerce Center Building at right and Lear Corporation at left. (RACER photo)The former Buick City complex in Flint now contains the Flint Commerce Center Building at right and Lear Corporation at left. (RACER photo)M1 Concourse racetrack in Pontiac. (RACER photo)M1 Concourse racetrack in Pontiac. (RACER photo)
The trust’s work hasn’t undone all the economic carnage inflicted by GM’s bankruptcy on struggling communities like Flint, Saginaw and Pontiac that were GM company towns for decades. 
GM cut 20,000 jobs, shuttered 14 assembly and parts plants and terminated the franchises of 2,000 dealerships in its bankruptcy reorganization, according to the MotorCities National Heritage Area.  
But a recent economic impact study commissioned by Racer found that tens of thousands of new jobs and billions of dollars in business investment have been generated at the former GM facilities. 
Nearly 82,000 permanent direct and indirect jobs with annual payrolls of $7.6 billion have been created at the former GM sites, an annual average of $92,700 per job.  
The new business investment has generated $63.6 billion in overall economic impact across the 14 states where GM had operations. 
 All the former GM’s 166 buildings—mostly factories, warehouses and offices—and 75% of the nearly 7,000 acres of vacant land have been sold, Rasher said. 
The buyers represent a mix of industries, creating a much-needed economic diversification in communities that were overly dependent on manufacturing. 
United Wholesale Mortgage employs 4,300 people at GM’s former sprawling Centerpoint engineering campus in Pontiac, the most of any sites sold by Racer Trust, according to the study. 
United Wholesale Mortgage in Pontiac. (RACER photo)
Most of the more than two dozen remaining properties are being marketed by Racer as potential sites for data centers, warehouses, and solar and battery storage facilities. Among them are former assembly and parts plant locations in Lansing, Saginaw and the Flint area. 
Rasher said he gets as many as 10 feelers a week from developers inquiring about those properties for possible data centers. 
“It’s like a gold rush right now,” Rasher told me when I spoke with him on Election Day. 
That could change with Democrats taking control of the U.S. House and Senate, as well as the Michigan Legislature and governor’s office in the blue tsunami. 
Strong opposition by voters to data centers needed to power artificial intelligence helped Democrats across the country defeat Republicans in last week’s election. 
But if the Democrats can work to restore economic policy certainty that businesses crave, the way could be cleared to sell the remaining properties RACER holds. 
“I truly believe that, based on inquiries from developers, uncertainty about the business climate, high interest rates and tariffs are causing them to hold off,” he said. 
Rasher said the sale of GM’s former facilities was a team effort involving federal state and local governments and their economic development arms. 
“I think this is a model for helping communities hurt by severe economic circumstances,” he said.

name: California
title: Olympics transit overhaul needs to support working Angelenos, not just tourists
description: The influx of infrastructure to prepare for the 2028 Olympics shouldn't just allow more people to reach L.A. It should give the city's essential workers reliable, safe transportation.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Shanice Joseph
Shanice Joseph is a Los Angeles-based writer and Watts native whose work explores community, identity and the experiences of working-class Angelenos.


On a day off from work this summer, I took the Metro D Line (which will always be the “purple” line to me) to L.A.’s newest rail station, Wilshire/Fairfax. I wanted to see the La Brea Tar Pits before the museum closed to undergo a $240 million upgrade in preparation for the 2028 Olympics. 
I love the idea that the La Brea Tar Pits and the rest of museum row is now a train ride away for little kids in Compton and Watts, where I grew up. But as I walked through the station and the museum that day, I wondered, Can I be excited while also questioning who we are building all of this for? 
I’ve spent my adult life working in the essential systems that keep L.A. moving. That includes cleaning airplanes overnight at Los Angeles International Airport and working a public safety job that has me answering strangers’ calls as they navigate emergencies.
Like so many Angelenos who do this important work, each day I am forced to ask the question: How am I going to get to work safely?
My commute takes me from Watts to the San Fernando Valley, where I work five unpredictable shifts each week, often during hours when safe public transportation simply does not exist. Routinely I navigate pitch-black darkness, isolated transit terminals and deserted freeways.
If I attempt to utilize the Metro system to get to work, I endure a 1.3-mile walk from my home to the bus stop. The streets of South L.A. are currently plagued by rampant copper wire theft, leaving entire arterial blocks of Main Street, Figueroa Street and Avalon Boulevard in absolute darkness. Walking these unlit corridors means navigating a landscape stripped of basic safety infrastructure.
Even on the transit system, I cannot let my guard down. On multiple occasions, I’ve opted to take the bus or train if it’s running (because Metro Rail does not operate on a 24-hour schedule) only to be met with a system that is dangerous, volatile and deeply unreliable. I have endured explicit, violent threats on and off the bus. I have sat on delayed trains watching the clock tick down, knowing I would be late or forced to miss work entirely.
Not only is that a strike against my own career stability — it is also a threat to public safety because of the nature of my work.
A few years ago, I finally purchased a car, hoping that would help. But driving comes with its own set of issues. I paid upward of $200 monthly for the privilege of parking near my workplace. Then there were the countless dollars I poured into the gas tank.
More terrifying than the financial drain was the physical peril of driving the Los Angeles freeway system at irregular hours. There I witnessed the chaotic breakdown of societal order. 
More than once, I swerved to avoid unhoused individuals running blindly across the freeway. One day, someone threw a brick off an overpass onto my car. Later, at a red light, the driver behind me accelerated into my bumper because she panicked over a bee. My Toyota Camry was totaled.
Owning a car didn’t solve my transportation insecurity. It simply changed what I was vulnerable to.
Just recently at a bus stop, a man carrying a pole approached and threatened me. While I made it out physically unharmed, I was shaken by the encounter and didn’t return to work for several days. That changed the questions I asked about transportation. As did my visit to the La Brea Tar Pits. 
While I might enjoy taking the train during regular business hours, if an emergency required me or another essential worker to clock in or out of work at 3 a.m., we couldn’t trust L.A. transportation to get us there.
I often think about L.A. as a living body. The Department of Water and Power is its heart, pumping water and electricity through millions of homes and businesses. Public safety is the immune system that prevents or helps heal sickness or injury. City Hall is the brain. And our streets, buses, rail lines and freeways form the circulatory system, carrying people where they need to go.
Each system depends on another. None functions without workers.
I hope we continue celebrating new stations and new rail lines as our city readies for the 2028 Olympics. But I also hope this influx of infrastructure doesn’t just allow more people to reach Los Angeles. I hope it gives the workers the city relies on the most better access to reliable and safe transportation to get us where we are needed.
This commentary was adapted from an essay produced for Zócalo Public Square.

name: California
title: CalMatters sues Shasta County over its refusal to disclose federal subpoena related to election ballots
description: Shasta County has refused to release a subpoena it allegedly received regarding June 2026 election results. CalMatters is suing to obtain a copy of the document.
text:
In summary
Shasta County has refused to release a subpoena it allegedly received regarding June 2026 election results. CalMatters is suing to obtain a copy of the document.


CalMatters and Shasta Scout are suing Shasta County over its refusal to comply with a public records request to release a federal subpoena served after the county’s outgoing elections chief questioned the integrity of the 2026 primary election.Attorneys for the First Amendment Coalition, representing both news organizations, filed suit Friday in Shasta County Superior Court.
As of Sunday, multiple Shasta County representatives did not reply to voice messages and emails for comment.“Transparency should be the default setting for every public official,” CalMatters managing editor John D’Anna said. “Citizens shouldn’t have to file suit to get their government to obey the law.
The suit argues that the public has a compelling interest to know “whether any such (federal) investigation is motivated by well-grounded allegations of wrongdoing” or whether the probe is based on no credible evidence and instead intended to “sow unwarranted doubts about elections.”
After the June election, Shasta County Registrar Clint Curtis drew the attention of the Trump administration by claiming ballots looked, felt and smelled funny, CalMatters and Shasta Scout reported. Curtis was running for reelection and was defeated by Joanna Francescut, a former Shasta County elections official.
In August he said he had put a padlock on the door where he stored the ballots, then threw away the key in an effort to preserve them as evidence. 
In September Curtis told several media organizations he received a federal grand jury subpoena related to the ballots, and that same month FBI agents arrived to inspect the room, Curtis said.
“I just showed them what we had,” Curtis told CalMatters in September. “The FBI never says anything to you, by the way … it’s information in and nothing out.”
CalMatters and Shasta Scout sought copies of the subpoena, which should detail what the grand jury is investigating. But the county rejected the news organizations’ California Public Records Act request, saying the subpoena is “shielded from disclosure” under federal law.
The lawsuit argues that the law only protects federal courts from sealing its own records, and “does not prevent the County … from disclosing the subpoena.” The county is therefore violating the state’s public records act by unlawfully withholding the subpoena, according to the lawsuit.
“Clint Curtis has embroiled Shasta County’s elections office in turmoil, conspiracy, and allegations of misconduct,” Shasta Scout managing editor Annelise Pierce said. “The people have a right to know what a federal grand jury seeks from our top election official.”
The lawsuit also noted that eight other counties, including Fresno, Imperial, Los Angeles Orange and San Bernardino, disclosed copies of federal grand jury subpoenas issued to their election officials. Those subpoenas are related to a wider effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to find evidence of noncitizens illegally voting in the runup to the midterm election.
“Shasta Scout and CalMatters have closely reported on the ongoing controversies at the county’s elections office,” said David Loy, the First Amendment Coalition’s legal director, in a statement.
“The county must disclose the subpoena so the people can see for themselves whether the grand jury investigation has any valid basis or is improperly contributing to unwarranted distrust in the integrity of elections,” Loy added.

name: California
title: After Silicon Valley spending spree, more moderate Democrats are heading to the Capitol
description: New tech-backed super PACs spent tens of millions of dollars boosting some Democrats over their more progressive opponents. Almost all of their favored candidates won their contests, despite voters’ broad distrust of AI and billionaires.
text:
In summary
New tech-backed super PACs spent tens of millions of dollars boosting some Democrats over their more progressive opponents. Almost all of their favored candidates won their contests, despite voters’ broad distrust of AI and billionaires. 


In April, Ada Briceño felt confident she’d win one of the top two spots in the Assembly District 67 primary race to represent parts of Orange and L.A. counties. The labor leader and former hotel worker had endorsements from the California Democratic Party, the Working Families Party and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. Internal polling showed she was solidly ahead of her closest Democratic competitor, Cerritos city councilmember Mark Pulido. 
Then the money started flowing. 
Between April 9 and the June 2 primary, special interests groups spent $9.2 million attacking Briceño and raising Pulido’s profile, with the majority coming from Airbnb, Meta, Google and cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen. Pulido’s campaign spent another $600,000. Two regional cardrooms spent $500,000 to support Briceño, but her campaign couldn’t compete. 
“He made it past the primary because of the $10 million that was spent against me. Absolutely,” Briceño said of Pulido. Pulido’s campaign did not respond to a direct message on social media or an emailed request for comment.
Pulido is part of a wave of at least nine business-backed Democrats who will be going to the Capitol after Silicon Valley companies and investors spent at least $50 million on races, much of it to help moderates triumph over more progressive, union-backed opponents. The nation’s blue wave extended to kicking several Republican incumbents out of their statehouse seats. But the backlash against billionaire spending did not extend to legislative races in California, despite the efforts of candidates and critics of tech spending to point it out.
Tech funders make gains
Grow California, a new independent expenditure committee principally funded by Larsen and venture capitalist Tim Draper, and California Leads, funded mostly by Meta and Google, spent $24 million and $17 million respectively backing moderate Democrats over more left-leaning Democrats. The two groups accounted for 30% of all independent expenditures on legislative races during a record year for political spending. 
“We are proud to see so many Leads backed candidates joining the California Legislature next year, and we aren’t taking our foot off the gas for 2028,” said Nathan Click, a California Leads strategist, in an emailed statement. Click declined to be interviewed and would not comment on the defeat of several Republicans the group had backed, including incumbent Sen. Tony Strickland, Assemblymember Greg Wallis and Ed Musgrove, a candidate for state Senate representing San Diego. 
Mobilizing Economic Transformation Across (Meta) California, a super PAC funded by Meta explicitly to support tech-friendly candidates, spent $2.6 million on five Democratic campaigns for the state Legislature, including three new lawmakers: Assemblymembers-elect Andrae Gonzalez and Annalisa Perea and Sen.-elect Scott Sakakihara, a former executive for Palantir Technologies who received the bulk of that spending. 
While META California’s stated goal is to elect people who will be receptive to “AI innovation,” California Leads and Grow California stress they are not advocating for any issues in particular.
“We’re trying to make a minority of the ideologues on both sides,” said Shaudi Fulp, a political strategist for Grow California.
“Our whole goal is that legislators are not a rubber stamp for any special interest — whether it’s tech, whether it’s public sector labor, whether it’s business.”
Grow California spent extensively in L.A. County’s Senate District 26, the seat vacated by progressive Democratic Sen. María Elena Durazo: $4.6 million to support Democrat Sara Hernandez, an attorney with more moderate positions on healthcare and new development than her Democratic opponent, Sarah Rascón. 
“It was David and Goliath … My Goliath was these outside tech corporate interests.”Progressive Democratic state Senate candidate Sarah Rascón
Durazo endorsed Rascón, while Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas endorsed Hernandez.
Like Briceño’s, Rascón’s campaign was dwarfed by her opponent’s independent expenditure committees. IEs backed by the California Nurses Association and California Environmental Voters spent $450,000 supporting her; a fraction of Hernandez’s $9 million.
“It was David and Goliath,” Rascón said. “My Goliath was these outside tech corporate interests.”
The environmental advocate said she was inspired to run in part because Durazo was one of the few people willing to take on corporate interests in the Legislature. 
She pointed to Durazo’s Senate Bill 716, which increased the amount local governments could fine property owners who violate health and safety ordinances in non-residential structures. She introduced the bill after a weeklong warehouse fire broke out in June in the working-class L.A. neighborhood of Boyle Heights, sickening hundreds of nearby residents. A coalition of business groups, including the California Chamber of Commerce, opposed the breadth of buildings that could receive a maximum fine and argued the bill could create very large costs for property owners.  
“I think it’s such a shame to lose this seat in a progressive district that was one of the last soldiers holding the line for working people,” Rascón said. 
Hernandez did not respond to a social media direct message and emailed request for comment, but in September she posted an Instagram video explaining how outside money works and saying she was proud her campaign didn’t accept contributions from crypto, big tech, or AI companies, among others.
“If it’s not from me, I didn’t approve it. Don’t rope me in with outside money,” she captioned the video.
The new normal
To some, the specter of new spending by tech interests has been a persistent cause for concern. 
“When they started announcing within the last year that they were going to be spending this money at the state level, that really freaked us out,” said Catherine Bracy, the chief executive of TechEquity Collaborative, a Bay Area nonprofit that advocates for tech industry regulation. She said the new spending is an extension of Silicon Valley’s increasing presence in California lawmaking. 
This fall, her nonprofit’s political advocacy arm, TechEquity Action, began a $1 million statewide ad campaign directing voters to thetruthabouttechmoney.com, which highlighted where the dollars were going statewide. 
“We’ve seen what happens when, for example, Elon Musk spends $450 million on national elections. People do not like it,” Bracy said, referring to Tuesday’s results. 
Still, she acknowledges there is daylight between the different tech backed-entities.  
Larsen, for instance, told KQED in October that he wants the state to “stop all new building” of data centers until there are more regulations on artificial intelligence.
However, his group, Grow California, spent millions to oppose Jackie Elward, a progressive candidate for Marin and Sonoma counties’ Assembly District 12 who said she wanted moratoriums on “anything related to AI.” That district is one of two in which the Grow California-backed candidate, Eric Lucan, was trailing in election returns. 
Sonoma State political science professor David McCuan said in that race, the spending backfired: Early and uncoordinated spending by Grow California and committees backed by real estate and insurance agents increased Elward’s name recognition, and voters’ distaste for tech money followed Lucan, despite his disavowal of it.
McCuan said all the statehouse spending is a strategy by Big Tech to get ahead of a public that’s increasingly skeptical about data centers and artificial intelligence. He expects the spending to grow and become more coordinated in the coming years.  
“Big Tech is trying to preempt what should be a difficult regulatory environment,” he said. 
As for whether the tech industry’s deep pockets will influence new legislators’ votes, UC Riverside political science professor Shaun Bowler said they’ll be a big factor, but not the only one.
“(Lawmakers) don’t just need money, they need to do things that will support the district or help the district,” he said. “One billionaire isn’t the same as 100,000 votes.”

name: California
title: L.A. had its worst mosquito year this decade. El Niño could make it even worse
description: California is seeing the highest level of West Nile Virus activity in five years. Next year could be worse.
text:
When temperatures rise above 70 degrees, tiny West Nile viral particles begin to rapidly replicate in the gut of Culex mosquitoes, which then go hunting for their next “blood meal,” injecting virus-laden saliva into their prey when they feast.
This year, California’s warm, wet summer and fall produced the most West Nile activity in five years. As of Nov. 6, the virus has seriously sickened 528 people and killed 32, according to the California Department of Public Health.
Most people who are infected never feel sick, but about 1 in 5 may develop fever, headache and body aches. For the rare few — 1 in 150 — things get serious: The virus can hitch a ride to the brain, causing inflammation, neurological problems and even death. There is no cure, only supportive medical care.  
Southern California bore the brunt of infections, with Los Angeles County accounting for more than half of all reported human cases.
Residents there may soon notice a reprieve from mosquitoes, as cooler nights slow both mosquito breeding and growth of the virus. But experts still worry about what comes next, as climate change and extreme weather create conditions for mosquito-borne illness to surge, particularly along the coast and in floodplains.
“We’re all scared of next year,” said Paula Macedo, chair of the Mosquito and Vector Control Association of California. “With the amount of activity that we already saw this year and having the forecast of being an El Niño year, we are all bracing ourselves.” 
Whether next year brings relief or another surge depends on a tangle of birds, mosquitoes and weather that even experts struggle to predict.
Coastal California at risk of increased disease
In September, a warm storm swept past Southern California’s coastal and inland regions. The outer tendrils of Hurricane Marie poured an inch-and-a-half of rain across much of the westside of Los Angeles; downtown L.A. broke a rainfall record from 1965. In the following days, temperatures reached a high of 104 degrees, with overnight lows failing to dip below 77 degrees. 
Mosquitoes thrived in the following days. The rainfall flushed mosquito-killing treatments out of more than 3,000 miles of underground storm drains, according to the Greater Los Angeles County Vector Control District. 
“One of our biggest sources for Culex (mosquitoes) are our underground storm drains,” said Susanne Kluh, the district’s general manager. “It’s pretty much 72 degrees down there and humid all year round.”
Beachgoers stand in thick humidity as Hurricane Marie moves along, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026, on Huntington Beach, southern Calif. (AP Photo/Ethan Swope)
The district treats storm drains monthly, but with the larvicide washed out to sea, mosquito populations surged. At one point this summer, Kluh said more than 70% of mosquitoes trapped for sampling carried West Nile virus. That share has fallen in recent weeks to about one-third. 
Research suggests that climate change will increase risk of West Nile transmission along Southern California’s coast. A UC Berkeley-led study of Los Angeles-area data from 2006 to 2016 found a narrow tipping point: when average temperatures stayed below about 70 degrees, the virus was much less likely to turn up in mosquitoes, and when they rose above about 73, it became much more likely. Higher temperatures were also linked to more human infections. 
Coastal Los Angeles sits right at that edge. Summer averages hover in the high 60s to low 70s, and a few degrees of warming can push it over. That’s precisely what happened this year. 
“The longer that those temperatures are appropriate, the more opportunity there can be for human cases,” said Tristan Hallum, scientific director for San Gabriel Valley Mosquito and Vector Control District.
The virus moves in a complex loop driven by birds, mosquitoes and weather conditions. A female mosquito feeding on an infected bird can ingest the virus and subsequently infect other birds and sometimes humans. But birds that have been previously infected and survived become immune to West Nile, and their blood no longer carries virus for feasting mosquitoes to consume. 
That immunity tends to produce a natural three- to five-year cycle of West Nile activity, meaning Los Angeles, Orange County and other areas with many cases may get a reprieve next year, but other parts of the state remain vulnerable.
Virus flourishes during extreme weather
Federal forecasters give a very strong El Niño a greater than 90% chance this winter, raising the odds of heavy rain, particularly in Southern California. That worries public health and vector control officials: if floodwaters linger into spring as temperatures rise, mosquitoes could boom. 
That’s happened before. In 2023, heavy precipitation and flooding filled the long-dry Tulare Lake basin in the Central Valley, submerging vast stretches of agricultural land and reviving wetland habitats. The lake persisted for roughly a year, temporarily changing bird migration patterns and behavior; it also created prime habitat for the state’s native Culex mosquitoes.
That year health officials recorded 433 human cases of West Nile.
Drought matters too, and in a counterintuitive way. In 2014 and 2015, more than 1,600 people contracted West Nile during some of the driest years on record. 


Protect yourself from West Nile virus
Simple precautions can reduce your risk, according to the state public health officials and vector control experts.

Dump standing water in the yard at least once per week. Common culprits include pet dishes, plant saucers, children’s toys, birdbaths and debris.
Treat permanent water sources such as small ponds with larvicides. Some vector control districts supply mosquitofish.
Use repellent with EPA-registered active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin or oil of lemon eucalyptus.
Wear long-sleeved shirts and long pants if you’ll be spending time outside between dusk and dawn.
Report dead birds particularly ravens, crows and California Scrub-Jays to the health department at westnile.ca.gov/report.

Know the signs: Seek medical care for a severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or muscle weakness, especially if you’re over 60.


“One hypothesis is that the dry conditions bring birds and mosquitoes into closer contact due to the water being more limited across the landscape,” said Chris Barker, a professor at UC Davis who studies mosquito-borne illnesses and helps run the state’s West Nile surveillance program.
Because West Nile depends on a shifting mix of birds, mosquitoes and weather, cases won’t climb steadily year after year as climate warms, Barker said. Instead, extreme weather — both floods and drought — will create more years when conditions line up for outbreaks, making the virus harder to fight. 
“Climate change has the effect of tipping the scales against us just a little bit more,” he added.
Experts seek vaccine
There is no vaccine to protect against West Nile virus. Aaron Brault, a top West Nile expert and researcher with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said in an email that the U.S. needs one. 
“Despite West Nile virus being an important cause of illness in the United States for more than 25 years, our overall toolbox is limited,” Brault said. 
The CDC accepted only written questions and would not make Brault available for an interview.
Repellent and long sleeves help to decrease risk, but people frequently forgo these measures, Brault said, and those measures “have not adequately reduced the number of West Nile virus disease cases or deaths in the United States.” 
The CDC is exploring new ways to combat West Nile and encourage development of a vaccine, new treatments and better diagnostic tests, but it’s difficult work. West Nile outbreaks are unpredictable, making it tough to run the large clinical studies vaccines require. 
“Viruses do defy us sometimes, especially the people trying to predict them,” Barker said. 
Climate change supercharges that uncertainty and makes it harder for the people trying to keep mosquito numbers low.
Vector control faces new challenges, limited funding
Vector control districts across California spend millions each year trapping and killing mosquitoes. Residents fund the work locally through property taxes, typically $4 to $10 a year, according to the Mosquito and Vector Control Association of California. New pests and longer mosquito seasons challenge their work.
The mosquitoes most Southern California residents swatted and scratched at this year were likely not the West Nile bearing Culex mosquito, but an invasive species called Aedes aegypti. 
Native Culex mosquito species bite between dusk and dawn and prefer birds to humans, though they’re opportunistic biters. In contrast, the black-and-white striped Aedes hunts during the day, and its meal of choice is human blood. It doesn’t transmit West Nile Virus, but it can spread other infectious diseases such as dengue, zika, chikungunya and yellow fever. 
Aedes is also harder to control. It breeds in as little as a teaspoon of water, and its eggs can also survive months of drought, reviving whenever wet weather returns. Some vector control districts in California have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars releasing sterile male Aedes mosquitoes to reduce the overall number of mosquitoes, taking away from the ability to fight Culex mosquitoes. 
Disasters can add to the strain. The Eaton fire, which destroyed 9,000 structures in 2025, left behind 1,400 stagnant swimming pools.
“Budget over time has been stretched really thin by having to respond to these additional mosquitoes and additional causes,” Macedo, with the Mosquito and Vector Control Association of California, said.
State law limits how much local governments can raise fees for these services, though some vector control districts have gone to voters to ask for more money.
Still, Macedo said, no budget can cover every backyard. 
“We cannot enter every property. We cannot treat every mosquito source,” she said. “We need people to understand how they can prevent the situation.”
Supported by the California Health Care Foundation (CHCF), which works to ensure that people have access to the care they need, when they need it, at a price they can afford. Visit www.chcf.org to learn more.

name: Nevada Current
title: Commentary: Democrats swept Nevada. Now protect all workers.
description: Aaron Ford defeated Governor Joe Lombardo, leading a historic Democratic sweep of every statewide office. Nevadans have delivered a clear mandate to Democratic leadership. Now, voters expect them to deliver tangible improvements to daily life and lower the cost of living. A meaningful portion of that political capital ought to be invested directly in protect[...]
text:
Nevada Democrats have a clear path to provide statutory safeguards for its growing freelance workforce. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Aaron Ford defeated Governor Joe Lombardo, leading a historic Democratic sweep of every statewide office. Nevadans have delivered a clear mandate to Democratic leadership. Now, voters expect them to deliver tangible improvements to daily life and lower the cost of living. A meaningful portion of that political capital ought to be invested directly in protecting the Nevadans who work for themselves.
That constituency includes nearly 100,000 independent workers, and nearly three times that when you include solo business operators. Standard social safety net programs are traditionally delivered through traditional employment structures, leaving self-employed individuals entirely on their own. When a client refuses to pay or contract work dries up, freelancers have no unemployment benefits to fall back on, no cost-effective legal avenues, and no PTO.
The state’s immediate priority should be passing guaranteed payment protections. When a client fails to pay a freelancer, there is no corporate payroll department to contact and no wage enforcement law to lean on. Freelancers are forced to resend invoices, send polite follow-up emails, and weigh whether pursuing unpaid earnings is worth risking the business relationship and hard-earned savings if there is any. 
Nevada should mandate written contracts, set strict payment deadlines, prohibit retaliation against workers who claim unpaid fees, and establish a clear right to sue delinquent clients. Proven models already exist: California’s Freelance Worker Protection Act, Illinois’s Freelance Worker Protection Act, and New York’s Freelance Isn’t Free Act require client payments according to contractual terms or within 30 days, backed by formal legal recourse.
Full disclosure: I serve on the board of the Freelancers Union, which actively advocated for these laws.
Securing affordable health insurance remains one of the most significant hurdles for self-employed workers. Without an employer to subsidize monthly premiums, freelancers absorb the entire expense directly. Rates for plans purchased through Nevada’s state health insurance exchange are set to increase by an average of 17% for 2027. While federal tax credits offset costs for some buyers, rate hikes disproportionately impact independent workers paying out-of-pocket.
Nevada already possesses a starting foundation: under a federally approved waiver, the state marketplace provides targeted premium relief to eligible residents. Nevada should expand this model by offering dedicated, state-funded premium assistance specifically tailored to freelancers, ensuring their solo health coverage costs remain manageable. 
Another critical vulnerability occurs during sudden work stoppages. Unlike traditional employees who can claim unemployment benefits after a layoff, independent workers in Nevada do not pay into the state unemployment trust fund and are legally barred from collecting assistance. Periods without contract work must be financed entirely through personal savings.
To bridge this gap, Nevada should establish a dedicated unemployment coverage framework for self-employed individuals, providing temporary income support between client projects. Because no state currently operates such a framework, designing it presents novel administrative questions. 
Specifically, verifying when contract work has legitimately stopped poses a hurdle: a California Employment Development Department study concluded that without standardized employer wage reporting, validating active work status is uniquely complex. However, mandatory written contracts, coupled with 1099 reporting requirements, would give Nevada the exact verification tools needed to solve this problem.
Paid leave presents a similar financial hazard when a freelancer experiences illness or welcomes a child, income halts entirely. States like Washington, Oregon, Massachusetts, and several others allow self-employed workers to opt into state-managed paid family leave programs. 
Nevada lawmakers should explicitly resolve this in the statutory text by naming independent contractors and granting them automatic coverage for paid leave, sick days, and disability benefits without requiring complex opt-in procedures. As legislative proceedings begin in February, lawmakers must ensure that “all workers” truly includes the self-employed workers.
Sustaining these protections requires a reliable funding mechanism, which should be financed by the hiring businesses. Contracting companies should be legally mandated to make automatic contributions into portable benefit accounts for every freelancer they engage. These accounts would remain tied to the individual worker across client relationships, funding health coverage, paid sick time, and disability protections. 
Corporate opponents will undoubtedly argue that mandatory benefit contributions raise hiring costs, which is accurate. Businesses frequently utilize contract labor specifically to lower payroll overhead by omitting benefit contributions. That cost savings comes directly at the expense of freelancer security, and closing that loophole is precisely the goal. 
Critics may also push to make benefit contributions voluntary. Nevada has already considered this approach: a voluntary portable benefits bill sponsored by Republican Senator Lori Rogich passed the Senate in 2025 before expiring at the end of the session. That proposal left employer contributions optional and allowed businesses to deduct contribution costs directly from freelancer pay upon written consent. Similar voluntary frameworks exist in Louisiana and Utah.
The core flaw of voluntary systems is economic: low participation rates inevitably drive up individual costs, discouraging enrollment. California offers elective disability insurance to self-employed residents, yet in 2023, only 1,509 individuals enrolled out of a total self-employed workforce of over one million. This dismal turnout demonstrates why opt-in models consistently fail to deliver real protection.
The Nevada Legislature convenes on February 1, 2027, and the official bill drafting list is filling rapidly. At present, no requested measure specifically references independent workers, freelancers, or the self-employed in its title, leaving general paid leave as the sole active policy discussion.
Key legislative leaders are well-positioned to champion these reforms. Elaine Marzola, the incoming Assembly Speaker, previously chaired the Assembly Commerce and Labor Committee, while Julie Pazina led the Senate Commerce and Labor Committee in 2025. Both committees hold jurisdiction over labor legislation.
Assemblymember Selena La Rue Hatch has pledged to reintroduce paid family leave legislation in 2027, providing an ideal vehicle to include freelance protections. Ultimately, Governor Aaron Ford holds final authority to sign these measures into law.
With unified control, Nevada Democrats have a clear path forward. Models from California, Illinois, and New York offer proven solutions for wage protections, leaving Nevada to craft statutory safeguards for its growing freelance workforce. 
Passing these protections is entirely a matter of political will. Democrats can either build an economy that works for everyone who labors in Nevada, or prove that independent workers simply don’t count.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT makes fuel cells that power data centers. Here’s what to know
description: CT has yet to see much hyperscale data center development, but it is home to two leading manufacturers of fuel cells that power them.
text:
Connecticut is playing a quiet role in powering the global build-out of data centers through the development of fuel cell power stations.
The global fuel cell market is expected to grow to around $30 billion in revenue by 2030, more than ten times the $2.8 billion in revenue reported last year, according to research firm Rystad Energy. Demand is largely coming from data centers, which require the kind of continuous, on-site power generation fuel cells provide.
While Connecticut has yet to experience widespread development of hyperscale data centers, it is home to two of the world’s leading manufacturers of fuel cells: Fuel Cell Energy in Danbury and Torrington and HyAxiom — a division of Doosan Group — located in South Windsor.
But what are fuel cells, and why are they suddenly of interest to data center developers?
How do fuel cells work?
Simply put, fuel cells create energy from a chemical reaction involving air and another fuel, usually hydrogen. The reaction produces water, electricity and heat.
From there, the process works similarly to a battery, with negative (anode) and a positive (cathode) ends surrounding an electrolyte layer. Hydrogen is delivered to the anode while air is sent to the cathode. Electrons travel through a circuit between the two ends, creating electricity.
Unlike a battery, fuel cells can operate around-the-clock without the need to recharge.
Fuels cells powered by natural gas must first break down methane into hydrogen and carbon dioxide, but they emit a lower volume of CO2 than traditional power plants that burn fossil fuels. (Fossil fuel-burning power plants also emit other air pollutants, such as nitrogen oxides and sulfur.)
For this reason, proponents tout fuel cells as an effective way to cut emissions while still providing essential power to homes, businesses, factories and, increasingly, data centers.
“That’s the biggest value piece of where fuel cells bring a real differentiator,” said Eric Strayer, the global head of sales at Fuel Cell Energy. “You don’t have a loud turbine combusting and, you know, vibrating at your site. It’s a quiet, electrochemical conversion of that natural gas into electricity and heat.”
Some critics, however, point out that fuel cells do rely on fossil fuels and related infrastructure, including natural gas pipelines.
How are they used?
The basic technology behind fuel cells has been around since the mid-1800s, a short time after the invention of batteries. A century later, Pratt and Whitney made hydrogen-oxygen fuel cells that were used to power the Service Module on NASA’s Apollo space missions.
Since the 1970s, the development of fuel cell technology has been driven by rising energy prices and the push for cleaner forms of electricity, according to the Los Alamos National Laboratory. In addition to providing electrical power, fuel cells can be used to power vehicles and heavy machinery.
Honda and Toyota both began selling hydrogen-fuel cell vehicles in the early 2000s. However, that technology has not become more widely available due to the high cost and limited availability of hydrogen refueling stations.
There are also different fuel cell designs based on the type of electrolyte used to produce the chemical reaction.
Fuel Cell Energy, for example, manufactures a molten-carbonate system with a minimum output of 1,250 kilowatts. Doosan, the parent company of HyAxiom, produces a 440-kilowatt solid-oxide fuel cell system.
What does the future hold?
Power fuel cells can be built small enough to fit on top of a tractor-trailer, allowing them to be transported and located nearly anywhere.
That’s made them attractive option for energy developers seeking to build in dense, urban communities or on former brownfield sites. Bridgeport, for example, is home to four different fuel cell power stations. 
In addition, modular designs allow fuel cells to be scaled to provide much larger quantities of power — one of the principal demands of data centers. 
For example, developers behind proposed data center projects in Beacon Falls, Colchester and Cromwell have all pitched using fuel cells to power those facilities instead of relying off the local power grid. So far, none of those projects have received approvals from state or local officials.
Elsewhere, the rush to construct and power new data centers is having local economic effects. At its manufacturing facility in Torrington, Fuel Cell Energy is currently hiring a around 100 workers as part of a ramp-up in production to meet the demand from data center developers.
