name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: The nation saw a blue wave this election. Idaho saw a ripple.
description: In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind. The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term. Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both […]
text:
Voters cast their ballots in the general election on Nov. 3, 2026, at the Calvary Baptist Church in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)In Idaho, a Republican stronghold, the closest Democrat in this year’s election to securing a seat in Congress or statewide office was 11 points behind.
The candidate, Ellie Gilbreath, was trying to stop Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson’s bid for reelection to a 15th term.
Across the country last week, Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress, won governorships in most states and made headway in state legislatures. 
Amid national blue wave, Idaho Democrats gain six legislative seats — flipping competitive districts

But by the time the national blue wave — or tsunami, as some are calling it — hit Idaho, the tide had turned it into a ripple.
Idaho Democrats made modest gains. They swept full control of three legislative districts, gaining six more legislative seats, a shift that does little to chip away at Republicans’ supermajority control of the Legislature. 
And a closer look at election results shows that across the board, Democrats captured slightly more votes against Republican incumbents in statewide office and congress, who easily won reelection. But in all of those races, Democratic victory was still far off. No Democrat has won a statewide office in the state since 2002, and the last Democratic congressman in Idaho served in 2010.
If Democrats want to upset decades of Idaho political history by winning a top of the ticket race, they have a long way to go.
On average, Democrats gained 6 points of the vote share in federal and state races compared to the last time those offices were up for election. Still, Idaho Democrats this year were an average of 27 points behind Republicans, according to an analysis of election results by the Idaho Capital Sun. 
Boise State University political scientist Jaclyn Kettler wasn’t surprised that the blue wave didn’t carry Democrats through in Idaho.
“Idaho is a solidly Republican state. We don’t tend to see too many competitive races” in the general election for statewide races, she said in an interview. “ … It’s just solid enough Republican that it’s hard for even a blue wave in other areas of the country to have too much influence, especially for those statewide races.”
The Idaho Democratic Party also boasted another gain: Democrats got more of the vote in 67 legislative races than they did in 2024.
This year’s election results are unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers, which meets Nov. 24.
 Idaho Democratic Party leader says the state saw a blue wave. Republican leader says state fended it off.

Idaho Democratic Party Chair Lauren Necochea said the state did indeed see a blue wave.
In this file photo, then-Assistant House Minority Leader Rep. Lauren Necochea, D- Boise, at the State Capitol building on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
“We’re a red state, where it looks different,” she said, adding that many conservatives had moved into the state in recent years.
Democrats, she said, reached out to many voters and it shows. 
“We were able to be specific about what we wanted to do as we campaigned. And I think voters are getting tired of the culture war rhetoric that Republicans rely on, and they’re looking for more common sense solutions to their everyday challenges. That’s where we were. We met voters where they were,” Necochea said.
Idaho Republican Party chairwoman Dorothy Moon gives a speech on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Idaho Republican Party Chairwoman Dorothy Moon said she saw minimal signs of the blue wave in Idaho. Turnout in some Democratic leaning parts of the state, she said, was up. But Republicans in higher office were reelected, and voters rejected Proposition 1, a ballot initiative that would’ve repealed the state’s near-total abortion ban, by a nearly 56% no vote. 
“I think we had a great night,” Moon said. “We fended off the blue wave.”
And she noted that Republicans maintained control of a North Idaho legislative district, District 6 that includes Moscow. Democrats ran for every legislative seat there.
Necochea said high Republican turnout for Prop 1 was a problem for Democrats. 
“Our hypothesis is that conservative churches galvanized conservative voters to go to the polls to vote against Prop 1,” Necochea said. “And absent Prop 1, there would not have been as much money and there wouldn’t have been electioneering from the pulpit driving voters to the polls.”
State data on who turned out to vote this year isn’t available yet. Nearly 99% of voters who cast ballots voted on the ballot initiative, state data shows.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 How did Democrats perform in Idaho elections this year? 

Ellie Gilbreath (Photo courtesy of Ellie Gilbreath)
The closest a Democrat got in Idaho to unseating a Republican was in the race against incumbent Simpson, a longtime congressman. Gilbreath, a Democrat, was only about 11 points behind Simpson, with 40.3% of the vote compared to his 51.7%. She outperformed Simpson’s last two Democratic challengers. (Two independents and a libertarian took 8% of the vote in the race this year.)
Necochea said that Gilbreath ran a “fantastic campaign focused on issues that Idaho voters care about: Making life affordable, protecting public lands, personal liberties.”
And, she said, Gilbreath ran in a congressional district that didn’t see as many conservatives moving in than the state’s other congressional district. 
“I think we have in her district more longtime Idahoans who lean conservative perhaps but are looking for common sense and common ground, and are willing to consider voting for a Democrat,” Necochea said. 
Gilbreath couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. 
In the race for the state’s attorney general, Democrat Lori Hickman had the smallest gains compared to recent Democratic challengers for the office. She picked up about 2.8 more points than the last Democratic challenger in 2022, Tom Arkoosh. 
And even though GOP incumbent Raúl Labrador had a commanding lead, the gap between him and Hickman, of 19.7 points, was smaller than many other challenges. But Hickman still outperformed Democratic challengers in the race for that office for the past three election cycles, back to 2014, eight years before Labrador was elected.
In some races, Democrats this year didn’t even have the best performance that Democratic candidates have put up in runs for that office in recent years. 
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens speaks to a crowd at Boise’s third No Kings protest on Saturday, March 28, 2026. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun)
In the governor’s race, Democrat Terri Pickens had the biggest swing — gaining 12 points against incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little compared to 2022 Democratic challenger Stephen Heidt. But Pickens performance, with 32% of the vote, was still behind Democrat Paulette Jordan’s 2018 run against Little when the seat was open. Jordan got 38% of the vote. 
In the race for Idaho’s first congressional district, Democratic challenger Kaylee Peterson performed about 3 points better than in her last run against incumbent Republican Rep. Russ Fulcher in 2024, and more than 2 points better than her first run against him in 2022. But she faced the biggest point gap: She was 35.5 points behind Fulcher. Peterson clinching nearly 28.8% of the vote this year was still shy of Democrat Christina McNeil’s 2018 run against Fulcher, where she got 30.8% of the vote.
In Idaho’s U.S. Senate race this year, the Democrat, David Roth, dropped out after pressure from supporters of independent candidate Todd Achilles; leaders of Ada County Democrats also asked Roth to withdraw. Achilles, a former Democratic state legislator, only performed slightly better than the last Democrat to challenge Risch in 2020, Jordan, who had also ran for governor. 
Achilles received about 33.5% of the vote, compared to Jordan’s 33.2%. In 2014, Democratic U.S. Senate challenger Nels Mitchell got more of the vote, 34.7%. 
Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles speaks with supporters at an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, at Iconic Bistro and Bar in Garden City. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Two Democratic candidates whose campaigns raised $0 — secretary of state hopeful Shawn Keenan, and state treasurer challenger Kevin A. Jones — outperformed the last Democratic run for those offices. (Keenan ran against Republican Phil McGrane in 2022, when the office had no incumbent.) 
“It tells me that even when voters weren’t sure about the details of the person on the ballot,” Necochea said, “and let’s face it, we sometimes have a four-page ballot, and you don’t always research every single candidate. Most people don’t have time to do that, but they were using that Democratic label as a clue that that was someone who wasn’t part of the Republican grift machine, was someone who’s going to be looking out for regular Idahoans, and so they used that clue to vote for them.”
Moon, head of the Idaho Republican Party, doesn’t see the state becoming politically competitive anytime soon.
“We’re gonna work very hard to maintain our Republican base, increase the numbers, broaden our base as well, and make sure the issues that are important to everybody here in Idaho, that we keep Idaho Idaho and keep it conservative,” she said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Ayoub: Now comes the governing part
description: Last week’s national “blue wave” stayed mostly off on Nebraska’s reliably red shores. The changing tide, however, moved closer.  That was not only evident in Democrat Denise Powell’s victory in the 2nd Congressional District, the state’s “Blue Dot,” but also in the vote totals of three closely watched races: for governor, U.S. senator and 1st […]
text:
The final day of the 2024 session of the Nebraska Legislature. (Paul Hammel/Nebraska Examiner)Last week’s national “blue wave” stayed mostly off on Nebraska’s reliably red shores. The changing tide, however, moved closer. 
That was not only evident in Democrat Denise Powell’s victory in the 2nd Congressional District, the state’s “Blue Dot,” but also in the vote totals of three closely watched races: for governor, U.S. senator and 1st Congressional District representative. Each winner did so with less than 51% of the vote as of this writing. 
In the 2022 governor’s race, the winning percentage was 59; in the U.S. Senate races in 2024, one of which was a special election, the percentages were 53 and 62; and in the Ist District election in 2024 the percentage was 60.
Change is afoot elsewhere. The NINO (nonpartisan in name only) Nebraska Legislature will no longer sport 33 GOP senators, a political cudgel supermajority and enough to end a filibuster. GOP senators will now number 30 (that’s likely but unofficial at this time), enough votes if everyone toes the party line to change the body’s rules or override a veto, the latter perhaps moot because the state’s corner office has a very red door.
Draw your own conclusions about what last week’s results mean for Nebraska, but across the country, voters clearly had change on their minds. I’m not smart enough to know for sure what the exact takeaways were. My best guess is that what American voters (including some Nebraskans) told exit pollsters was what most reasonable Americans already knew. 
Governing poorly has consequences.
People are tired of high prices, an incomprehensible war and bewildering tariffs. They have had enough of Congress capitulating to the White House. While they want immigration problems solved, they are not here for the administration’s policy of cruelty and violence. They reject taking food and medical assistance from the working poor. They do not believe some of us are more equal than others, and so have grown weary of the undermining or erasing of policies that promote diversity. They want our history, all of it, to be taught exactly as it happened, not rewritten to assuage the uninformed and the iconoclastic. They want AI-peddling, ring-kissing, data-center-building tech bros to stay in their lane and out of voters’ backyards. Finally, and most emphatically, they want the corruption to end.
Winning elections is the easy part; governing is the hard part. The winds of change may be softer in Nebraska than the gales blowing in Texas, Kansas and Iowa. Still, how a new Nebraska Legislature reads the prevailing breeze will be key to its success as it faces a variety of issues, including the daunting task of making a state budget add up with current and forecasted deficits. 
How a new, blue Congress navigates the next two years with a lame-duck GOP president whose policies took a serious beating at the ballot box will require a steely but deft hand. As we said above, voters want affordability, an end to wars and tariffs, and a return to food programs and healthcare options. And maybe throw a little agency into their own lives.
Some have already counseled that any investigations should wait until affordability issues are addressed. Maybe, but part of Congress’ responsibility is oversight, which it derives from Article I in the Constitution, the necessary and proper clause. Plus, Congress can’t multitask? Really? One senator scoffed at the notion of having to choose, reminding us that they can indeed “walk and chew gum at the same time.”  
Finally, especially given the change that is afoot even here in Nebraska, I offer a modest proposal with apologies to Jonathan Swift. Every elected official has a team of advisers (or at least should), those who gather information, read the tea leaves and offer opinions on policy, legislation, public relations and the aforementioned wafting political winds. 
The wise among these leaders should always have a “devil’s advocate” among their most trusted inner circle, someone who says no to groupthink, who reminds decision-makers of the consequences — especially the unintended ones — of a new idea that might become law, who tells not just the other side of the story, but even promotes it. 
Here’s why: The headline is the blue wave, and, as in any election, we had winners and losers. But unlike football, a footrace or fiddling contest, where there are winners and losers, whoever prevails at the ballot box doesn’t get a trophy or a medal or even a record contract.
They get a job … the description of which includes representing the hopes and dreams not simply for those who voted for them, but also those who voted against them and even those who didn’t vote.

title: Oklahoma tribal town town sues Kalshi amid prediction market contract dispute
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A small Oklahoma tribe is suing one of the nation’s largest prediction market companies in an effort to invalidate a business agreement that they claim was not authorized by its governing committee. The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town and Samuel Marshall Jr., who claims he is the rightful chief of the tribe of about […]
text:
The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town's flag flies Oct. 27, 2026 at the Indian Flag Plaza outside the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A small Oklahoma tribe is suing one of the nation’s largest prediction market companies in an effort to invalidate a business agreement that they claim was not authorized by its governing committee.
The Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town and Samuel Marshall Jr., who claims he is the rightful chief of the tribe of about 400, sued Kalshi, its CEO Tarek Mansour, Wilson Yargee, and Michael Stopp to block a potentially lucrative agreement that allows the tribe to develop and operate a prediction market app, known as PokkeTrades. Prediction markets allow people to wager on pretty much everything from the outcome of sporting events to political races to the weather.
The lawsuit asks a tribal judge to declare that the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town is not bound to any agreement for PokkeTrades and that Yargee, who claims he’s the legitimate chief, and his administration have no authority to authorize it. 
The tribe and Marshall wrote in its lawsuit filed in Muscogee (Creek) Nation District Court that Yargee and Stopp did not have permission from the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town’s governing committee to enter into the agreement with Kalshi. 
The lawsuit alleges Marshall is the legitimate chief, not Yargee. Yargee was removed from office in 2021 and has been falsely representing himself as the chief of the tribal town based about 90 miles southeast of Oklahoma City in Wetumka, the lawsuit alleges.
Oklahoma tribal leadership fight puts Kalshi’s prediction markets at center of dispute

It also alleges that the tribe’s governing body never ratified the agreement Yargee entered into with Kalshi, making it invalid.
Yargee’s agreement with Kalshi has forced Marshall and town officials to spend time and money correcting the record, disrupted business relationships, “damaged its commercial goodwill” and created confusion about town leadership, according to the complaint. The tribe is seeking a temporary restraining order, compensation for damages and correction of Yargee’s claims, among other requests. 
The tribe’s lawsuit also draws on an 1825 law from the Creek Nation that prohibited “bad talk” against the chief. Marshall requests that the court recognize this as a “civil Bad Talk claim” against the defendants who misrepresented their roles, therefore injuring the Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town and chief. 
The Alabama Quassarte Tribal Town’s enrolled members hold dual citizenship at the Muscogee (Creek) Nation. The tribe was one of several tribal towns part of what was previously known as the Muscogee Nation Confederacy. 
Yargee though claims he is the rightful chief of the tribe. He previously told Oklahoma Voice that as chief, he had the right to enter into the agreement. 
Tribal election results were not immediately publicly available, but both Marshall and Yargee claim to have won reelection in 2025, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs lists both men as chief.
Kalshi, who promoted the gaming partnership with the tribe last month as one of its first partnerships with Native American tribes, stands by its agreement, said Jacki McGavick, a Kalshi spokesperson, on behalf of the company and Mansour.
She said the tribe’s governing council signed off on the agreement.
Prediction markets ‘undermine’ Oklahoma tribal gaming compacts, association says

Stopp, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation who serves as Yargee’s vice president of economic development, said in a statement on behalf of himself and Yargee that this is just the latest lawsuit filed by Marshall’s administration. 
Stopp said he and Yargee expect the court to dismiss the case as it has dismissed previous cases brought by Marshall’s administration. 
A previous lawsuit filed in this court between Marshall and Yargee over rightful leadership was dismissed over a lack of jurisdiction because both parties failed to waive their right to sovereign immunity, which protects recognized tribes from federal, state and tribal lawsuits without their explicit consent. Marshall has waived his and the town’s sovereign immunity for this lawsuit. 
“It would be helpful for a court competent jurisdiction to stop the Marshall faction from continuing to make these claims,” Stopp said. 
He said that if the court doesn’t immediately throw out the case, they will reevaluate their legal strategy which could include a waiver of sovereign immunity.

title: Commentary: Only ripples from the blue wave reached Oklahoma, but the GOP should acknowledge the erosion
description: Before the dust even had a chance to settle in last week’s elections, Republican House Speaker Kyle Hilbert proclaimed the results “demonstrate that Oklahomans continue to believe in the conservative principles, priorities and leadership that have helped move our state forward.” Republicans may have emerged maintaining control of all statewide and federal of[...]
text:
Voters fill out ballots for the midterm election at the Millwood Field House on Nov. 3, 2026, in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)Before the dust even had a chance to settle in last week’s elections, Republican House Speaker Kyle Hilbert proclaimed the results “demonstrate that Oklahomans continue to believe in the conservative principles, priorities and leadership that have helped move our state forward.”
Republicans may have emerged maintaining control of all statewide and federal offices and commanding supermajorities in the Legislature, but voters didn’t actually signal that they embrace the GOP’s “conservative principles, priorities and leadership.”
In fact, I think they did the opposite. If Republicans are too shortsighted to recognize the as-yet small speck on the horizon is actually a freight train of doom hurdling toward, then they’re going to be in big trouble over the next decade.
The 2026 elections should be construed as a warning shot across the bow for the GOP. A prudent leader would consider it a sign that it’s time for the party to take some time to rethink whether its  “priorities” and “conservative principles” actually align with what voters want and need.
Here’s why:

Five Republican state House incumbents lost to Democrats on election night. Typically Democrats don’t even win contests for seats in both chambers that the incumbent is vacating. For five incumbent Republicans to be unseated by Democrats is unusual and a red flag that the tide is beginning to shift.
The state’s most populous counties — Tulsa and Oklahoma — turned blue Tuesday night. Those counties also said “no thanks” to some of their current Republican state lawmakers. Oklahoma County residents actually elected a Democratic slate of candidates and booted their longtime Republican county assessor from office. A political expert once told me that shifts in voting patterns in Oklahomans living in urban and suburban areas are typically harbingers of broader political change in the state. When those areas change from blue to red or red to blue, the rest of the state slowly follows.  
Republicans almost lost control of two seats in the U.S. House. Democrat Jena Nelson fell only about 3,300 votes short of upsetting Republican U.S. Rep. Stephanie Bice in Oklahoma’s 5th Congressional District, which includes parts of Canadian, Oklahoma, Logan, Lincoln, Pottawatomie, and Seminole counties. For context, the contest drew over 264,500 voters. Bice barely won despite the GOP-controlled Legislature’s previous efforts to gerrymander the district to guarantee Republican victories. In the 1st Congressional District, Republican Mark Tedford managed to win by only about 10,700 votes in an area that represents Tulsa, Creek, Rogers and Wagoner counties.
Voters again squashed legislators’ state questions. For the third time in as many months, Oklahoma voters rejected the “conservative principles” that state lawmakers claimed that their supporters espoused. It turns out that Oklahomans don’t want Republicans to be able to put their fingers on the scale when it comes to judicial selections or want state officials to muck around with property taxes — the primary local revenue stream that schools, counties and municipalities rely on to keep the lights on. And interestingly, those “conservative principles” that legislators were convinced Oklahomans wanted didn’t just lose by a little. Voters destroyed them. The effort to rig the judicial selection process lost by 480,000 votes. A question that would have reduced how much property taxes could grow lost by over 91,000 votes. Lawmakers would be wise to keep that in mind when Republican Governor-elect Mike Mazzei starts putting pressure on them to eliminate property taxes for some Oklahomans, and the next time they’re tempted to put issues on the ballot. Voters are proving to be increasingly skeptical of legislative ballot measures.
Texas. Voters living in what has long been considered a Republican stronghold, elected a slate of Democrats to legislative, statewide, and even the U.S. Senate. It was part of a partisan shift that occurred across the country states that have long been red.  

In short, any prudent Republican should view last Tuesday as a sign that when the GOP plows ahead with these so-called “conservative principles” the loss of five legislative seats may likely be only the beginning.
Oklahomans are sick and tired of being among the worst in the nation for public education outcomes, healthcare, incarceration rates and pretty much everything else that impacts people’s quality of life. They’re sick of politically connected people getting special treatment. They’re sick of officials diverting public money to pay for private education while watching their local schools subsiding on scraps. They’re sick of lawmakers putting measures on the ballot in an attempt to change things voters have already put in the state Constitution. 
And they’re exhausted by the continuing increase in prices of everything from their insurance to a tank of gas to nearly everything on their grocery list.
They want our state and federal leaders to focus on what actually matters. They want them to espouse the now ancient Republican value of local government control, which means to stop screwing around with revenue streams that run the level of government we all see close.
They want smaller class sizes and better public schools.
They want this to be a state where college graduates want to remain five years after graduating. Right now, an increasing number are fleeing for greener pastures, which is not a good sign.
To do that will mean making financial investments, not cutting taxes.
Because it will cost money to keep hospitals open, fix our roads and bridges, retain quality teachers and cut class sizes. 
They’ll need to respect voters who voted to expand Medicaid. 
And they’ll have to prove that they listen to the voters that put them there instead of the lobbyists funding their campaigns or an out-of-touch future governor who casually spent almost $13 million of his own money on the election like it was nothing while most people are struggling in this economy. 
There is time to divert that freight train of doom, but to do that Republicans have to look a little bit deeper than the fact they again won all statewide offices Tuesday night. And they’ll have to move away from their hero-like worship of President Donald Trump, stop being his backup band the Trumpettes and think about what our state really needs.
If Republicans can’t do that, in two years, their legislative losses are going to be more than five seats. In four years, it could cost them even more: congressional or statewide offices (Remember: Bice initially ran for a congress in a district that a Democrat won in 2018.).
Oklahoma voters are tired of losing. They want to be winners just like the GOP candidates were last week.
And if things aren’t getting better in two or four years, they will have no choice but to blame those so-called Republican “conservative principles” and the officials who purport to espouse them.

title: Idaho Legislature’s budget committee meets in Moscow, Lewiston this week
description: Members of the Idaho Legislature’s joint budget committee are meeting in Moscow and Lewiston for three days this week as they gear up for the 2027 legislative session.  Although the Idaho Legislature is not in session, the Joint FInance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, normally conducts a spring and fall tour at locations around the state during […]
text:
The door to the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee room at the Idaho State Capitol building is pictured on Jan. 6, 2023. (File photo by Otto Kitsinger for the Idaho Capital Sun)Members of the Idaho Legislature’s joint budget committee are meeting in Moscow and Lewiston for three days this week as they gear up for the 2027 legislative session. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Although the Idaho Legislature is not in session, the Joint FInance-Appropriations Committee, or JFAC, normally conducts a spring and fall tour at locations around the state during the legislative off season.
JFAC is a powerful legislative committee made up of 10 members each from the Idaho House of Representatives and Idaho Senate. Each year, the committee is responsible for setting every budget for every state agency and department. 
Last year, JFAC and Gov. Brad Little enacted budget cuts for almost all state agencies and departments. Other than K-12 public schools, most state agency budgets were cut by 4% in the fiscal year 2026 budget and 5% in the fiscal year 2027 budget. 
JFAC will begin working on the new fiscal year 2028 budget in January.
As preparation for the work that will come during the regular legislative session, JFAC members will participate in budget briefings, audit updates and working tours to inspect state facilities during this week’s meetings.
Deep dives on the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare budget request, the wildfire season and fire suppression costs, a briefing on new state correctional facilities and tours of the Port of Lewiston, Lewis-Clark State College and University of Idaho are planned throughout the week.
“The Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee is pretty much working year round because government is a year-round process and funding government and making sure it is funded appropriately demands a lot of time from the committee,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chair of JFAC.
 Where is the Idaho Legislature’s budget committee meeting?




Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



This week’s meetings will not be livestreamed online, said Keith Bybee, the Idaho Legislative Services Office’s budget and policy analysis manager. That means the only option to follow the committee is to attend in person. 
JFAC’s first meeting of the week begins Tuesday at 3 p.m. Pacific Time Tuesday in the Idaho-Palouse Room at the Best Western University Inn, 1516 Pullman Road in Moscow (the full agenda and schedule is embedded at the bottom of this article).
Wednesday’s meeting begins at 8 a.m. Pacific Time inside the student union building on the University of Idaho’s Moscow campus.
JFAC will move to Lewiston on Thursday, starting at 8:30 a.m. Pacific Time at Independent School District No. 1 in Lewiston before moving on to the Idaho State Veterans Home, 821 21st Ave., in Lewiston. 
Grow said the working tours of state facilities, public schools, colleges and universities give legislative budget writers a chance to see first hand how government funding is put to use. 
“That gIves us opportunities to visit certain sites that are of interest in an effort to see how the appropriations have been utilized and to assure us that the money that was appropriated went for good and appropriate purposes in accordance with state law,” he said. 
 JFAC will have new members during 2027 Idaho legislative session

There will be changes coming to JFAC for the 2027 legislative session. Five of the 20 members of JFAC who served during the 2026 legislative session will not be returning in 2027, either because they retired, they lost their primary election in May or they lost in November’s general election. 
The JFAC members who will not return in 2027 include Sens. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle; Glenneda Zuiderveld, R-Twin Falls; Cody Galloway, R-Boise; Rep. Steven Miller, R-Fairfield and Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello. 
Grow said Republican legislative leaders will appoint new members to JFAC during the Idaho Legislature’s organizational session, which begins Dec. 3.
After that the 2027 regular session of the Idaho Legislature begins Jan. 11.

name: WyoFile
title: The first Wyoming Boys’ School trial starts today. Follow along with our coverage.
description:
The trial concerns the case of Blaise Chivers-King, one of six former boys’ school residents who accused school staff of physical and psychological abuse. Another former resident’s claims of improper isolation will go to trial at the end of the month.
The post The first Wyoming Boys’ School trial starts today. Follow along with our coverage. appeared first o[...]
text:
Do you have questions about this story? Or information to share? Reach out to Maya Shimizu Harris at maya@wyofile.com.
After more than two years of litigation, the first trial concerning alleged abuse at the Wyoming Boys’ School begins today. 
This trial concerns the case of Blaise Chivers-King, who is one of six former boys’ school residents who lodged complaints against the facility in 2024, accusing staff of physical and psychological abuse. The school, which detains delinquent boys ages 12 to 21, is a 38-acre residential facility near Worland that’s overseen by the Wyoming Department of Family Services. 
Chivers-King, who served two stints of roughly 11 months each at the Boys’ School between the ages of 15 and 17, alleged Wyoming Boys’ School staff violated his 14th Amendment rights by placing him in isolation, using excessive force and infringing on due process. U.S. District Judge Scott Skavdahl ruled in October that some, but not all of his claims, could go to trial.
The defendants, which include the Wyoming Boys’ School, the Wyoming Department of Family Services and individual boys’ school staff members, argued that “every instance of claimed ‘isolation’ served a legitimate purpose and was not excessive in relation to that purpose.” Staff who placed Chivers-King in isolation assert they should be protected by qualified immunity — a type of legal immunity that protects government officials from lawsuits under some circumstances.
Skavdahl disagreed, pointing to evidence that some uses of isolation “were, or became, simply punishment or unrelated to management of a safety threat.” He emphasized how staff placed Chivers-King “in isolation for predetermined amounts of time, which is at least arguably unrelated to the legitimate purpose of managing a child who is physically violent or attempting suicide.” That Chivers-King remained in isolation even after he changed his behavior, Skavdahl noted, could raise questions for a jury about its use for a legitimate purpose. 
Last month, Skavdahl denied the defendants’ request to bar the term “solitary confinement” during trial, though he said he would “listen carefully” to ensure the term isn’t used to “inflame the jury.” 
The defendants will also be required to bring physical examples of items related to former resident Blaise Chivers-King’s claims of excessive force and isolation, including a “spit mask,” mechanical restraints and riot gear, as well as a mattress and magnets used in the school’s detention rooms.
Skavdahl ruled Wednesday that some of the claims of improper isolation by another former resident, Dylan Tolar, can go to trial. While Tolar alleged four boys’ school staff members violated his 14th Amendment rights by putting him in isolation, the claims against just two of those staffers — Elsa Olson and John Schwalbe — will go to trial. Although Olson and Schwalbe never placed Tolar on detention status, which is the facility’s “most restrictive disciplinary status,” “whether conditions constitute impermissible isolation is based on facts, not a facility’s (or an expert’s) labels,” Skavdahl wrote in his order. 
The judge wrote that “a rational jury could conclude Olson and Schwalbe impermissibility placed Mr. Tolar in punitive isolation” because that isolation was similar to what’s described in other juvenile isolation cases: “a long stretch of time in which a child is not allowed out of his room and may be restricted in other ways as to entertainment, exercise, and the like.” 
Tolar’s trial is scheduled to start Nov. 30. 
I’ll be at the U.S. District Court of Wyoming in Casper this week keeping you up to date on what’s happening with the Chivers-King trial. You can follow my coverage here at WyoFile.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: The collapse of GOP voters for Blackburn in TN. Two years later, and 1M fewer votes.
description: The top Tennessee Republican received nearly 1 million fewer votes in 2026 than 2024, a turnout collapse that reverberated down-ballot, costing the GOP half a dozen state House seats and effectively neutralizing the party’s mid-cycle redistricting of the state’s U.S. House map. Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn garnered roughly 1.9 million votes in her landslide r[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, acknowledging supporters at her downtown Nashville victory party on Nov. 3, 2026, was elected to be Tennessee's first woman governor in Tuesday's election. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The top Tennessee Republican received nearly 1 million fewer votes in 2026 than 2024, a turnout collapse that reverberated down-ballot, costing the GOP half a dozen state House seats and effectively neutralizing the party’s mid-cycle redistricting of the state’s U.S. House map.
Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn garnered roughly 1.9 million votes in her landslide reelection victory for U.S. Senate in 2024, but two years later, the coalition powered by President Donald Trump that delivered her an impressive statewide win has almost disappeared. 
Blackburn received around 950k votes in the governor’s race, defeating her Democratic challenger by 2.5%, and in the process became the first Tennessee governor to win less than 50% of the vote since before World War II. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Kent Syler, a political science professor at Middle Tennessee State University, said Rutherford County was at the center of the GOP’s long night.
Blackburn, U.S. Sen. Bill Hagerty, and U.S. Rep. Scott DesJarlais, in his likely narrow defeat to Democrat Victoria Broderick, all lost Rutherford County. Democrats also flipped three state House seats in the county.
“It was a complete surprise,” Syler said.
Democrats in Tennessee didn’t receive more votes in any county in 2026 than in 2024. Instead, nearly a million Republican voters chose not to vote for Blackburn, primarily in Tennessee’s urban and suburban counties. 


Turnout for midterm elections is typically much lower than for presidential elections, particularly in the Trump era, because Trump drives rural Republican turnout at record levels. Trump and Blackburn won their 2024 elections, each garnering 64% and 63, respectively in Tennessee.
During Tuesday’s election, Blackburn received 45% of the vote, a 19% drop in two years.
Dawn Schluckebier, an advocacy director with the nonpartisan think tank ThinkTennessee, said the narrow margins of victory for Republicans were the biggest takeaway of the night. 
“This is something we haven’t experienced in Tennessee in a while,” Schluckebier said. “Overall competitiveness across the board.”
2026 looks a lot like 2018, except for Blackburn
Hagerty won his reelection to the U.S. Senate Tuesday with 55% of the vote, roughly by the same margin Blackburn won her first U.S. Senate election in 2018.
The 2018 midterm election is the closest comparison to 2026 because it featured the same president and an open governor’s race in Tennessee. But turnout in 2018 was slightly higher in total votes and percent of electorate than in 2026. 
In Tuesday’s selection, the difference between Blackburn’s narrow gubernatorial victory and Hagerty’s easy win comes down to David Hatley, an independent candidate. Hatley explicitly targeted Blackburn and the conservative vote by spending nearly $12 million of his own cash.
When combined, Blackburn and Hatley received about 1.15 million votes in the governor’s race, and Hagerty received 1.14 million. 
State Rep. John Ray Clemmons, a Nashville Democrat who chairs the party’s state House Democratic caucus, said Blackburn was uniquely unpopular. 
“Our polling consistently showed four unpopular things in Tennessee were Trump, Blackburn, toll lanes and (private school) vouchers,” Clemmons said.
Visual: The partisan lean of Tennessee’s proposed new U.S. House map

Blackburn, legislative leaders pushed gerrymander that nearly cost Republicans five U.S. House seats
After redrawing Tennessee’s U.S. House map in May, Republicans hoped to increase their advantage from 8-1 congressional seats to 9-0. But after Tuesday’s results, it looks like the party will still hold an 8-1 advantage. 
Broderick, the Democratic nominee in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District, leads DesJarlais, the Republican, by 285 votes, with roughly 700 provisional ballots still to be counted.
Erin Covey, the head of the Cook Political Report’s U.S. House ratings, said Broderick’s win would be “the reddest seat that Democrats flipped last night,” with Trump winning the district by 24% in 2024. Cook is a nonpartisan election-rating organization that analyzes federal and gubernatorial races.
District 4 was one of six seats redrawn in May, as state Republicans, with a push from Blackburn and Trump, tried to gerrymander the state’s congressional map to win every U.S. House seat. 
But to do so, Republicans had to shrink their margins in six seats, all of which Republicans won by 5% or less Tuesday.
On a smaller scale, state Republicans’ 2022 redistricting in Rutherford County, designed to increase their state House seats, likely led to the loss of three of the county’s five districts.
The county has been subtly shifting toward Democrats as the population has increased and it’s become a hub for workers who can’t afford to live in Nashville. In August, eight Democrats won seats on the Rutherford County Commission, a harbinger of November’s results. 
The state House Democratic caucus actively tried to flip seats in Clarksville, Knoxville and Memphis, but the wins in Rutherford came as a surprise. 
Syler said the Republican redistricting effort in 2022 could, in hindsight, be called a mini-dummymander, which refers to when a party goes too far to gerrymander seats so that, in wave elections, it loses districts it otherwise would have safely held under previous maps. 
For example, in Rutherford, a packing of Democratic votes probably leads the party to lose one seat, not three. 
“Republicans got greedy in Rutherford,” Syler said.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama voters approve four constitutional amendments by varying margins
description: Alabama voters approved four statewide amendments last Tuesday, though some had an easier time of passage than others.  Amendment 1 sets guidelines for lieutenant governor vacancies. Under the amendment, the state could hold an election for lieutenant governor if the office becomes vacant within the first two years following an election. Should the lieutenan[...]
text:
The Alabama State Capitol as seen on Nov. 24, 2025, in Montgomery, Alabama. During the 2026 midterm election, Alabama voters approved four statewide constitutional amendments. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama voters approved four statewide amendments last Tuesday, though some had an easier time of passage than others. 
 Amendment 1 
Amendment 1 sets guidelines for lieutenant governor vacancies. Under the amendment, the state could hold an election for lieutenant governor if the office becomes vacant within the first two years following an election.
Should the lieutenant governor’s seat become vacant more than 60 days before the 2028 election, an election for the office could be set. Prior to passage of the amendment, voters would not choose a new lieutenant governor until 2030. 
The measure also allows the Legislature to set the lieutenant governor’s salary by resolution and requires travel funds expended by legislators to be approved by officers elected by the House and Senate.
According to the Alabama Secretary of State’s Office, the amendment passed with 987,299 (65.4%) votes in unofficial returns.
Jerome Dees, Alabama policy director at Southern Poverty Law Center, said in an interview Thursday afternoon his concern with the amendment came from the salary piece of the amendment.
“I think that just kind of goes to sort of a broader concern amongst the sort of electorate about just accountability of the Legislature and potential for pettiness if any sort of grievances arise between that part of the executive branch and the legislature,” Dees said.
 Amendment 2 
Amendment 2, which allows for public county school boards to consolidate, passed with just 50.2% of the vote in unofficial returns. 
Under the measure, two or more county school boards of education can begin a merger process if all the boards agree. Should 25% of qualified voters in the counties object to the merger, it would be placed on the ballot. It could only go forward if a majority of voters in the affected counties approve it.
Alabama amendment would authorize county school board mergers

Allison King, government relations manager for the Alabama Education Association, said in an interview Thursday the organization has not heard of any school boards looking to consolidate.
“We’re not aware right now of any school systems, county systems that are planning to consolidate, and it’s a permissive option only with buy-in from school boards and constituents,” King said.
Dees said one area of concern for the amendment could be a lack of resources, including funding for all of the schools under the consolidated districts, particularly with the state CHOOSE Act, which extends income tax credits to families to pay for nonpublic education, including private school tuition.
“I think some of those fears are grounded in reality, particularly in light of the increased siphoning of funds that we will continue to see over the next couple of years as a result of the CHOOSE Act,” he said.
Transportation and childcare arrangements could also pose a problem if schools consolidate.
 Amendment 3 
Amendment 3 mandates public school boards in the state to require schools to have policies for daily recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance and for student-led prayer.
The amendment passed with 62.6% of the vote according to unofficial election data.
Alabama law has required schools to conduct the Pledge of Allegiance at the start of the day in K-12 schools since 1976, and federal law prevents schools from forcing students to recite the Pledge. Students are already allowed to conduct prayer on school grounds. Students could not be required to participate in prayer and could opt out.
King said teacher protections being in place were important for AEA when the bill was moving through the Legislature.
“When we were watching that piece of legislation, what’s permissible for the students is fine, but we want to protect our employees in making sure that they’re not at risk,” she said.
Alabama legislator proposes amendment on Pledge of Allegiance, school prayer

Dees said Amendment 3 is “dangerously close” to violating the First Amendment.
“If I am somebody who is not of a Christian faith, and my child is in a school where there is mandatory sort of prayer, what does that look like for my child?” Dees said. “Is my child allowed to pray in whatever faith tradition they may have, or if my family is of no faith tradition, is that prayer that’s now mandatory in school going to be in violation of my right to not have any particular faith? So I think we’re going to potentially see some real issues with that.”
Dees also said the amendment’s opt-out provision was likely “the Legislature’s effort to try and kind of circumvent any sort of First Amendment violations.
“What does it look like if I am a student and I am the only one who is opting out?” he said. “I think there’s going to be real discussion and debate over sort of what that sort of government interference and government sponsorship of one particular religion over another, even if you are allowing others to sort of opt out, you are now having a child removed from the sort of learning space so that you can engage in religious activity.” 
 Amendment 4 
The last statewide amendment, Amendment 4, requires school boards to broadcast or perform “The Star-Spangled Banner” once a week in public schools.
The amendment passed with 58.6% of the vote according to unofficial election results.
Dees, who worked on amendment language when the bill was moving through the Alabama Legislature, said the national anthem should be performed in its entirety. The rarely-sung third stanza of “The Star-Spangled Banner” has been seen as a defense of slavery. 
“We are all patriotic, but I think again, kind of hearkening back to 2024 and the passage of anti-CRT (critical race theory), anti-DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) legislation. I think that we have to be clear about what the history of the country is, so that we can truly work towards making it better,” Dees said
Both Dees and King said during interviews that these amendments don’t address larger problems in schools.
“We’re fine with them passing, but we need to be realistic about these are not things that are going to move the needle for public education in the state of Alabama,” King said. “Protecting instructional time, supporting teachers when these kids have major discipline issues and are beating them up, making sure that we are helping kids with reading and math, making sure that we’re protecting planning time so that teachers can adequately get done all the paperwork they need to get completed.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota lawmaker seeks limits on Flock-style cameras
description: A North Dakota lawmaker is planning to propose a bill to regulate the use of controversial automated license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, across the state. “I have a lot of constituents who reach out on a nearly daily basis who are very concerned about this, and they want them banned,” said Sen. Jamie […]
text:
A Flock camera is shown mounted on a city light pole near the corner of 45th Street and 13th Avenue in Fargo on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Dan Koeck/For the North Dakota Monitor)A North Dakota lawmaker is planning to propose a bill to regulate the use of controversial automated license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, across the state.
“I have a lot of constituents who reach out on a nearly daily basis who are very concerned about this, and they want them banned,” said Sen. Jamie Selzler, D-Fargo. “People do not want these at all.”
Rather than banning the cameras, Selzler’s bill would implement “reasonable regulations” on their use, he said. The lawmaker said he’s working on the proposal with a bipartisan group of legislators.
Under the bill, law enforcement agencies would have to publicly disclose the locations of these cameras and provide a 30-day public notice before installing a new one. They also wouldn’t be allowed to install cameras near schools, places of worship or hospitals, and agencies would only be able to keep data for 14 days.
The bill would also criminalize intentional misuse of the technology and require there to be an open investigation before an officer is able to run a search through the cameras’ database.
Sen. Jamie Selzler, D-Fargo, speaks on the Senate floor during a special session of the Legislature on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“It’s putting guardrails in place to protect the public from abuse or overreach by law enforcement,” Selzler said.
Selzler said he hasn’t worked with law enforcement on the bill yet, but he plans to as the 2027 session nears. He said he hopes law enforcement will be on board with the idea.
“If I were law enforcement, I would be worried about law enforcement overreach causing these to be completely banned,” he said.
Nationwide, there’s been growing opposition to the cameras, which capture images or videos of vehicles, read their license plates and compare their information against databases.
Opponents argue the devices are a violation of privacy because of their ability to store data about drivers’ locations over time. In several high-profile cases nationally, law enforcement officials have also been accused of using the cameras to stalk former romantic partners. 
Selzler was one of several dozen attendees at a “Flock Talk” event hosted in Fargo last month by the Faith & Conviction Coalition.
The event brought together residents and a panel that included Horace City Councilmember Chad Chalmers. The Horace City Council voted in September to take down the city’s Flock cameras. It was the first community in the Fargo metro area to do so, according to Erin Powers, an organizer of the event.
Chalmers said that while many may think of these cameras as being “just license plate readers,” what he saw in Horace would suggest otherwise. 
“We had two Flock Falcons, which are license plate readers, and one of them was what’s called a Condor. It’s got pan-tilt-zoom, and it can do full live video,” he said. 
Which North Dakota cities have Flock-style cameras?
The Monitor reached out to police departments in North Dakota’s largest cities to ask whether they use automated license plate readers.
Fargo declined an interview but pointed to its Flock Transparency Portal page, which includes a section with frequently asked questions and links to the department’s policy. It does not share camera locations.
In its ALPR camera policy, the Fargo Police Department says “locations are considered exempt records and not open to public review pursuant to this policy and North Dakota Century Code.”
A spokesperson confirmed via email that in addition to the 21 stationary Flock cameras listed on the website, the Fargo Police Department has 61 squad cars outfitted with ALPR cameras from another brand. The department also has five pan-tilt-zoom cameras installed in downtown Fargo.
Pan-tilt-zoom cameras, which record live video, “include a feature called Guardian Mode, which uses AI to detect motion and follow that movement, vehicle or pedestrian, until the subject is no longer in view,” according to the online page. “This feature does not use facial recognition or compare images to any database.”
However, the city doesn’t use that mode because its pan-tilt-zoom cameras are “positioned in busy public areas where movement is constant,” according to the city’s Flock page. 
Flock surveillance cameras raise constitutional questions, bipartisan US senators say

The Grand Forks Police Department told the Monitor it doesn’t have any stationary or car-mounted automated license plate readers. 
West Fargo also declined an interview, but in a statement, a spokesperson said the West Fargo Police Department has had ALPR cameras since 2024. It has 48 stationary cameras and four car-mounted cameras. 
“To ensure proper use of the system, an audit is conducted monthly and is reviewed by the Intelligence Supervisor. All information obtained through the Flock system is also verified by a supervisor before any additional law enforcement action is taken,” according to the statement. 
The Bismarck Police Department has ALPR cameras on all 43 of its squad cars. They were turned on this past spring, according to Lt. Luke Gardiner. He said the department doesn’t own any stationary cameras but does have access to several cameras at Kirkwood Mall.
In Dickinson, the police department’s squad cars have all been outfitted with ALPR cameras since 2023. Deputy Police Chief Matthew Hanson said the city also has three stationary cameras, two of which are up and running. 
“The one thing that makes our system a little bit different than Flock is our system is only operated by us,” Hanson said. “We don’t share our information with anybody else.”
He said the cameras have been a “huge lifesaver” during challenging investigations, including last fall, when several rounds were fired in a trailer court and eyewitnesses were not willing to give statements.
“It was going into our city-owned camera systems and finding a vehicle of interest that ultimately led us to the case,” Hanson said.
The cameras have also helped officers solve cases despite long-term understaffing, Hanson said.
Minot doesn’t have any stationary ALPR cameras, but it did install them on its squad cars this year. City spokesperson Jennifer Kleen said the data is housed in the department’s systems and can’t be accessed by the company the city works with.
Kleen said the city also has an oversight committee, composed of city councilmembers and community members, that meets every month to review the police department’s use of the technology. 
In Williston, the police department has 31 cameras installed on its patrol vehicles in addition to two “quick-deploy” cameras that can be moved around and “placed in specific locations when needed to assist with investigations or targeted enforcement,” according to city spokesperson Calli Stellmacher.
Stellmacher said the city’s officers are required to “do their due diligence” and not arrest someone based solely off of a hit from an ALPR camera.
Opponents’ concerns
Chalmers, the Horace city councilmember, said he trusts law enforcement. But he said the cameras tested the balance of security and liberty, and “when it comes down to it, liberty comes before security.”
“If we have no liberty, we will have no security. Governments throughout history have killed more people than criminals have,” Chalmers said. “I’m not saying our government’s going to be doing that anytime soon, but we certainly don’t want to set them up with tools (to do so).” 
Members of the Faith & Conviction Coalition brought anti-Flock signs to a Flock Talk event in Fargo Oct. 16, 2026. Event attendees were encouraged to join the group’s protests against the use of Flock cameras around the metro area. (Photo by Ceilidh Kern/For the North Dakota Monitor)
Kellan Benson, a Fargo attorney who also participated in the Flock Talk panel, said that while people don’t typically have a right to privacy in public spaces — such as public roads — the “mosaic of information” that these cameras are able to collect and store could amount to an invasion of privacy. 
He also argued that while many ALPR cameras don’t have facial recognition technology, the fact that drivers can be so easily linked to their cars means tracking a car’s movements around a city is more or less the same as tracking a person’s movements.
A recent case in which facial recognition aided an investigation that led to a Tennessee woman being charged with bank theft in Fargo shows how relying on this kind of technology can harm people, Benson said. 
It also demonstrates cities’ liability, he added. After charges against Angela Lipps, the Tennessee woman, were dropped, she sued the city and a police detective for $10 million.
Governments passing laws and regulations — such as requiring warrants and a case number before officers can access camera systems, and limiting access to a few trained and trusted officers — could help to protect citizens from overreach, the panel speakers said.
Another concern, Benson said, is that law enforcement agencies aren’t the only ones with access to databases full of information captured by ALPR cameras. 
Some of the companies that sell the cameras and lease the software, such as Flock, also have access, Benson said, adding that a contract provision preventing Flock from sharing data with third parties may not be enough.
“I have trouble with the fact that that’s not a law. That’s a contract provision. Who’s enforcing that part of the contract?” Benson said.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Federal cuts hobble efforts to prevent overdoses from contaminated drugs
description: GREENVILLE, N.C. — When the federal funding ran dry, Diannee Carden Glenn’s options were few. Carden Glenn is the director of ekiM for Change, a volunteer-run public health organization that works to prevent overdoses in Greenville and surrounding rural communities. For much of the past decade, she relied on funding from the federal Substance Abuse […]
text:
Diannee Carden Glenn is the director of ekiM for Change, a volunteer-run public health organization in eastern North Carolina. With federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration funding no longer available for street-drug test strips, she must now come up with the money on her own. (Taylor Sisk for KFF Health News)GREENVILLE, N.C. — When the federal funding ran dry, Diannee Carden Glenn’s options were few.
Carden Glenn is the director of ekiM for Change, a volunteer-run public health organization that works to prevent overdoses in Greenville and surrounding rural communities. For much of the past decade, she relied on funding from the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration to buy drug test strips, used to check for contaminants in the street-drug supply.
But in April, the federal agency sent out a “Dear Colleague” letter announcing that organizations like hers could no longer use its money to buy test strips for fentanyl, xylazine, medetomidine, or other substances that heighten the risk of overdose, particularly when the user is unaware of what they’re consuming.
Carden Glenn’s options?
“Well, I’m 81 years old, and I get Social Security,” she said, “so I use my Social Security. And I’m lucky to have a husband who can support me.” She also has other retirement income; she allocates that to ekiM’s work as well. Occasionally, she receives a donation. The federal funding was a little more than $15,000 a year.
Carden Glenn’s small organization is part of the “harm reduction” movement, which aims to help people who use drugs stay safe. Opponents argue that distributing test strips and similar supplies abets drug use and detracts from abstinence-based recovery. Proponents counter that checking street drugs for contaminants is a proven way to prevent overdoses, particularly with so many unknown drugs now in the supply. While fentanyl is ubiquitous, front-line workers are also commonly discovering that drugs sold on the streets unexpectedly contain methamphetamine and an increasing number of ultrapotent synthetic drugs, including carfentanil, medetomidine, and nitazenes.
Research has indicated that people who use test strips are more likely to engage with other harm reduction services and strategies, such as carrying naloxone and not using drugs alone.
At a church in Durham, North Carolina, outreach workers use a Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy machine to test the contents of street drugs. (Taylor Sisk for KFF Health News)
In North Carolina, the federal agency was the state opioid response program’s exclusive funding source for fentanyl and xylazine test strips, which were then distributed to organizations across the state. These cuts are part of a more than $300 million reduction in federal funding for overdose prevention and treatment initiatives nationally.
North Carolina is among the states that permit such groups to use a variety of drug-checking tools. Carden Glenn’s organization typically hands out test strips for fentanyl, xylazine, and medetomidine. The strips can cost $1 or more apiece, depending on the type. Giving away several hundred a week adds up.
Test strips are one in a spectrum of tools that are being utilized throughout the state.
Each Friday afternoon, 100 miles west of Greenville, team members of the North Carolina Harm Reduction Coalition arrive at Elizabeth Street United Methodist Church near downtown Durham with a toaster-oven-sized contraption called a Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy machine. The device allows for more thorough examination than test strips, providing insight into the varied, sometimes startling contents of drugs brought in by the people who use them or by their friends, family, or advocates.
Jennifer Carroll is an associate professor of anthropology at North Carolina State University who partners with the Harm Reduction Coalition to evaluate testing results from such equipment. The university received funding from the North Carolina Collaboratory to enable this work. The utility of the technology excites her; each new drug sample presents a mystery.
Those who visit the testing site range from regular to occasional users. Often, they have no clue what might be found in a sample. “It just feels nice being able to offer this to people, and for them to have the power of having that knowledge,” Carroll said.
“We see quinine, lidocaine, tetracaine,” she said while seated behind the testing machine on a Friday afternoon in January. “We see tranquilizers like xylazine and medetomidine. We occasionally see gabapentin show up, but it’s not common. We occasionally see heroin.”
The machine isn’t perfect, she said. For example, it might miss traces of medetomidine in cocaine that a test strip would detect. So the staffers keep strips on hand.
For more comprehensive testing, the team sends samples to the Street Drug Analysis Lab at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, known more commonly as “Nab’s Lab,” in recognition of Nabarun Dasgupta, the lab’s director and recipient of a 2025 MacArthur Fellowship “genius grant.”
Dasgupta and his team use an instrument that provides more thorough analysis, offering confirmation of the chemical formula of a sample. Since the lab’s launch in 2022, they’ve detected some 500 unique substances in the drug supply. From rural Edgecombe County, for example: levamisole, a medication primarily prescribed to treat worm infestation in animals. From Asheville: the industrial chemical BTMPS, used to protect plastics from ultraviolet exposure.
Pearson Ripley with the harm reduction organization Steady Collective in Asheville said keeping up with the flow of adulterants in the drug supply is probably the foremost challenge today for those doing this work. For a time, the biggest problem was the emergence of fentanyl. But people have learned to adjust to its effects, he said. Now it’s the unknown complexity of the supply.
Look at graphs charting the composition of street-drug samples, Ripley said, “and it’s just, bam, stepping up every single year in the number of substances found in a supply.”
Thus, those on the front lines say, the urgent need for easily accessible drug testing.
Carroll emphasized the critical role street-drug suppliers can play in drug-checking initiatives.
“We’re still a very nascent service in North Carolina,” she said; those relationships have yet to be established. “But in many other places that have been offering this service longer, some of their most impactful relationships around the service are with drug suppliers who are like, ‘I want to be able to communicate what I’m selling to other people so that no one is surprised.’”
Dasgupta has been impressed with street-drug checking strategies conceived and launched in rural communities, which he calls “engines of ingenuity.” He cites Holler Harm Reduction in rural western North Carolina, “where they’re going to people’s houses and doing driveway drug checking. That’s cool.”
The Good Mind Initiative, serving Indigenous communities across North and South Carolina, holds monthly community socials at the United Katehnuaka Longhouse at which as many as 300 people convene for fellowship, food, first aid kits, naloxone, condoms, and more. Throughout the month, Good Mind Initiative staff distribute supplies.
“Our identity, our culture, our language, our songs, our dances are integral to our healing and to our ability to help each other reduce harm,” said Kaya Littleturtle, the initiative’s program manager. So too were test strips, which they no longer have the money to provide.
His organization holds fundraising events, including target-shooting contests in which the prizes are turkey or other types of meat. He acknowledged, though, that it would take a lot of fundraising to replace the lost federal money.
Kaya Littleturtle is program manager of the Good Mind Initiative, which provides services to Indigenous communities across North and South Carolina. (Taylor Sisk for KFF Health News)
In July 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stipulating that federal grants not be spent on “‘so-called’ harm reduction” efforts, writing that they “only facilitate illegal drug use and its attendant harm.”
That order and subsequent funding cuts have contributed to what North Carolina Harm Reduction Coalition executive director Elyse Powell calls “an incredibly hostile time” for critical services.
And there’s a ripple effect. Carroll said she has had interactions with federally qualified health centers that have said they’re not allowed to participate in an event that has the term “drug checking” associated with it.
In May, U.S. Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) sent a letter — co-signed by four fellow senators and 16 members of the House of Representatives, all Democrats — to the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration asserting that its recent directive “defies evidence showing that harm reduction for substance use reduces overdose deaths and dangerous infections, threatening to reverse years of progress in combating the overdose epidemic.”
“To abandon harm reduction is to do so at our own peril,” he wrote.
Markey also noted that the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has acknowledged that test strips can be “the difference between life or death.”
Margaret Bordeaux is a longtime advocate for harm reduction efforts. “I know people who have done amazing things, incredible work, to really advance drug testing here in North Carolina, and the impact that’s having on communities,” she said. “I know exactly what happens when those resources aren’t available in communities. We lived through it, and to think that we’d have to go through it again is sad. It’s sad.”
Littleturtle agrees. “It’s just a hard time right now, because of politics, and politics should never get in the way of saving lives,” he said. “But it does.”
KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas Explained: What is the legislative ‘supermajority’?
description: Arkansas Democrats didn’t claim any statewide or federal victories in last week’s midterm election, but they made gains in the state Legislature that could have major implications. The party won 10 seats in the state House and flipped another Republican-held seat in the Senate. The GOP still holds a majority of seats in both chambers […]
text:
Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders gives her State of the State address in the House of Representatives chamber at the Arkansas State Capitol in Little Rock, Arkansas on Wednesday, April 8, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Arkansas Democrats didn’t claim any statewide or federal victories in last week’s midterm election, but they made gains in the state Legislature that could have major implications.
The party won 10 seats in the state House and flipped another Republican-held seat in the Senate. The GOP still holds a majority of seats in both chambers of the Legislature, but the gains may give Democrats leverage on budget negotiations that they haven’t had in a decade.
Here’s a look at the advances Democrats made at the statehouse level and what it means for next year’s legislative session:
 
What gains did Democrats make in the Legislature?
Democrats’ victories give them 30 seats in the 100-member House and ends the Republican supermajority in the chamber. 
A supermajority is when one party has enough members to clear a required vote threshold without needing votes from an opposing party. 
Passing most appropriations bills, which authorize agencies to spend state money, requires at least three-fourths support in the House and Senate. That means 75 votes in the 100 member House and 27 in the 35-member Senate.
With Arkansas Republicans’ House supermajority lost, a changed dynamic

Not every budget bill has to clear this hurdle. The appropriation for public school funding only needs a simple majority. So does the proposed Revenue Stabilization Act, the must-pass state budget bill that spells out spending priorities based on revenue.
In the Senate, Democrats are below the three-fourths threshold. They hold seven of the chamber’s 34 filled seats. One seat in the chamber is vacant following former Republican Sen. Jonathan Dismang’s resignation earlier this year. A special election to fill the vacancy is scheduled for Dec. 15. 
 
Why does breaking the supermajority matter?
For the past 10 years, Republicans have been able to pass most budget bills without needing any Democratic votes.
For most budget bills, that hasn’t been an issue. Most appropriations bills are relatively noncontroversial and haven’t prompted partisan fights.
But it can factor into debates over key policy issues, especially the state’s hybrid Medicaid expansion. The appropriation for Arkansas’ Medicaid program has struggled to clear the three-fourths vote needed in past years, facing multiple failed votes that centered around some GOP lawmakers’ opposition to the expansion.
Live coverage: Arkansas 2026 election

That vote margin even prompted former Republican Gov. Asa Hutchinson and legislative leaders to concoct an unusual parliamentary trick. It involved Hutchinson using his line-item veto authority to strike language that would have ended the healthcare program.
Lawmakers in the minority party have also used the high bar needed for appropriations to block spending bills to highlight their objections to certain programs. Before they were the majority, House Republicans in 2011 temporarily blocked appropriations for several agencies including the History Commission and the Crime Lab to show their displeasure with state spending levels under then-Democratic Gov. Mike Beebe. 
 
How will this new dynamic affect the Legislature?
The biggest impact of Democrats’ increased numbers could be on the debate over Medicaid expansion. 
The Trump administration last week gave the state a six-month extension of the program, which provides health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income residents. 
That gives lawmakers a short window to come up with a replacement for the program, which the federal government declined to renew for a longer period of time.
Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion

Medical providers have said that ending the program would be devastating for the state’s health system, which is already strained. 
But the main two alternatives — moving enrollees to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid or a managed care program — could also face significant resistance.
Republicans’ loss of the supermajority could also factor into discussions about prison overcrowding. 
GOP Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders put her plan for a 3,000-bed prison in Franklin County on hold after facing legislative resistance that included some Republican lawmakers.
It could also complicate budget discussions about the governor’s school voucher program, which has faced opposition from Democrats and some Republicans in the Legislature.
It may not factor as much in non-budget legislation, most of which only needs a simple majority to pass.
The top Democrat in the House, Rep. Andrew Collins, last week said the midterm results give the party more influence but that they still hope to find common ground with Republicans on some issues.
Sanders has said she also would find ways to work with Democrats, and cited bills she’s backed that received bipartisan support such as a measure guaranteeing free school breakfast to students and another banning students’ use of cellphones in schools.
