name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH trans teens ask federal judge to pause rule banning Medicaid-funded gender-affirming care
description: In August, the Trump administration issued a new rule: no Medicaid funding for most types of gender-affirming care for children. Now, a group of transgender New Hampshire girls are suing the federal government to reverse the change, and U.S. District Court Judge Steven McAuliffe is deciding whether to pause the rule during the yearslong legal […]
text:
Chris Erchull speaks to reporters outside the federal courthouse in Concord after an Oct. 30 hearing. He and his colleagues were asking Judge Steven McAuliffe to pause a federal rule banning Medicaid-funded gender-affirming care for children. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)In August, the Trump administration issued a new rule: no Medicaid funding for most types of gender-affirming care for children.
Now, a group of transgender New Hampshire girls are suing the federal government to reverse the change, and U.S. District Court Judge Steven McAuliffe is deciding whether to pause the rule during the yearslong legal battle the lawsuit is likely to entail.
The rule came from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services in August and took effect Oct. 13. The ban encompasses transition surgery and hormone blockers for those under 18. President Donald Trump and Republican Party leaders claim gender dysphoria isn’t real, a position at odds with most major medical organizations.
During a hearing in Concord’s federal courthouse last month, attorneys from a coalition of nonprofits, including GLBTQ Legal Advocates and Defenders (commonly known as GLAD) and the ACLU of New Hampshire, pushed McAuliffe to grant a temporary injunction to pause the rule.
One of the trans teenagers, using the pseudonym “Kylie Coe,” has been struggling in school as her body changes without the puberty blockers she used to receive through Medicaid, her attorney, GLAD’s Chris Erchull, told the judge. Blockers cannot undo changes, he emphasized, but can only prevent them. Erchull said as her body begins to change again, classmates are starting to see her as a boy. 
“Most of Kylie’s classmates only know her as a girl,” Erchull said.
For that reason, he said, it’s urgent that the court pause the rule.
However, Erchull spent most of the hearing trying to establish the lawsuit’s legal merits, giving the first look into how the case will be litigated. At the core of that argument is the EPSDT, or early and periodic screening, diagnostic and treatment mandate. In 1967, Congress required Medicaid to cover any services medically necessary to sufficiently offer early and periodic screening, diagnostics and treatment. Erchull argued that the law forbids the Trump administration from cutting the services.
“Congress cannot have intended EPSDT to apply except when the president disagrees,” he said.
Erchull argued that, based on previous precedent, qualified medical providers and states — not the federal government — determine what is medically necessary. He pointed out that medical providers overwhelmingly support this kind of care.
“That can’t be right,” McAuliffe retorted. “The system isn’t at the whim of any healthcare provider that says this is medically necessary. Someone has to make those decisions.”
The U.S. District Court, District of New Hampshire, Aug. 27, 2025. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
The judge appeared skeptical that CMS was unable to make those decisions entirely.
“We all understand the concept that agencies don’t legislate,” he said. “But I’m having trouble with your argument.”
McAuliffe appeared to see gender-affirming care as different, on a legal basis, from most types of care covered under the EPSDT standard because of the political issue it’s become.
“They’re overriding Congress’ mandate?” he asked. “OK, show me the mandate. … I don’t see anything in there about gender dysphoria. That’s a sociopolitical issue.” 
In 2025, the New Hampshire Legislature banned this type of gender-affirming care for children. However, it grandfathered in kids who were already receiving the care. The ban became a point of contention during the hearing as McAuliffe interrogated Erchull on why the ban doesn’t mean that the state  — which Erchull argued is responsible for, alongside providers, determining medical necessity — deems the care medically unnecessary. Erchull argued that because his specific clients — four teenage transgender girls and their families — were grandfathered in, that means the state deemed it necessary for them.
Stephen Tagert, a trial attorney for the Department of Justice, represented the federal government in the hearing.
“This is not about any sort of ban (on gender-affirming care),” he said. “This is about whether the federal government pays for it.”
McAuliffe appeared skeptical.
“It’s an effective ban,” he said. “Name me a state that has continued to fund the care. There’s none.”
McAuliffe also questioned why CMS was doing this now. He pointed out that the federal government regularly approves New Hampshire and other states’ Medicaid plans and it approved this one before. Why, he asked, is it suddenly intervening after already having approved the plan?
Tagert said the question “is irrelevant because New Hampshire and the federal government are aligned.” He pointed to the state’s 2025 ban.
The judge asked him to specify the federal government’s legal authority. Tagert argued that because the government has the authority to ensure medically necessary care is covered, it has the authority to ensure medically unnecessary care isn’t. He called it “two sides of the same coin.”
He seemed to lose the judge.
“Coming in here, I generally agreed with you,” McAuliffe told Tagert, “until I came in here and heard it’s the rule that’s the problem.”
The parties disagreed about whether the federal government followed the proper steps — allowing sufficient public comment, meaningfully considering alternative courses of action, etc. — an issue that’s likely to be fought over for many months.
After the hearing, Erchull told reporters outside the courthouse that “the judge really did seem to understand the harm that’s going to come to the families that we represent in this case and seemed to understand how significant it is for them and their entire futures to be able to continue accessing the care that they desperately need as young people struggling with gender dysphoria.”
Federal judges are known to be vigorous in their questioning of both parties in court, making it difficult to parse whether a judge is buying an attorney’s overall argument.
“By the end of the oral arguments, I think that we had convinced the judge to take a closer look at what EPSDT actually requires,” he continued, “which is a very sweeping mandate that requires Medicaid cover basically every medically necessary treatment or procedure that a young person might need.”
Tagert declined to speak to the Bulletin after the hearing.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island Blood Center workers seek union election over staffing and pay concerns
description: Justin Madden works as a driver for the Rhode Island Blood Center, helping to set up, operate and take down the mobile blood drives that pop up across the Ocean State. “We have a very important job,” Madden said in a recent phone interview. Madden wishes there were a few more people in his department […]
text:
An employee at the Rhode Island Blood Center in Providence checks the IV line in the arm of a donor on Monday, Dec. 15, 2025. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)Justin Madden works as a driver for the Rhode Island Blood Center, helping to set up, operate and take down the mobile blood drives that pop up across the Ocean State. 
“We have a very important job,” Madden said in a recent phone interview.
Madden wishes there were a few more people in his department doing that important work with him. The longtime driver believes better starting wages at the blood center would help fill those vacancies — something which a union could help achieve, Madden said. 
On Oct. 30, Teamsters Local 251 formally petitioned for a union election to represent a proposed unit of 175 workers at the Blood Center.
The Blood Center’s leaders and some of its workers, however, have different interpretations about how the campaign has played out thus far. 
“Our employees are essential to our mission, and we recognize and respect their rights under federal labor law,” a Blood Center spokesperson said in an unsigned Nov. 5 statement. “It is up to employees to decide whether they want to be represented by a union, and we have encouraged them to ask questions and make their own informed decisions.”
The nonprofit Rhode Island Blood Center was founded in 1979, and collects and supplies blood and blood products to more than 60 hospitals in Rhode Island and Connecticut, according to its website. 
The petition describes the proposed bargaining unit as including full-time, part-time and per diem employees in roles ranging from donor technicians and drivers to laboratory, administrative and maintenance staff.
Two employee groups — those who work in hospital services and the call center — are currently excluded from the union’s proposal, Teamsters organizer Virginia Tavares said in a Nov. 5 phone interview and follow-up email. Tavares said management wants those groups included and the union is disputing their inclusion.
Local 251 has requested an in-person election Nov. 18. In a Nov. 5 follow-up email, Tavares said the date “is now being disputed because the attorney is unavailable until after Thanksgiving.”
The Blood Center statement said it has received the petition and is working with the National Labor Relations Board on “the logistics and details of that election.”
Madden described subpar staffing and compensation as the underlying reasons to organize. 
He’s worked with the Blood Center for more than a decade, and his schedule is inherently a liquid one. His hours follow the needs of blood drive sponsors, whose own timetables dictate when Madden’s shifts begin and end.
Madden said his department is missing four full-time, 40-hour employees and one part-timer who works 20 hours weekly. Better starting pay would help keep staff on board and relieve some of the pressure on workers like him, Madden argued.
“You raise the floor, then you can have people stay longer,” Madden said. “That would alleviate a lot of this pressure that’s on people [who are] overworked. That would be the biggest thing.”
Madden said just talking about organizing has led to some improvements. Before, if someone called out, the mobile unit might be down a worker for the day. Now, he said, replacements show up much faster.
“Ever since we started this whole union talk….[that] replacement shows up within the hour, which is kind of interesting because that’s something they could have been doing the entire time,” Madden said. 
Madden cited improved health plan options and time-and-a-half policies as an additional benefit of unionization. He was also concerned about the presence of outside consultants he and organizers say were brought in to discuss unionization with employees.
“They cross paths with somebody from my department daily,” Madden said. “It’s aggravating too because people can see the writing on the wall and know these people are getting paid, and this is money that potentially could have went to us.” 
Blood Center leaders have also held meetings and town hall-type events meant to supply information on unionization. Madden described the meetings as voluntary.
The Blood Center spokesperson did not include information in its email addressing questions about which consultants the Blood Center had retained, what services they performed or how much they were paid. 
A Sept. 30 email reviewed by Rhode Island Current showed Blood Center leadership instructing managers to inform employees that they may be required to sign a union authorization card to attend an informational union meeting during the first weekend of October. 
The Blood Center confirmed in an earlier Oct. 6 statement to Rhode Island Current that an email had been sent to employees. 
“We had received information that employees may be required to sign a union authorization card to attend, and we wanted to inform our employees that they should be able to gather information without feeling pressured to sign anything,” the statement read.
Teamsters organizer Tavares denied that signing a card was required to attend, and said it was “false information spread by management and the anti-union consultants to intimidate workers into attending their meetings.”
“Workers are not required to sign authorization cards before attending any of our meetings,” she wrote in her Nov. 5 email. “These meetings are simply an opportunity to educate employees about our union, answer their questions, and explain the organizing process.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: For runoffs, Louisiana voters selected Democrats with conservative records on social issues
description: Louisiana Democrats have promised to capitalize on the surprisingly strong showing for their candidate, Jamie Davis, in the U.S. Senate election during the governor’s race in 2027. But the party still has two Congressional races left to run this year, with Democratic candidates advancing to the Dec. 12 runoffs for the 5th and 6th U.S. House districts.
text:
The two Democrats, state Rep. Pat Moore, of Monroe, and former Baton Rouge Metro Council member Chauna Banks, who have advanced to the runoff election on Dec. 12, 2026 (Photo by John Gray/Verite News)Louisiana Democrats have promised to capitalize on the surprisingly strong showing for their candidate, Jamie Davis, in the U.S. Senate election during the governor’s race in 2027. But the party still has two Congressional races left to run this year, with Democratic candidates advancing to the Dec. 12 runoffs for the 5th and 6th U.S. House districts.  
The country is in the midst of a “blue tsunami” election cycle where Democrats have won House seats in unlikely places across the nation. Leveraging that enthusiasm for these two remaining races could be complicated, however, since the remaining Democratic candidates’ views on abortion and LGBTQ+ rights are out of step with those of most of the party’s activists and donors. 
State Rep. Pat Moore, D-Monroe, and state Rep. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, will face each other in the 5th district runoff after receiving 18% and 17% of the vote respectively Tuesday. Former Baton Rouge Metro Council member Chauna Banks, a Democrat, and state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, will see each other in the 6th district race, after receiving 19% each of the vote. 
Moore and Banks, both Black women, are antiabortion and have opposed measures to provide protections to LGBTQ+ people. Neither received the state Democratic Party’s endorsement in the primary election, in part because they had views that contradicted those of many Louisiana Democratic State Central Committee members. 
“I think it makes it harder for them to raise money from traditional Democratic sources of fundraising,” said Mary Patricia Wray, a political consultant who ran Democratic campaigns for former Gov. John Bel Edwards, Public Service Commissioner Foster Campbell and U.S. House Rep. Cleo Fields, D-Baton Rouge. 

“A lot of out-of-state donor networks are not going to want to participate,” she said. 
In Louisiana, Democratic candidates are typically dependent on out-of-state donation to run competitive campaigns. 

Almost 86% of Davis’ Senate race campaign donations came from outside Louisiana, according to an analysis by Open Secrets, a nonpartisan organization that tracks political spending nationally. His top donor state was California, which had contributed $478,000 compared to  $400,000 from Louisiana donors as of Oct. 15, according to the analysis. 
Both races would be uphill battles for any Democratic candidate regardless of their views. While Moore and Banks finished first in their respective primary elections, that’s mostly because the Republican vote was split among more candidates than the Democrats had in each race. 
In the 5th district, six Republican candidates, including Firment, collectively received 62% of the vote over three Democrats, including Moore. In the 6th district, six Republicans, including Miguez, collectively received 57% of the vote over three Democrats, including Banks, and a Libertarian. 
 Controversial votes


Since joining the Louisiana House in 2019, Moore has favored legislation that places restrictions on abortion access. In an interview this week, she said she considered herself to be an antiabortion legislator. 

Moore said her family history has shaped her opposition to abortion. Her own mother gave birth to her at the age of 14 after being raped, she said. 

“[My mother] could not have a relationship with me. She couldn’t love me, touch me or name me, but she gave me life,” she said. 
In 2019, Moore voted with the majority of the Louisiana House to pass an earlier version of Louisiana’s current abortion ban that would have prohibited the procedure if a fetal heartbeat was detected. Abortion rights advocates had opposed the legislation, saying it could effectively ban all abortions, since most people don’t discover a pregnancy until after a heartbeat can be identified. 

During debate over the bill that year, Moore spoke about her mother on the House floor while advocating against an amendment, which failed, that would have eased abortions restrictions in cases where a pregnancy resulted from rape or incest. 
Louisiana’s current abortion ban law passed in 2022, a few weeks before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and allowed states to outlaw the procedure. Moore was absent for the vote on that legislation. 
On LGBTQ+ legislation, Moore voted in favor of a state ban on gender-affirming care for minors  and a prohibition on K-12 school employees using transgender and nonbinary students’ preferred pronouns without parental permission in 2023. 

She was absent for the vote on Louisiana’s transgender sports ban in 2022 and split her votes on “Don’t Say Gay” legislation, which restricts public school employees’ from discussing LGBTQ+ issues with students. In 2023, Moore supported such a bill that was vetoed, but then she voted against similar legislation in 2024, which passed into law. 
Moore said her approach to a few social issues might not align with the national Democratic party, but most of her stances, such as reversing cuts to the Medicaid program and reinstating food assistance funding, line up with the party’s platform overall. 
“The reason I’m a Democrat is because this is a party that’s inclusive, even if we don’t agree,” Moore said. 
As a Baton Rouge Metro Council member from 2013 to 2024, Banks was not faced with votes on abortion like Moore. But in an interview Thursday, Banks said she believes “life begins at conception” and considers herself pro-life. 
“I have the same views on abortion that I have on the death penalty,” Banks said. 

While Banks generally opposes abortion, she said there are circumstances in which an abortion should be allowed. For example, she said a person should be allowed to terminate a pregnancy if it is going to threaten their life. 

Banks challenged the notion that Democrats generally favor abortion rights. 
“I don’t know what the Democratic view on abortion is,” she said this week. 

In 2014, Banks voted against a so-called “fairness ordinance” that came before the Baton Rouge Metro Council to prohibit discrimination against people based on sexual orientation or gender identity in areas of housing, employment and public accommodations. The measure failed 8-4, with Banks voting in the majority. 

In an interview this week, Banks said she doesn’t personally categorize people based on their sexuality and has never seen an LGBTQ+ person suffering discrimination. She said she would like to see data and evidence of discriminatory practices against LGBTQ+ people. 
 Louisiana has a history of conservative Democrats

Moore and Banks are not alone among Louisiana Democrats in terms of having more conservative views on social issues. John Bel Edwards, the only Democrat to win a statewide office since 2008, also opposed abortion and signed the state’s strict abortion ban into law in 2022. 

Yet the state Democratic party went so far as to rescind its initial endorsement of Moore in September on a technicality, in part because members were uncomfortable with her views on abortion, Democratic Chairman Randal Gaines said last month. They decided to back Antonio Wilson, who favored abortion rights, instead.  

On Wednesday, Gaines said he expects the party will endorse both Moore and Banks in the runoff election, since they are the only Democrats running. For that to happen, the Democratic State Central Committee will have to take an endorsement vote some time in the few weeks. 

While Democratic committee members may have more progressive views on social issues, Gaines said party voters in the 5th and 6th districts don’t necessarily share those views. 

“Pat Moore is a conservative Democrat whose platform is perfect for that district,” he said. “A lot of our Democratic voters have more conservative views.” 

Public Service Commissioner Davante Lewis, a Black Democrat who is the only openly gay person serving in elected office state government, agreed. Democrats in Louisiana should lean toward being more inclusive, he said. 

“When you have a big tent, there are people that aren’t going to agree with all portions of the tent,” said Lewis, who is considering a run for governor next year.

name: National
title: States push short-term insurance as healthcare costs climb
description: Earlier this year, Madison Harden-Stein and her colleagues at the Georgetown University Center on Health Insurance Reforms posed as consumers interested in buying insurance as part of a secret shopper study. They found that insurance brokers and sales representatives often pushed short-term health insurance plans with limited coverage, and used misleading an[...]
text:
Elvia Macedo, a Medi-Cal patient, gets a check-up with Dr. Oscar Casillas at Martin Luther King Jr. Community Hospital in Los Angeles in 2022. Some conservative states are promoting short-term health plans for people who have been priced out of Obamacare or who stand to lose their Medicaid coverage in the coming year due to federal changes. (Photo by Pablo Unzueta for CalMatters)Earlier this year, Madison Harden-Stein and her colleagues at the Georgetown University Center on Health Insurance Reforms posed as consumers interested in buying insurance as part of a secret shopper study.
They found that insurance brokers and sales representatives often pushed short-term health insurance plans with limited coverage, and used misleading and inaccurate information to make them more appealing. The deceptive sales tactics made it difficult to make an informed decision about what they’d be signing up for.
“It was very confusing to understand what they were even marketing,” said Harden-Stein, an assistant research professor.
But as insurance costs skyrocket for many, consumers could see more such plans in the coming year.
Conservative states are making it easier for insurance giants to sell cheap, short-term healthcare plans with limited coverage — potentially sticking buyers with thousands of dollars in unexpected medical bills.
The push follows a spike in Obamacare premiums after Republicans allowed federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year. Meanwhile, millions of people stand to lose Medicaid coverage in the coming year due to federal changes.
Some Republican state and federal officials are pitching the plans as a cheaper alternative to the comprehensive coverage sold on the marketplaces created under the Affordable Care Act.
Earlier this year, Mississippi Insurance Commissioner Mike Chaney announced he wanted to make short-term plans more accessible by offering them through a state-operated customer portal.
“The goal here is to give Mississippi consumers more choices,” Chaney said in a September statement.
“We should not assume that every Mississippian has the same health insurance needs,” he said. “Some people need comprehensive coverage with broad benefits and protections. Others may need a lower-cost option to bridge a temporary gap in coverage.”
The percentage of people without health insurance is growing

But critics call them “junk plans.” They say shoppers may be drawn in by low premiums and copayments without fully understanding that they lack the consumer protections people have come to expect since the Affordable Care Act. The 2010 law created regulated health insurance markets and banned insurers from denying coverage, dropping policies, or charging higher rates to people with preexisting health conditions.
Short-term, limited duration health plans have been around for decades, intended as stopgap insurance for people between jobs or who are waiting for their employer-sponsored insurance to kick in. The plans usually have cheaper premiums and copayments, but cover fewer services.
They don’t have to cover maternity care, mental health treatment or prescription drugs.
And insurers are allowed to drop a person’s coverage due to preexisting conditions, or limit the amount paid out per service. They can charge higher premiums for certain people. Research has found some plans charge women up to 19% more than men for the same coverage, which isn’t allowed under ACA-compliant plans.
Under these types of plans, people with chronic conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure, or who are pregnant, can’t get coverage.
Restrictions on the plans have seesawed as the Obama and Biden administrations limited the plans to just a few months’ duration and the Trump administration relaxed those rules.
Most recently, the Trump administration announced in August 2025 it would not enforce Biden-era rules that limited the duration of short-term plans to a few months, and encouraged states to do the same.
Shortly after, states including Arkansas and Oklahoma said they would allow insurers to sell short-term plans that last less than a year, and allow them to be renewed up to three years, greatly extending the “short-term” nature of the plans.
Consumer advocates say brokers and insurance agents have used misleading or outright false information to entice consumers into purchasing the plans, which later surprised them with thousands of dollars in medical bills.
And while these plans can be lucrative for insurers, critics warn they will drive up costs for everyone else.
Jennifer Snow, the national director of government relations and policy at the National Alliance on Mental Illness, said someone like her 18-year-old son, who does not have complex health needs, could be considered an ideal candidate for short-term insurance.
But “you need those healthier people in the overall market to balance out the risk of people who need a lot more healthcare in a given year.” said Snow, who is also a consumer representative with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners.
States face tight timeline as feds unveil new Medicaid work requirement rules

Health insurance works by spreading healthcare expenses across a large group. If insurers divert healthier people into cheaper, short-term plans, that leaves sicker people who need more expensive care in the risk pool for the comprehensive plans, leading insurers to raise those rates to cover those costs.
And, she said, short-term plans rarely cover mental health care, even though about half of people will have a mental health condition over their lifetime — coverage for which usually isn’t included in short-term plans.
“At the end of the day, we are all human,” she said, “and we have healthcare needs that are going to be unpredictable.”
Better than nothing?
Insurance giant UnitedHealthcare will begin offering a handful of short-term plans through Mississippi’s state-run portal by early next year.
Those plans could benefit some of the 200,000 Mississippians who left the ACA marketplace in the past year, said Chaney, the insurance commissioner.
But that exodus from the ACA marketplace is largely the result of recent federal action.
Last year, the ACA saw its highest-ever enrollment of 24 million people, thanks to enhanced premium tax credits made available by the American Rescue Plan Act in 2021 and later extended through the end of 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act.
Those subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes. But they were designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, and the GOP-controlled Congress allowed them to expire at the end of last year.
As a result, premiums jumped. Then marketplace enrollment dropped by 13%, according to federal data, indicating rates were no longer affordable for many. For example, a 60-year-old couple with an annual income of $85,000 suddenly faced annual premiums of $22,600 this year, instead of the roughly $7,225 they paid with enhanced premium tax credits, according to an analysis from the Bipartisan Policy Center.
Already the share of uninsured, working-age adults is growing. Eleven percent of adults ages 19-64 now have no insurance, up from 8.9 percent just two years ago, according to a new analysis from the Commonwealth Fund, a health policy nonprofit.
Given these realities, some insurance is better than none at all, Chaney and other officials have said.
Short-term plans are currently sold in 36 states, according to the most recent analysis from KFF, a nonprofit health policy and research organization.
Five states ban them: California, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey and New York. Nine other states, plus the District of Columbia, require they adhere to stricter consumer protection requirements, and no short-term plans are currently available in those states.
But in the states that allow them, more officials are exploring ways to expand access.
Tennessee lets insurers offer short-term plans on its state ACA marketplace, with some minimum coverage requirements. States including Alabama, Florida, Missouri and Ohio have passed laws in recent years that allow farm bureau health plans, similar to short-term insurance.
Experts expect cheaper ACA-alternative plans will proliferate, as the feds continue loosening restrictions.
‘Skeevy marketing’
After a year-long investigation into short-term plans, a congressional committee released a report in 2020.
It found that most insurers yanked coverage if they determined an enrollee had a prior health condition or risk factors they should have disclosed when applying for the plan, and some insurers denied claims for people who developed previously undiagnosed medical conditions after enrollment.
Some states have tighter rules around deceptive marketing practices, said Harden-Stein.
“But it’s a bit of a whack-a-mole situation,” she said. “You can take down one group that has these skeevy marketing tactics, but they might pop up again under another business name. That’s what makes the regulation of this difficult” without stricter federal rules like those in the ACA.
Democratic wins put Medicaid expansion back in play in holdout states

Short-term plans are lucrative for insurance companies, because by staying outside of ACA rules, they can pick and choose whom they insure and avoid roadblocks to denying coverage.
And while federal law generally allows insurers to only keep about 15-20 cents of every premium dollar collected for ACA-compliant plans, short-term plans have no such restrictions, meaning insurers can keep more of an enrollee’s monthly premiums and pay less toward medical claims.
As healthcare costs rise and with little appetite at the federal level to increase financial help paying for it, experts expect to see short-term plans proliferate in the coming years as states relax their rules and more people settle for “better than nothing” health insurance.
But cheaper doesn’t necessarily mean more affordable, Harden-Stein cautioned.
“It may not necessarily be the affordable option in the long run because it doesn’t offer that comprehensive coverage.”
Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida’s statewide seats remain red. How?
description: Republicans mostly staved off what Gov. Ron DeSantis called a “meteor strike” of national Democratic success last week. During what the governor called “probably the most difficult electoral environment that Republicans will face in quite some time,” he praised Florida as the only large state with a conservative tilt to “hold the line.” DeSantis didn’t […]
text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis hosted a news conference on Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, at the Florida Capitol following the midterm elections. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Republicans mostly staved off what Gov. Ron DeSantis called a “meteor strike” of national Democratic success last week.
During what the governor called “probably the most difficult electoral environment that Republicans will face in quite some time,” he praised Florida as the only large state with a conservative tilt to “hold the line.”
DeSantis didn’t accept the title of Republican “savior” when asked the next morning whether the word applied, but he launched a national press tour to share his opinions about Florida’s still-red status and the state of the national GOP.
Susan MacManus, professor emerita of political science, addresses the Capital Tiger Bay Club on Jan. 31, 2023, in Tallahassee. (Photo by Michael Moline/Florida Phoenix)
Regarding the return to office of Florida’s red statewide officials, Susan MacManus, political science professor emerita at the University of South Florida, pointed first to the 1.5 million more registered Republicans in the state.
“There’s a lot to be said about why that was the case,” MacManus said, although their wins were narrower compared to four years ago.
“When you have a 1.5 million edge, even though you have a plummeting turnout rate, which Republicans did, you could still lose a lot but still win,” MacManus said.
Florida Republicans turned out 62.6% of their registered voters, while Florida Democrats turned out at a rate of 68.4%, according to Fresh Take Florida. Just shy of 50% of the rest of registered voters turned out, compiling an overall 60.8% turnout rate.
In 2022, the state reported that 54% of eligible voters cast ballots in the General Election. In 2018, 63% voted, and in 2014, 51%.
Why did Florida’s red-tint shine different from the rest of the country, DeSantis asked himself.
“I think the answer is, is that we built up a record of achievement, we’ve earned trust from a number of our voters, that even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line and prevent the worst from happening here,” DeSantis said.
MacManus pointed to the “major spurt” in voter registration for Republicans that came with the COVID-19 pandemic, crediting it in part to the governor as “more and more people” were moving to Florida and “liked what the governor here was doing in terms of public policies and parental rights and some of those other things.”
When DeSantis took office in 2019, Democrats had more than a quarter of a million more registered voters than Republicans. The most recent data, now with two months left for the DeSantis administration, show a GOP advantage of 1.55 million.
“The governor’s popularity has always exceeded that of [President Donald] Trump in Florida, and him entering and finally endorsing the statewide candidates tapped into that feeling of comfort in him saying that these are good people,” MacManus said.
The result of statewide GOP control remained the same, but the margins shrank. In 2022, DeSantis won his reelection by more than 19 points. Then-Attorney General Ashley Moody won by more than 20% and the GOP candidates for chief financial officer and commissioner of agriculture won by nearly 20%, too.
Candidate for governor Byron Donalds speaks at a rally in Tallahassee one week before the election, Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
Last week, Republican Byron Donalds won by about 1.3% to become governor-elect, while GOP candidates for attorney general, chief financial officer, and commissioner of agriculture won by 2.2% or less. Attorney General James Uthmeier and Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia were in that cohort, both DeSantis appointees who faced their first election for their posts.
The strong Democratic voter turnout, paired with no-party-affiliated voters who cast votes for Democrats, helped shrink the gap.
“We don’t have facts yet, but we think a lot of that NPA vote came from both young people and Latinos,” MacManus said of those voters who went with the Democrats, “because we know, registration-wise, those groups have sizable portions of NPAs.”
During DeSantis’ media appearances last week, he criticized congressional Republicans for insider trading, votes against releasing the Epstein files, and overall productivity. Democratic turnout, he said, was not a mandate for progressive policies but rather a rebuke of the sitting administration.
“My whole characterization of this election comes down to one phrase,” MacManus said. “A lot of people wanted new faces in high places, pure and simple.”

Florida House
The Florida House remains under GOP control, but the party no longer holds a supermajority. Democrats increased their share of the 120-member body to 50. Before the election, they held 34 seats. In the 40-member Florida Senate, Democrats flipped one seat, sending them into the 2027 session with 13 Democratic senators. There is one vacant seat with a special election still to be called.
DeSantis, noted Dan Weldon, a GOP candidate for Florida House who lost, “was nowhere to be seen on the campaign trail” for “countless down ballot races.”

This should not be treated as a victory lap for Gov. DeSantis. This was the worst election cycle in Florida in decades. He could’ve saved countless down ballot races by helping boost GOP turnout.
We’re a team & our captain was nowhere to be seen on the campaign trail. https://t.co/9SAdZsUTkc
— Tampa Dan (@TampaDan) November 4, 2026

Outgoing Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez, a Republican, and DeSantis sparred for the past two years over priorities. Following Tuesday’s election results, DeSantis called Perez “a rotten speaker.”
“I didn’t get involved with the Florida House races. You know, we’ve just had differences of opinion over the last two years. It is what it is,” DeSantis said the day after the election. “They had a little bit harder time on it, but those are just choices people make.”
Amendment 3
The day after the election, DeSantis credited his party’s voter registration margin and Amendment 3’s placement on on the ballot for GOP victories in Florida.
Despite earlier hesitation to campaign, DeSantis hosts event supporting Amendment 3

Amendment 3, which passed, will dramatically reduce taxes homesteaded property owners pay, reducing revenue collected by local governments.
DeSantis initially claimed he would sit out campaigning in support of Amendment 3, although he said he’d vote for it. Eventually, though, he hosted events to vocalize his support for the amendment.
On Amendment 3, DeSantis “had some influence, of course,” MacManus said. “But I think the major influence was the personal calculations of voters that, look, here’s a chance for me to make a little bit of a dent in my sorry budget at the moment.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Utility regulation: too much or not fast enough?
description: In 2022, America’s utilities planned for about 24 gigawatts of new peak electricity demand over the following five years. By 2025, according to the consulting firm Grid Strategies, their forecasts called for 166 gigawatts, more than six times as much. Data centers account for more than half of that growth, and manufacturing is the next […]
text:
Duke Energy broke ground on the  Cayuga Energy Complex Project in Vermillion County in May 2026. (Photo from Duke Energy)In 2022, America’s utilities planned for about 24 gigawatts of new peak electricity demand over the following five years. By 2025, according to the consulting firm Grid Strategies, their forecasts called for 166 gigawatts, more than six times as much. Data centers account for more than half of that growth, and manufacturing is the next largest driver.
Those forecasts describe a different industry from the one I helped regulate. During my years on the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, the question before us was usually whether a utility was building too much. Today’s question is how quickly a growing economy can get the power it needs, and on what terms, and the public-interest standard that answers both has held steady.
When I joined the commission in 2018, American electricity demand had grown at well under 1% a year for two decades. Indiana’s coal fleet, which had supplied 90% of the state’s electricity as recently as 2010, was aging, and by 2020 its share had fallen to about 53%. Our work was to pace that transition: how quickly old plants should close and what should replace them.
The clearest test of that era came from Evansville. Vectren (now CenterPoint) had coal units scheduled to retire in 2023, so the issue was how much to build in their place and in what form. Its own forecast showed customers’ demand on the hottest summer days growing by fewer than 100 megawatts over 17 years, yet it proposed a single plant of roughly 850 megawatts, enough for about three-quarters of that peak, at a cost of $781 million. In 2019, the commission denied the request, and our order explained why. It found that the request for bids had been “unduly restrictive,” ruling out combinations of smaller resources; that one facility would have carried most of the utility’s baseload; and that the plant’s economics depended on wholesale market sales with no firm contracts behind them, a revenue stream the order called “a speculative influence that we find must be materially discounted.”
‘Big five’ Indiana utilities defend rates in regulator questioning

That caution followed from how utilities earn money. A regulated utility earns an return on what it builds and owns, while power it buys from others under contract generally earns it nothing. The arrangement attracts the long-term investment the industry needs and inclines a utility toward building. Our job was to check that inclination before customers paid for a plant they might never use.
When we decided the Evansville case, we believed we were serving through the most consequential period in the industry’s history, which we called the energy transition. Our order considered how a changing industry might leave customers with an uneconomic plant, yet every change we imagined pointed toward the plant becoming unnecessary. Our decision fit the record before us, but within seven years, a short time for plants built to run 40, the outlook reversed, and a forecast like today’s would have made for a very different record.
Today the pressure runs toward building, and talk of transition has given way to talk of abundance. Data centers and new manufacturing are the kind of investment states compete hard to attract, and available power has become the first filter in choosing a site.
Under that pressure, the commission’s job is to test need on the record. A faster pace does not lower the utility’s burden of proof or the duty to keep rates fair for Hoosier households and businesses. Cost causation protects both: large new customers carry the cost of serving them, backed by long-term commitments, so households are not left holding the bill if that demand never arrives.
Expectations of regulators have also risen with their audience. Utility cases that once drew mainly lawyers and analysts now draw public comment and press coverage. That attention is healthy, because customers pay for every decision, and it rewards decisions that can be explained plainly and defended on the evidence.
Whether the question is how much to build or how fast, the answer has to come from the record, built through sworn testimony and cross-examination, with the state’s consumer advocate at the table for customers and the utility required to prove its case. That design weighed flat demand in 2019 and suits the growth Indiana is pursuing now. Forecasts will keep changing, and a public, evidence-based process remains the surest way for a state to build quickly and build well.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: RI budget and policy director Brian Daniels resigns
description: After shaping a dozen state budgets across three administrations of different political parties, Rhode Island Management and Budget Director Brian Daniels is hanging up his purple tie. Daniels, who goes by the handle @PurpleTieRI on X, is leaving his post on Dec. 11, according to an Oct. 30 resignation letter sent to Gov. Dan MCKee’s […]
text:
Brian Daniels, director of Rhode Island’s Office of Management and Budget, speaks with reporters at the Powers Building in Providence on Jan. 15, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)After shaping a dozen state budgets across three administrations of different political parties, Rhode Island Management and Budget Director Brian Daniels is hanging up his purple tie.
Daniels, who goes by the handle @PurpleTieRI on X, is leaving his post on Dec. 11, according to an Oct. 30 resignation letter sent to Gov. Dan MCKee’s office and shared with Rhode Island Current. Daniels’ resignation was first reported by Ted Nesi at WPRI-TV 12.
“Serving as OMB Director has been an inspiring and rewarding experience, but it is not a role that I can perform indefinitely,” Daniels wrote. “Having contributed to twelve budgets under three Governors, I now plan to take some time off to enjoy a quiet holiday season with loved ones and then explore new frontiers.”
His resignation from the $222,000-a-year job leaves another vacancy for Governor-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes to fill once she takes office. It’s not uncommon for cabinet members and gubernatorial staffers to leave their positions ahead of a change in administration, but Daniels has endured through multiple election cycles and changes in the governor’s seat.
A Rhode Island native with more than two decades of experience in local, state and federal government, Daniels arrived on Smith Hill in 2010 as policy director for then-Gov. Lincoln Chafee, a former Republican who turned independent. 
His career in the state budget office began in 2012 as director of performance management, a position he held through the 2014 election that brought in Gov. Gina Raimondo. Daniels took a five-year reprieve from state budget work from 2017 to 2021 to head the Rhode Island League of Cities and Towns, but returned under the McKee administration in November 2021 as director of the management and budget office.
In his resignation letter, Daniels cited the creation of a state supplemental rainy day fund created with the fiscal 2024 budget, and use of federal COVID relief funds for capital projects and debt retirement, as accomplishments of the budget office.
“This discipline has been hailed by bond rating agencies and ultimately led Fitch to upgrade the State’s general obligation bond rating from AA to AA+,” Daniels wrote. 
Other measures implemented under Daniels’ watch include standardized performance measures and quarterly progress tracking for state agencies; data analytics tools to identify and prevent waste and abuse in benefit programs; and oversight of $1 billion in federal pandemic aid.
Rhode Island Health and Human Services Secretary Richard Charest also resigned to lead Roger Williams Medical Center and Our Lady of Fatima Hospital.
Even before winning the election, Foulkes has been outspoken about her plans to hire a new state transportation director who has no connections to state government — an indirect jab at former Rhode Island Department of Transportation Director Peter Alviti Jr., whose political career — and absence of infrastructure expertise — came under scrutiny in the wake of the Washington Bridge closure. Alviti retired in February.
But Foulkes has not commented publicly on her plans for other cabinet directors, including someone to help craft her first budget proposal as governor, which will be unveiled in January.







“The OMB director is a priority position for the Governor-elect to fill,” Jon Carvalho, a spokesperson for Foulkes’ transition team, said in an email Friday. “In the last 24 hours, Governor-elect Foulkes and her transition team have already received more than 200 applications from professionals interested in serving in the administration, and are already reviewing filling key roles and beginning a process to start interviewing in the coming weeks.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Senatobia officer who fatally shot toddler had a history of aggressive, volatile policing
description: A Kohen Wiley memorial was erected outside the Walmart in Senatobia, Miss. where the toddler was fatally shot.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mukta Joshi is a reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow. Joseph Cranney is a reporter at Verite News. Both report for the Deep South Today Investigative Reporting Center in collaboration with The Times.
SENATOBIA – The Mississippi police officer who fatally shot a Black toddler in a Walmart parking lot this summer had a history of aggressive behavior and escalating traffic stops into violent confrontations, an examination of more than a dozen incidents captured on video reveals.
The videos show the officer, Hunter Foster, quickly ramping up encounters that began over minor infractions: resorting to physical force without warning, cursing at people and sometimes pointing his gun at them.
Kohen Wiley, 1, was shot and killed in a Walmart parking lot in Senatobia, Miss. Credit: Veronica Roberson
Foster came under scrutiny in June when he and four other officers ran out of the Walmart in Senatobia and surrounded a car as two young women tried to flee. Foster ran and stood in front of the car and then opened fire as it drove toward him, video shows, and continued to fire as it passed him. One of the bullets struck and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, who was sitting in his mother’s lap in the passenger seat.
Foster was the first officer to point his gun at the car, and the only one to open fire. In October, Attorney General Lynn Fitch declined to bring charges against Foster, 33, saying in a press release that the officer’s actions had been justified. He resigned from the police department later that week.
The death of a Black toddler at the hands of Foster, a white police officer, was another episode in what many residents describe as a painful history of policing in the state.
It also raised questions about the proportionality of the police officers’ response. The women had been accused by employees of shoplifting a box of Pampers Easy Ups and baby clothes.
Reporters for The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News interviewed Foster’s former colleagues and reviewed lawsuits, court records and police reports to catalog other incidents in which he used force over his seven-year career in law enforcement.
A memorial for 1-year-old Kohen Wiley outside the Walmart in Senatobia, Miss., where the toddler was fatally shot.  Credit: Rory Doyle/The New York Times
The examination included video from 12 incidents from his time at the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office, the only agency among Foster’s former employers that provided detailed records in response to a public records request. Reporters also reviewed video footage included in two federal lawsuits Foster was named in, and from an incident flagged by community members in which Foster shouted profanities at a group of women when responding to a report of domestic violence.
Foster was patient and polite at the beginning of most of the encounters, even when the motorists he had pulled over were unruly or intoxicated. But several incidents quickly devolved into violence, with Foster tackling, punching or drawing his Taser or firearm in response to minor provocations.
The encounters reviewed by the news organizations represent a small sample of Foster’s interactions with the public. But three policing experts who separately examined the videos at our request said they raised questions about Foster’s aggression,  temperament and professionalism.
Foster’s behavior displayed “an orientation toward going to force almost without warning,” said Michael Gennaco, a former federal civil rights prosecutor who now operates a police oversight consultancy in California. In several of the videos, Gennaco said, Foster appeared “out of control.”
In one case, Foster tackled a man after he didn’t immediately put his hands behind his back, then punched him at least 14 times while he was pinned to the ground.
In another, Foster continued to yank on a man’s arm while he screamed in pain. Foster was attempting to detain him after detecting a discrepancy with his vehicle tags.
After reporters shared a detailed summary of this article’s findings, Foster’s lawyer, Martin Zummach, briefly replied that some of the characterizations of his client’s behavior was slanderous, though he didn’t respond to a list of questions, or follow-up phone and email messages.
Zummach has described the Walmart shooting as “unfortunate,” but maintained that Foster did not know there was a child in the car, and that he had acted in defense of himself and other officers.
In most of the cases reviewed by the news organizations, Foster filed reports to explain why he felt physical force was necessary. Those descriptions did not always line up with what video evidence showed.
And the Walmart parking lot incident was not the first time that Foster said a vehicle had posed a threat. He was one of several officers named in a lawsuit accusing them of falsifying incident reports to say that a driver, who officers later beat, had accelerated his car, “almost running” one of them over. But video shows the car never drove toward, or nearly hit, any of the officers. 
In court papers, Foster, who did not participate in the beating, denied knowing that any part of his report was inaccurate. The lawsuit was settled in 2022 for an undisclosed amount.
‘Traumatic, traumatic experience’
Foster grew up in northeastern Mississippi, the son of a longtime law enforcement officer. He went to high school about an hour east of Starkville, in Caledonia, where he was a lineman on the football team.
He spent several years in the Army National Guard before switching to law enforcement in 2019, working for three departments over the next seven years in northern Mississippi. 
Hunter Foster, right, received an award from the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office in 2023, when he worked there as a deputy. He later went to work for the Senatobia Police Department. Credit: DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office via Facebook
Most of Foster’s former coworkers and supervisors declined to answer our questions, citing the sensitivity of the fatal shooting.
Two of his former colleagues in Senatobia described Foster as a good officer with an even demeanor. An ex-girlfriend with whom Foster shares a child said he was “a good person and an amazing father,” but declined to answer more questions. “It seems like everyone has already painted an awful picture of him,” she said. 
From 2021 to 2024, Foster worked at the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office, where he built a reputation as a prolific patrol officer.
Two years in a row, he won an award for issuing the most DUI citations of any officer in the state of Mississippi. In one month in 2022, he wrote more than 150 traffic citations, an average of about seven per workday, court records show.
Laterrius Inge was violently detained by Hunter Foster in 2022 after pulling over with car trouble. Credit: Rory Doyle/The New York Times
On a Sunday afternoon in 2022, Laterrius Inge encountered Foster on a county road just outside Memphis. Inge said the used Camaro he recently purchased had started jerking, so he pulled over. Foster pulled up just as Inge popped open the hood.
Body-worn camera footage shows the two chatting calmly at first, but things change after a dispatcher informs Foster that the license plate on the car doesn’t match the Camaro, and that he can’t be identified by the name he had given.
Without warning, Foster reaches out to cuff his left hand.
Inge asks why he is being detained. Instead of answering, Foster repeatedly says “Stop,” raising his voice, the video shows.
“I ain’t did nothing! What are you doing?” Inge asks, raising his right hand in surrender. Foster, still holding Inge by his handcuff, points his Taser, threatening to shock Inge if he doesn’t turn around.
Foster then grabs Inge by his arm and shoves him against the car. Inge crumples to the ground and wails in pain for nearly 10 minutes, repeatedly screaming, “My wrist!” At one point, footage shows, Foster drags Inge by his handcuffs across the pavement, tearing his hoodie.
Inge With Captions
Foster later wrote in his report that he had dragged Inge to get him on his stomach, but that he kept rolling on his back, refusing to give up his right arm.
Matt Steffey, a criminal and constitutional law professor at Mississippi Christian University who helped draft the state’s rules on criminal procedure, said the video could be “a training video on how not to conduct a traffic stop.” He noted that the officer did not ask Inge to put his hands behind his back before cuffing or dragging him.
Inge was charged with careless driving, failure to surrender his driver’s license, being an uninsured motorist and having a switched tag. In an interview, he said that Foster had caused a shoulder injury that still requires treatment.
“It was a traumatic, traumatic experience,” he said.
‘Why are you beating me up?’
Experts who reviewed the footage said that Foster appeared to have escalated some situations without cause or warning.
One night in 2023, he stopped a man named Jonathan Fields on the side of a highway over an improper vehicle tag. Footage from the incident was captured on the squad car’s dashboard camera.
Foster asks if Fields has a gun in the car. He says that he does, and Foster asks where it is. (Mississippi is an open carry state.)
In his incident report, Foster wrote that Fields had “grabbed the firearm.” The action isn’t clear from the footage, but Fields can be heard saying, “I was just trying to show you where it’s at.”
Audio from the footage captures Foster berating and cursing at Fields for touching the gun. Then, the officer tells him to step out of his Chevrolet sedan. When Fields doesn’t immediately exit, seven seconds later, Foster draws his gun and points it at Fields until he complies, the footage shows.
Fields Intro With Captions
A few moments later, Foster tells Fields not to move while he questions him about having marijuana in the car. When Fields takes a few steps toward his car, a second deputy tells him to stop. When he does, the officer tries to handcuff him, Fields waves his hands away, and Foster tackles him to the ground.
In his incident report, Foster later wrote that the man had “ripped” his arms away from the other deputy.
Foster punches Fields at least 14 times while the other officer holds him down. “Why are you beating me up?” Fields yells.
Fields With Captions
In his use-of-force report, Foster called his punches “distractive,” delivered when he felt Fields tense his body, which he interpreted as part of an effort to fight back.
Steffey, the law professor, noted that Foster began striking Fields before asking him for his hands.
“That looks like assault,” Steffey said.
Another night, in 2023, Foster pulled over an Uber driver for failing to dim his high beams. Footage shows officers eventually ordering a passenger out of the car, too, after Foster said he smelled marijuana.
Then, all of a sudden, Foster shoves the passenger face down toward the hood of a squad car, grabbing the back of his neck.
Alexander With Captions
The second officer pulls the man’s hands above his head while instructing him to put his hands behind his back. In the ensuing struggle, Foster punches him at least six times, including before giving the man any clear commands.Barbara Attard, a policing consultant and former Independent Police Auditor for the city of San Jose, said Foster’s use of force that day was “totally inappropriate” and “excessive.”
Four months later, Foster arrived at a scene where two other officers were trying to get a man out of his car in his driveway. Within 13 seconds of arriving, Foster opens the door and pulls the unarmed man from his vehicle, tackling him to the ground, dashboard camera footage shows.
Washington With Captions
Foster later curses at the man for attempting to record the interaction on his cellphone.
‘Can you please stop cussing?’
By the time Foster started working in Senatobia, the city of roughly 8,400 people — 40 percent of whom are Black — was already reeling from a string of policing controversies.
In 2023, the city’s chief of police, who is white, was caught on camera barging into a Black man’s home and choking him. The chief at the time said officers had believed a fleeing suspect to a shooting was hiding there. The same year, the department faced criticism after its officers arrested a 10-year-old Black boy for urinating in a parking lot. The chief said that officers had violated their training.
The following year, two Black teenage girls accused the chief of shouting “get your Black ass out of the road” when he arrested them outside a public housing complex. The year after that, a Black woman was thrown to the ground by an officer after she parked in a handicapped spot in the same Walmart parking lot where Kohen was later killed. City leadership voted to remove the chief.
So when news broke in June that a white officer had killed a Black toddler in a dispute over shoplifting, many residents saw the incident as part of a pattern of racist policing. 
Things intensified in August when The Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News obtained internal department complaints alleging that Foster had used racially offensive language toward his colleagues. In September, we revealed the police chief at the time had routinely used racist slurs in texts to a colleague. That chief was pushed out too.
Kenesha Herron was outside a home in Senatobia in May when Hunter Foster approached her and other women and launched into an expletive-filled tirade. She is wearing a shirt for Kohen Wiley. Credit: Rory Doyle/The New York Times
Experts noted that Foster frequently stopped Black motorists over minor infractions, like not having a license plate light, then accused them of drug use before searching them and their cars. Those actions carry the hallmarks of pretextual stops, which some states have placed heavy restrictions on, though not Mississippi.
Experts agreed that the most problematic incident they reviewed was in response to a domestic call in early May that was captured on body-worn camera footage and recently obtained by reporters.
Within a minute of arriving at a home in a predominantly Black neighborhood in Senatobia, where a woman had accused her child’s father of hitting her, Foster launches into an expletive-filled tirade.
Upon learning the man accused of assault had left, Foster immediately raises his voice at her and other women standing outside, who are Black, calling them a “bunch of motherfuckers.”
Johnson With Captions
“Can you please stop cussing?” Kenesha Herron, the mother of the man who had left, asks. “No, cause I’m sick of this shit,” he says.
He accuses the group of women, who are standing with two children, of trying to hide the man. “I’m tired of y’all doing this,” Foster says.
“Tired of who doing what?” Kenesha Herron, the man’s mother, asks, having interpreted Foster’s comment as being racially motivated. She later said in an interview that she had “never felt so openly hated” because of her skin color.
Moments later, Foster tells other officers he’s sick of “this place,” adding another expletive, video shows.
“He’s the kind of officer that is to blame for the fact that communities of color have no confidence in public safety,” said Gennaco, the former civil rights prosecutor.Foster’s body-worn camera footage shows him apologizing to Herron after their altercation. “I’m sorry for being loud with you,” he says. “Sometimes things get heated.”
Sheelagh McNeill of The New York Times and Julie Lee of Mississippi Today contributed reporting.
