title: Racine mayor Cory Mason won’t run for reelection
description: Racine Mayor Cory Mason won’t run for a fourth term, he announced Friday, making room for new leadership in Wisconsin’s fifth-largest city. Mason made the announcement Friday, on the eve of the 20th anniversary of his first election, when he won the race to represent the city in the state Assembly Nov. 7, 2006. Mason, […]
text:
Racine Mayor Cory Mason, photographed in 2024. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Racine Mayor Cory Mason won’t run for a fourth term, he announced Friday, making room for new leadership in Wisconsin’s fifth-largest city.
Mason made the announcement Friday, on the eve of the 20th anniversary of his first election, when he won the race to represent the city in the state Assembly Nov. 7, 2006.
Mason, a Democrat, left the Assembly in 2017 after running in a special election to succeed John Dickert as mayor of Racine, a nonpartisan office. Dickert left in mid-term to take another job. Mason went on to win a full four-year term in 2019 and again in 2023.
“After 20 years, it’s time to pass the torch of leadership to the next generation,” Mason said in an interview.
Mason said he will remain in office until his current term ends in April. The  decision not to run again was one he and his family made recently, he said. Mason and his wife, Rebecca, a Racine estate planning and elder law attorney, have three children in high school.
“It’s important to have work-life balance, and I’m looking forward to the next chapter where I can have a little bit more of that moving forward,” Mason said.
Mason will leave office in the first months of unified Democratic control of the governor’s mansion and both houses of the state Legislature for the first time since Republicans won all three in 2010. That could open the door to policies that Democrats have advocated for years to no avail, such as sending more shared revenue dollars to cities including Racine.
It’s a contrast to most of Mason’s tenure in the Assembly, dominated particularly by the fight over Act 10, the law that then-Gov. Scott Walker introduced early in his first term stripping most collective bargaining rights from public employees except for police and firefighters.
Reflecting on his tenure as mayor, Mason identified nearly 20 accomplishments, leading with the completion of a community center and health clinic to serve a northwest side district of Racine. That same district is also the site of a major affordable housing project. 
Mason also listed a city work internship for young people, a jobs program to connect potential workers with construction trades and reductions in gun violence.
Still in progress is a longer-term project that he hopes will get picked up by the next mayor: establishing commuter rail service connecting Milwaukee and cities to the south, Racine and Kenosha.
Federal funds provide the bulk of the financing, which Mason said is a slow-moving process. Two decades ago, a similar commuter rail project for the corridor foundered when Republican state lawmakers balked at the plan.
“You need a muscular and robust partnership with the Wisconsin Department of Transportation to make a project to this scale go forward,” Mason said. “So we’re very excited about Gov. David Crowley for many reasons,” including his openness to improved public transportation, “and then having a Legislature that cares deeply about it.”
Trevor Jung, who won his race for the state Senate on Tuesday, is currently Racine’s transit director. “I know he shares my passion for this project and I’m really excited for him to advocate for this up in Madison,” Mason said.
Mason didn’t discount a return to politics, but turned aside speculation about possible races in the next four years.
Asked whether he might join the incoming Crowley administration, he said, “I don’t have anything definitive lined up, but I’ve not ruled anything out either.”
There’s one exception — becoming a lobbyist. “I did rule that out as the next thing that I would do,” Mason said. “But that notwithstanding, you know I’m excited to figure out what the next chapter of my life looks like.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Acton win heralds new policy era for Ohio
description: After last week’s election results, Ohio will be returning to divided government for the first time in half a generation. Less than three hours after polls closed in Ohio, the Ohio Capital Journal called the race for governor. At the time I wrote this commentary, former state health director Amy Acton leads Vivek Ramaswamy by […]
text:
Dr. Amy Acton became the first Democrat in 20 years to lead Ohio after winning the governor’s race Tuesday, Nov. 3, at a rally in Cleveland. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)After last week’s election results, Ohio will be returning to divided government for the first time in half a generation.
Less than three hours after polls closed in Ohio, the Ohio Capital Journal called the race for governor. At the time I wrote this commentary, former state health director Amy Acton leads Vivek Ramaswamy by nearly 8 percentage points with 99 percent of the total votes counted.
Acton has put forth a platform of policy priorities that look to reorient state policy, and successes in the Ohio House of Representatives give her a bloc that can back up her veto pen. As Candidate Acton moves to Governor Acton, there are a number of policy issues where we could see changes that would impact people’s lives in a concrete way.
 Education and Property Taxes

Ohio has been grappling with this tradeoff over the past few years. Record increases in housing valuations have led to a backlash against property taxes at the same time that the state has been working to equalize its school funding. Acton has prioritized fair school funding but will have to contend with headwinds with school finance’s most important tool in Ohio: property taxes.
Acton will face this challenges in the first few months of her governorship, with school funding questions being central to state budget negotiations.
 Poverty Reduction

The Acton campaign has emphasized anti-poverty tax credits as a “day one” priority for the administration. These are changes that will have to happen in collaboration with a potentially hostile General Assembly. While Governor DeWine was successful in negotiating an expansion to the Earned Income Tax Credit early in his first term, he introduced a Child Tax Credit last year that was immediately removed from the budget by House leaders.
This is a potential place for collaboration between Acton and legislative leaders. Leaders are interested in tax relief, and if that can be brought about through support for low-income households, this could be an opportunity for compromise during budget negotiations.
 Health Care

Governor Kasich famously bucked his party a decade ago by engineering a quiet approval for Medicaid expansion in the state, bringing around $8 billion of federal dollars for healthcare services into the state per year and providing health insurance coverage to 670,000 Ohio residents. Since then, legislators have worked to reduce the state’s investment in Medicaid, including passing a budget clause last year that will immediately remove coverage for those residents if the federal government changes policy to provide a dollar less than it provides for Medicaid today. I’m 
Acton has proposed medical debt relief, reducing administrative barriers to Medicaid enrollment, and using state purchasing power to reduce prescription drug costs. While some of this could be focuses for the state budget, many health care strategies may be possible through executive action. The options could grow in the second half of her term if Democrats take the White House in 2028, opening options for new waivers with the federal Department of Health and Human Services.
 Energy

Acton has proposed a moratorium on data center development and requiring developers to cover their own energy costs. She has also said she wants to appoint people to the public utilities commission that focus on ratepayer protection. This is likely to be an ongoing discussion as the question of data center development is not going away in Ohio any time soon. With the widespread backlash against data center development, there are opportunities for the new administration to work together with legislative leaders to ensure the benefits of new development outweigh their costs.
The first test of Ohio’s new divided government will come during next year’s budget negotiations. Acton will have opportunities to shape education, taxation, health care and energy policy, but each step she takes will come with fiscal and political tradeoffs. How those tradeoffs are resolved will determine how much this election concretely changes the lives of Ohio residents.

title: Commentary: Florida bucked the trend toward sanity
description: Not subtle. Not nuanced. Americans launched an almighty middle finger at the Mob Boss of Mar-a-Lago, repudiating him and his congressional Flying Monkey squad. The Bible-spouting Pharisee Mike Johnson will no longer be Speaker of the House; the sclerotic Chuck Grassley will no longer chair the committee that placed Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch on […]
text:
Republican Byron Donalds celebrates his win in the Florida governor race on Nov. 3, 2026, flanked by his wife, Erika, and running mate Bryan Ávila. (Photo via Donalds Facebook page)Not subtle. Not nuanced.
Americans launched an almighty middle finger at the Mob Boss of Mar-a-Lago, repudiating him and his congressional Flying Monkey squad.
The Bible-spouting Pharisee Mike Johnson will no longer be Speaker of the House; the sclerotic Chuck Grassley will no longer chair the committee that placed Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch on the U.S. Supreme Court; and no longer will Congress sign off on obscene funding for the Iran war.
MAGA myrmidons crashed and burned in Trump-voting states across the nation — not Florida, of course, but we’ll talk about that in a minute.
Ohio, for example, where tech bro Vivek Ramaswamy saw nothing wrong with running an attack ad starring the estranged mother of opponent Amy Acton, a woman who defended her husband even though he’d been indicted for raping Amy when she was 12.
Or Texas, for God’s sake. Texas, a state so red it puts cheap Santa suits to shame, spurned Ken Paxton, Trump’s hand-picked Senate candidate.
The epically sleazy Paxton, who was impeached by his own party, got taken to the woodshed by a fresh-faced seminarian with a strong resemblance to Opie Taylor.
Elon Musk must be sick as a parrot. He burned through millions of dollars trying to get his Texas supplicants elected, to no avail. Now, SpaceX and Tesla stock is heading downhill and Texas’ new Democratic government is likely inclined to investigate him, his dodgy finances, his campaign donations, and his environmentally disastrous space city.
Now that Texas is no longer friendly to the bazillionaire oligarch and professional baby-daddy, what do you want to bet Musk moves to Florida?
All the best authoritarian creeps end up here: Trump, his boys, the Kushners, Jeff Bezos, and Flávio Bolsonaro.
But Iowa? Kansas? Seriously? Kansas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
New new South
South Carolina hasn’t chosen a Democratic senator since Fritz Hollings was re-elected in 1998. It’s got one now.
The South, land of slavery-excusing, abortion-banning, vaccine-hating, and mandating religious instruction in public schools is getting bluer.
They’re still counting in the Mississippi Senate race, where Democrat Scott Colom leads incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. His lead is small, but y’all, this is Mississippi, a state Trump won by more than 20 points in 2024.
In North Carolina, voters flipped a U.S. Senate seat, gave Democrats the majority in the state House of Representatives, and made substantial gains in the state Senate.
In Georgia, the top offices are now as blue as deep water.
Democrats hold both U.S. Senate seats, have taken control of the state House of Representatives, and elected the nation’s first Black woman governor.
Then there’s Florida, which never fails to disappoint.
While most the country rejected Donald Trump’s toxic regime, Florida bucked the trend toward sanity and stuck with Republicans.
Byron Donalds made history as the state’s first Black governor.
This should be a proud accomplishment, except the man is a Trumpist to the core.
During the campaign, he inched away — a little — from references to Trump’s endorsement.
Trump’s approval rating was (and is) in the low-to-mid 30s.
However, once Donalds won, the sucking-up resumed. The man who likes to call Trump “Daddy,” declared: “Mr. President, I want you to hear from Florida that we are still red!”
And Trump is still a racist.
Even Florida shifted
Florida could have made more history by electing Angie Nixon, who’d have been our first Black senator.
Instead, we chose former Attorney General Ashley Moody, appointed to serve out Marco Rubio’s term after he was elevated (if that’s the right word) to be Trump’s secretary of state.
James Uthmeier, appointed to fill the attorney general post after Moody decamped for D.C., won his election, too.
He’s a self-proclaimed devout Christian, yet remains proud of “Alligator Alcatraz,” that giant human rights violation of a prison camp in the Everglades.
Government inspectors (Trump administration inspectors!) found the facility abused detainees, some of whom accused the state of “torture.”
Uthmeier can now continue his mission to shut down drag shows, ban Judy Blume novels, instruct bishops in Roman Catholic theology, and defend himself against accusations of misdeeds in the HOPE Florida scandal.
Still, Florida was not a total bust for Democrats.
These races were far closer than they should have been, given how this state has been blindly electing Republicans for the past 30-odd years.
Angie Nixon was less than three percentage points behind Ashley Moody. That’s a major shift: Marco Rubio beat Val Demings by 6.5 percent in 2022 and Rick Scott’s 2024 margin over Debbie Murcasel-Powell was over 12 points.
The last time he ran, Ron DeSantis romped (an unseemly image, but still), beating Charlie Crist by nearly 20 points.
David Jolly got within 1.3 percentage points of Donalds.
As for Uthmeier, his win over José Javier Fernandez was thread-slim, despite having more than three times as much campaign cash.
There’s more (qualified) good news for Dems.
If Republicans prevail in the two neck-and-neck races that are, at the time of writing, still too close to call, the party make-up of Florida’s congressional delegation will remain the same as it was last year.
‘Oops’
But Republicans thought they could grab even more seats.
Remember that redistricting stunt they pulled to pad their numbers and get rid of the likes of Kathy Castor, the long-time representative from Tampa Bay?
It didn’t quite go as planned.
Three of the four redrawn districts went to Democrats; incumbent Darren Soto leads in the fourth.
Nationwide, what the gerrymandering Republicans thought was a sure bet to net them more seats blew up in their faces.
Most of their redrawn districts went to Democrats.
As the Texan sage and failed presidential candidate Rick Perry once said, “Oops.”
Despite Florida’s Cabinet remaining DeSantisite, Republicans have lost their supermajority in the House and their total control of the Senate is teetering on the brink after Maitland Mayor John Lowndes whipped incumbent DeSantis acolyte Jason Brodeur, one of the most powerful politicos in the state.
The question will be: Will Florida Republicans get a clue and realize they’re not as popular as they used to be?
During a post-election press conference, DeSantis congratulated Florida (and, by extension, himself) for bucking the national trend, while warning the midterms were “as close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years.”
Scary! His party has lost two key states, Ohio and Texas: “If the Republican Party doesn’t have Texas as an anchor, then we are not going to be viable moving forward.”
Texas was always what Florida wanted to be when it grew up.
But, as DeSantis boasted, “Our line of scrimmage held better here in Florida.”
Amendment 3
He’s even more pleased Amendment 3, his pet anti-local government project, passed.
Appealing to greed usually works: Voters have chosen to dismantle our property tax system.
Homeowners will be happy to get the extra cash, though the one-third of Floridians who rent won’t get anything out of this.
And nobody will like it when their local taxes and fees shoot up to fund basic services, when the potholes don’t get fixed, law enforcement loses officers, firefighters get laid off, libraries and neighborhood clinics close, cultural events are canceled, and parks neglected.
None of that matters to DeSantis. Amendment 3 is his calling card for another presidential bid, an accomplishment he thinks he can run on.
But Florida might not remain the Ghost of Texas Past DeSantis and the Republicans want it to be.
This year shows even the reddest of reds can fade.
The presidential race in 2028 may bring another Democratic opportunity in Florida.
Ashley Moody must run again to keep her U.S. Senate seat. It’s possible she’ll again face Angie Nixon.
Given the stinking miasma of the Trump administration will still be hanging over Republicans in general, and Moody in particular, Nixon could prevail this time.
Perhaps the Florida Democratic Party — long a by-word for dysfunction — will look across the border at Georgia, where Black women hold the top state offices, and learn.
The national Democratic Party may finally (finally!) invest in the state, recruiting good candidates, growing the voter base one citizen at a time, and spending actual money here.
It won’t be easy, obviously, but the midterms have blown a chill wind through Republican Florida.
As the good old Game of Thrones saying goes, “Winter is coming.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT Republicans need a reckoning, not excuses
description: If CT voters were convinced we offered a credible alternative, more would have supported us.
text:
Connecticut Republicans didn’t just lose an election Tuesday. We suffered a political slaughter the likes of which we have never seen. 
While a national Democratic wave contributed to the outcome, the magnitude of our defeat demands more than excuses. It demands an honest reckoning.

Timothy Herbst

First, Ryan Fazio deserves our gratitude and respect. When others declined to step forward, Ryan accepted the enormous challenge of running for governor in an unfavorable political environment. He worked tirelessly, traveled the state, and made a serious case for fiscal responsibility and economic opportunity. He knew the odds and answered the call anyway. His courage, commitment, and extraordinary work ethic deserve admiration.
But honoring Ryan’s effort cannot substitute for examining why Republicans lost so decisively.
Perhaps the greatest frustration is the disconnect between voters’ concerns and their choices at the ballot box. Connecticut residents repeatedly identified taxes, the cost of living, and exorbitant utility bills among their most pressing problems. Yet those concerns did not translate into accountability for the party that has controlled the governorship and both legislative chambers since 2011.
Donald Trump didn’t create Connecticut’s public benefits charge on electric bills. State policymakers did. Trump didn’t design Connecticut’s tax structure or determine Hartford’s spending priorities. Connecticut’s elected leaders did. Trump didn’t enact the state laws that have stripped control of zoning from local communities. Gov. Ned Lamont and Democratic legislators did.
Donald Trump certainly didn’t create Connecticut’s longstanding and shameful achievement gap in our public schools. That problem predates his presidency by decades and remains unresolved after 16 years of Democratic control in Hartford. And now, with proposals for regionalized school districts back on the table, I fear Hartford may seek to strip communities of local control over their schools as well.
At some point, Lamont and Democratic legislative majorities must be held accountable for the problems they have failed to solve. Certainly, national economic forces matter. But opposition to Donald Trump appears to have overwhelmed almost everything else. For many voters, national political passions superseded an examination of Connecticut’s governing record.
Yet Republicans cannot simply blame Trump or the electorate. If voters were convinced we offered a credible alternative, more would have supported us.
That is our failure to address.
The Republican Party needs rebuilding from the bottom up. It starts with our Republican Town Committees and the members representing each district on the Republican State Central Committee. Many have served faithfully for years, even decades, and deserve appreciation. But 20 years in the same position should not be mistaken for 20 years of progress.
Republicans in every district must examine who represents them on State Central. Are they recruiting new people, bringing fresh ideas, expanding our reach, and building a party capable of winning? Or have these positions become comfortable seats occupied by the same familiar faces election after election?
There is another fundamental problem that Republicans must confront: the tremendous disconnect between our Republican elected officials, our Republican Town Committees, and the Republican State Central Committee. I witnessed this firsthand when I ran for governor eight years ago. Too often, these groups operate in separate silos rather than functioning as parts of a unified political organization. Elected officials, party leaders, and grassroots activists should be working toward common objectives, communicating regularly, and supporting one another. If we cannot get on the same page within our own party, how can we possibly expect to prosecute a successful statewide campaign in an increasingly difficult political environment?
And then there is the destructive culture of infighting that has plagued Connecticut Republicans for far too long. Democrats certainly have their own personality conflicts, ideological divisions, and internal disagreements. But when an election approaches, they generally find a way to put those differences aside and unite around the common objective of winning. 
Connecticut Republicans, by contrast, too often form a circular firing squad, spending more time attacking fellow Republicans than challenging the opposing party. Personal grievances, factional rivalries, and old political scores become more important than the larger mission. This mindset has to be expurgated from the Connecticut Republican Party once and for all. Healthy debate and honest disagreement make a political party stronger. Personal vendettas and political score-settling only make it weaker. We will never build a credible governing alternative until we learn that winning elections requires discipline, mutual respect, and a willingness to put the party’s broader interests ahead of individual egos.
We need new blood, new energy, and a new generation willing to do the hard work of rebuilding. Town committees must become engines of candidate recruitment, fundraising, and community engagement. District Republicans must take responsibility for choosing State Central representatives committed to growing the party rather than preserving the status quo.
There may be one silver lining in this otherwise disastrous election. With overwhelming legislative majorities, Connecticut Democrats, particularly their progressive wing, may interpret the results as permission to pursue a more ambitious agenda. I suspect progressives like Josh Elliott will view this election as a mandate to push their agenda further left. Governor Lamont strikes me as a genuinely nice man. But being a nice man and having the political will to stand up to the most ideological members of your own party are two different things. Whether he will exercise that restraint remains an open question.
Republicans should prepare for renewed debates over taxes on investment income and high earners, costly energy mandates, government spending, and further erosion of local decision-making authority. These are potential battles, not inevitable outcomes. We must challenge proposals on their merits and offer practical alternatives.
The political landscape will eventually change. Donald Trump will not be a presidential candidate in 2028. Although his influence will persist, Democrats cannot assume that opposition to him will indefinitely overshadow scrutiny of their own governing record.
But Republicans cannot simply wait for Democrats to overreach.
We must rebuild a coalition that includes independents and the pragmatic, fiscally responsible Democrats once represented by Joe Lieberman. These voters want affordable electricity, reasonable taxes, safe communities, good schools, and competent government. Our message must be grounded in common sense and kitchen-table economics, not national grievances or ideological purity tests. We must demonstrate that Republicans can govern better, not merely complain louder.
Ryan Fazio did his part. Now the rest of us must do ours.
No one is entitled to a seat on State Central. No one is entitled to lead simply because they’ve always been there. And no Republican should confuse loyalty to the party with loyalty to the people who currently occupy its positions.
The time for excuses is over. The time for new blood is now. If we aren’t willing to clean house and make meaningful changes within our own party, we have no business asking Connecticut voters to trust us to lead the state.
Timothy M. Herbst was the First Selectman of Trumbull from 2009-2017 and ran for Governor of Connecticut in 2018.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Election season is done. Holiday season is approaching. And lawmakers still have dozens of big decisions to make.
description: It’s a new phenomenon for the Legislature to have this much unfinished business this close to the end of the two-year session.
text:
THERE’S NO PLACE like the State House for the holidays.
It’s easy to forget amid all the hubbub of a national blue wave and a nine-question state ballot, but with the election now past, the Legislature has a long list of business left to accomplish in the eight holiday-punctuated weeks remaining before the 2025-2026 term draws to a close.
“Long” might actually be an understatement. There are 12 House-Senate negotiating panels still working to finalize compromise bills, plus a late-moving spending proposal needed to close the state’s financial books. But because legislative leaders prefer to cram multiple topics into each omnibus package, the number of discrete policy decisions still in play reaches into the dozens.
By our count, there are more than 40 significant policy choices the Democrats who control Beacon Hill need to make before the final gavel rings out on January 5, 2027, ranging from whether to upzone the entire state for duplex development to whether to ban the sale of dogs, cats, and rabbits in pet stores. Any bill left unfinished by the term’s end will expire, and lawmakers will need to start the process from scratch after they’re sworn in for the 2027-2028 session.
Our tally may be exhausting, but it is not exhaustive. We did not include every one of the discrepancies in spending between House and Senate legislation, which are more granular.
It’s a lot to track, even for professional Beacon Hill-watchers.
Because almost everything is now in the hands of conference committees, the actual policy decisions will essentially be made behind closed doors by only a handful of Democrats. Each panel is working to iron out differences between the underlying House and Senate versions of a bill; once its members reach agreement, the rest of the Legislature will only get a chance to vote up or down on the final accord — usually with no more than a day or two’s notice on the actual substance — without making any further changes.
House Speaker Ron Mariano said Friday that the negotiating teams are ” making progress and working hard.”
“It’s important to understand that these are complex policy decisions that take time, and often many conversations and meetings to resolve,” Mariano said in a statement to CommonWealth Beacon. Stretching the timeline, he added, gives lawmakers “more time to work diligently to reach the best possible policy outcomes — understanding that the content of the final product is far more important than reaching an agreement quickly solely for the sake of doing so.”
It’s a new phenomenon for the Legislature to have this much unfinished business this close to the end of the two-year session. For decades, lawmakers set themselves an earlier deadline, writing into their internal rules that no formal sessions can take place after July 31 in the second year of the term. Roll call votes can only happen in a formal session, so the rule effectively meant the only lawmaking that could occur after the cutoff date needed to be uncontroversial enough to win unanimous support.
Prior generations of lawmakers created the deadline almost immediately after a stinging controversy about lame-duck session shenanigans. Weeks after the 1994 election, with only a bit more than a month left in the legislative term, Republican Gov. Bill Weld suddenly filed legislation authorizing a 55 percent pay raise for lawmakers even though, as CommonWealth’s Dave Denison put it, he was previously “on record as being cool to the idea.” The Legislature quickly approved the measure, and days later, they also advanced a tax cut bill that had been quietly amended to include a capital gains tax cut — a Weld priority that had long failed to gain traction.
After drawing intense criticism for what struck many as a quid pro quo exchange, lawmakers the following year codified a new rule: Formal sessions, and therefore major business of any kind, must end by July 31 in the term’s second year. Republican Rep. David Peters of Charlton, who self-identified as “one of the loudest critics of the system,” at the time called the new deadline “one of the most significant reforms I’ve seen since I’ve been in the building,” according to a 1995 State House News Service report.
Three decades later, the current crop of legislative leaders decided the rule was worth tweaking after a pair of especially chaotic sprints to the finish line. In both 2022 and 2024, the House and Senate headed into July 31 with several major bills stuck in conference committee. Still hoping to strike deals, lawmakers kept the sessions going well past sunrise on August 1, then adjourned with some matters still unresolved.
This term, lawmakers agreed to a different approach. The Legislature’s new rules still require major bills to get an initial round of approval in both the House and Senate by July 31, but as long as conference committee negotiations started by that date, lawmakers can reconvene in a formal session any time before the term ends to greenlight a final compromise version.
Lawmakers sent 12 different matters into conference committees by the deadline this term. None produced any agreements by Election Day, leaving essentially the entire pile of business that was unfinished on August 1 to be decided in lame-duck sessions — including a potential rewrite of a public records ballot question voters just approved in a landslide.
“The whole point behind the July 31 extension for conferences was to take the pressure off the last couple of weeks and say, ‘We’re close here, if we meet a few more times on this, we can wrap this up before the end,’” Mariano said in the summer.
It’s safe to say the pressure is back on.
